It's a good story, and the bishop is indeed said to lie near the front door, but the famous line about being walked over may be a later embellishment.

The churchyard outside the wall is one of the oldest Catholic burial grounds in the city. Its graves stopped taking new burials in the 1800s, as the city banned burials in lower Manhattan for health reasons and moved the dead to big new cemeteries in Brooklyn and Queens. That's why the Catholic dead of later generations lie in Calvary Cemetery, in Queens, and why this patch of old trees and leaning stones feels like a time capsule.

If you take one of the catacomb tours, look closely at the names on the vault doors. They are a who's who of early Catholic New York.

stops.title: The Bowery
stops.text:
You're on the Bowery, one of the oldest roads in New York. Its path follows a Lenape trail, and the Dutch named it after the word bouwerij, meaning farm, because it led to the farms north of town, including Governor Peter Stuyvesant's.

In the early nineteenth century, the Bowery was a lively, working class entertainment strip, a rival to the more genteel Broadway. It had theaters, beer gardens, oyster bars, and dime museums. The Bowery Theatre, which opened in 1826, was famous for raucous crowds and melodramas. The Bowery Boys, a working class gang and youth subculture, swaggered up and down the street in high hats and slicked hair, and became stock characters in plays and later movies.

In 1878, the Third Avenue elevated railway was built above the Bowery. The El cast the street into permanent shadow and noise, and the neighborhood declined. By the early twentieth century, the Bowery had become the most famous skid row in America, lined with flophouses, cheap lodging houses where men rented cages or cots by the night, along with missions and saloons. The Bowery Mission, which opened in 1879 and still operates at 227 Bowery, is one of the oldest rescue missions in the country. For much of the twentieth century, saying someone ended up on the Bowery meant they had hit bottom.

Look at the grand building with the classical columns and arched entrance at 130 Bowery, near Grand Street. This was the Bowery Savings Bank, designed by McKim, Mead and White and completed in 1894. It was a savings bank for working people, built in a monumental style meant to reassure depositors that their small savings were safe. Today it's an event space.

Also notable is the building that looks like a stack of offset white boxes, at 235 Bowery. That's the New Museum, a contemporary art museum designed by the Japanese firm SANAA and completed in 2007. Its arrival marked the transformation of the Bowery from skid row to an art and luxury corridor.

The Bowery is also famous today for its restaurant supply district, a stretch of shops selling commercial kitchen equipment, from industrial mixers to stacks of plates. If you're a serious home cook, it's worth a browse. And farther north is where the punk club CBGB once stood, which you can visit on the East Village tour.

deeper.title: Mose the B'hoy, and a Songwriter's Last Days
deeper.text:
In the 1840s, the Bowery gave American popular culture its first great urban hero, and twenty years later it took one of its greatest songwriters.

The hero was Mose. He was a Bowery B'hoy, as they said it, a working class young man in a red flannel shirt and a tall hat, with his hair slicked into curls called soaplocks, a volunteer fireman who loved a fight and loved his girl, Lize. Mose first appeared on stage in 1848, in a play called A Glance at New York, and audiences went wild. The actor Frank Chanfrau played him in sequel after sequel. Mose was brash, funny, loyal and proud, and the real Bowery boys in the audience saw themselves. He was the ancestor of every streetwise New York character since, from the Dead End Kids to sitcom cab drivers.

The songwriter was Stephen Foster, the author of Oh! Susanna, Camptown Races, and Beautiful Dreamer, the most famous American composer of his time. Foster sold his songs outright for small sums and earned little from their success. By the early 1860s, he was living alone in New York, drinking heavily and selling songs for a few dollars each. In January 1864, in a cheap hotel on the Bowery, he fell in his room and was badly hurt. He died a few days later at Bellevue Hospital, at the age of thirty seven. In his pocket was a worn purse with thirty eight cents and a scrap of paper on which he had written five words: dear friends and gentle hearts. It may have been the start of a song.

The Bowery's reputation was summed up by a hit song of 1891, called simply The Bowery, which warned that they say such things and they do strange things on the Bowery, and ended, I'll never go there anymore.

deeper.title: Under the El: Skid Row and a Missing Subway
deeper.text:
For nearly eighty years, an elevated railway ran above the Bowery, and when it came down, it took a promise with it.

The Third Avenue El was finished over the Bowery in 1878. Its tracks covered almost the whole width of the street, dropping ash, oil and noise on the sidewalks below. Rents fell, and the Bowery filled with the businesses that cheap rents attract: pawnshops, saloons, and lodging houses. By the early twentieth century, the Bowery had dozens of flophouses that could sleep thousands of men a night. The cheapest spaces were cubicles a few feet wide, with walls that stopped short of the ceiling and chicken wire stretched over the top, rented for a few cents a night.

The men who lived here were not all drunks. Many were laborers between jobs, seamen ashore, old men on tiny pensions, and veterans. During the Depression, the Bowery's missions served huge breadlines, and after World War Two, the street became the national symbol of men who had fallen through the cracks.

In 1955, the El was torn down, and light fell on the Bowery for the first time in generations. The city had promised a replacement: a new subway under Second Avenue, first planned back in 1929. Money for it was raised in a bond issue in 1951, and then spent on other projects. Construction finally started in the 1970s, and stopped during the city's fiscal crisis, leaving sealed tunnel sections buried in East Harlem and downtown. Only in 2017 did the first piece of the Second Avenue subway open, on the Upper East Side. Down here, the promise is still waiting.

deeper.title: Look Closer: A Mural Wall and a Graffiti-Covered Bank
deeper.text:
Walk a few blocks north along the Bowery, and two buildings tell the story of how the street went from skid row to art destination.

At the northwest corner of the Bowery and Houston Street, look for the big painted wall. In 1982, the young artist Keith Haring painted a mural there, a riot of his dancing cartoon figures. It was soon painted over. In 2008, a developer who owned the wall had Haring's mural recreated, and since then the wall has been repainted every few months by street artists from around the world. Whatever is on it today is a temporary exhibition, and you're seeing it for a limited run.

A little farther north, at 190 Bowery, at the corner of Spring Street, stands a heavy granite bank building from 1898, built for the Germania Bank. For decades it looked abandoned, its doors and walls thick with graffiti. In fact, it was a home. In 1966, the photographer Jay Maisel bought the whole building, six floors and about seventy rooms, for around a hundred thousand dollars, and lived and worked there with his family for nearly fifty years, letting the graffiti accumulate outside. In 2015, he sold it for about fifty five million dollars, which says everything about what happened to the Bowery and to New York real estate in between.

On the way, notice how many restaurant supply stores still line the street, with stacks of pots and steel tables on the sidewalk. And look up at the facades. Above the storefronts, many buildings still carry the cornices and window decorations of the 1800s, from the years before the El darkened the street.

stops.title: The Tenement Museum
stops.text:
You're now on Orchard Street, standing near 97 Orchard Street, the building that houses the Lower East Side Tenement Museum.

The building was constructed in 1863 by a German immigrant named Lucas Glockner. It's a typical tenement: five stories plus a basement, with four apartments per floor, each about three hundred twenty five square feet, divided into three small rooms. Only one of those rooms had windows to the outside. At first, there was no indoor plumbing at all: residents used outhouses in the backyard, and water came from a pump. Over about seventy years, from 1863 to 1935, an estimated seven thousand people from more than twenty countries lived in this one building.

In 1935, rather than comply with new housing laws, the landlord evicted the residents and sealed the upper floors. The apartments stayed closed for over fifty years. In 1988, the historian Ruth Abram and her colleague Anita Jacobson found the building and discovered the sealed floors almost like a time capsule, with layers of wallpaper, linoleum, and objects left behind. They founded the museum, which has restored individual apartments to tell the stories of specific families who actually lived there: a German Jewish dressmaker abandoned by her husband during the Panic of 1873, Italian Catholic immigrants, Sicilians, Eastern European Jews, Irish, and later families.

The building's history is also the history of housing law. Reformers horrified by tenement conditions pushed a series of laws. The Tenement House Act of 1879 required that every bedroom have a window, which led landlords to build the so-called dumbbell tenement, with narrow air shafts pinched into the middle of the building. The shafts were dark, foul, and often filled with garbage. Then the Tenement House Act of 1901 required much larger courtyards, indoor toilets for each apartment, and better fire safety. That 1901 law is considered one of the founding pieces of American housing regulation.

Orchard Street itself was the center of a famous pushcart market. By the early 1900s, hundreds of peddlers lined the streets selling everything from pickles and herring to hats, fabric, and pots. In the mid-twentieth century, Orchard Street became known as a bargain shopping district, especially on Sundays, since many Jewish merchants closed on Saturdays for the Sabbath.

The museum offers guided tours of the apartments, and if you have the chance, they're one of the most moving and intimate history experiences in the city.

deeper.title: The Families of 97 Orchard
deeper.text:
The Tenement Museum doesn't tell history through famous people. It tells it through the families who actually lived in this building, and a few of their stories are worth knowing before you go in.

In 1869, an Irish couple, Joseph and Bridget Moore, lived here with their children. That year, their infant daughter Agnes died of malnutrition. The Moores had come from a country devastated by famine and found poverty here too, and anti-Irish prejudice everywhere.

In 1874, during the depression that followed the Panic of 1873, a German Jewish shoemaker named Julius Gumpertz walked out one morning and never came back. His wife, Nathalie, raised their children alone, working as a dressmaker in the apartment, and years later, she won an inheritance from her husband's family in Germany and moved her family uptown.

In the 1890s, Harris and Jennie Levine ran a small garment shop in their apartment, with several workers sewing in the same rooms where the family ate and slept. It was a sweatshop in the literal sense: home and work in one hot, crowded space.

In 1918, a Lithuanian Jewish family, the Rogarshevskys, lost the father, Abraham, to tuberculosis, the great killer of the tenements. And in the 1930s, during the Great Depression, a Sicilian Catholic family, the Baldizzis, lived here until the landlord evicted everyone in 1935. Their daughter Josephine, who grew up in the apartment, came back decades later to help the museum recreate it, remembering where the furniture stood and how her mother cooked.

Together, these families tell the American story in one stairwell: different languages, the same narrow rooms, and the same hope of moving out and up.

deeper.title: How a Tenement Worked
deeper.text:
Look up at the buildings on Orchard Street, and with a little knowledge you can read how they were built and lived in.

Almost every tenement here sits on a standard city lot, twenty five feet wide and a hundred feet deep. Builders covered as much of it as the law allowed. A typical building of the 1860s like number 97 had four apartments on each floor, two in front and two in back, with a narrow staircase up the middle. In each apartment, only the front room had windows to the outside. The bedrooms in the middle were dark.

Water at first came from a pump in the backyard, and the toilets were outhouses back there too. Over the decades, laws forced upgrades: a cold water tap in each hallway, then, in the early 1900s, toilets in the hallways, shared by two families. Bathtubs were rare. People went to the public baths that the city built after 1900, some of which still stand around here.

Look at the fronts of the buildings. The iron fire escapes were required by law after the 1860s, and families used them as balconies, places to sleep on hot summer nights, and shelves for laundry and food. Up at the top, the decorative cornices of pressed metal were bought from catalogs and bolted on to make cheap buildings look prosperous. Many facades also have stone or cast decorations around the windows, chosen from builders' pattern books.

The ground floors were usually shops or saloons, often a few steps down from the street, and the cellars held workshops, storerooms, and sometimes more people. At number 97, a German family named Schneider ran a beer saloon in the basement for years in the 1860s and 1870s, and the museum has rebuilt it. It was a place to drink, eat, cash a paycheck, and hear the news from home.

deeper.title: The Kosher Meat War of 1902
deeper.text:
In May 1902, the women of the Lower East Side went to war over the price of meat, and they wrote a new chapter in American protest.

The trigger was a sudden jump in the price of kosher beef, from about twelve cents a pound to eighteen, blamed on the big meat packers. For families who already lived on the edge, it meant no meat at all on the Sabbath table. On May 14th, a group of neighborhood women, led by two housewives named Fanny Levy and Sarah Edelson, met near Pike and Monroe Streets and agreed: nobody would buy kosher meat until the price came down.

The next morning they took to the streets. Women organized door to door, patrolled the butcher shops, and stopped other women from buying, sometimes by pulling meat out of their hands and throwing it into the street. Some shop windows were broken. Newspapers reported crowds in the thousands, and police arrested dozens of women.

The boycott spread to Brooklyn, Harlem, Newark, Boston and Philadelphia. The women formed a committee, held mass meetings in synagogues, and pressed rabbis to back them. By early June, prices had come down somewhat, and the boycott ended.

Historians see it as a dress rehearsal for what came next on these streets: the rent strikes of the early 1900s, the great garment strikes, and the idea that immigrant women, without votes or money, could organize and win. The tactics they invented, from picket lines at shop doors to neighborhood committees, would be used again and again.

stops.title: Eldridge Street Synagogue
stops.text:
In front of you, on Eldridge Street, is a building that seems almost out of place among the tenements around it: a tall facade with a great rose window, horseshoe arches, and Moorish and Gothic details. This is the Eldridge Street Synagogue, completed in 1887.

It was the first great synagogue built in America by Eastern European Jews. Before this, most synagogues for the new immigrants were tiny congregations meeting in rented rooms or converted churches. This building was a statement. Its builders, mostly working class immigrants who had prospered a little, wanted to show that they had arrived and that Judaism had a permanent place in America. On the High Holidays at the turn of the century, the sanctuary was reportedly packed with worshippers, with crowds spilling into the street.

The Moorish Revival style, with its horseshoe arches and geometric patterns, was popular for synagogues across Europe and America in the nineteenth century. It evoked the era of Muslim Spain, sometimes remembered as a golden age for Jewish culture, and set synagogues apart from the Gothic style of Christian churches.

As the Jewish population moved away to Brooklyn, the Bronx, and the suburbs, the congregation shrank dramatically. By the 1950s, the main sanctuary was closed off, and the remaining worshippers met in the smaller basement chapel. Pigeons lived in the sanctuary, and the building deteriorated badly. In the 1980s, preservationists launched a long effort to save it, and after a restoration of about twenty years, it reopened in 2007 as the Museum at Eldridge Street.

Look at the great round window on the facade. The original window had been lost, and in 2010 it was replaced with a new stained glass window designed by the artist Kiki Smith with the architect Deborah Gans, featuring a field of stars on a blue background.

The synagogue now sits at the edge of Chinatown. On the surrounding blocks you'll see Chinese signs, groceries, and businesses, mixed with traces of the old Jewish neighborhood: an old building cornerstone with Hebrew lettering, a former matzo bakery, a sign over a doorway. It's a compact lesson in how New York neighborhoods layer one community atop another.

deeper.title: Look Closer: Inside the Sanctuary
deeper.text:
If the museum is open, go inside and climb to the main sanctuary. Here is what to look for.

At the far end, on the east wall facing Jerusalem, is the ark, the great carved cabinet where the Torah scrolls are kept, with a lamp burning before it. In the middle of the room is the bimah, the raised platform where the Torah was read aloud, so that the reading happened in the midst of the congregation rather than at the front.

Look up and around. On three sides runs the women's balcony. In Orthodox practice, men and women prayed separately, and the women's gallery let them see and hear everything from above. The walls and ceilings are painted with stenciled patterns, and in places, painted marble and painted woodwork imitate costlier materials that the congregation couldn't afford. The brass chandeliers were built to burn gas and were later wired for electricity.

Then look down. Near the old wooden pews, the floorboards are worn into shallow hollows. Guides here will tell you they were worn by the feet of generations of men swaying as they prayed, the traditional motion called shuckling. Whether every hollow came from prayer, or some from simple foot traffic, it's hard to stand there and not imagine the crowds of 1900.

Finally, turn around and face the rose window above the entrance. When light comes through Kiki Smith's window of stars, it fills the back of the sanctuary with blue. The restorers decided to leave some of the old damage visible, a patch of original paint here, a worn surface there, so that the building shows its age honestly. It's not a replica of 1887. It's a survivor.

deeper.title: Two Catholic Brothers and a Moorish Synagogue
deeper.text:
One of the surprises of the Eldridge Street Synagogue is who designed it: two Catholic brothers from Germany.

Peter and Francis William Herter were young immigrant architects who had designed only a few buildings in the city when the congregation hired them in 1886. They had never designed a synagogue. They went on to a long career, mostly designing the very kind of building that surrounds this one: tenements, many of them still standing on the Lower East Side.

For the synagogue, they drew on a style that was hugely popular for synagogues in Germany and Central Europe in the nineteenth century: the Moorish Revival, with horseshoe arches, stripes and geometric ornament borrowed from the Islamic architecture of Spain. Great synagogues in Berlin, Vienna and Budapest had been built in this style, and so had New York's Central Synagogue on Lexington Avenue, finished in 1872 for a congregation of established German Jews.

For a Jewish congregation, the style did several things at once. It set the building apart from Christian churches, it recalled Jewish life in medieval Spain, and it announced, with all its towers and finials, that this congregation was here to stay.

But look closely at the facade and you'll see the Herters mixed their sources freely. The rose window is Gothic, the arches Moorish, and the round-arched windows Romanesque. Architects of the time weren't worried about purity. They wanted a building that would stand out on a street of plain brick tenements and make a statement. They succeeded: more than a century later, this building still stops people on the sidewalk.

deeper.title: The Chief Rabbi's Funeral
deeper.text:
The world that built this synagogue was proud, pious and divided, and one day in 1902 shows all three.

In 1888, a group of Orthodox congregations on the Lower East Side brought a famous scholar from Vilna, Rabbi Jacob Joseph, to be the chief rabbi of New York's Orthodox Jews. They hoped he would bring order to a chaotic religious scene, especially in the supervision of kosher meat. It went badly. When the rabbi's backers tried to pay for supervision with a small fee on kosher meat, many immigrants resented it, other rabbis refused to accept his authority, and the effort fell apart. Rabbi Joseph spent his last years ill and poor.

When he died, in July 1902, the neighborhood gave him one of the largest funerals New York had ever seen. Tens of thousands of mourners followed his coffin through the streets. As the procession passed a big printing press factory on Grand Street, workers there threw scrap metal and other objects from the windows and sprayed the crowd with water. When mourners fought back, the police waded in, and many officers beat the mourners instead of the attackers. Around two hundred people were hurt.

The Jewish community was outraged, and for once it was united. Mass meetings demanded justice. The mayor appointed an investigating committee, which criticized the police harshly.

Historians see the riot as a turning point. It showed the Lower East Side's Jews that they needed to organize politically to protect themselves, and they did, with organizations, voting blocs and leaders who could stand up to City Hall.

stops.title: Seward Park & the Forward Building
stops.text:
You're at Seward Park, at the corner of Essex Street and East Broadway. Opened in 1903, it's often cited as the first permanent, municipally built public playground in the United States. Reformers argued that children of the tenements had nowhere to play but the street, and that parks with organized play would make them healthier and keep them out of trouble. On opening day, crowds of children reportedly swarmed the playground.

Now look at the tall building across the street at 175 East Broadway, with ornate carvings and the name FORWARD across the top. This was the headquarters of the Jewish Daily Forward, known in Yiddish as the Forverts. It was founded in 1897, and under its legendary editor, Abraham Cahan, it became the most widely read Yiddish newspaper in the world. At its peak in the 1920s, it had a circulation of around a quarter million copies.

The Forward was socialist, pro-union, and passionately engaged in teaching immigrants how to become Americans. It ran English lessons, advice on etiquette and hygiene, and serialized fiction by writers including Isaac Bashevis Singer, who later won the Nobel Prize. Its most famous feature was the Bintel Brief, meaning a bundle of letters, an advice column where readers wrote in with their problems: husbands who had abandoned them, children who refused to keep kosher, dilemmas of love, work, and faith in a new country. It's one of the great primary sources of immigrant life.

Look closely at the facade. Above the entrance, there are relief portraits of socialist figures, including Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. Today the building has been converted into luxury condominiums, which says something about how far the neighborhood has traveled.

Nearby on East Broadway is the Educational Alliance, a settlement house founded by established German Jews to help the newer Eastern European arrivals assimilate. It offered classes, libraries, art lessons, and a gym. Among the young people who passed through it were artists and performers who went on to shape American culture.

The garment unions also had deep roots here. The International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union, founded in 1900, drew much of its strength from Jewish and Italian women working in shops on these streets. In 1909, tens of thousands of shirtwaist makers went on strike in what became known as the Uprising of the Twenty Thousand. Two years later, the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire, which you'll hear about on the Greenwich Village tour, killed one hundred forty six workers, many of them young women from this neighborhood.

deeper.title: Abraham Cahan's Newspaper
deeper.text:
The Forward was the voice of the Lower East Side, and for nearly half a century it was the voice of one man, Abraham Cahan.

Cahan was born in 1860 near Vilna, in the Russian Empire, and fled to America in 1882 as a young radical with the police on his trail. He learned English fast, taught it to other immigrants, and began writing in both languages. His novella Yekl, a story of a Jewish immigrant couple pulled apart by Americanization, was turned many decades later into the film Hester Street. His novel The Rise of David Levinsky, about a poor immigrant who becomes a rich garment manufacturer and finds himself empty inside, is still read as one of the great immigrant novels.

As editor of the Forward from the early 1900s, Cahan made a radical choice: he wrote in plain, everyday Yiddish, the language people actually spoke, rather than the formal Yiddish of intellectuals. He mixed socialism with practical advice, gossip with literature, and he understood that an immigrant newspaper's job was to help readers live in America.

He also gave the paper its home. The ten-story Forward Building went up in 1912, towering over the tenements of East Broadway. Its facade carries four portraits of socialist thinkers: Marx and Engels, whom you heard about, and the German labor leaders Ferdinand Lassalle and Wilhelm Liebknecht.

Cahan ran the paper into the 1940s and died in 1951. The Forward moved uptown in 1974. A Chinese church owned the building for years, and then it became apartments. The newspaper itself survived, shrinking, and today it publishes online in English and Yiddish.

deeper.title: Clara Lemlich and the Uprising
deeper.text:
The garment strike of 1909 began with a young woman pushing her way to a stage, and it changed the American labor movement.

Clara Lemlich was a Ukrainian Jewish immigrant in her early twenties who worked in the shirtwaist shops, where young women sewed the fashionable blouses of the era for long hours and low pay, often paying for their own needles and thread and being fined for mistakes. She had already been beaten on a picket line by thugs hired by her employer.

On November 22nd, 1909, the union held a mass meeting at Cooper Union. Speaker after speaker, many of them men, urged caution. Then Lemlich climbed onto the platform and spoke in Yiddish. She said she was a working girl, one of those on strike against intolerable conditions, that she was tired of talk, and that she moved for a general strike. The hall erupted.

The next day, thousands of workers walked out, and within days, the strike had grown to some twenty thousand, maybe more, mostly young Jewish and Italian women. They picketed through a freezing winter. Hundreds were arrested. Wealthy women, including the banker's daughter Anne Morgan and the suffragist Alva Belmont, joined them, raising money and showing up at night court. Newspapers called these supporters the mink brigade.

By February 1910, most shops had settled, with shorter hours and better pay, and the union's membership soared. But some of the biggest shops, including the Triangle Waist Company, refused the demand for safer conditions. A year later, the Triangle fire killed one hundred forty six workers. Clara Lemlich spent the rest of her life organizing, for suffrage, against high rents, and for the cause of working people.

deeper.title: Lillian Wald's Nurses on the Rooftops
deeper.text:
A few blocks south of here, on Henry Street, a young nurse from Rochester changed the way America takes care of its poor and its children.

In 1893, Lillian Wald was teaching a home nursing class on the Lower East Side when a little girl led her to a tenement where the girl's mother lay sick in a filthy room. Wald later said that this was her baptism of fire. She and a fellow nurse, Mary Brewster, moved into the neighborhood to live among their patients. With money from the banker Jacob Schiff, she opened a house at 265 Henry Street, which became the Henry Street Settlement.

Wald's nurses went into tenements to care for the sick at home, charging little or nothing. To save time and avoid endless stairs, they often traveled from building to building across the rooftops. Wald coined the term public health nurse for what they did. She pushed the city to put nurses in the public schools, and the experiment worked so well that school nursing spread across the country.

She had an eye for causes. She campaigned against child labor and was among those who first proposed a federal Children's Bureau, created in 1912. She championed playgrounds like Seward Park, supported unions and women's suffrage, and opposed America's entry into the First World War. The settlement started a theater, the Neighborhood Playhouse, and music classes that grew into a music school.

The Henry Street Settlement still operates today, out of the same row of houses, and the Visiting Nurse Service that grew out of Wald's rooftop nurses is still caring for New Yorkers at home.

stops.title: Katz's, Russ & Daughters & Houston Street
stops.text:
You're now on East Houston Street, which, a New Yorker will tell you, is pronounced HOW-ston, not like the city in Texas. It is named after William Houstoun, a Georgia delegate to the Continental Congress.

On the corner of Houston and Ludlow is Katz's Delicatessen, founded in 1888. It's one of the last of the great Jewish delis that once filled these streets. You take a ticket at the door, order from a counterman who slices your pastrami by hand, and the counterman will usually give you a sample while he works. A tip, traditionally, earns you a thicker sandwich. During World War Two, when the owners' sons were serving overseas, Katz's coined the slogan Send a salami to your boy in the army, and shipped salamis to soldiers. And yes, the famous scene in the 1989 movie When Harry Met Sally was filmed here. A sign hangs over the table where it happened.

A few doors west is Russ and Daughters, an appetizing shop, opened in 1914 by Joel Russ, a Polish immigrant who began by selling herring from a pushcart. Note the distinction: in New York Jewish food culture, a delicatessen sells meat, and an appetizing store sells fish and dairy, things you eat with bagels, like smoked salmon, herring, whitefish, and cream cheese. The separation comes from kosher dietary law, which prohibits mixing meat and dairy. Russ and Daughters was also notable as one of the first businesses in the country to have Daughters in its name. Joel Russ had no sons, and he made his daughters partners in the 1930s.

Also on Houston Street is Yonah Schimmel Knish Bakery, which has been baking knishes, dough pockets stuffed with potato, kasha, or other fillings, since 1910. It looks like it hasn't changed much since then.

These three businesses are survivors. In 1920, the Lower East Side had dozens of delis, appetizing stores, bakeries, and dairy restaurants. Most closed as the Jewish population left. The ones that remain survived by becoming destinations, drawing visitors from all over the world.

deeper.title: Pastrami, Pickles and the Egg Cream
deeper.text:
The foods that made this neighborhood famous each have a story, and a few have a legend attached.

Pastrami came from Romania and Moldova, where pastrama was a way of preserving meat, often goose or mutton, by salting, seasoning and drying it. In New York, cheap beef took over. Brisket or navel is cured in brine for weeks, rubbed with pepper and coriander, smoked, then steamed until tender. A popular story says a butcher named Sussman Volk introduced pastrami to New York in 1888, after a Romanian friend gave him the recipe in exchange for storing his luggage. It's a nice tale, and impossible to confirm.

Pickles were everywhere. Barrels of sour and half-sour cucumbers sat on the sidewalks of Essex and Orchard Streets, and pickle men sold them from the brine with their bare hands. A few pickle sellers still carry on, and every fall the neighborhood holds a pickle festival.

Bagels came with the Jews of Poland. For much of the twentieth century, New York's bagels were made by hand by a small union of Jewish bakers, who guarded their trade fiercely and often passed their jobs down from father to son. Machines eventually broke their hold.

And then there's the egg cream, a fizzy drink of milk, seltzer and chocolate syrup, containing neither egg nor cream. Nobody knows where the name came from. A candy store owner on Second Avenue named Louis Auster is often credited with inventing it in the 1890s, but there are rival claims and rival theories, including one that the name is a garbled Yiddish phrase.

Pick one of each, and you have a Lower East Side lunch that has barely changed in a century.

deeper.title: Names: Loyalists, War Heroes and SoHo
deeper.text:
The street names around here are a map of history, if you know how to read them.

Before the Revolution, much of this land was the farm of the De Lancey family, wealthy merchants and politicians. James De Lancey sided with the British, and after the war, New York State confiscated his estate and sold it off in lots. His name survives anyway, on Delancey Street, and so does his orchard, on Orchard Street.

Rivington Street is named for James Rivington, who printed the leading Loyalist newspaper in British-occupied New York. There's a twist. Historians have long suspected that Rivington was secretly passing information to George Washington's spies, and after the war, he stayed in New York unharmed, which suggests that someone was protecting him.

Then look at the streets between the Bowery and Allen Street: Chrystie, Forsyth, Eldridge and Allen. They were named in 1817 for young American officers who died in the War of 1812, a war now mostly forgotten, which once mattered enough to rename a neighborhood.

Houston Street, as you heard, honors William Houstoun, and New Yorkers still pronounce it his way. Kenmare Street, a few blocks west, was named for the Irish hometown of the mother of Big Tim Sullivan, the Tammany boss of the Bowery. Even the neighborhoods have invented names. SoHo, south of Houston, was coined by a city planner in the 1960s. Nolita, north of Little Italy, came from real estate agents in the 1990s. And Loisaida, the Puerto Rican name for the Lower East Side, was spread by the poet Bimbo Rivas in the 1970s.

deeper.title: Ludlow Street, from the Jail to the Velvet Underground
deeper.text:
Ludlow Street, the narrow street beside Katz's, has had more lives than most streets in the city.

At its southern end, near Broome Street, stood the Ludlow Street Jail, a county jail for debtors and civil prisoners. Its most famous inmate was Boss Tweed, who died there in 1878. The jail closed in the 1920s, and a high school was built on the site.

In the tenement years, Ludlow Street was as crowded as any in the neighborhood, lined with shops on the ground floors and sweatshops above. In the 1960s, its cheap, run-down apartments drew a different kind of immigrant: young artists and musicians. In 1965, the Welsh viola player John Cale shared an apartment at 56 Ludlow Street, and that's where he and a young songwriter named Lou Reed rehearsed with friends and began forming the Velvet Underground, one of the most influential rock bands ever.

Through the 1980s and 1990s, Ludlow Street became one of the centers of a downtown scene of small bars, galleries and music clubs, with names like Max Fish and Pianos, where bands played to a few dozen people and sometimes went on to fame.

Today, the street's mix is typical of the new Lower East Side. A hundred-year-old tenement may hold a cocktail bar on the ground floor and expensive apartments above, next to a new glass hotel, across from a shop that has sold the same goods for decades. Walk its length, and you pass through a century and a half of the neighborhood's history in about five minutes.

stops.title: Essex Market & the Williamsburg Bridge
stops.text:
End your walk at Delancey and Essex Streets, near the Manhattan entrance of the Williamsburg Bridge.

Essex Market, now in a modern building at the Essex Crossing development, has its roots in a reform by Mayor Fiorello La Guardia. In the 1930s, the streets of the Lower East Side were still clogged with thousands of pushcart vendors. La Guardia, the son of an Italian father and a Jewish mother from Trieste, wanted to modernize the city and clear the streets. He created a system of enclosed public markets, where vendors could rent stalls with refrigeration and running water. The original Essex Market opened in 1940, across the street. In 2019, it moved into the new building here.

Essex Crossing itself has an unusual history. In 1967, the city demolished tenements on several blocks here for an urban renewal project, displacing hundreds of mostly Puerto Rican and Jewish families, with a promise that they could return to new housing. But politics stalled the project, and for nearly fifty years the land sat empty, mostly as parking lots. It was one of the largest undeveloped city-owned sites in Manhattan. Construction finally began in the 2010s, with a mix of market rate and affordable housing, a park, offices, and the market.

Now look up at the Williamsburg Bridge, rising above Delancey Street. When it opened in 1903, it was the longest suspension bridge in the world, surpassing the Brooklyn Bridge. It was also the first major suspension bridge with towers made entirely of steel rather than stone. Its builders went for strength over beauty, and critics at the time considered it ugly.

But the bridge transformed both sides of the river. It gave the crowded Lower East Side an escape route. Tens of thousands of Jewish families moved across it to the Williamsburg section of Brooklyn, so many that the bridge was sometimes nicknamed the Jews' highway. Today, Williamsburg is home to a large Hasidic community, as well as the young, artsy population that made it famous in the 2000s. You can walk across the bridge on its pedestrian path, and pick up the Williamsburg and Greenpoint tour on the other side.

Look back at Delancey Street as you go. It was widened for the bridge approach, and it became a busy commercial strip of bargain stores. The 1988 movie Crossing Delancey took its title from the idea that crossing this street, from the old neighborhood to the uptown world, was the defining journey for the children of immigrants. It still is, in a way. The story of the Lower East Side is the story of people arriving, working, saving, and eventually crossing over to somewhere else.

deeper.title: Fiorello La Guardia, the Little Flower
deeper.text:
The man who built this market was the most popular mayor in New York history, and almost nothing about him was typical.

Fiorello La Guardia, whose first name means little flower, was born in Greenwich Village in 1882, but grew up mostly in Arizona, where his father was an army bandmaster. As a young man, he worked at American consulates in Hungary and in the port city of Fiume, then came back to New York and worked as an interpreter at Ellis Island while studying law at night. He spoke Italian, Yiddish, German and Croatian, and he campaigned in all of them.

He was short, loud and tireless, a Republican who backed Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal and fought Tammany Hall. Elected mayor in 1933, he served three terms. He smashed slot machines with a sledgehammer for the newsreels, chased gangsters out of the city's markets, rebuilt parks and bridges with federal money, and gave his name eventually to an airport. During a newspaper delivery strike in 1945, he read the Sunday comics aloud on the city's radio station, doing the voices himself, so the children wouldn't miss them.

The pushcarts were one of his targets. He thought they were unsanitary, chaotic and a traffic hazard, and he also wanted to give vendors a better life. His answer was a string of enclosed public markets, with stalls, running water and refrigeration: this one on Essex Street, opened in 1940, La Marqueta in East Harlem under the railroad viaduct, and the market on Arthur Avenue in the Bronx, which is still the heart of the Bronx's Little Italy.

Some vendors hated leaving the streets. But the markets lasted, and several of them still operate.

deeper.title: Building the Williamsburg Bridge
deeper.text:
The Williamsburg Bridge was built fast and cheap, nearly burned before it opened, and nearly fell apart eighty years later.

Its chief engineer, Leffert Buck, had built bridges across canyons in South America, and he designed this one for heavy traffic: two tracks for elevated trains, two for trolleys, roadways and walkways. To save money and time, he used steel towers instead of masonry ones, and a stiff, boxy truss to carry the deck. Critics hated how it looked. But it opened in 1903 as the longest suspension bridge in the world.

In November 1902, with the cables in place, a fire broke out in the wooden scaffolding at the top of the Manhattan tower. Crowds watched it burn from the streets below, and engineers feared that the heat would ruin the cables. The fire burned itself out, the damaged wires were checked and repaired, and the bridge opened a year later.

The bridge's real problem came later and more slowly. The cables had been made of wire that wasn't galvanized, without a protective coating of zinc, and over the decades, water and salt went to work. By the 1980s, inspectors found cables badly rusted and steel beams rotted through. In April 1988, the city closed the bridge to cars and trains, at a moment's notice, fearing it could not safely carry them. Some engineers argued it should be torn down and replaced. Instead, the city rebuilt it, piece by piece, over many years, while keeping it partly open.

Today the bridge carries the J, M and Z trains, cars, and some of the busiest bike lanes in the country. Walk or bike up its long ramp and you'll understand why: the view of Manhattan from the top is worth every step.

deeper.title: Sonny Rollins on the Bridge
deeper.text:
In 1959, one of the greatest jazz musicians in the world disappeared from the scene, and he could be found, if you knew where to look, on the walkway of the Williamsburg Bridge.

Sonny Rollins was already a star of the tenor saxophone, with acclaimed albums behind him, when he decided he wasn't good enough. He stepped away from performing and recording to work on his playing. He lived in an apartment on Grand Street, near here, and he worried that practicing for hours a day would disturb his neighbors, including a woman who was expecting a baby. So he took his horn up onto the bridge.

For about two years, day and night, in all kinds of weather, Rollins practiced on the walkway, high above the East River, with the subway trains rumbling past. He said later that the bridge was the perfect place: he could play as loud as he wanted, and the noise of the trains and boats pushed him to play bigger. Passersby occasionally stopped to listen. Most had no idea who he was.

When he came back, in 1962, he named his comeback album The Bridge. It's considered one of the great records of its era.

Rollins played into his eighties and became one of the last living giants of his generation of jazz. So as you walk up the bridge's ramp, imagine the sound of a tenor saxophone floating over the rumble of the trains.

overview:
If you want to understand how America absorbed the great waves of immigration of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, there is no better place to walk than the Lower East Side.

For about a century, from the 1840s to the 1920s, these streets were among the most densely populated places on Earth. At its peak, around 1900, parts of the Lower East Side packed in several hundred thousand people per square mile, a density that rivaled or exceeded the most crowded parts of Bombay or London at the time. They lived in tenements, five and six story walk-up buildings built to squeeze as many families as possible onto a standard twenty five by one hundred foot city lot.

The first great wave was German. By the 1850s, the area east of the Bowery and north of Division Street was known as Kleindeutschland, Little Germany. It was one of the largest German speaking cities in the world, with its own beer halls, newspapers, theaters, and gymnastic clubs. Over time, prosperous Germans moved uptown, to Yorkville and elsewhere, a migration accelerated by a terrible tragedy in 1904 that we'll talk about on the East Village tour.

Then came the Eastern European Jews. Between about 1880 and 1924, around two and a half million Jews came to America, fleeing poverty and pogroms in the Russian Empire, Austria-Hungary, and Romania. A large share of them came first to these streets. They brought Yiddish, a garment industry built on small workshops, a passionate radical politics, and a culture of newspapers, theater, and debate. At the same time, Italians, mostly from southern Italy and Sicily, settled just to the west, around Mulberry Street, in what became Little Italy.

This was where the garment industry was born, in crowded sweatshops in tenement apartments. It was where the labor movement found some of its fiercest organizers. It was also where urban reformers, horrified by conditions, pushed the laws that shaped how cities everywhere build housing, requiring windows, air shafts, toilets, and fire escapes.

After immigration restrictions in 1924, the neighborhood slowly emptied. Puerto Rican families arrived after World War Two, giving the area east of Avenue A the name Loisaida, a Spanglish rendering of Lower East Side. Chinatown expanded from the south. And in the last few decades, the neighborhood has become a destination for bars, galleries, and restaurants, with new towers rising alongside the old tenements.

As you walk, look for the fire escapes zigzagging down the fronts of buildings, the decorative cornices at the tops of tenements, which landlords used to make cheap buildings look respectable, and the old Jewish delis and appetizing shops that have survived a century of change.

title: Hudson Square, Tribeca & SoHo
blurb: Freight terminals, telecom fortresses, the butter-and-egg district, cast-iron palaces, and the first passenger elevator.

stops.title: St. John's Terminal & Hudson Square
stops.text:
You're near the corner of West Houston Street and West Street, beside the long, massive building that stretches south along the river. This is St. John's Terminal, and if you work at Google New York, you may know it well from the inside.

The name goes back to St. John's Park, which once existed a few blocks south of here. In the early 1800s, Trinity Church built a grand chapel, St. John's Chapel, and laid out a private, fenced square around it, modeled on London's elegant residential squares. It became one of the most fashionable addresses in the city. But in 1867, Trinity sold the park to Commodore Cornelius Vanderbilt, who paved it over and built a giant freight terminal for his Hudson River Railroad. The chapel was demolished in 1918. The fashionable families had already fled uptown.

Trains used to run down the middle of the West Side streets, at street level. Tenth Avenue, in Chelsea, was nicknamed Death Avenue because of the number of people killed by freight trains. In the 1930s, the New York Central Railroad built the West Side Improvement Project, which lifted the trains onto an elevated viaduct. That viaduct is what we now know as the High Line. Its southern end was right here: freight trains rolled directly into the second floor of this building, which opened in 1934, so that goods could be unloaded straight into storage.

As trucking took over, the rail line was cut back. The southern portion, including the connection to this building, was demolished in the early 1990s. If you look at the building's north end, you may notice where the old rail tracks once entered.

In recent years, Google acquired and rebuilt the terminal as a major office, adding new floors above the old freight structure. It's part of a broader reinvention of Hudson Square. The neighborhood, much of which is still owned by Trinity Church's real estate arm, was the printing district for most of the twentieth century. The big industrial buildings with heavy floors, built to hold the weight of printing presses, now hold offices for media and tech companies. The Walt Disney Company has also built its New York headquarters a few blocks south.

As you head south, you'll pass the entrance to the Holland Tunnel, which opened in 1927 under the Hudson River to Jersey City. It was the first mechanically ventilated underwater vehicle tunnel in the world. Its chief engineer, Clifford Holland, died during construction, possibly from the stress and exhaustion of the job, and the tunnel was named after him. Huge ventilation buildings on both sides of the river exchange the air inside the tunnel every ninety seconds.

deeper.title: The Chapel, the Commodore and the Bronze
deeper.text:
You heard how Trinity Church sold St. John's Park to Cornelius Vanderbilt in 1867. Here's what became of the pieces.

Start with the chapel. St. John's Chapel was finished in 1807, designed by the brothers John and Isaac McComb, with a columned portico and a tall steeple rising over the park. It stayed even after the park became a freight yard, though its congregation dwindled. In 1892, Trinity's leaders announced plans to tear it down, and the remaining parishioners rebelled, joined by New Yorkers who simply loved the building. Their pastor, Philip Brown, led the holdouts until his death in 1909. It was one of the city's earliest fights to save a historic building. In the end, the street won. When the city widened Varick Street for the new subway, the chapel's portico stood in the way, and the whole building came down in 1918. If you ride the 1 train, look for the mosaics in the Canal Street station that remember it.

Then the depot. Vanderbilt's freight depot went up in 1868, and the next year he unveiled a monument New Yorkers never forgot: an enormous bronze sculpture across the front of the building, crowded with steamships, locomotives and scenes from his career, with a statue of the Commodore himself standing in the middle. It was designed by Albert De Groot, who had once captained one of Vanderbilt's steamships, and sculpted by Ernst Plassmann. Critics found it ridiculous: a monument a man had raised to himself, on top of a freight shed.

The statue outlived the depot. In 1929, it was moved to Grand Central Terminal, the family's grandest monument, where it still stands on the south side of the building, above Park Avenue. The depot was later torn down, and its land became the exit plaza of the Holland Tunnel. When you see cars pouring out of the tunnel and around the traffic circle a few blocks south of here, you're looking at the ground where the city's most exclusive park once stood.

deeper.title: Trinity Church, Landlord
deeper.text:
Much of the ground around you belongs to a church, and that church is one of the great landlords of New York.

Trinity's fortune began in 1705, when Queen Anne granted the parish a large farm on Manhattan's west side, land that had passed from the Dutch to the English crown. Over the next two centuries, the city grew over it. Trinity sold some of the land, gave some away for other churches and for King's College, which became Columbia University, and leased much of the rest on long leases, collecting ground rent while others built.

In the early twentieth century, the city cut through the neighborhood. Seventh Avenue was pushed south, Varick Street was widened, and the subway was dug underneath. Trinity and its neighbors put up big, heavy loft buildings, and printers filled them. For decades, the presses here turned out magazines, books, catalogs, stock certificates and phone books, and typesetters, binders and paper merchants clustered around them.

When printing moved away, the area was rebranded in the 1990s as Hudson Square, after the old park. Trinity pushed for a rezoning, approved by the city in 2013, that allowed apartments alongside offices. Then, in 2015, the church went into partnership with an unexpected investor: Norway's sovereign wealth fund, which invests that country's oil money. The fund paid about one and a half billion dollars for a stake of nearly half in eleven of Trinity's office buildings here.

So as you walk south, you're crossing land granted by an English queen to a church, now shared with a Norwegian oil fund and filled with tech companies. Look at the buildings as you go. Many still have their freight elevators, loading docks and huge steel-framed windows, built to light the press rooms. The rents pay for Trinity's churches, programs and charitable grants, as the land has done for more than three hundred years.

deeper.title: Clifford Holland's Tunnel
deeper.text:
The Holland Tunnel was one of the great engineering feats of its time, and it cost the lives of the two men who first led it.

When construction began, in 1920, no one had ever built a long underwater tunnel for cars. The hard part wasn't the digging. It was the air. Car exhaust carries carbon monoxide, and in a tube more than a mile and a half long, with thousands of cars passing every hour, drivers could be poisoned. The engineers worked with the United States Bureau of Mines and with scientists from Yale University, who tested the gas on volunteers to learn how much people could safely breathe. Their answer was a new kind of ventilation: fresh air blown in through ducts beneath the roadway, and foul air drawn out through the ceiling, around the clock.

The digging itself was done by sandhogs, who pushed huge steel shields through the mud beneath the river, working in compressed air to hold back the water, and lined the tunnel behind them with rings of cast iron.

The chief engineer, Clifford Holland, was thirty six when he took the job, and he drove himself without rest. In 1924, worn out, he went to a sanatorium in Michigan to recover, and died there of a heart attack at forty one, just before the two halves of the tunnel were due to meet under the river. His successor, Milton Freeman, died of pneumonia a few months later. A third engineer, Ole Singstad, finished the job, and went on to build the Queens Midtown and Brooklyn Battery Tunnels.

The tunnel opened in November 1927. Before any cars were let in, about twenty thousand people walked through it, for the thrill of strolling under the Hudson. It was named for the man who didn't live to see it, and the ventilation system his team designed became a model for road tunnels around the world.

stops.title: Hook & Ladder 8 & the Heart of Tribeca
stops.text:
At the corner of North Moore Street and Varick Street stands a small, ornate Beaux-Arts firehouse. This is the home of Hook and Ladder Company 8, completed in 1903. With its red doors, rusticated stone, and elaborate cornice, it shows how seriously the city took its civic architecture at the turn of the century. Even a firehouse was meant to look like a small palace.

The building became internationally famous as the headquarters of the paranormal exterminators in the 1984 film Ghostbusters. Fans still come here to take pictures, and the firefighters inside have embraced the connection; there's often a Ghostbusters sign displayed inside.

But this firehouse also has a quieter history. The firefighters of Ladder 8 responded to the World Trade Center on September eleventh, 2001. Fire stations throughout lower Manhattan lost members that day.

Tribeca itself, as a name, is a recent invention. In the 1970s, artists began moving into the abandoned warehouses south of Canal Street, following the same path as in SoHo. Real estate brokers and residents called the area the Triangle Below Canal, and shortened it to Tribeca. Today it is one of the most expensive neighborhoods in the United States, home to celebrities and finance executives who live in converted warehouses with eighteen-foot ceilings.

After September eleventh, the neighborhood, just north of the World Trade Center, was deeply affected. To help bring people back downtown, the actor Robert De Niro, the producer Jane Rosenthal, and the investor Craig Hatkoff founded the Tribeca Film Festival in 2002. De Niro had long been invested in the neighborhood: his company, Tribeca Productions, was based in a former coffee warehouse nearby, in what's now called the Tribeca Film Center.

As you walk the streets around here, North Moore, Franklin, White, and Walker, notice the dense collection of handsome nineteenth century warehouses, many with their loading docks still intact. These buildings once held dry goods, textiles, and groceries on their way to stores across the city and the country.

deeper.title: The Firehouse That Was Cut in Half
deeper.text:
This firehouse looks perfectly proportioned, but you're looking at only half of the building that opened here in 1903.

When Ladder 8 moved in, the firehouse was twice as wide, with two big doors, and the rigs were pulled by horses. In the firehouses of that era, the horses lived in stalls on the ground floor, behind the apparatus, and the firefighters slept upstairs, ready to slide down a brass pole. When the alarm bell rang, the horses were trained to step out of their stalls and take their places in front of the rig, where harnesses hanging from the ceiling dropped onto their backs. A good company could be rolling in moments.

Then came the subway. Around 1913, the city widened Varick Street for the new line being dug beneath it, and the firehouse was in the way. Rather than move the company, the fire department cut the building down to fit. The half nearest Varick Street was taken down, a new wall went up along the new sidewalk, and the front you see on North Moore Street, with its single big door, is the half that survived. The same street widening doomed St. John's Chapel, a few blocks north.

The horses didn't last much longer. The department replaced them with motor rigs through the 1910s, and in 1922, the last horse-drawn engine in the city made its final run, in Brooklyn, with a ceremony to mark the end of an era.

The firehouse itself has been well looked after. In the late 2010s it was renovated for about six million dollars, while Ladder 8 spent about three years in a firehouse in SoHo. Then the company moved back home, and its rig still squeezes out of that single door onto North Moore Street, to answer calls all over lower Manhattan.

deeper.title: Ghostbusters and the Movie Firehouse
deeper.text:
In 1984, a comedy about three scientists who lose their university jobs and go into business catching ghosts made this firehouse one of the most famous buildings in the world.

In the film, the three buy a run-down old firehouse for their headquarters. Dan Aykroyd's character, Ray, falls in love with it and slides down the pole, and the team parks their converted 1959 Cadillac ambulance, the Ecto One, in the bay.

Here's a movie secret. Only the outside was filmed here. Most of the interior scenes were shot in Los Angeles, in an old downtown firehouse that had been taken out of service, Fire Station 23, which fans still visit on the West Coast.

The movie also caught a real moment in New York. In the 1970s, during the city's fiscal crisis, the fire department shut down companies across the city, and lower Manhattan was full of empty industrial lofts that a team of oddballs could rent for very little. Under the jokes, Ghostbusters is a movie about downtown real estate.

The firefighters here have made peace with their fame. Inside, they display half of an actual sign used in the sequel, Ghostbusters Two, from 1989. When Harold Ramis, who played Egon, died in 2014, they hung a Ghostbusters sign outside in his memory. And in 2021, a fan group from Buffalo raised money for a new, weatherproof copy of the famous logo, a ghost inside a red circle with a slash through it, and gave it to the firehouse.

If you'd like more of the movie's New York, it opens at the main library on Fifth Avenue at Forty Second Street, with its stone lions, and Sigourney Weaver's character lives in the grand apartment building at 55 Central Park West, where the film's final battle takes place on the roof.

deeper.title: Triangles, Lofts and Landmarks
deeper.text:
You heard that Tribeca is short for Triangle Below Canal. The story behind the name is odder than it sounds.

In the early 1970s, during a fight over zoning, the residents of one small, triangle-shaped block just south of Canal Street, between Church Street and Broadway, formed a group they called the Triangle Below Canal Block Association. They soon shortened that to the Tribeca Block Association. Other accounts credit city planners with the name. Either way, by the mid 1970s it was in print, and it had spread to the whole district, west to the river and south to Chambers Street. That area isn't a triangle at all. It's a lopsided four-sided shape. The name stuck anyway.

The artists who moved into Tribeca's empty warehouses mostly lived there illegally, in buildings zoned for manufacturing. In 1982, the state passed the Loft Law, which protected tenants who had moved into commercial lofts and required landlords to bring the buildings up to the code for homes. It let many of the pioneers stay, but it couldn't stop the neighborhood from changing around them.

Preservationists, meanwhile, went to work on the buildings themselves. In 1991 and 1992, the city created four historic districts here, Tribeca West, East, North and South, protecting hundreds of the warehouses and stores you're walking past. That's why these streets still look much as they did a century ago, even as lofts with eighteen foot ceilings sell for tens of millions of dollars.

Real estate agents have been trying to repeat the trick ever since, inventing names for every corner of the city. A few, like Nolita, for North of Little Italy, have caught on. Most fade away. Tribeca lasted, partly because it sounds good, and partly because the people who lived here embraced it.

stops.title: Harrison Street & the Lost Washington Market
stops.text:
You're on Harrison Street, near Greenwich Street. Look at the row of small brick houses with peaked roofs and dormer windows. These are Federal-style townhouses, built in the late 1700s and early 1800s, when this was a residential neighborhood for merchants and artisans. Several of them weren't originally here: in the 1970s, as urban renewal swept through the area, a few of these historic houses were moved from nearby Washington Street to save them from demolition and reassembled here.

That urban renewal was aimed at what was once the largest wholesale food market in the city: the Washington Market. Founded in the early 1800s, it spread over many blocks along the Hudson waterfront. By the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, it was the place where much of New York's fresh food, fruits, vegetables, meat, poultry, came into the city by boat and rail and was sold to grocers, restaurants, and pushcart peddlers. The area was chaotic, crowded, and notoriously congested, with trucks jammed in the streets day and night.

In the 1950s and 60s, city planners decided the market was obsolete and should move to a modern facility. The wholesale produce trade moved to Hunts Point in the Bronx in the 1960s, where it still operates as one of the largest food distribution centers in the world. Most of the Washington Market area was demolished. Part of it became the site of the original World Trade Center. Part became Independence Plaza, the large apartment towers you see nearby, and part became Manhattan Community College.

Just to the south and east, the area around Duane Park, a small triangular park, was the city's butter and egg district. Dairy wholesalers clustered around here, and the old warehouses still bear names of food businesses on their facades. Duane Park itself has a curious origin: the city bought the land from Trinity Church in 1797 for the price of five dollars. It was originally part of a farm owned by a Dutch woman named Annetje Jans in the 1600s.

One survivor of the food trade was the Bazzini nut company, which roasted and sold nuts in Tribeca from the late 1800s until the 2000s, when it, too, moved out to the Bronx, and its building became apartments. Today, the only market in Washington Market Park is the playground. But walk around and you'll see the old names, still carved into stone.

deeper.title: What They Sold at Washington Market
deeper.text:
Picture this neighborhood at four in the morning around 1900. You'd hardly be able to move, and you'd smell the market before you saw it.

Wagons, and later trucks, jammed every street. Dealers sold by the crate and the barrel to grocers, hotel chefs, restaurant owners and pushcart peddlers, who loaded up before dawn and fanned out across the city. There were mountains of oysters and clams, barrels of apples, crates of oranges and bananas off the ships, butter and cheese from upstate farms, and live chickens by the thousands.

In the nineteenth century there was also an enormous trade in wild game. A butcher named Thomas De Voe, who kept a stall at the Jefferson Market in Greenwich Village, published a book in 1867 called The Market Assistant, describing everything sold in the markets of New York and other eastern cities. It lists venison and bear meat, wild turkeys, ducks and geese, and a long list of small birds, robins among them, sold by the dozen. It's a picture of a time before game laws, when almost anything that ran, flew or swam could end up on a New York table.

Some dealers specialized in a single thing: eggs, or poultry, or turtles and terrapin for the rich soups that fancy restaurants served. Many of these businesses were family firms, handed down for generations.

The market was also a mess. Food spoiled in the gutters, carts and trucks blocked the streets for hours, and each middleman along the way added to the price. For decades, reformers argued that New Yorkers paid more for their food because of it, which is part of why the city finally moved the trade to the Bronx.

Look around for the clues that remain: metal canopies over the sidewalks, where crates were stacked out of the rain, loading platforms at the height of a wagon bed, and the names of old food companies, still carved or painted on the buildings.

deeper.title: Butter, Eggs and the Mercantile Exchange
deeper.text:
Walk to the corner of Harrison and Hudson Streets and look for the red brick building with the tower over its entrance. It was the home of a market that grew from butter and eggs into oil.

In 1872, dairy merchants in this district founded the Butter and Cheese Exchange of New York, so they could trade under agreed rules, grades and prices. Eggs were soon added, and in 1882 the exchange took a grander name: the New York Mercantile Exchange. In the mid 1880s it moved into this building, designed by Thomas Jackson in a style called Queen Anne, and traders shouted their bids on the floor inside for about ninety years.

For much of the twentieth century, the exchange's biggest business was potato futures: contracts to buy or sell Maine potatoes at a set price on a set date. Then, in 1976, traders who had sold contracts for May potatoes failed to deliver them, the largest default the futures markets had ever seen. The scandal nearly ruined the exchange.

It survived by reinventing itself. It left this building for the new World Trade Center, and began trading contracts on heating oil, and then, in 1983, on crude oil. That crude oil contract became one of the most closely watched prices on earth. When you hear on the news that the price of oil rose or fell, it's often the price set by a market that began with butter, a few steps from where you're standing.

In 2008, the exchange was bought by its great rival, the Chicago Mercantile Exchange. Its old home here has been converted to new uses, but look up at the tower over the Harrison Street entrance, recently restored with a new copper spire. It's a monument to the butter and egg men.

deeper.title: Annetje Jans and the Endless Lawsuit
deeper.text:
You heard that Duane Park was once part of a farm owned by a Dutch woman named Annetje Jans. For nearly two centuries, people claiming to be her heirs tried to take that farm back.

Annetje Jans came to New Netherland around 1630 with her first husband, Roelof Jansen. In 1636, the Dutch governor granted them a farm of about sixty two acres, just outside the little town of New Amsterdam, along the shore of the Hudson, beginning near today's Warren Street and running north toward Canal Street. After Roelof died, Annetje married the minister of the Dutch church, Everardus Bogardus, and the land became known as the Domine's farm, the minister's farm.

She died in 1663. In 1671, her heirs sold the farm to the English governor, Francis Lovelace. All of them signed the deed, except the family of one son, Cornelius Bogardus, who had died a few years before. That missing signature was the seed of the legend.

The farm passed to the English crown, and in 1705 Queen Anne granted it to Trinity Church. As the city grew over it, the land became some of the most valuable on earth, and Annetje's descendants multiplied into thousands of families across America. Many grew up hearing that they were the rightful owners of lower Manhattan, cheated out of their inheritance by a church.

They went to court again and again. In 1749, one descendant simply moved onto part of the old farm, and lost when Trinity took him to court. Another case, begun in 1830, dragged on until 1847 before it was dismissed. Trinity won every time, in part because the church had held the land openly for so long. Still the legend lived on, and through the nineteenth century, promoters collected money from hopeful descendants to pay for new lawsuits.

So the legend is checked: no court ever accepted the heirs' claim. But the story is true in another way. Annetje Jans's farm really is under your feet, and Trinity's fortune really did grow from it.

stops.title: Telecom Fortresses: 33 Thomas Street & 60 Hudson
stops.text:
At the corner of Thomas Street and Church Street, look up at the strangest building in Tribeca: a massive, windowless tower of concrete and granite, with no windows at all, just a few vents near the top. This is 33 Thomas Street, completed in 1974 for AT&T, and originally known as the Long Lines Building.

It was designed to house telephone switching equipment, not people. Its architects designed it to withstand a nuclear blast and to be self-sufficient for up to two weeks in a disaster, with its own fuel and water supplies. Its floors are unusually tall, to accommodate large equipment. In 2016, an investigation by The Intercept and a documentary drew on leaked documents to report that the building was likely a site where the National Security Agency monitored international communications. Whatever happens inside, it remains one of the city's great architectural enigmas, a building designed for machines.

A short walk away, at 60 Hudson Street, stands another telecom landmark: the Western Union Building, completed in 1930. Look at its brickwork. The bricks shift gradually in color from dark at the bottom to light at the top, in a subtle gradient, an Art Deco flourish. Western Union was the telegraph monopoly of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the company that wired news, stock prices, and money across the country. This building was its headquarters and its nerve center.

Today 60 Hudson is one of the most important internet hubs in the world, a so-called carrier hotel. Dozens of telecommunications companies and data networks connect their equipment inside, because the building sits at the junction of major fiber optic routes. The same reasons that made it valuable for telegraph lines a century ago, being a central point where cables converge, make it valuable for internet traffic today. When you send data from New York to London, there's a decent chance it passes through this building.

There's a nice continuity here. Western Union's telegraph, AT&T's telephones, and today's fiber optic networks have all occupied the same few blocks of Tribeca. The infrastructure of communication is sticky: once the cables are in the ground, the buildings keep their importance, even when the technology inside changes completely.

deeper.title: Western Union and the Telephone It Turned Down
deeper.text:
Western Union was the most powerful communications company in America for half a century, and the most famous story about it is almost certainly made up.

The company grew in the 1850s by buying up and merging small telegraph lines. In 1861 it completed the first telegraph line across the continent, and two days later, the Pony Express, which had carried mail on horseback across the West, announced it was shutting down. Western Union carried news for the papers, orders for the railroads, and stock prices for brokers. A young Thomas Edison worked as a telegraph operator, and later invented machines for the company.

Now the story. In 1876, Alexander Graham Bell's backers are said to have offered his telephone patent to Western Union for a hundred thousand dollars, and to have been turned down. A memo is often quoted, supposedly from a Western Union committee, saying that the telephone had too many shortcomings to be seriously considered as a means of communication. That memo is almost certainly a fake. It surfaced decades later, and no one has ever found an original. There may have been an informal offer, and Western Union certainly didn't buy the patent. But the company wasn't blind to telephones. It quickly hired Edison and others to build telephones of its own and went into the business, until 1879, when it settled a patent lawsuit with Bell's company and agreed to leave telephones to Bell, in return for a share of the rental fees.

Western Union carried on with telegrams for another century. It introduced the singing telegram in the 1930s, and grew into a business that sends money around the world. It sent its last telegram in 2006.

Its old headquarters at 60 Hudson Street still hums with wires, but the messages passing through them now belong to the internet.

deeper.title: The Wires Under Your Feet
deeper.text:
Look up as you walk around here and notice what you don't see: telephone poles and overhead wires. Their absence has a story.

By the 1880s, the streets of lower Manhattan were a tangle of wires. Telegraph companies, telephone companies, stock ticker services, fire alarm systems and the new electric light companies each strung their own lines on their own poles, some of them as tall as ninety feet and carrying dozens of crossbars. On some streets the wires were so thick they darkened the sky. The most dangerous were the high voltage lines for the new electric arc lights.

The state ordered the wires buried in the 1880s, but the companies dragged their feet. Then the Blizzard of 1888 brought down poles and wires all over the city. And in October 1889, a Western Union lineman named John Feeks was electrocuted while working high on a pole at Centre and Chambers Streets, near City Hall. His body hung in the tangle of wires above a horrified crowd.

That was the end of the poles. Mayor Hugh Grant sent crews with axes to chop down the poles of companies that wouldn't comply. The wires went into underground conduits, which New Yorkers called subways years before the trains took that name. One of the companies formed to build and run them, the Empire City Subway Company, founded in 1891, still manages the conduits for telephone and internet cables under Manhattan's streets.

When fiber optic cables arrived a century later, many of them were pulled through those same old ducts. That's part of why buildings like 60 Hudson Street became internet hubs. The paths under these streets lead to them, as they once led to the telegraph headquarters.

So every manhole cover you pass is a door into another city below, full of copper, glass fiber and history.

deeper.title: Ralph Walker's Palaces for Wires
deeper.text:
Three of the finest Art Deco buildings in lower Manhattan were built for the companies that carried words and voices, and one architect designed all three.

Ralph Walker was a young designer at the firm of McKenzie, Voorhees and Gmelin when the New York Telephone Company asked for a new headquarters in the early 1920s. His Barclay Vesey Building, finished in 1926 beside today's World Trade Center, was the first skyscraper to treat the city's new zoning rules, which made tall buildings step back as they rose, as a chance for drama instead of a burden. It's often called one of the first Art Deco skyscrapers.

Then came 60 Hudson Street for Western Union, finished in 1930, with the brickwork you heard about, shading from dark to light as it rises. And a few blocks north of here, at 32 Avenue of the Americas, Walker enlarged an older building and gave it new fronts for AT&T's long distance service, finished in 1932.

If you have a few minutes, walk up and look into its lobby, which is an official city interior landmark. One wall holds a tiled map of the world, its continents separated by oceans but tied together by lines of wire, under the words: Telephone wires and radio unite to make neighbors of nations. Overhead is a glittering ceiling of glass mosaic by Hildreth Meière, the artist who covered the banking hall at One Wall Street in red and gold, with figures of the continents and messengers linked by golden lines. It's an office building, so you may only be able to look in from the door.

Walker was proud and opinionated. Frank Lloyd Wright, who admired very few architects, reportedly called him the only other honest architect in America. In 1957, when the American Institute of Architects turned one hundred, it created a special award for him, and The New York Times called him the Architect of the Century. Today he's half forgotten, but his telephone palaces are still here, still full of wires.

stops.title: Greene Street Cast Iron
stops.text:
