Welcome to SoHo, and to Greene Street, one of the most beautiful streets in New York. Look at the facades on both sides: rows of columns, arches, and ornate details, stacked five or six stories high. Most of this is not stone. It's cast iron.

Here's a test: if you carry a small magnet, put it against one of the columns. It'll stick.

Cast iron architecture flourished in New York from the 1850s to the 1880s. It was an early form of mass production in building. Foundries cast facade pieces, columns, capitals, window frames, cornices, from molds, and those parts could be ordered from a catalog, shipped to the site, and bolted together. This allowed builders to imitate the look of expensive carved stone palaces, Venetian, French, or Italian Renaissance, at a fraction of the cost. It also allowed for large windows, since the iron was strong enough to carry loads with thin supports. In an era before electric light, big windows meant more daylight for workers.

Two names to know are James Bogardus, an inventor who promoted cast iron construction in the 1840s and 50s, and Daniel Badger, whose Architectural Iron Works produced facades for buildings across the country.

The buildings were usually painted to look like stone, often in cream, gray, or white. Look for 28 to 30 Greene Street, a grand building with a mansard roof, known as the Queen of Greene Street, and farther north, 72 to 76 Greene Street, known as the King of Greene Street, with its tall columns and projecting central bay.

These buildings mostly housed textile and dry goods businesses: wholesalers of fabric, clothing, and household goods. Ground floors held showrooms. Upper floors held stock or light manufacturing. Despite the iron, fires were common, since the contents were flammable and the iron could buckle under heat. Firefighters called the district Hell's Hundred Acres.

By the 1960s, the buildings were nearly empty. That's when artists came. They found the open loft floors perfect for large canvases and sculpture. Look for small signs reading A.I.R. near the doorways of some buildings, short for Artist in Residence. They told firefighters that people, not just goods, lived in the building, which was important in buildings never designed for residential use.

deeper.title: The Highway That Would Have Erased SoHo
deeper.text:
You heard that Robert Moses wanted to run an expressway along Broome Street, a few blocks south of here. Here's how close it came.

The Lower Manhattan Expressway was first proposed in the early 1940s, and for years it was official city policy. As planned in the 1960s, it would have been ten lanes wide, much of it raised above the streets, slicing across the island. Estimates at the time said it would displace about two thousand families and some eight hundred businesses, many of them small manufacturers employing thousands of workers. The buildings on this street would have stood in its shadow, if they survived at all.

The opposition was a patchwork: families in Little Italy and on the Lower East Side, small business owners, churches, preservationists, artists quietly living in lofts, and the writer Jane Jacobs, who had already fought Moses in Greenwich Village. In April 1968, at a state hearing on the plan, Jacobs and other protesters rushed the stage, and the stenographer's tape was torn up and scattered. Jacobs was arrested and charged with inciting a riot, among other things. The charges were later reduced.

In 1969, Mayor John Lindsay, who had once supported the road, withdrew his backing, and a couple of years later the expressway was finally wiped off the city's plans.

Without the highway hanging over it, the neighborhood could finally plan a future. The city legalized artists' lofts in 1971, and in 1973 the cast iron district was protected. If Moses had won, you might be standing beside a wall of concrete pillars, in the roar of trucks. Instead you're on one of the most beautiful streets in America.

deeper.title: Hell's Hundred Acres
deeper.text:
You heard that firefighters called this district Hell's Hundred Acres. Here's why, and how that reputation nearly doomed it.

The cast iron fronts made the buildings look solid, but behind them most had wooden floors and joists, and they were packed with bales of cloth, paper and rags. When a fire took hold, iron columns could crack when cold water from the hoses hit them, and whole fronts could come down. Firefighters learned to keep their distance.

The deadliest fire came on March 19th, 1958, at 623 Broadway, a few blocks east of here. Flames trapped workers at the Monarch Underwear Company on the upper floors. The building had no sprinklers, and twenty four people died, a short walk from the site of the Triangle Shirtwaist fire, nearly half a century later. Mayor Robert Wagner called for laws requiring sprinklers in loft buildings, and the city tightened its rules.

Fires like that gave the district's critics ammunition. In 1962, a civic group, the City Club of New York, published a report called The Wastelands of New York City, which described this area as a commercial slum, ready to be cleared. But when the city asked a planner named Chester Rapkin to study the district, he found something else: hundreds of small businesses employing thousands of workers, in jobs that depended on cheap space near the center of the city. His 1963 report helped make the case against tearing it all down. Rapkin is also credited with the district's nickname: SoHo, for South of Houston.

So the district survived its reputation. Today almost every building on this street has sprinklers and fire escapes, and the hundred acres are among the most valuable in the world.

deeper.title: Look Closer: Reading a Cast Iron Street
deeper.text:
Stand on Greene Street and look for the details most shoppers walk right past.

Start at your feet. The street is paved with Belgian blocks, rectangular granite paving stones laid to stand up to iron wagon wheels and heavy loads. People call them cobblestones, but true cobblestones are rounded stones from riverbeds.

Look at the vault lights in the sidewalk, the small round glass lenses set in iron plates. Many have turned a pale purple. That's because the glass contained manganese, which slowly turns violet after decades in the sun.

Now look at the bottoms of the iron columns on the building fronts, just above the sidewalk. Many carry small raised plates with the names and addresses of the foundries that cast them, names like Cornell, or Badger's Architectural Iron Works, cast right into the building like a signature.

Then walk to the corner of Prince Street and look at the wall of 112 Prince Street that faces Greene Street. Count its windows, columns and cornices. Almost all of them are paint. In the mid 1970s, the artist Richard Haas painted that blank brick wall to match the building's real cast iron front around the corner, with more than fifty painted windows. Look for the painted cat in one of them. The architecture critic Ada Louise Huxtable called the mural a triumph. It was Haas's first outdoor mural, and after four decades of weather it was carefully repainted, and rededicated in 2024.

That wall sums up SoHo: artists making something beautiful out of a blank industrial wall, in tribute to the buildings they had come to love.

stops.title: The Haughwout Building & the First Passenger Elevator
stops.text:
At the corner of Broadway and Broome Street stands one of the most important commercial buildings in American history: the Haughwout Building, completed in 1857.

Look at the facade. It's a cast iron recreation of a Venetian palace, inspired by the Sansovino Library in Venice, with rows of arched windows framed by columns, repeated over five stories. The rhythm is hypnotic, and it's one of the purest expressions of the cast iron style.

The building was built for E. V. Haughwout and Company, a retailer of fine china, glassware, silver, and chandeliers. It was a luxury store, comparable to Tiffany and Company, which was located nearby on Broadway at the time. Haughwout's customers reportedly included the White House: the company is said to have supplied china for Mary Todd Lincoln.

But the building's real claim to fame is inside. In 1857, it became the first commercial building in the world to install a passenger elevator, built by Elisha Graves Otis. A few years earlier, at the 1854 Crystal Palace exhibition in New York, Otis had staged a dramatic demonstration. He rode a platform high into the air and then had the rope holding it cut. Instead of plunging, the platform stopped, held by his safety brake, a spring-loaded mechanism that locked into the guide rails if the cable failed. All safe, gentlemen, he reportedly announced.

The problem with early elevators wasn't lifting; it was falling. Otis solved the problem of trust. Without the safety elevator, the skyscraper would have been impossible, because no one would rent an office on the twentieth floor if they had to climb twenty flights of stairs, or if they feared riding up a rope. The Haughwout elevator, powered by a steam engine in the basement, was the first step toward the vertical city.

The company Otis founded, the Otis Elevator Company, became the largest elevator maker in the world, and still is one of the leaders. You've probably ridden in one of its elevators today. Look for the name on the inspection plate the next time you step into an elevator in an office building.

Broadway itself, through SoHo, was once a premier shopping street of the city, before the retail center migrated north to Ladies' Mile and later to Fifth Avenue. In a way, the boutiques here now have returned the street to what it was in the 1850s.

deeper.title: Elisha Otis, the Man Who Made Falling Safe
deeper.text:
The man who made skyscrapers possible was a tinkerer who never lived to see one.

Elisha Graves Otis was born on a farm in Vermont in 1811 and drifted through many trades: wagon driver, mill builder, wagon and carriage maker, and inventor of small machines. In 1852 he was working as a master mechanic at a bedstead factory in Yonkers, just north of the city, when he had to work out how to move heavy equipment to the upper floors. Hoisting platforms were common, but workers feared them, because when the rope broke, the platform and everything on it fell.

His answer was simple and brilliant. He fixed a wagon spring to the top of the platform, attached to the hoisting rope. As long as the rope pulled taut, the spring stayed bent. If the rope snapped, the spring straightened and pushed two catches outward into toothed rails on either side of the shaft, locking the platform in place. He started a small business making safety hoists, and in 1854 he took one to the Crystal Palace exhibition, on the site of today's Bryant Park, for the famous demonstration you heard about.

Otis died in 1861, at forty nine, only four years after the Haughwout elevator went in. His sons, Charles and Norton, built up the company. Otis elevators went into hotels, stores and office towers across the country. In 1889 the company built elevators that climb the curving legs of the Eiffel Tower, and in the twentieth century, Otis elevators carried people up the Empire State Building and the original World Trade Center.

The safety elevator changed how buildings were valued, too. Before elevators, the best rooms were on the lower floors, and the top floors went to servants and the poor, who had to climb. After elevators, the top floors became the most desirable of all. The penthouse is, in a sense, an Otis invention.

deeper.title: Broadway's Marble and Iron Palaces
deeper.text:
In the 1850s, this stretch of Broadway was the most fashionable shopping street in America, and the stores along it helped invent the way we still shop.

It began a little south of here, at Broadway and Chambers Street, where an Irish immigrant named Alexander Turney Stewart opened his Marble Palace in 1846: a huge store faced in white marble, often called the first department store in America. Stewart sold an enormous range of goods under one roof, at fixed prices, with no haggling, behind big plate glass windows. It was a place where respectable women could spend a day shopping on their own. Stewart became one of the richest men in the country.

Rivals soon lined Broadway north into SoHo. Lord and Taylor and Brooks Brothers both had stores at Broadway and Grand Street, a block south of here. Tiffany and Company was a couple of blocks north, at 550 Broadway, with a carved wooden figure of Atlas holding up a clock over its entrance. That Atlas clock moved uptown with the company, and it still stands over the door of its flagship on Fifth Avenue.

Just across Broadway and up the block stood the St. Nicholas Hotel, opened in 1853, one of the most luxurious hotels in the world, with hundreds of rooms and marble and gilding everywhere.

And Haughwout's sold fine china, silver and glass. In May 1861, the new first lady, Mary Todd Lincoln, came to New York on a shopping trip to refurnish the White House, and ordered a state dinner service of French porcelain, decorated by Haughwout's with a wide border in a fashionable purplish pink called solferino, around the arms of the United States. Pieces of it survive in the White House collection and in museums.

The shopping district kept moving north. By the 1870s, the big stores had moved up to Ladies' Mile, near Union Square, and SoHo became a district of wholesalers and warehouses. It took a century for the shoppers to come back.

deeper.title: Look Closer: A Venetian Palace in Iron
deeper.text:
Stand across Broadway from the Haughwout Building and give it a slow look. It repays the time.

The architect was John Gaynor, and most historians credit the iron to Daniel Badger's Architectural Iron Works. Notice how one unit, an arched window framed by small columns and set between larger columns, repeats across the Broadway front and down the long Broome Street side, dozens of times, floor after floor. That repetition was the whole point of cast iron. Once the molds were made, every additional window was cheap.

In Venice, the library it imitates was carved from stone. Here, the iron was painted to look like stone, so that shoppers would see a palace, not a factory product.

Now find the big clock on the Broadway side. Stores of the time liked to put clocks on their buildings, as a public service and an advertisement at once. Look closely at how it writes the number four. Most clocks with Roman numerals use four strokes, I I I I. This one uses the proper Roman form, I V.

Then look at the windows themselves. The iron could carry the building's weight on slender supports, so most of the front is glass, letting daylight deep inside. That mattered in a store whose customers were examining fine china and crystal, decades before electric light.

The building had a hard twentieth century. The store moved out, the iron rusted, and some of the ornament was lost. It was one of the first buildings the city protected under its new landmarks law, in 1965, and in the early 1990s, its iron fronts were carefully restored.

And remember what's inside: the place where the first safe passenger elevator went into service, in 1857, the first step toward the skyscrapers uptown.

stops.title: The Little Singer Building & SoHo's Galleries
stops.text:
On Broadway, just north of Prince Street, look for the building at 561 Broadway with an unusual facade: a delicate lattice of green-painted iron, terracotta, and huge sheets of glass, with ornamental balconies. This is the Little Singer Building, completed in 1904 and designed by Ernest Flagg.

It was built for the Singer Manufacturing Company, the maker of the famous sewing machine. Singer is one of the great stories in American business history. Isaac Merritt Singer, a colorful inventor and actor with a complicated personal life, patented improvements to the sewing machine in the 1850s. But his business partner, Edward Clark, a lawyer, came up with the innovations that made the company a giant: installment payments, which allowed families to buy an expensive machine a little at a time, and a direct sales force. Singer became one of the first truly multinational American companies, with factories and salesmen around the world. It also helped transform the garment industry, making mass production of clothing possible, including in the sweatshops of the Lower East Side.

Flagg's design here was strikingly modern: the facade is mostly glass, with a thin metal framework, anticipating the glass curtain walls of twentieth century skyscrapers. A few years later, Flagg designed the much taller Singer Tower downtown, which in 1908 was briefly the tallest building in the world. Tragically, that tower was demolished in 1968, among the tallest buildings ever deliberately demolished at the time.

Look around you now at SoHo's streets: Prince, Spring, Mercer, Wooster, West Broadway. In the 1970s and 80s, this was the center of the art world. The dealer Leo Castelli, who championed artists like Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg, Roy Lichtenstein, and Andy Warhol, opened a gallery at 420 West Broadway in 1971, and dozens of galleries followed. Artists like Donald Judd bought entire buildings here. Judd's home and studio, at 101 Spring Street, a cast iron building he bought in 1968, is preserved as a museum.

In 1977, a gourmet food store called Dean and DeLuca opened on Prince Street, introducing many Americans to imported cheeses, olive oils, and specialty foods. The store became an emblem of the neighborhood's transformation. By the 1990s and 2000s, most of the galleries had moved to Chelsea, driven out by rising rents, and SoHo became a high end shopping district. Apple opened its first New York store in a former post office on Prince Street in 2002.

Before you leave, look up at the cornices, columns, and window frames above the shop signs. The ground floors have changed many times, but the iron facades above have watched over all of it: textile merchants, firefighters, artists, collectors, and shoppers.

deeper.title: Isaac Singer's Complicated Life
deeper.text:
The Singer sewing machine was a model of reliability. The life of the man behind it was anything but.

Isaac Merritt Singer was born in upstate New York in 1811, left home as a boy, and spent years as a touring actor and a part-time machinist. In 1850, in a Boston machine shop, he was asked to look at a sewing machine that didn't work well. In about eleven days, he redesigned it, with a needle that moved straight up and down, an arm that held the needle over the cloth, and a foot to hold the fabric in place. He patented it in 1851.

The sewing machine business quickly became a war of patents, with Singer, Elias Howe and others suing each other. In 1856, they settled it in a new way: they pooled their patents and shared the fees, so that all of them could keep making machines. It's often called the first patent pool in American business.

Singer's private life was a scandal even by the standards of the time. He kept several families at once, with different women, sometimes under different names, and fathered about two dozen children. When the scandals became public, his partner Edward Clark, a proper lawyer, insisted that Singer step back from the company, and Singer moved to Europe. He built a mansion in Paignton, on the English coast, and died there in 1875, very rich.

Now a legend. Singer's young widow, Isabella Boyer, a striking Frenchwoman, is often said to have been the model for the face of the Statue of Liberty. The sculptor, Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, never said who posed for it, and many historians think the face is closer to his own mother, Charlotte. So the Isabella story is a nice one, but unproven.

deeper.title: The Galleries and the Earth Room
deeper.text:
SoHo's great gallery era is mostly over, but two works of art from it are still here, and they're among the strangest and most wonderful things in New York.

The first gallery in SoHo was Paula Cooper's, which opened on Prince Street in 1968 with an exhibition that raised money for the movement against the Vietnam War. Leo Castelli followed in 1971, as you heard, and through the 1970s and 1980s, SoHo was where artists showed new work, from minimalism and conceptual art to the big paintings of the 1980s boom. On Saturday afternoons, West Broadway was crowded with collectors.

Now the survivors. At 141 Wooster Street, a short walk from here, climb to the second floor and look through the doorway at the New York Earth Room, a work by the artist Walter De Maria, installed in 1977. It's a large loft filled with dirt, twenty two inches deep, about two hundred fifty cubic yards of earth, and nothing else. The room smells like a forest after rain. The Dia Art Foundation has kept it for decades, raking and watering it, and lets visitors see it for free for much of the year.

At 393 West Broadway, you can see another De Maria work, The Broken Kilometer, from 1979: five hundred polished brass rods, laid in five rows across a gallery floor, which together would stretch for one kilometer.

There's something perfect about these works surviving in SoHo. They take up a great deal of very expensive space and do nothing but sit there, being beautiful. In one of the most valuable neighborhoods in the world, a room full of dirt is the ultimate luxury.

deeper.title: Ernest Flagg's Glass Front
deeper.text:
The Little Singer Building looks decades ahead of its time, and its architect, Ernest Flagg, was a man of strong ideas.

Flagg trained in Paris at the École des Beaux-Arts, the great school of classical architecture, and designed grand buildings in that style, like the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington and much of the Naval Academy in Annapolis. His brother-in-law was the publisher Charles Scribner, and Flagg designed the Scribner company's buildings on Fifth Avenue. But he was an engineer at heart, interested in fireproofing, ventilation and how to make cities healthier.

The Little Singer Building shows the engineer. Its front is a light frame of iron and steel, painted green, filled with sheets of glass, with delicate balconies and panels of terracotta. Instead of hiding the frame behind stone, Flagg made it the design.

He also thought about the city as a whole. As skyscrapers rose, he worried they were turning streets into dark canyons. He proposed that tall buildings be allowed to rise without limit only if their towers covered a small part of their lots, leaving light and air around them. His slender Singer Tower downtown, finished in 1908, was meant to show how. The city's first zoning law, in 1916, adopted a version of the idea, letting towers rise without limit over a quarter of the lot, and that rule helped shape the tower-topped skyscrapers of the 1920s and 1930s.

Flagg also designed small, fireproof stone houses for ordinary families, and built himself an estate on Todt Hill, on Staten Island. He died in 1947. Twenty one years later, his Singer Tower was torn down, and he was spared the sight.

overview:
This walk covers three neighborhoods that share one big story: how industrial Manhattan became residential Manhattan.

For most of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the area west of Broadway and south of Houston Street was a working landscape. Along the Hudson River were piers, freight rail yards, and warehouses. Tribeca was the center of the city's wholesale food trade, with butter, eggs, cheese, and produce moving through enormous markets. SoHo was a district of textile and dry goods warehouses and small factories, housed in some of the most beautiful commercial buildings ever built in America, with facades made of cast iron. Hudson Square, just to the north and west, was the city's printing district, filled with presses that produced everything from magazines to phone books.

After World War Two, that economy faded. Container shipping moved the port to New Jersey. Manufacturing left the city. Trucks replaced freight trains. Buildings emptied out. City planners in the 1950s and 60s viewed much of SoHo as a slum of decaying industrial buildings, and Robert Moses planned to run an elevated expressway right through it, along Broome Street, connecting the Holland Tunnel with the Manhattan and Williamsburg Bridges.

Artists saved it. They had discovered that these empty factory floors, with high ceilings, big windows, and cheap rents, made ideal studios. They moved in, often illegally, since the buildings weren't zoned for residential use. Together with preservationists and activists like Jane Jacobs, they helped defeat the Lower Manhattan Expressway in the 1960s. In 1971, the city legalized artists living in lofts, and in 1973, SoHo's cast iron buildings were protected as a historic district. Galleries followed the artists. Then boutiques followed the galleries. Then the bankers, celebrities, and luxury brands followed the boutiques. The artists who saved SoHo were mostly priced out of it, a cycle so familiar that urbanists sometimes call it the SoHo effect.

Tribeca went through a similar transformation a little later, and the name itself, short for Triangle Below Canal Street, was coined in the 1970s. Hudson Square is in the middle of its own reinvention, as media and tech companies, including Google and Disney, have built major offices in its old industrial buildings.

As you walk, look for things that reveal the old industrial life: loading docks raised to the height of a truck bed, metal canopies over sidewalks where goods were unloaded, old painted signs on brick walls, and the glass-studded vault lights set into the sidewalks, which let daylight into basements below.

title: Greenwich Village
blurb: Washington Square, the Triangle fire, the folk revival, Stonewall, Jane Jacobs, and the original Bell Labs.

stops.title: Washington Square Park & the Arch
stops.text:
You're in Washington Square Park, the heart of Greenwich Village.

This land has a grim past. From 1797 to 1825, it served as a potter's field, a burial ground for the poor, the unknown, and victims of yellow fever. Archaeologists estimate that thousands of people may still be buried beneath the park, and bones are occasionally unearthed during construction work. Public executions were also held in the area, and a large old English elm in the northwest corner is called the Hangman's Elm, though historians doubt anyone was actually hanged from it.

In 1826, the city converted the field into a parade ground and later a public park, and wealthy families built elegant homes around it. Look at the north side of the park, along Washington Square North. The row of red brick Greek Revival townhouses, built in the 1830s, is known as The Row. This was old money New York. The novelist Henry James was born nearby, and his 1880 novel Washington Square captured the world of these houses.

Now look at the marble arch at the foot of Fifth Avenue. In 1889, for the centennial of George Washington's inauguration, a temporary wooden arch was built here. It was so popular that the city commissioned a permanent version, designed by Stanford White, of the firm McKim, Mead and White, and completed in 1892. It's modeled on the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. Two statues of Washington, as general and as president, were added to the north face in the following decades. In 1917, a group of artists, including Marcel Duchamp, climbed to the top of the arch through an internal stairway and declared the Free and Independent Republic of Washington Square, a classic Village prank.

The park was also the site of a major battle over the future of cities. For years, Fifth Avenue traffic ran right through the park, under the arch. In the 1950s, Robert Moses proposed extending Fifth Avenue as a sunken highway through the center of the park. Local mothers, led by Shirley Hayes and joined by Jane Jacobs, organized a campaign against it. Not only did they win, but by the early 1960s, traffic was banned from the park entirely. It was one of the first major defeats of Moses's highway plans.

The park has long been a stage for music and protest. In 1961, when the city tried to ban folk singing in the park, hundreds of musicians and fans gathered in defiance, a confrontation sometimes called the Beatnik Riot. The city backed down. Today, the fountain area is still filled with musicians, performers, chess players, and students from New York University, which surrounds the park and owns many of the buildings around it.

deeper.title: The Arch, Up Close
deeper.text:
Walk over to the arch and look closely. You heard that the marble arch replaced a much loved wooden one. Its cornerstone was laid in 1890, and it was formally dedicated in 1895.

Look up at the winged figures carved into the spaces above the curve of the arch. They're by the sculptor Frederick MacMonnies. Then look along the top for an inscription, words attributed to Washington: Let us raise a standard to which the wise and the honest can repair. The event is in the hand of God.

Now walk around to the north side, the side facing Fifth Avenue, to see the two statues of Washington. As you face the arch from Fifth Avenue, on the left, on the eastern pier, is Washington as commander in chief, by Hermon MacNeil, from 1916, with figures of Fame and Valor at his back. On the right is Washington as president, from 1918, with figures of Wisdom and Justice, by Alexander Stirling Calder. New Yorkers often call them Washington at War and Washington at Peace.

That second sculptor comes from a remarkable family. His father, Alexander Milne Calder, made the giant statue of William Penn on top of Philadelphia's City Hall. His son, Alexander Calder, became one of the most famous artists of the twentieth century, known for his hanging mobiles. Three generations of sculptors, and the middle one is right here.

Notice, too, how late the statues came. Stanford White's plans had called for sculpture on the piers, but for about twenty years after the dedication the piers stood bare, until these two groups were finally carved.

Finally, go back into the park, stand south of the arch, and look north through it. The arch frames the start of Fifth Avenue, for generations the city's grandest street, so that the avenue begins with a ceremonial gateway at the edge of a village.

deeper.title: The Hangman's Elm and the Potter's Field
deeper.text:
You heard that historians doubt anyone was hanged from the old elm in the northwest corner of the park. Walk over and look at it anyway. It's an English elm, and the city's parks department estimates it's more than three hundred years old, which would make it one of the oldest trees in Manhattan.

The stories attached to it come in several versions. In one, traitors were hanged from its branches during the Revolution. In another, it served as the gallows when this was a potter's field. The trouble is the map. Until 1827, the ground where the tree stands was private farmland, outside the burial ground, and the city added it to the square only after the cemetery had closed. No record shows anyone hanged from it.

There was, though, an execution in the potter's field itself, and it's well documented. Rose Butler, an enslaved teenager, was convicted of setting a fire in the house of the family who held her. The fire did little damage and hurt no one, but she was sentenced to death, and the courts upheld the sentence. She was hanged on a gallows built in the field, in front of a huge crowd, and buried in the ground nearby. Her story is far less famous than the tree's, and far more certain.

The burial ground itself is no legend either. Some estimates put the number of people buried here as high as twenty thousand. When workers dug the foundation for the arch's eastern pier in 1890, about ten feet down they found human bones, a coffin, and a gravestone dated 1803.

So if you sit on a bench here, you may be sitting above some of those forgotten New Yorkers, near a tree that is famous for something it almost certainly never did.

deeper.title: Painters on the Square
deeper.text:
For more than half a century, one of America's greatest painters climbed four flights of stairs on the north side of this square to get to work.

Edward Hopper moved into the top floor of number 3, Washington Square North, in 1913, and lived and painted there until his death in 1967. His wife, the painter Josephine Nivison Hopper, joined him after they married in 1924. The building was a walk-up heated with coal, and the coal had to be hauled up four flights of stairs. Hopper painted the city as a place of quiet and solitude: empty streets in early morning light, lit windows at night, people alone in rooms. You can feel this neighborhood in much of it.

Hopper's first one-man show opened in January 1920 at the Whitney Studio Club, a block from the square on West Fourth Street. It sold nothing. The club was founded by the sculptor and heiress Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney, who bought and showed the work of living American artists when most museums wouldn't. In 1931 she opened the Whitney Museum of American Art in a row of houses on West Eighth Street, a block north of the square. The museum later moved uptown, and now stands at the foot of the High Line, but its first home is still there, now an art school, the New York Studio School. And the Whitney today holds the largest collection of Hopper's work anywhere.

Hopper was far from the first artist drawn here. In 1857, a few blocks north on West Tenth Street, the architect Richard Morris Hunt built the Tenth Street Studio Building, one of the first buildings in America designed especially for artists. Winslow Homer, Frederic Church and John La Farge all worked there. It was torn down in 1956.

So when you look at the dignified houses of the Row, imagine a tall, silent painter climbing the stairs with a load of coal, to a room where he painted the loneliness of the modern city.

stops.title: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory
stops.text:
At the corner of Washington Place and Greene Street, look at the ten-story building, now owned by New York University and known as the Brown Building. On the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors of this building was the Triangle Waist Company, a factory that made women's blouses, called shirtwaists.

On the afternoon of Saturday, March twenty-fifth, 1911, near closing time, a fire broke out on the eighth floor, probably from a discarded cigarette or match in a bin of fabric scraps. The fire spread with terrifying speed through piles of cotton and tissue paper. Workers on the eighth floor escaped. Workers on the tenth floor, including the owners, escaped to the roof. But on the ninth floor, the workers were trapped. One exit door was locked, reportedly to prevent theft and unauthorized breaks. The single flimsy fire escape collapsed under the weight of people trying to flee. The fire department's ladders only reached the sixth or seventh floor.

Crowds on the street watched as workers, many of them young Jewish and Italian immigrant women, some in their teens, jumped from the windows to escape the flames. In less than half an hour, one hundred forty six people died.

The owners, Max Blanck and Isaac Harris, were tried for manslaughter and acquitted. But the fire galvanized the city. Huge crowds marched in a funeral procession through the streets. The state created a Factory Investigating Commission, led by state legislators Robert Wagner and Al Smith, which pushed through dozens of new laws on fire safety, sprinklers, working hours, and factory conditions.

One eyewitness was a young social reformer named Frances Perkins, who happened to be having tea nearby and ran to the scene. She later said the New Deal began on that day. Perkins went on to become Franklin Roosevelt's Secretary of Labor, the first woman to serve in a presidential cabinet, and was a driving force behind Social Security, the minimum wage, and limits on working hours.

Look at the building's corner. You may see a series of small plaques, and on the anniversary each year, people gather here and chalk the names of the victims on the sidewalk. A permanent memorial was installed on the building in 2023, with ribbons of steel bearing the victims' names.

deeper.title: The Shirtwaist Kings
deeper.text:
You heard that the owners, Max Blanck and Isaac Harris, were tried and acquitted. In the trade they were known as the Shirtwaist Kings, and their story shows how the garment business worked.

The shirtwaist was the fashion of the age: a tailored blouse worn with a long skirt, made popular around 1900 by the confident Gibson Girl of magazine illustrations. Millions were sold, and New York was the center of the trade. Blanck and Harris were immigrants who had started small and built Triangle into one of the biggest blouse makers in the city, with hundreds of workers.

In 1909, Triangle was one of the shops where the great shirtwaist strike began, the walkout that grew into the Uprising of the Twenty Thousand. Many shops settled and recognized the union. Triangle's owners never did.

At the manslaughter trial, their lawyer, Max Steuer, one of the best trial lawyers in the city, had a key survivor, Kate Alterman, repeat her vivid testimony again and again, then suggested to the jury that her words sounded rehearsed. The jury acquitted both men in less than two hours.

The civil cases ended even worse for the families. In 1914, twenty three lawsuits brought by victims' families were settled for seventy five dollars per life lost. Meanwhile, the owners' insurance had paid them about sixty thousand dollars more than their reported losses, roughly four hundred dollars for every worker who died.

And in 1913, Max Blanck was in court again, this time for locking a door during working hours at his new factory. He was fined twenty dollars.

It's a story about two men, but also about a whole system: an industry with almost no rules, laws that barely punished anything, and workers with little power, until the fire changed the politics of the state.

deeper.title: The Elevator Men
deeper.text:
In the chaos of the Triangle fire, two men kept going back into it.

Joseph Zito and Gaspar Mortillalo ran the passenger elevators in the building. When the fire broke out, they began running their small cars up toward the burning floors, cramming in as many workers as they could and bringing them down to the street, again and again, as smoke filled the shafts. Some workers, desperate, jumped down the elevator shaft itself. Finally, the rails of one elevator buckled in the heat, and the cars could no longer climb.

No one knows exactly how many people they saved. Estimates for Zito alone run from about a hundred to a hundred and fifty. Their courage was reported in the newspapers at the time, but their names are far less known than the owners'.

Others helped too. On the tenth floor, where the owners had their offices, people fled up to the roof. In a taller building next door, used by New York University, a law professor and his students found ladders and helped the workers climb from the factory roof up to safety.

And there were the firefighters, who arrived within minutes, and found that the nets they held out could not hold people falling from so high.

When you stand at the corner, look at the building's entrance and imagine those two small cars rising into the smoke. The names on the memorial are the people who were lost. Many of the people who lived owed their lives to two elevator men who wouldn't stop.

deeper.title: Naming the Dead
deeper.text:
In the hours after the fire, the bodies were carried to a pier on the East River at Twenty Sixth Street, where a temporary morgue was set up, and laid out in rows of coffins. Through the night and the days that followed, long lines of people filed past, searching for daughters, sisters, sons and friends. Some victims could be recognized only by a ring, a shoe, or a detail of their clothing. The youngest of the dead were fourteen years old.

A handful of bodies could not be identified at all. On April 5th, 1911, unions and community groups organized a funeral procession for them, and in a cold, driving rain, hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers turned out, marching or standing silently along the route. The unidentified victims were buried together at the Evergreens Cemetery in Brooklyn.

For nearly a century, six of them stayed nameless. Then a researcher named Michael Hirsch spent years combing through old newspapers, records and family histories, and in 2011, just before the hundredth anniversary of the fire, he announced their names: Max Florin, Fannie Rosen, Dora Evans, Josephine Cammarata, Maria Lauletti and Concetta Prestifilippo. A new marker with their names was unveiled at the cemetery on April 5th, 2011, a hundred years to the day after the march in the rain.

Today every one of the hundred and forty six has a name. You heard that people chalk those names on the sidewalk here each year. A project called Chalk also sends volunteers to the sidewalks in front of the buildings where the victims lived, scattered across the city, so that each name returns, for a day, to the place that person called home.

So the memorial on this corner isn't only about how they died. It's also about a long, stubborn effort, lasting a century, to remember exactly who they were.

stops.title: MacDougal Street & the Folk Revival
stops.text:
You're on MacDougal Street, just south of Washington Square, the center of Village bohemia for over a century.

In 1916, a group of writers and artists moved their small theater company from Cape Cod to MacDougal Street and became the Provincetown Players. Their most important discovery was a young playwright named Eugene O'Neill, whose early plays were first performed here. The Provincetown Playhouse building still stands on MacDougal, south of the park, though it's been rebuilt by NYU.

On the corner of MacDougal and Minetta Lane, look for Minetta Tavern, which opened in 1937 and was a hangout for writers like Ernest Hemingway, E. E. Cummings, and Ezra Pound, at least according to legend. Nearby, Caffe Reggio, open since 1927, claims to have introduced the cappuccino to America, and its antique espresso machine is on display. Minetta Lane follows the curve of the buried Minetta Brook, which still flows underground.

In the 1950s and 60s, the coffeehouses of MacDougal and Bleecker Streets became the stage for the folk revival. Places like the Gaslight Cafe, the Café Wha?, and, a few blocks away on West Fourth Street, Gerde's Folk City, hosted open mic nights where young musicians performed for tips, often passing a basket. A nineteen-year-old from Minnesota named Bob Dylan arrived in the winter of 1961 and began playing at Café Wha?. Within a year, after a glowing review in the New York Times of a show at Gerde's, he had a record contract. Others who played these clubs included Joan Baez, Dave Van Ronk, Phil Ochs, Peter, Paul and Mary, and Simon and Garfunkel. The Café Wha? also gave an early stage to a guitarist then calling himself Jimmy James, who soon became known as Jimi Hendrix.

The Beat writers were here too, in the 1950s. Jack Kerouac, Allen Ginsberg, and Gregory Corso read poetry at coffeehouses and drank at bars like the San Remo, which stood at the corner of MacDougal and Bleecker.

Comedy has its own history on these blocks. Comedians like Woody Allen, Bill Cosby, and Richard Pryor performed in Village clubs in the 1960s, and the Comedy Cellar, on MacDougal, opened in 1982 and is still among the most famous comedy clubs in the country. Big name comedians often drop in unannounced late at night.

deeper.title: Dave Van Ronk, the Mayor of MacDougal Street
deeper.text:
If the folk revival had a center of gravity on these blocks, it was a big, bearded, gravel-voiced singer named Dave Van Ronk.

Van Ronk grew up in Brooklyn and Queens, played in traditional jazz bands, shipped out as a merchant seaman, and by the late 1950s was singing old blues and folk songs in the coffeehouses here. He was a teacher as much as a performer. Younger musicians came to him to learn guitar parts and old songs, and to argue about music and politics. When Bob Dylan arrived in 1961, Van Ronk took him under his wing, let him sleep on his couch, and helped him get work at the Gaslight. Dylan later called him the king of the street.

Van Ronk told one story about their friendship many times. He had worked out his own arrangement of an old song, The House of the Rising Sun, and planned to record it. Dylan learned it and put it on his own first album before Van Ronk got the chance. Then, in 1964, a British band, the Animals, had a worldwide hit with a version that followed the same arrangement, and Dylan stopped playing the song, because audiences assumed he was copying the Animals. Van Ronk loved telling that story.

Van Ronk never became a star, and he didn't seem to mind. He kept playing the Village for decades, until his death in 2002. His memoir, The Mayor of MacDougal Street, was finished after his death by the writer Elijah Wald, and it inspired the Coen brothers' 2013 film, Inside Llewyn Davis, set in the Village folk world of the early 1960s.

In 2004, the city named a corner of Sheridan Square, where Barrow Street meets Washington Place, Dave Van Ronk Street. If you're heading west toward Christopher Street, look for the sign.

deeper.title: Little Africa
deeper.text:
Before this was an Italian neighborhood, and long before it was a bohemian one, the streets around Minetta Lane were a center of Black New York.

The roots go back to the 1600s, when the Dutch granted farmland in this area to formerly enslaved Africans. Later, the path along Minetta Brook was known as the Negroes' Causeway.

In the nineteenth century, after slavery finally ended in New York State in 1827, a Black community grew up here, on Minetta Lane and Minetta Street, and along Bleecker, Thompson and Sullivan Streets. It was crowded and poor, but it was a real community, home to waiters, laborers, laundresses, sailors and musicians. New Yorkers called it Little Africa. In 1890, the reformer Jacob Riis described it in his book How the Other Half Lives, mostly as a slum, with the condescension of his time.

The community was pushed and pulled away. After the Draft Riots of 1863, when white mobs attacked Black New Yorkers across the city, many families left Manhattan. Later, rising rents and new waves of immigrants pressed on those who stayed. By the turn of the century, Black New Yorkers were moving north, first to the Tenderloin, in the West Twenties and Thirties, and to San Juan Hill, near today's Lincoln Center, and then to Harlem. Italian immigrants filled the tenements they left behind, and within a generation, Little Africa was almost forgotten.

There's little to mark it now. But as you walk along Minetta Lane, remember that the Village's long history of outsiders making a home here didn't begin with the bohemians. It began with people who had far fewer choices about where they could live.

deeper.title: Bleecker Street's Italian Village
deeper.text:
Walk a block or two south and west of here, onto Bleecker Street, and you'll find what remains of the South Village's Italian past, much of it in the form of food.

By 1900, the blocks south of Washington Square had become one of the largest Italian neighborhoods in the city. Life centered on the church of Our Lady of Pompeii, on Carmine Street, whose parish was founded in 1892 to serve Italian immigrants. Its pastor for more than three decades, Father Antonio Demo, helped newcomers find their footing in a new country, and the little square beside the church, where Bleecker, Carmine and Sixth Avenue meet, is named Father Demo Square.

The food shops followed the people. Along Bleecker Street, you can still find a pork store, Faicco's, that has been making sausage for more than a century, and a cheese shop, Murray's, open since 1940 and now known across the country. Bakeries sell cannoli and pignoli cookies, and pizza by the slice gets folded and eaten on the sidewalk.

The Italian cafés on these streets were serving espresso long before the Beat poets and folk singers made coffeehouses the center of Village life. When the folk clubs of the 1960s needed cheap basements and storefronts, many of them found space in these Italian blocks, and the landlords, the neighbors and the musicians didn't always get along. Some older residents complained about the noise and the crowds, and those complaints were part of the background to the 1961 fight over folk singing in Washington Square.

Today the Italian population has thinned, and many of the old social clubs are gone. But stop in for a sandwich or a pastry, and you're tasting the neighborhood that sat between Little Africa and the folk revival, and outlasted both.

stops.title: Jefferson Market Library & Patchin Place
stops.text:
At the corner of Sixth Avenue and West 10th Street, look up at the fairy tale building with a tall clock tower, pointed arches, and colorful bands of brick and stone. This is the Jefferson Market Library, a branch of the New York Public Library. But it wasn't built as a library.

Completed in 1877, it was a courthouse, the Third Judicial District Courthouse, designed by Frederick Clarke Withers and Calvert Vaux, who also co-designed Central Park. Its style is Victorian Gothic, inspired by the writings of the English critic John Ruskin, who championed colorful, richly decorated medieval architecture. In an 1880s poll of architects, it was voted one of the most beautiful buildings in America. The tower housed a fire lookout and bell. The court handled the petty crimes of the neighborhood: drunkenness, prostitution, and street disputes.

After the courts moved out in the 1940s, the building sat empty and was slated for demolition. In the late 1950s and early 60s, neighborhood residents, including the poet E. E. Cummings, campaigned to save it, and it was converted into a library, opening in 1967. It was one of the early victories of the preservation movement in New York.

Next door, where the lovely Jefferson Market Garden is now, stood the Women's House of Detention, a massive Art Deco jail that operated from 1932 to 1974. Inmates would shout down to friends and family on the sidewalk, and passersby would shout back. Among the women held there were the political activist Angela Davis and the writer Dorothy Day. It was demolished in 1974, and the community turned the site into a garden.

Across Sixth Avenue, on West 10th Street, look for a small iron gate leading to a little dead-end street of brick houses. That's Patchin Place, built in the 1840s. Its tiny houses became home to an astonishing number of writers. E. E. Cummings lived at number four for about forty years. The novelist Djuna Barnes lived at number five for decades. The journalist John Reed, who wrote Ten Days That Shook the World about the Russian Revolution, also lived here. Around the corner is a similar alley called Milligan Place.

Notice also the old gas lamp at the end of Patchin Place, one of the last gas street lamps in the city, now converted to electricity.

deeper.title: The Committee to Start the Clock
deeper.text:
You heard that neighbors saved this building from demolition. Their campaign began with something small: a clock that didn't work.

By the late 1950s, the clock in the tower had stopped, a sad sign over an empty building. A Village resident named Margot Gayle decided to start there. With a group of neighbors, she formed a committee with a gloriously long name: the Committee of Neighbors to Get the Clock on Jefferson Market Courthouse Started. One Christmas, they sent Mayor Robert Wagner a telegram that played on the song All I Want for Christmas Is My Two Front Teeth. What they wanted was their clock.

It worked. In October 1960, the clock started again. The clock was a symbol, and once the neighbors had won it, they set their sights on the whole building. In 1961, a new group formed, the Committee for a Library in the Courthouse, and it persuaded the city to turn the courthouse into the library you see today.

Margot Gayle went on to become one of the city's great preservationists. She was a leader in the fight to protect SoHo's cast iron buildings, and she founded a group called the Friends of Cast Iron Architecture to champion them, at a time when many people saw those buildings as old factories ready for the wrecking ball.

Her method is worth remembering. Instead of starting with a huge demand, she started with something everyone could agree on, a stopped clock on a neighborhood landmark, and built from there. Each small win made the next, bigger one possible.

Look up at the tower. If the clock is keeping time, it's partly because a neighbor thought a stopped clock was a bad sign for a neighborhood.

deeper.title: The House of D
deeper.text:
The garden next door stands on the site of the Women's House of Detention, which everyone called the House of D. You heard that Angela Davis and Dorothy Day were held there. Many others passed through too.

The jail held women awaiting trial or serving short sentences, and it was famously overcrowded. Ethel Rosenberg was held here after her arrest in 1950, during the espionage case in which she and her husband, Julius, were convicted and later executed. Afeni Shakur, a member of the Black Panther Party, was held here as one of the Panther 21, accused of plotting bombings, and spent part of her time here pregnant with her son, the future rapper Tupac Shakur. She defended herself at trial, and she and her codefendants were acquitted in 1971.

Historians have also recovered another side of the House of D. Many of the women held here were lesbians, or didn't fit the gender rules of their time, and were arrested for it, or for sex work, or simply for being poor. The writer Hugh Ryan, in a history of the jail published in 2022, argues that it was a central place in queer New York, just a few blocks from the Stonewall Inn. The shouted conversations between the windows and the sidewalk that you heard about included lovers, and the street outside became a meeting place in its own right.

Conditions were harsh, and complaints mounted. In 1965, a college student named Andrea Dworkin, arrested at a protest against the Vietnam War, spoke out about brutal treatment by the jail's doctors. Her account made the newspapers and added to the pressure to close the jail, which finally happened in the early 1970s.

Today, roses grow where the jail once stood, in a garden tended by volunteers.

deeper.title: The Market Behind the Name
deeper.text:
Why is a library called Jefferson Market? Because for nearly a century, this block was a market, named for Thomas Jefferson.

In 1833, the city opened a public market here, one of the neighborhood markets where New Yorkers bought meat, fish, vegetables and butter from licensed stall keepers. Over the market rose a tall wooden fire lookout tower with a big bell. Watchmen scanned the rooftops of the growing village, and when they spotted smoke, they rang the bell in patterns that told firefighters which part of town to run to.

One of the butchers who took a stall here when the market opened, Thomas De Voe, stayed for nearly forty years and became the great historian of the city's markets. In 1862 he published The Market Book, a history of New York's public markets, and a few years later The Market Assistant, a guide to every kind of food sold in them, from game birds to oysters. He went on to become the city's superintendent of markets.

In the 1870s, the city replaced the old wooden sheds with a whole civic complex in the same colorful Victorian style: the courthouse you see, a jail behind it, and a new market hall. The courthouse tower took over the old lookout's job. The market carried on into the twentieth century, but neighborhood markets were giving way to grocery stores, and in the late 1920s the market and the old jail were cleared to make way for the Women's House of Detention.

So the name over the library door remembers a place where Villagers once haggled over chickens and cabbages, under a watchtower keeping an eye out for fire.

stops.title: The Stonewall Inn & Christopher Park
stops.text:
You're on Christopher Street, at Christopher Park, a small triangle of green. Across the street is the Stonewall Inn.

In the 1960s, gay life in New York was largely hidden and heavily policed. It was illegal for bars to serve alcohol to people believed to be gay, and police regularly raided gay bars, arresting patrons, especially those who wore clothing that didn't match their perceived gender. Because legitimate businesses avoided serving gay customers, many gay bars were run by the Mafia, which paid off the police. The Stonewall Inn was one of them: a dingy, unlicensed bar with watered-down drinks, but one of the few places where gay men, lesbians, drag queens, and transgender people, many of them young and poor, could dance together.

In the early morning hours of June twenty-eighth, 1969, police raided the Stonewall. This time, the patrons didn't scatter. A crowd gathered outside and began to resist, throwing coins, bottles, and bricks. The police barricaded themselves inside the bar. The confrontations continued for several nights, with crowds of hundreds and then thousands. Among those involved, according to many accounts, were activists including Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera, who became prominent figures in the movement that followed, though the details of who did what on which night are still debated.

The uprising didn't begin the gay rights movement, which had existed in quieter forms for years, but it transformed it into a more militant, visible, mass movement. Within months, new organizations formed. On the first anniversary, in June 1970, activists organized the Christopher Street Liberation Day march, from here to Central Park. That march is considered the first gay pride parade, and pride marches held every June around the world commemorate Stonewall.

In 2016, President Barack Obama designated the Stonewall National Monument, the first national monument dedicated to LGBTQ history. It includes Christopher Park and the surrounding streets.

In the park, look for the white statues by the sculptor George Segal, called Gay Liberation: two standing men and two seated women, cast in bronze and painted white. They were commissioned in 1979 and installed here in 1992 after years of controversy.

Christopher Street itself is one of the Village's oldest streets, named for Charles Christopher Amos, an heir to an eighteenth-century estate. Walk west along it toward the Hudson, and you'll see the shops and bars that made it the main street of gay New York for decades.

deeper.title: The Sip-In at Julius'
deeper.text:
You heard that bars could be punished for serving gay customers. Three years before Stonewall, a few blocks from here, activists challenged that rule with a quieter kind of protest, and it worked.

The State Liquor Authority treated gay customers as a sign of a disorderly bar, so bartenders routinely refused to serve anyone they suspected of being gay. In April 1966, three members of the Mattachine Society, one of the country's early gay rights groups, Dick Leitsch, Craig Rodwell and John Timmons, decided to challenge the rule the way civil rights activists in the South had challenged segregated lunch counters. They called it a sip-in, and they brought reporters.

The men went from bar to bar, announcing that they were homosexual and asking to be served. At Julius', at the corner of West Tenth Street and Waverly Place, the bartender set out glasses, heard their declaration, and put his hand over the top of a glass. A photographer caught the moment, and the picture of that hand became famous.

The protest made the New York Times. The city's Commission on Human Rights said that gay people had the right to be served in bars, and court decisions over the next few years made it harder for the state to punish a bar just because its customers were gay. It didn't end police harassment, as the Stonewall raid would show. But it was an early step toward gay bars that could operate openly and legally.

Julius' is still pouring drinks, and it's one of the oldest gay bars in the city. In 2022, the city made it an official landmark, for what happened at its bar.

Craig Rodwell, one of the three, opened the Oscar Wilde Memorial Bookshop in 1967, one of the first bookstores devoted to gay and lesbian writers. After Stonewall, he helped propose the march you heard about, the one that became the first pride parade.

deeper.title: Who Threw the First Brick?
deeper.text:
Ask who started the Stonewall uprising, and you'll get many answers. You heard that the details are still debated. Here's what the debate is about.

The most famous story says that Marsha P. Johnson, the Black drag queen and activist, threw the first brick, or a shot glass, at the police. But in an interview years later, Johnson herself said that by the time she got there, the uprising had already started. Sylvia Rivera, her friend and fellow activist, also told dramatic stories about that night, but her accounts changed from one telling to the next, and historians still argue about what she saw.

Another account centers on a woman dressed in men's clothes, who fought back as police pushed her toward a patrol wagon, and called out to the crowd to do something. Many people believe that woman was Stormé DeLarverie, a performer who later worked as a bouncer and was known around the Village as a protector of lesbian bars and the women in them. DeLarverie said in interviews that it was her, but it's never been confirmed.

You heard that the crowd threw coins. Many accounts say those coins carried a message: they mocked the payoffs the police took from the bar's owners.

Johnson and Rivera's greatest importance came afterward. In 1970 they founded a group called STAR, Street Transvestite Action Revolutionaries, which sheltered homeless young people, and for decades they fought to keep transgender people, especially transgender people of color, at the center of the movement.

Whoever threw the first brick, the uprising belonged to the whole crowd on the street that night: young, poor, many of them homeless or gender nonconforming, and out of patience.

deeper.title: The Stonewall's Many Lives
deeper.text:
The building across the street has been a pair of stables, a bakery, a restaurant, a Mafia bar, and the heart of a national monument.

It's actually two buildings, numbers 51 and 53 Christopher Street, built in the 1840s as stables. In 1930 they were joined at the ground floor and housed a bakery, and a few years later a restaurant opened here called Bonnie's Stonewall Inn.

By the mid 1960s, the restaurant had closed, and men connected to the Genovese crime family took over the space. In 1967, Tony Lauria, known as Fat Tony, reopened it as a gay bar. You heard it had no liquor license. To get around that, it called itself a private bottle club, and patrons signed a book at the door, often with made-up names. There was no running water behind the bar, so glasses were rinsed in tubs and used again, and the police usually tipped off the owners before a raid.

After the uprising, the bar didn't last long. It closed within months, and for years the space was rented to a string of other businesses, while the uprising itself grew into legend. A new bar took the old name in the 1990s.

Recognition came slowly, then all at once. In 1999, the building and the streets around it were listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and the next year they became a National Historic Landmark. In 2015, the city made the Stonewall Inn an official landmark, the first in New York designated mainly for its place in gay history. The national monument followed the next year.

Look at the front of the building and notice how modest it is: two plain old stables, joined and painted, with a sign over the door. History doesn't always choose grand buildings. Sometimes it chooses the place where people finally refused to leave.

deeper.title: St. Vincent's and the AIDS Years
deeper.text:
A few blocks north of here, at Seventh Avenue and Twelfth Street, stood a hospital that was woven into the life of the Village for a century and a half.

St. Vincent's Hospital was founded in 1849 by the Sisters of Charity, and it cared for the city in some of its worst moments. In 1912, survivors of the Titanic were brought here. On September 11th, 2001, its doctors and nurses lined up stretchers on the sidewalk, waiting for the wounded from the World Trade Center, most of whom never came.

In the 1980s, the hospital was at the center of another crisis. As AIDS spread through the city, and hit gay men in neighborhoods like this one especially hard, St. Vincent's opened what is often described as the first and largest AIDS ward on the East Coast, in 1984. Many of the Village's young men died there. The nurses and doctors who cared for them, at a time when much of the country looked away, are remembered with deep gratitude.

The hospital closed in 2010, deep in debt, and its buildings were turned into apartments. Across the street, on a triangle of land at Seventh Avenue, Twelfth Street and Greenwich Avenue, the New York City AIDS Memorial was dedicated on World AIDS Day, December 1st, 2016. A white steel canopy rises over a fountain, and the granite paving around it is engraved with lines from Walt Whitman's poem Song of Myself, arranged by the artist Jenny Holzer.

If you have a few minutes, walk up and stand under it. It's a quiet place in the middle of a busy intersection, for remembering a generation the Village lost.

stops.title: Bedford Street: Chumley's & the Narrowest House
stops.text:
You're now in the quiet, winding heart of the West Village, around Bedford and Commerce Streets.

At 86 Bedford Street, look for a door with no sign. This is Chumley's, a former speakeasy. Opened by Leland Stanford Chumley in 1922, during Prohibition, it had hidden entrances, trapdoors, and escape routes so patrons could vanish if the police arrived. The bar became a literary hangout: writers including John Steinbeck, William Faulkner, Willa Cather, and John Dos Passos are said to have drunk here, and the walls were lined with book jackets of authors who'd been regulars.

Chumley's is also connected to a well-known piece of slang. To eighty-six something means to get rid of it, or to throw someone out. One popular story claims it comes from this address: when the police were coming, the bartender would shout eighty-six it, telling customers to leave through the Bedford Street door. Etymologists are skeptical, and there are many competing explanations, but it's a good story.

Down the street, at 75 and a half Bedford Street, is a building you might walk right past: a red brick house only about nine and a half feet wide, among the narrowest houses in New York. It was built in 1873 in what had been a carriage alleyway between two houses. The poet Edna St. Vincent Millay, who won the Pulitzer Prize in 1923, lived here in the 1920s. The actor John Barrymore and, according to some accounts, the cartoonist William Steig and the anthropologist Margaret Mead also lived here at various times.

Around the corner, at 38 Commerce Street, the Cherry Lane Theatre, founded in 1924 in a former brewery and box factory, is among the oldest continuously operating Off-Broadway theaters in New York. It has premiered works by playwrights including Samuel Beckett, Edward Albee, and Sam Shepard.

Look around at the old houses, the angled streets, and the trees. This part of the Village feels like it was built for walking, and it was. The street pattern predates the city grid, and it's the reason this neighborhood has stayed so intimate.

deeper.title: Edna St. Vincent Millay
deeper.text:
You heard that the poet Edna St. Vincent Millay lived in the narrowest house on this street. In her day she was one of the most famous poets in America, and a symbol of a new kind of freedom.

Millay grew up poor in Maine, raised by her mother, a nurse, and she became famous young: she was twenty when her long poem Renascence was published, in 1912. She got her unusual middle name from St. Vincent's Hospital in New York, which had saved her uncle's life just before she was born. Her friends called her Vincent.

After college, she moved to Greenwich Village in 1917, acted with the Provincetown Players, and wrote poems that captured the mood of young women in the years after the First World War: independent, witty, and a little reckless. Her most famous lines, from a short poem called First Fig, are about a candle that burns at both ends. It will not last the night, she wrote, but it gives a lovely light.

In 1923, the year of her Pulitzer Prize, she married Eugen Boissevain, a Dutch businessman who was devoted to her career, and the two lived for a time in the tiny house here. In 1924, she joined a group of theater friends in founding the Cherry Lane Theatre, around the corner.

Millay and Boissevain soon moved to a farm in upstate New York called Steepletop, where she lived for the rest of her life. She died there in 1950. But the image of her in this little house, a famous poet in a home barely wider than a hallway, sums up the Village of the 1920s: talented, poor or pretending to be, and determined to live differently.

deeper.title: Look Closer: Bedford and Commerce Streets
deeper.text:
These few blocks hold some of the oddest and oldest houses in Manhattan. Here's what to look for.

Start at 77 Bedford Street, at the corner of Commerce Street, right next to the narrow house, a plain little house with a brick front. It was built in 1799, and it's often called the oldest house in the Village. Its early owners included Harmon Hendricks, a copper merchant who served as Paul Revere's agent in New York. The brick is only skin deep: it was added in 1836 to the older wooden house underneath.

Walk up Bedford to number 102, and you'll see something out of a fairy tale: a half-timbered house with two steep peaks, known as Twin Peaks. It began as a plain house around 1830. In 1925, a designer named Clifford Reed Daily, with money from the banker Otto Kahn, rebuilt it as a whimsical home and studios for artists, a little Alpine fantasy dropped onto a Village street.

Then walk to 39 and 41 Commerce Street, two matching houses with mansard roofs, standing apart with a garden between them. Legend says a sea captain built them for two daughters who couldn't stand each other. It's a good story, with no evidence behind it. They were built in the early 1830s for a milkman, and the mansard roofs were added decades later.

Finally, walk to the corner of Bedford and Grove Streets and look up at the apartment building at number 90. You may recognize it. It's the building shown as the characters' home in the television comedy Friends.

As you go, notice the details that survive on the older houses: low doorways, small windows under the roofline, and iron railings worn smooth by two centuries of hands.

deeper.title: Thomas Paine's Lost Bones
deeper.text:
A short walk from here, at 59 Grove Street, a plaque marks the place where one of the most important writers of the American Revolution died, nearly forgotten.

Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense, published in 1776, persuaded thousands of Americans to support independence. His series The American Crisis, which begins These are the times that try men's souls, was read aloud to Washington's troops. But his later book, The Age of Reason, which attacked organized religion, made him one of the most despised men in America. When he came back from France in 1802, many old friends shunned him.

He spent his last months in Greenwich Village, poor and ill, and died on June 8th, 1809, in a small wooden house where 59 Grove Street now stands. Only a handful of people came to his funeral. The house is long gone. The bar in the building there now is a piano bar called Marie's Crisis, named in honor of his pamphlets.

The Village didn't entirely forget him. A nearby street was named Reason Street, after his book. New Yorkers slurred it into Raisin Street, and it was later renamed Barrow Street.

Now the legend, and it's mostly true. Paine was buried on his farm in New Rochelle, north of the city. In 1819, an English admirer, the radical journalist William Cobbett, dug up the bones and shipped them to England, planning to build a grand memorial. The memorial was never built. After Cobbett died, the bones passed through other hands, and then they vanished. Over the years, people have claimed to own pieces of him, a skull here, a jawbone there, a lock of hair. None of the claims has been proven.

So one of the men who argued America into existence has no known resting place. He has a plaque on a quiet Village street, beside a bar where people gather around the piano and sing show tunes late into the night.

stops.title: Bell Labs at Westbeth
stops.text:
Walk toward the Hudson, to the block bounded by West, Bethune, Washington, and Bank Streets, and you'll find a massive complex of connected industrial buildings. Today it's called Westbeth, the largest artists' housing complex in the world. But for most of the twentieth century, this was the headquarters of the most important industrial research laboratory in history: Bell Telephone Laboratories.

The buildings were originally built for Western Electric, the manufacturing arm of AT&T. Beginning in 1925, when Bell Labs was formally established as AT&T and Western Electric's research division, this complex served as its headquarters. Engineers and scientists here worked on just about everything related to communications, and a remarkable list of breakthroughs came out of this site.

In 1927, AT&T engineers demonstrated long-distance television transmission, sending live images of Herbert Hoover, then Commerce Secretary, from Washington to an audience in New York. Bell Labs and Western Electric developed sound systems for motion pictures, and the technology helped launch the talkies, including the 1927 film The Jazz Singer. Engineers here developed high-fidelity sound recording and improved vacuum tubes. In 1937, a Bell Labs mathematician, George Stibitz, built an early binary adding circuit on his kitchen table, a precursor to digital computing; his later relay computers were built in this era of Bell Labs. And during World War Two, the labs worked on radar and other military technology.

Look closely at the building on the West Street side. An elevated freight railway, what is now the High Line, used to run right through the building. Trains passed through a tunnel in the building's structure.

After World War Two, Bell Labs moved most of its operations to a campus in Murray Hill, New Jersey, where scientists would invent the transistor in 1947, a device that made modern electronics possible. Later came the laser, the solar cell, the UNIX operating system, and the C programming language, along with work that earned several Nobel Prizes. If you work in tech, this is your ancestral home.

In 1970, the buildings were converted into Westbeth, subsidized housing and studios for artists, with support from the J. M. Kaplan Fund and the National Endowment for the Arts. The architect Richard Meier, then early in his career, designed the conversion. Generations of painters, dancers, musicians, and writers have lived here. The choreographer Merce Cunningham's dance company had its studio on the top floor for decades.

It's a very Village kind of story: a building where engineers once invented the future of communication, now filled with people imagining the future of art.

deeper.title: The Call Across the Continent
deeper.text:
Long before Bell Labs got its name, this building was full of engineers working on one enormous problem: how to make a voice travel across a continent.

The building belonged to Western Electric, and in 1907 the engineering staffs of Western Electric and its parent company, AT&T, were brought together here, at what was then 463 West Street. Their task was to stretch the reach of the telephone. Over long distances, the electrical signal of a voice grew weaker and weaker, until nothing was left.

The answer came from a strange new device, the vacuum tube. An inventor named Lee de Forest had built a tube he called the Audion, and AT&T bought the rights to use it. A young physicist here, Harold Arnold, turned it into a reliable amplifier, and engineers placed these amplifiers at stations along the line, boosting the voice as it traveled.

On January 25th, 1915, the transcontinental line opened. In New York, Alexander Graham Bell, the inventor of the telephone, picked up the receiver and repeated the words from his first call, nearly forty years earlier: Mister Watson, come here, I want you. In San Francisco, his old assistant, Thomas Watson, is said to have answered that it would take him five days to get there now.

That October, engineers from this building tried something bolder. From a navy radio station in Arlington, Virginia, they sent a human voice across the Atlantic. Listeners at the Eiffel Tower in Paris heard it, faintly. They had no way to talk back, so they answered by telegraph.

The vacuum tube amplifier became the heart of radio, sound movies and long distance calling for half a century. And when Bell Labs was founded in 1925, it grew out of this same engineering department, in this same building.

deeper.title: Machines That Talk and Listen
deeper.text:
The engineers here were fascinated by sound: how we hear it, how we speak, and how a machine might do both.

In the 1920s, a physicist named Harvey Fletcher led research here into human hearing, measuring how loud sounds seem at different pitches, and working on hearing tests and hearing aids. That work led toward stereo. Fletcher's team worked with the Philadelphia Orchestra and its famous conductor, Leopold Stokowski, and in 1933 they carried a concert over telephone lines from Philadelphia to an audience at Constitution Hall in Washington, through three separate channels and three sets of loudspeakers, so that listeners could hear where each instrument was. In 1940, they demonstrated stereo recordings at Carnegie Hall.

Another engineer, Homer Dudley, worked on taking speech apart. Beginning in the late 1920s, he developed the vocoder, which broke a voice into its basic components so that it could be sent more efficiently and rebuilt at the other end. Then he built a machine that could speak with no human voice at all: the Voder, shown at the 1939 World's Fair in Queens. A trained operator played it like an organ, with keys and a foot pedal, and astonished crowds heard it say whole sentences.

The vocoder went to war. During the Second World War, Bell Labs built its principles into a secret system called SIGSALY, which scrambled the telephone conversations of Allied leaders, including Winston Churchill and Franklin Roosevelt, so the enemy couldn't listen in.

After the war, the vocoder found a second life in music, giving robotic voices to electronic and pop records, most famously those of the German band Kraftwerk.

So when you hear a synthesized voice on your phone, or a robot voice in a song, or music that seems to surround you from every side, you're hearing ideas that took shape in this building.

deeper.title: Discoveries on West Street
deeper.text:
Some of the most important ideas of the twentieth century were worked out in this building, by people most of us have never heard of.
