In 1927, two physicists here, Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer, fired a beam of electrons at a crystal of nickel and found that the electrons scattered in patterns, the way waves do. It was proof that particles of matter can behave like waves, one of the strange central ideas of quantum physics. Davisson shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1937, the first of the many Nobel Prizes for work at Bell Labs.

That same year, an engineer named Harold Black was riding the ferry across the Hudson to work here when an idea came to him for making amplifiers far more stable and faithful. He sketched it on the only paper he had, a blank space in his copy of the New York Times. That idea, the negative feedback amplifier, became a foundation of modern electronics.

Around the same time, John Johnson discovered that every electrical circuit hums with a faint, unavoidable noise, caused by the jiggling of electrons in the warmth of the wire itself, and his colleague Harry Nyquist explained it with an equation. Nyquist's name is also attached to a rule at the root of digital sound: how often a signal has to be measured to capture it completely.

During the Second World War, the British codebreaker Alan Turing came here in 1943 to study the secret system for scrambling the voices of Allied leaders. While he was here, he often ate lunch in the cafeteria with a young Bell Labs mathematician named Claude Shannon, and the two talked about machines, minds and information. Five years later, Shannon published the paper that founded information theory, the mathematics behind every text, photo and video you send.

Look up at these plain industrial walls and imagine the conversations behind them.

stops.title: Jane Jacobs's Hudson Street & the White Horse Tavern
stops.text:
Walk east to Hudson Street, near West 11th Street. At 555 Hudson Street, look for a modest three-story building. In the 1950s and 60s, this was the home of Jane Jacobs, the writer and activist whose 1961 book, The Death and Life of Great American Cities, changed how the world thinks about cities.

Jacobs wasn't an architect or a planner. She was a journalist with an extraordinary eye. Sitting at her window and walking her neighborhood, she observed how city streets actually worked. She described what she called the sidewalk ballet of Hudson Street: shopkeepers opening their stores, children walking to school, workers on lunch break, bar patrons late at night. She argued that busy streets with mixed uses, short blocks, old buildings, and density created what she called eyes on the street, a natural, informal safety and vitality. This directly contradicted the planning orthodoxy of the time, which favored tearing down old neighborhoods, separating uses, and building towers in parks surrounded by highways.

Jacobs also put her ideas into action. She helped lead the fights against Robert Moses's projects: the road through Washington Square Park, the designation of the West Village for urban renewal, and the Lower Manhattan Expressway through SoHo. She won all three. She later moved to Toronto, where she lived until her death in 2006. Her ideas are now the foundation of modern urbanism, and if you've ever heard a planner talk about walkability or mixed-use neighborhoods, you're hearing Jane Jacobs.

A few steps away, at the corner of Hudson and West 11th Street, is the White Horse Tavern, which dates to 1880. In the 1950s, it became a haunt of writers. The Welsh poet Dylan Thomas was a regular, and according to legend, in November 1953, after drinking at the White Horse, he returned to the Chelsea Hotel and fell ill. He died a few days later. The extent to which drinking at the White Horse was responsible is debated, but the bar has embraced the legend. Jack Kerouac, James Baldwin, Norman Mailer, and Bob Dylan were also among its patrons.

Stand here for a moment and watch the street. People walking dogs, neighbors chatting at the corner, delivery workers, people sitting at sidewalk tables. That's the sidewalk ballet Jane Jacobs described, still going on more than sixty years later, on the same street, in the neighborhood she fought to save.

deeper.title: Saving the West Village
deeper.text:
You heard that Jane Jacobs helped defeat the plan to designate the West Village for urban renewal. Here's how that fight went.

In early 1961, the people of this neighborhood learned that the city wanted to study it for urban renewal. To planners at the time, that meant declaring an area blighted and clearing it for new housing projects. Blocks like these, with old houses, small factories and corner bars, were exactly what planners considered obsolete.

Neighbors formed the Committee to Save the West Village, and Jacobs became one of its leaders. They knew that once an area was officially labeled a slum, demolition was hard to stop, so they fought the label itself. They gathered evidence that the neighborhood was healthy, busy and loved. They packed public hearings. They pointed out that the people who would be displaced had never been asked.

The fight was fierce. In October 1961, at a stormy hearing, the City Planning Commission voted its approval anyway, while furious residents shouted their protests. But the pressure kept building, and within a few months the city dropped the plan.

The neighbors then went further. They drew up their own plan for new housing that would fit the neighborhood: modest walk-up buildings on vacant lots and old industrial sites, without tearing down homes. It took more than a decade. The result, the West Village Houses, forty two small brick apartment buildings near the river, finished in the 1970s, had a rocky start, squeezed by budget cuts and delays. But it was a rare thing: housing designed with a neighborhood rather than imposed on it.

The episode became a model for neighborhood fights across the country. And today, the blocks that were nearly cleared are among the most sought-after places to live in America.

deeper.title: Jane Jacobs, Before Death and Life
deeper.text:
The woman who changed how the world thinks about cities had no degree in planning, and no college degree at all.

Jane Butzner was born in 1916 in Scranton, Pennsylvania. She moved to New York in the mid 1930s, in the depths of the Depression, and took whatever work she could find, as a stenographer and freelance writer. She wrote articles about the city's working districts, the fur district, the flower district, the leather district, learning how neighborhoods actually made a living. She took classes at Columbia for a couple of years, but never finished a degree.

She married an architect, Robert Jacobs, in 1944, and a few years later they bought the modest building here on Hudson Street and fixed it up themselves. In 1952 she joined the magazine Architectural Forum, where she wrote about the great housing projects and urban renewal schemes of the time. The more of them she saw, the less she believed in them. She noticed that the new projects were often empty and unsafe, while old, messy streets like her own were full of life.

In 1958, she wrote an article for Fortune magazine called Downtown Is for People, attacking the planners' visions for city centers. It caught the attention of the Rockefeller Foundation, which gave her a grant to write a book. That book, The Death and Life of Great American Cities, came out in 1961 and opened with a line that announced a fight: This book is an attack on current city planning and rebuilding.

In the late 1960s, opposed to the Vietnam War and determined that her sons would not be drafted, she moved her family to Toronto. She became a Canadian citizen, and she helped stop a highway there too.

deeper.title: Sir Peter Warren's Greenwich
deeper.text:
Walk a block north to the little triangle where Hudson Street meets Eighth Avenue, called Abingdon Square, and you'll find a clue to who owned this land before it was a neighborhood.

In the 1740s, much of what's now the West Village belonged to Sir Peter Warren, an Irish-born officer in the British navy who had grown rich on prize money from capturing enemy ships. He married into a prominent New York family, the De Lanceys, and put together a country estate here of around three hundred acres, with a mansion near the river. Greenwich was then quiet countryside, a few miles north of the city.

Warren went back to Britain, became an admiral and a member of Parliament, and died in 1752, leaving his American lands to his daughters. One of them, Charlotte, married an English nobleman, Willoughby Bertie, the Earl of Abingdon, and that's where Abingdon Square got its name. Warren himself is remembered in Warren Street, far downtown in Tribeca.

Over the following decades, the estate was divided and sold off in lots, and some of its old boundaries and lanes live on in the angled streets you've been walking.

There's a nice twist to the name. The Earl of Abingdon was no friend of the British government's war against the colonies. During the Revolution, he spoke and wrote in defense of the Americans' rights. So this little square, in a neighborhood that has always welcomed dissenters, is named for an English lord who took the rebels' side.

overview:
Greenwich Village has been, for more than a century, the place where America's rebels, bohemians, and dissenters came to live. Before that, it was literally a village.

In the eighteenth century, Greenwich was a separate rural hamlet, a couple of miles north of the city, with country estates and farms. Its growth was driven by fear. In the early 1800s, yellow fever and cholera epidemics repeatedly swept through crowded lower Manhattan, and residents fled north to the healthier air of Greenwich. During the epidemic of 1822, banks and businesses relocated here temporarily; Bank Street is said to take its name from banks that set up offices there. Many people who came during the epidemics stayed.

Because the Village developed before the 1811 street grid, its streets follow old property lines, country lanes, and a buried stream called Minetta Brook. That's why the West Village is a maze of angled streets, and why, famously, West 4th Street crosses West 10th, 11th, and 12th Streets, something that should be geometrically impossible on a grid. The maze kept out through traffic and kept rents low, and that, in turn, attracted artists.

By the early twentieth century, the Village was America's bohemia. Writers, painters, radicals, feminists, and free-love advocates crowded its cheap rooming houses and cafés. Eugene O'Neill's early plays were staged here. The radical magazine The Masses was published here. In the 1950s, the Beat poets gathered in its coffeehouses, and in the 1960s, the folk revival was born on MacDougal Street, launching Bob Dylan and many others. The Village was also home to one of the earliest and most visible gay communities in America, and in 1969, it became the birthplace of the modern gay rights movement at the Stonewall Inn.

The Village is also where the modern historic preservation movement and modern urbanism found one of their greatest voices: Jane Jacobs, who lived on Hudson Street and who defeated Robert Moses's plans to remake the neighborhood.

Today, the Village is one of the most expensive places to live in the country, and the bohemians largely can't afford it. But its street life, its historic buildings, and its sense of being a small town inside a big city have been carefully preserved, in large part thanks to the fights you'll hear about on this walk.

title: Meatpacking, the High Line & Chelsea
blurb: Slaughterhouses to fashion, the Oreo's birthplace, Google's freight-terminal offices, the Titanic's pier, and Hudson Yards.

stops.title: The Meatpacking District
stops.text:
You're on the cobblestone streets of the Meatpacking District, near Gansevoort Street and Washington Street.

Look up at the metal canopies sticking out over the sidewalks from many of the buildings. These were built to shelter meat as it was unloaded and hung on hooks. If you look closely, you might still spot the steel rails and hooks that carried carcasses into the buildings.

The district's name comes from its role as a center of meat processing. By 1900, there were reportedly around two hundred fifty slaughterhouses and packing plants in the area, serving the hotels, restaurants, and butcher shops of the city. Animals arrived by train and boat, and meat went out by truck and cart.

The area's oldest name is Gansevoort, after Fort Gansevoort, a small fort that stood near the river in the early nineteenth century. The fort was named after Peter Gansevoort, a Revolutionary War hero. His grandson was the novelist Herman Melville, who, after his literary career faded and Moby-Dick failed to find an audience, took a job as a customs inspector on the New York docks. For nearly twenty years, the man who wrote one of the greatest American novels inspected cargo on the waterfront, including at a pier on Gansevoort Street, the street named for his own grandfather.

Gansevoort Market, an earlier market building, was a major wholesale center. In the mid-twentieth century, the meat trade began to decline, as refrigerated trucks and national meatpacking companies made the old local system obsolete. By the 1980s, the neighborhood was gritty and partly abandoned at night, known for underground gay clubs, sex clubs, and late night street activity.

Then the neighborhood flipped. In 1999, the French bistro Pastis opened here, and it became a celebrity hangout. Shows like Sex and the City featured the neighborhood. Fashion designers and boutiques arrived, including Diane von Furstenberg and Stella McCartney. Hotels and restaurants followed. A handful of meat businesses still operate here, in a cooperative building, but they're a small presence compared to the luxury stores.

As you walk the streets, notice the contrast between the cobblestones and old brick warehouses and the sleek glass buildings now rising among them.

deeper.title: Melville on the Waterfront
deeper.text:
You heard that Herman Melville, the author of Moby-Dick, spent nearly twenty years as a customs inspector on these docks. Here's how one of America's great novelists ended up checking cargo.

Melville was born in New York in 1819, the grandson of two heroes of the Revolution. When he was a boy, his father's business failed and his father died, and the family fell on hard times. As a young man, Herman went to sea. He sailed on a whaling ship to the South Pacific, deserted it, and lived for a time among the islanders of the Marquesas. His first book, Typee, based on those adventures, was a hit in 1846, and for a few years he was a celebrity.

Then his books grew stranger and more ambitious, and readers drifted away. Moby-Dick, published in 1851, sold poorly and puzzled many reviewers. By the 1860s, Melville was in debt and needed a steady income.

In December 1866, he was appointed an inspector of customs for the port of New York, at four dollars a day. For the next nineteen years, he walked the wharves along the Hudson, checking cargo and paperwork, through summer heat and winter wind.

He never stopped writing. In his off hours he wrote poetry, including a book-length poem called Clarel, about a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. After he retired, he began a short novel about a young sailor, Billy Budd. When he died in 1891, he was nearly forgotten. Billy Budd sat unpublished among his papers until 1924, when a new generation of critics rediscovered him, and his reputation soared.

So as you walk toward the river, picture a gray-bearded inspector with a notebook, checking crates on a pier at the end of a street named for his own grandfather, with no idea that his whale book would one day be called the great American novel.

deeper.title: The White Fort
deeper.text:
Gansevoort Street is one of the oldest names on this part of the waterfront, and it began with a fort.

In 1812, as war with Britain loomed again, a small fort was finished on the riverbank here, between what are now Gansevoort and West Twelfth Streets. It was built of red sandstone, with openings for twenty two cannon, but its walls were whitewashed, so New Yorkers called it the White Fort. Officially, it was named Fort Gansevoort, after Peter Gansevoort, a hero of the Revolution, who died that same year.

Gansevoort's fame came from the summer of 1777. As a young colonel, he commanded Fort Stanwix, in the Mohawk Valley of upstate New York, when a British force and its Native American allies laid siege to it. Gansevoort refused to surrender. After about three weeks, the British gave up and withdrew, a blow to the British campaign that ended in defeat at Saratoga that fall.

A legend grew up around the siege: that the defenders stitched together an American flag from scraps, including soldiers' shirts and a woman's red petticoat, and that it was the first Stars and Stripes ever flown in battle. The story is told with pride in upstate New York, but historians can't confirm what that flag looked like, or whether it was the Stars and Stripes at all.

The White Fort here never fired a shot in anger. The British never attacked Manhattan during the War of 1812, and by the 1850s the fort was gone, swallowed by the growing waterfront.

All that remains is the name: on the street, on the old market, and on the whole district, which for a long time was simply called Gansevoort. And through Peter Gansevoort's grandson, Herman Melville, the name reaches into American literature too.

deeper.title: Florent and the Night Market
deeper.text:
For more than twenty years, the most famous place to eat on these cobblestones was a diner that never closed.

In 1985, a Frenchman named Florent Morellet took over an old luncheonette on Gansevoort Street called the R and L, which had been feeding meat workers since 1943. He kept the counter and the booths, renamed it Florent, and stayed open twenty four hours a day. Its menu, designed by the graphic designer Tibor Kalman and his studio, is now in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art.

At the time, the neighborhood was rough. By day, butchers in bloody white coats pushed carcasses along the overhead rails. By night, the streets belonged to clubgoers, drag queens, sex workers, artists and night owls. Florent fed all of them, often at the same time. Meat workers on the early shift sat beside people coming home from the clubs.

The diner became a gathering place for gay New York, especially in the worst years of the AIDS crisis. Morellet learned in 1987 that he was HIV positive, and he did something remarkable. On the board where the restaurant listed its daily specials, in little plastic letters, he posted his own T-cell count, the number doctors used to track the disease, along with jokes and puns. For many customers facing the same diagnosis, that board said that they weren't alone, and that there was nothing to hide.

Morellet also became an activist for the neighborhood. He helped found the group whose campaign led the city, in 2003, to protect the old market buildings as the Gansevoort Market Historic District. But the popularity he helped create drove rents sky-high, and in 2008, when his landlord demanded far more, Florent closed. The space became a clothing store.

So as you walk past the boutiques, imagine a lit diner window at four in the morning, a butcher and a drag queen sharing the counter, and a menu board that told the truth.

stops.title: The Whitney & the Start of the High Line
stops.text:
You're at the southern entrance to the High Line, at Gansevoort Street, next to the Whitney Museum of American Art.

The museum, the large, asymmetrical building with steel cladding and outdoor terraces stepping down toward the river, was designed by Renzo Piano and opened here in 2015. The Whitney's story begins with Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney, a sculptor and heiress who collected the work of living American artists. In 1929, she offered her collection to the Metropolitan Museum of Art. The Met declined. So in 1931, she founded her own museum, in Greenwich Village. The Whitney later moved to Midtown and then to a famous building on Madison Avenue, before coming here. Its Biennial exhibition is one of the most important surveys of contemporary American art.

Now look at the elevated structure above you, the High Line.

As you heard in the overview, the railroad tracks were lifted off the street in the 1930s as part of the West Side Improvement Project, which removed over a hundred street-level crossings. The new elevated line, completed in 1934, ran from St. John's Terminal in Hudson Square up to the rail yards at 34th Street. It ran through the middle of blocks rather than over the avenues, and it passed directly into factories and warehouses, so trains could unload right inside buildings.

As trucking took over, rail traffic dwindled. The last train, reportedly carrying a load of frozen turkeys, ran in 1980. The southern section was demolished. The rest sat abandoned for nearly twenty years, and wild grasses, flowers, and small trees took root on the old tracks.

Property owners wanted it torn down. In 1999, two neighborhood residents, Joshua David and Robert Hammond, met at a community meeting and founded Friends of the High Line to save it. Initially, the idea seemed absurd. But photographs by Joel Sternfeld of the wild meadow growing on the tracks helped capture the public imagination. The city, under Mayor Michael Bloomberg, embraced the project. The first section opened as a park in 2009.

The design, by the landscape architecture firm James Corner Field Operations with the architects Diller Scofidio and Renfro, kept the old rails in places and used planting by the Dutch designer Piet Oudolf, who chose grasses and perennials inspired by the self-seeded landscape that grew there during the abandoned years.

The High Line became an instant hit, and a catalyst for development. Billions of dollars in new buildings went up alongside it. It also became a symbol of a broader debate about how public improvements can drive gentrification. Even its founders have acknowledged that the park benefited wealthy newcomers more than longtime residents of nearby public housing.

deeper.title: The Last Cowboy of Tenth Avenue
deeper.text:
You heard about Death Avenue, and the West Side Cowboys who rode ahead of the trains. Here's how that strange job came to an end.

For most of a century, freight trains rolled through the streets of the West Side, down Tenth and Eleventh Avenues, among wagons, pushcarts and children. The toll was terrible. By one count, the trains had killed more than four hundred people by the early 1900s, and newspapers and neighborhood groups campaigned for years to get the tracks off the street.

For a long time, the railroad's answer was the cowboys. A rider on horseback went ahead of each train, waving a red flag by day and a red lantern by night, to warn people out of the way. It was a slow, old-fashioned fix in one of the most modern cities on earth.

The real fix took decades of argument, and money from the city, the state and the New York Central Railroad. You heard that the elevated line opened in 1934. But a stretch of street-level track lingered on Eleventh Avenue, and so did the cowboys.

The last ride came in March 1941. A twenty one year old rider named George Hayde, on a horse called Cyclone, led a train of fourteen cars loaded with oranges up the avenue. After that, the job was gone for good.

Today, the High Line's old tracks are planted with wildflowers, and people stroll above the traffic. But the viaduct was built because so many people died on the streets below it. For a while, the only thing standing between the trains and the crowds was a young man on a horse with a red flag.

deeper.title: The Museum and the Flood
deeper.text:
Look at the Whitney's building, and you might not guess that it's built like a ship ready for a storm.

Renzo Piano, the Italian architect who also designed the New York Times Building, shaped the museum to fit this odd corner of the city. On the east side, it steps down toward the High Line in a series of outdoor terraces, where you can stand among sculptures with the city behind you. On the west side, facing the river, it's heavier and more industrial, clad in steel panels, like the warehouses that once surrounded it. And at the entrance, the building lifts up and hangs over the plaza, so the street seems to flow right under it.

The museum was still under construction in October 2012, when Hurricane Sandy pushed the Hudson River into these streets. Millions of gallons of river water poured into the building's basement. The museum and its engineers went back to work and added a whole system of flood defenses.

The most remarkable piece is a door. On the building's west side, facing the river, is a flood door fourteen feet tall and twenty seven feet wide, built like a watertight door on a ship, and designed so that a single person can close it in an emergency. When a big storm is coming, crews can also put up a temporary aluminum flood wall around the building. Piano wanted all of it to stay out of sight, so most visitors never notice it.

It's a sign of the times. This waterfront was built to bring cargo in from the river. Now its newest buildings are designed to keep the river out.

deeper.title: The Gardens on the Tracks
deeper.text:
Look at the plants along the High Line. They look wild, as if they'd seeded themselves. That's the idea.

When the trains stopped in 1980, the viaduct became an accidental meadow. Seeds blew in on the wind or arrived with birds, and tough plants took root in the gravel between the rails: grasses, wildflowers, even small trees. You heard that photographs of that wild landscape helped win support for saving the line.

When the park was designed, the Dutch garden designer Piet Oudolf set out to capture that feeling, not by copying it, but by composing it. He is a leader of a style sometimes called the New Perennial movement, which uses grasses and long-lived flowering plants arranged as if in a natural meadow, and values how plants look in every season, not just when they bloom. On the High Line, he used hundreds of kinds of plants, many of them native to North America, in a series of zones suited to the changing sun, shade and wind along the line.

Watch how the gardens change through the year. In spring come bulbs and fresh green shoots. In summer, the flowers and grasses are at their height, buzzing with bees. In fall, the grasses turn gold and copper. And in winter, instead of cutting everything down, the gardeners leave the dried stems and seed heads standing, where they catch the frost and feed the birds.

Then, each year in late March, gardeners and volunteers do what's called the spring cutback, clearing away the old growth so the new season can come through. Even then, they leave some stems standing, because native bees and other pollinators nest inside them.

So the High Line's gardens are a kind of performance: a designed wilderness, tended every day to look as if no one tends it at all.

stops.title: Little Island & Pier 54: The Titanic's Destination
stops.text:
Walk to the river, along the Hudson River Park, to the park built on what look like giant concrete tulips rising out of the water. This is Little Island, which opened in 2021. It was designed by the British designer Thomas Heatherwick and funded largely by the media mogul Barry Diller and his wife, the fashion designer Diane von Furstenberg. Its undulating surface is held up by about one hundred thirty two concrete pots on piles, and it contains lawns, gardens, and an amphitheater.

But look just south of it, at the remains of an old pier and a steel archway. That arch is the last remnant of Pier 54, and it carries one of the great stories of the steamship era.

In the early twentieth century, this stretch of the Hudson, from about 12th to 23rd Streets, was home to the Chelsea Piers, a set of grand ocean liner terminals designed by the architects Warren and Wetmore, who also designed Grand Central Terminal. They opened in 1910 and were used by the great transatlantic lines, including Cunard and White Star.

In April 1912, the White Star Line's new ship, the Titanic, was headed for these piers on its maiden voyage. It never arrived. After it struck an iceberg and sank, the Cunard ship Carpathia rescued about seven hundred survivors and brought them here to Pier 54 on the night of April eighteenth. Thousands of people crowded the waterfront in the rain, waiting for news of their loved ones.

Three years later, in May 1915, another famous ship left from Pier 54: the Cunard liner Lusitania, bound for Liverpool. Off the coast of Ireland, it was torpedoed by a German submarine and sank, killing nearly twelve hundred people, including over one hundred Americans. The sinking helped turn American public opinion against Germany and toward entry into World War One.

Look for the word Cunard still faintly visible on the steel arch. The great piers declined after ocean liners moved to larger terminals farther north in the 1930s, and air travel eventually ended the transatlantic liner era. A few blocks north, the Chelsea Piers complex has been converted into a giant sports and entertainment center.

Also nearby is Pier 57, a former marine terminal that has been redeveloped and now includes offices for Google, a food hall, and a rooftop park. It's another example of how the old maritime infrastructure of the west side has been transformed.

deeper.title: The Night the Carpathia Came In
deeper.text:
You heard that the Carpathia brought the Titanic's survivors here. Its part in the story began with a lucky moment.

Late on the night of April 14th, 1912, the Carpathia's wireless operator, a young man named Harold Cottam, had been up on the bridge and missed the Titanic's first calls for help. Back in his cabin, getting ready for bed, he listened in one more time, and heard them. He ran to wake his captain, Arthur Rostron.

The Carpathia was about fifty eight miles away. Rostron turned the ship around and drove it at top speed through waters full of ice, with extra lookouts posted, while the crew prepared blankets, hot drinks and the dining rooms for survivors. The Carpathia reached the scene in the dark before dawn, after the Titanic had gone down, and spent hours picking up survivors from the lifeboats.

Then came the slow trip back to New York, with the world desperate for news. On the evening of April 18th, in a cold rain, the Carpathia steamed up the Hudson. It didn't go straight to its own pier. First it went to the White Star Line's pier, a little to the north, to leave behind the Titanic's empty lifeboats. Then it came back here, to Cunard's Pier 54, and tied up at about half past nine.

Survivors came down the gangways into a crush of relatives and reporters. Some were met by family. Many had become widows that week. Relief groups were waiting to help the many who had lost everything.

Captain Rostron became a hero. Congress awarded him a gold medal, and a group of survivors, led by Margaret Brown, the woman later remembered as the Unsinkable Molly Brown, presented him with a silver cup. So the arch here also remembers a ship that turned toward the ice when another was in trouble.

deeper.title: The Lusitania's Last Sailing
deeper.text:
You heard that the Lusitania sailed from this pier in May 1915, and was sunk by a German submarine. The warning came in the morning newspapers.

On Saturday, May 1st, the day the ship was to sail, a notice from the German Embassy appeared in New York papers. It reminded travelers that Germany and Britain were at war, that the waters around the British Isles were a war zone, and that anyone sailing there on British ships did so at their own risk. In some papers, it was printed right next to Cunard's advertisement for the Lusitania's sailing.

Some passengers were alarmed, and a few canceled. But most shrugged it off. The Lusitania was one of the fastest ships on the ocean, and many people believed no submarine could catch her. The ship left the pier a little after noon, delayed by the transfer of passengers from another ship.

Six days later, on May 7th, off the southern coast of Ireland, a single torpedo struck. The great liner sank in about eighteen minutes.

The sinking caused fury in the United States, but not war, at least not yet. Three days later, President Woodrow Wilson gave a speech in Philadelphia in which he said that there is such a thing as a man being too proud to fight. Critics mocked the line. Wilson sent Germany a series of stern protests, and his Secretary of State, William Jennings Bryan, resigned rather than sign one of them, fearing it would drag the country into war.

The United States didn't enter the war until April 1917, nearly two years later, after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare. But the Lusitania became a rallying cry, used on recruiting posters and in speeches for the rest of the war.

So this pier saw off one of the turning points of the century, on a spring day, with a warning in the newspaper that almost everyone ignored.

deeper.title: Westway and the Striped Bass
deeper.text:
The park you're standing in exists partly because of a fish.

By the 1970s, the old elevated West Side Highway along the river was falling apart. In 1973, a section of it collapsed near Gansevoort Street under the weight of a truck. The piers along the shore were rotting. Planners proposed a grand replacement called Westway: a highway buried in a tunnel inside new land, made by filling in the Hudson along this shore, with parks, apartments and offices built on top.

Westway had powerful supporters, and well over a billion dollars of federal highway money behind it. But opponents argued that the money would be better spent on subways and buses, and environmental groups went to court. Their unlikely champion was the striped bass. Young striped bass spend the winter in the sheltered water among the old piers, and filling in the river would destroy that refuge.

In 1982, a federal judge, Thomas Griesa, blocked the project, ruling that government agencies had played down the harm to the fish. The agencies tried again, and in August 1985 Griesa ruled against them a second time, finding that testimony they had given was tainted. The next month, facing a deadline, New York gave up on Westway and traded the federal highway money for transit and local roads.

Instead of a buried highway, the West Side eventually got a surface boulevard, and the river's edge got a park. In 1998, the state created Hudson River Park, which runs along the shore from Battery Park City up to Fifty Ninth Street, and includes the water around the old piers, where fish and other river life are protected.

So when you see the rows of old wooden pilings sticking out of the water, don't think of them only as ruins. For the young striped bass, they're shelter, and they helped save this shoreline.

stops.title: Chelsea Market: The Birthplace of the Oreo
stops.text:
You're at Chelsea Market, the block-long complex of brick buildings between Ninth and Tenth Avenues and 15th and 16th Streets. Walk inside and look at the exposed brick, iron beams, and old pipes. This was a factory, and a historic one.

In 1898, several large baking companies merged to form the National Biscuit Company, later known as Nabisco. Its headquarters and main bakery were here, in a complex of about eighteen buildings that eventually spread over several blocks. The company pioneered mass-market packaged foods. Its first major national brand, launched in 1898, was the Uneeda Biscuit, a soda cracker sold in an innovative package lined with waxed paper to keep it fresh, at a time when crackers were usually sold loose from barrels. Nabisco's advertising campaign for Uneeda was one of the first large-scale national ad campaigns in American history.

And in 1912, the bakers here created a new cookie: two chocolate wafers with a cream filling, called the Oreo. Nobody knows for sure where the name came from. The Oreo went on to become the best-selling cookie in the world. Animal Crackers and Fig Newtons were also produced by Nabisco in this era. A plaque on the Ninth Avenue side commemorates the Oreo's birth on this block, and the street outside has at times been nicknamed Oreo Way.

Nabisco moved its manufacturing to a modern plant in New Jersey in 1958, and the buildings were used by other businesses. In the 1990s, a developer, Irwin Cohen, converted the ground floor into a food hall and market, which opened in 1997 as Chelsea Market. He kept many industrial details, including a waterfall made from a pipe. The upper floors became offices for media companies and tech firms.

In 2018, Google bought Chelsea Market, for a reported price of about two point four billion dollars, one of the most expensive real estate deals for a single building in New York at the time. It's now part of Google's Chelsea campus.

Note that the High Line passes right through the building's western side. When the rail viaduct was built, Nabisco had loading docks connected directly to the tracks, so flour and sugar could come in and finished products could go out without ever touching the street.

deeper.title: The Cracker in the Raincoat
deeper.text:
You heard that the National Biscuit Company sold its Uneeda Biscuit in a sealed package, backed by one of the first big national ad campaigns. The man behind that strategy was a Chicago lawyer named Adolphus Green.

In the 1890s, the cracker business was a war. Regional bakeries fought over territory, cutting prices until nobody made money. Bankers and bakers merged them into larger and larger groups, and in 1898, the biggest of those groups combined into the National Biscuit Company. Green became its first president.

Green decided that instead of fighting over price, the company would build a brand. He wanted a cracker that was exactly the same everywhere, sold under one name, in a package that kept it fresh. The company called its package the In-Er-Seal, a cardboard box with a waxed paper lining.

The name came from the company's advertising agency, N. W. Ayer and Son, which registered Uneeda at the end of 1898. Early in 1899, ads began appearing that simply asked, Do you know Uneeda Biscuit? Then came the mascot: a little boy in a rain slicker, carrying a box of crackers through a downpour. The message was that the crackers inside stayed dry, whatever the weather.

It worked spectacularly. Uneeda Biscuits sold in enormous numbers, and the cracker barrel began to disappear from American stores. The idea that a company could sell the same packaged food, under the same name, in every store in the country, now seems obvious. In 1899, it was new, and much of it was worked out in these buildings.

The boy in the raincoat became one of the most familiar faces in American advertising. Look carefully at old brick walls, here and in other cities, and you can still sometimes find faded painted signs for Uneeda Biscuit.

deeper.title: The Oreo's Mysteries
deeper.text:
The Oreo became the best-selling cookie in the world, and almost everything about its beginnings comes with a question mark.

Start with the fact that it wasn't first. In 1908, four years earlier, a rival company, Sunshine Biscuits, had introduced Hydrox: two chocolate cookies with a cream filling. When the Oreo arrived in 1912, it was, in effect, an imitation. But Nabisco had bigger bakeries and a bigger advertising budget, and over the decades the Oreo buried its rival. Today, many people assume Hydrox was the copy.

The first Oreos were sold on March 6th, 1912, to a grocer in Hoboken, New Jersey, just across the river.

Then there's the name. You heard that nobody knows where it came from. The theories are fun. One says it comes from or, the French word for gold, because the early packages were gold colored. Another points to a Greek word for mountain, because an early test version was shaped like a little hill. Another notices the letters r and e, from the word cream, sandwiched between two O's, like the filling between two cookies. Nabisco has never settled the question.

And then there's the design. The pattern stamped on today's Oreo dates to 1952, and is generally credited to a Nabisco employee named William Turnier, who is said to have started in the company mailroom. Over the years, people have read secret meanings into the little crosses and circles, linking them to the medieval Knights Templar or to secret societies. There's no evidence that anyone at Nabisco meant any of that, and the company has never explained the design.

So the next time you twist one open, remember that you're holding a small mystery that started on this block.

deeper.title: Look Closer: A Bakery Built in Layers
deeper.text:
Step back outside and look at Chelsea Market from the street. It isn't one building but a patchwork, built in stages over about half a century, by several different architects, as the bakery kept growing.

The oldest parts date from the late nineteenth century, sturdy brick buildings with rows of arched windows. As the business boomed, the company kept adding buildings until the complex filled the whole block. In 1904, a railroad spur was routed right through the complex, so freight cars could pull up inside.

Now walk toward Tenth Avenue. When the elevated freight line was built in the early 1930s, Nabisco rebuilt its whole Tenth Avenue side, designed by its own architect, Louis Wirsching Junior, so that the new tracks could pass straight through the building. That's why the High Line seems to tunnel through Chelsea Market today. Freight cars could stop inside to deliver flour and sugar, and leave with boxes of crackers and cookies.

Look up, too, for the bridge over Tenth Avenue. The bakery reached across the avenue to the building on the other side, and a walkway bridge crosses high above the traffic.

As you look, notice how different the pieces are: different bricks, different windows, different heights. Each one marks a moment when the company needed more room, and the whole block records the growth of one of America's first giant food companies.

stops.title: 111 Eighth Avenue: Google's Freight Terminal
stops.text:
Across Ninth Avenue, filling the entire block from Eighth to Ninth Avenues and 15th to 16th Streets, is a massive Art Deco building: 111 Eighth Avenue. If you work at Google, you may know this building very well.

It was completed in 1932 as the Port Authority Commerce Building, also called the Union Inland Terminal Number One. The Port Authority of New York, which built bridges and tunnels, wanted a freight distribution hub where trucks coming through the new Holland Tunnel could drop off goods. The building was designed so trucks could drive right inside and ride oversized elevators up to the upper floors, delivering goods directly to warehouses on each floor. Its floors are enormous and built to carry very heavy loads.

At about three million square feet, it was one of the largest buildings in the city by floor area. In fact, at the time it was built, it was among the largest buildings in the world by floor space. It covers an entire city block.

Later, the building became a hub for a different kind of freight: data. In the internet age, its central location, huge floors, strong structure, and electrical capacity made it a major hub for telecommunications and data centers, like 60 Hudson Street downtown.

In 2010, Google bought the building for about one point nine billion dollars, at the time one of the largest single-building sales in the country. Google had been leasing space here since 2006, and the building became the core of its New York operations. It's now joined by other Google buildings in the neighborhood: Chelsea Market, Pier 57, and St. John's Terminal in Hudson Square.

There's something poetic about this. The building was designed to make the movement of physical goods more efficient, and it now houses engineers building the software that moves information around the world. And it's not unique. Up and down the west side, buildings designed for freight have found new life as offices for tech companies, because the same things that made them good for freight, big floors, high ceilings, strong structures, and lots of power, make them good for modern offices too.

deeper.title: Union Inland Terminal Number One
deeper.text:
You heard that this building was built by the Port Authority as a freight terminal. To understand why, it helps to know what the Port Authority was for.

New York's harbor is shared by two states, and for decades New York and New Jersey squabbled over it while freight piled up. Most of the railroads from the west ended on the New Jersey side of the Hudson, so goods had to cross the river on barges and ferries, an expensive, slow and chaotic system. In 1921, the two states signed a compact creating the Port of New York Authority, an independent agency to run the region's port and transportation as one system. It was one of the first agencies of its kind in the country.

The Port Authority's early projects changed the region: two bridges to Staten Island, then the George Washington Bridge in 1931, and control of the new Holland Tunnel, which had opened in 1927. Trucks could now drive under the river. So the Port Authority imagined a new kind of freight hub: a terminal in the middle of Manhattan, where trucks would carry goods to and from the railroad lines and the shipping piers on the Hudson, instead of every shipper making its own trips to the waterfront.

This building was the result. Its ground floor and basement were the terminal, Union Inland Terminal Number One, and the floors above were rented out as warehouses and workshops. Trucks drove into giant elevators, said to be the largest truck elevators ever built at the time, able to lift forty thousand pounds, and rode up to the tenants' doors. The name, Number One, shows the planners were thinking big.

As trucks took over from trains, the freight terminal faded, and the Port Authority eventually sold the building. But its strength and size kept it useful, first for manufacturers, then for the telephone and internet companies, and now for Google.

So this massive block is a monument to a big idea about freight, and to a building so well made that it kept finding new lives.

deeper.title: The Meet-Me Room
deeper.text:
Somewhere in this building is a room where the internet shakes hands.

You heard that 111 Eighth Avenue became a hub for telecommunications and data. Here's what that means. The internet isn't one network. It's thousands of networks, run by phone companies, cable companies, internet providers, banks and tech firms. For data to pass from one network to another, their cables have to physically meet somewhere. Buildings where many networks come together are called carrier hotels, and the room inside where they connect is called a meet-me room. There, in long rows of locked cabinets, a technician can link two networks with a single cable, called a cross connect.

This building had what the carriers wanted: huge, strong floors to hold heavy equipment, plenty of electric power, and a central location near the fiber-optic cables that run under the city's streets. Around the turn of the century, its owners turned much of it into telecom space, and its meet-me room was once said to be the largest in the city.

When Google bought the building in 2010, many people assumed it wanted the network connections. In fact, it was mainly after the office space, and the telecom tenants stayed on, with long leases. So today, software engineers work on some floors, while on others, racks of humming equipment pass data from one network to the next.

The next time a message from your phone reaches a friend across town, there's a fair chance it passed through a room like this one, maybe this very one, where cables from rival companies are plugged in side by side.

stops.title: The Hotel Chelsea
stops.text:
On West 23rd Street, between Seventh and Eighth Avenues, look for the red brick building with ornate iron balconies and a vertical sign reading Hotel Chelsea.

It was built in 1884 as one of the city's first cooperative apartment buildings, and for a time it was among the tallest buildings in the city. In the 1880s, West 23rd Street was the heart of New York's theater district, with theaters and music halls lining the street. Within a couple of decades, the cooperative had failed, and the building became a hotel.

Over the twentieth century, the Chelsea became legendary as a residence for artists, writers, and musicians, many of them on long-term stays. Its manager for many years, Stanley Bard, was known for letting struggling artists pay their rent late, or even with artwork, which covered the walls of the lobby.

The list of residents is remarkable. Mark Twain and O. Henry are said to have stayed here. The poet Dylan Thomas was living here when he fell ill in 1953. Arthur C. Clarke worked on 2001: A Space Odyssey while staying here. Andy Warhol filmed parts of his 1966 film Chelsea Girls here. Leonard Cohen wrote a song about an encounter at the hotel with Janis Joplin. Patti Smith and Robert Mapplethorpe lived here in the late 1960s, as she describes in her memoir Just Kids. Bob Dylan, Jimi Hendrix, Madonna, and many others passed through.

The hotel's history also has darker chapters. In October 1978, Nancy Spungen, the girlfriend of the Sex Pistols bassist Sid Vicious, was found stabbed to death in their room. Vicious was charged with her murder but died of a heroin overdose before trial.

The hotel closed to new guests in 2011 for a long and contentious renovation, during which some long-term residents remained. It reopened in 2022 as a luxury hotel.

Also on this street, look for the Chelsea's neighbor, the old YMCA building, and the site of the Grand Opera House, which once stood on Eighth Avenue and was owned by the notorious financier Jim Fisk, who ran the Erie Railroad from offices there. In 1872, Fisk was shot dead by a rival in love and business at a hotel on lower Broadway. Chelsea has always been full of drama.

deeper.title: A Palace of Shared Apartments
deeper.text:
You heard that the Chelsea was built as one of the city's first cooperative apartment buildings. The idea behind it came from its architect, Philip Hubert.

In the 1880s, respectable middle class New Yorkers lived in private houses if they could afford them. Apartments were associated with crowded tenements, and many people thought living in one was not quite proper. Hubert and his partner, James Pirsson, set out to change that. They designed a series of buildings they called Home Clubs. Instead of renting from a landlord, a group of members would pool their money to build a fine apartment house together, each owning a share.

The Chelsea was the grandest of them. Look at its red brick front, its rows of iron balconies, and its steep roofline with gables and tall chimneys. Inside, a famous staircase winds up through the full height of the building.

For about twenty years, the cooperative worked. But the neighborhood changed as the theaters moved uptown, money grew tight, and the cooperative went bankrupt in the early 1900s. By 1905, the building had become a hotel, with many long-term residents, which is how it came to house so many artists and writers.

Hubert's idea outlived his building's cooperative. Today, cooperative ownership is the most common way people own apartments in Manhattan. So when you see a movie scene of nervous buyers being grilled by a co-op board, you're watching the descendants of Philip Hubert's Home Clubs.

deeper.title: When Twenty-Third Street Was Broadway
deeper.text:
You heard that West Twenty-Third Street was once the center of the American theater. In the years after the Civil War, this was the place to see a show.

The great actor Edwin Booth, the most famous Hamlet of his time, built his own theater at the corner of Twenty-Third Street and Sixth Avenue, and opened it in February 1869. It was meant to give serious drama a worthy home. Booth's name carried a heavy shadow. His younger brother, John Wilkes Booth, had assassinated President Lincoln four years earlier, and Edwin had left the stage for months afterward. His new theater was admired, but it was a financial disaster. Booth went bankrupt, and the theater closed in 1883.

Two blocks west, at the corner of Eighth Avenue, a businessman named Samuel Pike opened Pike's Opera House in 1868. Within a year, it belonged to Jim Fisk and Jay Gould, who renamed it the Grand Opera House, the theater you heard about where Fisk kept the offices of the Erie Railroad.

Later came vaudeville. In 1889, the showman F. F. Proctor opened a theater on this street, between Sixth and Seventh Avenues, offering a mix of singers, comedians, acrobats and animal acts that ran one after another from late morning until night, so you could walk in at almost any hour.

Then, as the theaters moved north toward Herald Square and Times Square, the street's glory faded. Some of the old theaters became movie houses, and the young film business found space in the neighborhood's lofts.

So as you walk along Twenty-Third Street, past the drugstores and apartment buildings, imagine carriages lined up outside the theaters on a winter night, a century and a half ago.

deeper.title: Jim Fisk, Prince of Erie
deeper.text:
You heard that Jim Fisk owned the Grand Opera House on Eighth Avenue, and was shot by a rival. His life was even wilder than that.

Fisk grew up in Vermont and started out as a peddler, selling goods from a wagon, and made money in the cotton trade during the Civil War. He was loud, stout, flamboyant and funny, with a waxed mustache and a diamond on his shirt front, and he loved an audience.

In 1868, Fisk teamed up with the quiet, calculating Jay Gould and the old speculator Daniel Drew to fight Cornelius Vanderbilt for control of the Erie Railroad. Vanderbilt kept buying Erie stock, and the Erie men kept issuing more of it. When a judge friendly to Vanderbilt ordered their arrest, they fled across the Hudson to Jersey City, taking the company's books and millions of dollars in cash. The battle, known as the Erie War, ended with Gould and Fisk in control of the railroad.

Fisk and Gould then bought the opera house, and Fisk ran the railroad from offices inside, while producing shows on the stage below.

In 1869, the two men tried to corner the market in gold. When the government sold gold to break the scheme, prices collapsed on September 24th, a day remembered as Black Friday, and many investors were ruined. Fisk and Gould came through largely unharmed, and Fisk barricaded himself inside the opera house.

His downfall was personal. Fisk kept a mistress, an actress named Josie Mansfield, and she took up with his business partner, Edward Stokes. The quarrel turned into lawsuits, and then into violence. On January 6th, 1872, Stokes shot Fisk on a staircase at the Grand Central Hotel on lower Broadway. Fisk died the next day, and his body lay in state at his opera house, where crowds lined up to see him.

He was thirty six years old.

stops.title: Clement Clarke Moore's Chelsea
stops.text:
You're now in the Chelsea Historic District, near Ninth Avenue and West 21st Street. Look at the full block of green lawn and Gothic buildings, the campus of the General Theological Seminary, the oldest seminary of the Episcopal Church.

The land was donated to the seminary in 1827 by Clement Clarke Moore, who owned the Chelsea estate. Moore was a scholar of Hebrew and Greek who taught at the seminary. He's best known, though, for something else: he's generally credited with writing, in 1822, the poem A Visit from St. Nicholas, which begins, Twas the night before Christmas. The poem helped create the modern American image of Santa Claus, with his sleigh, eight reindeer, and trip down the chimney. Some scholars have argued that another writer, Henry Livingston Junior, actually wrote it, but Moore's authorship is the traditional view.

Moore had good reason to develop his land. When the city's street grid was imposed in 1811, Ninth Avenue was cut through the middle of his estate. He was furious, but he made the best of it, dividing the land into lots and selling them with strict covenants about what could be built: residential houses only, with setbacks from the street, and no stables or factories. That's why this area has such elegant, consistent rows of townhouses.

Walk along West 20th Street, between Ninth and Tenth Avenues, to see Cushman Row, a row of Greek Revival houses built in the 1840s by a merchant named Don Alonzo Cushman, a friend of Moore's. Look for the small, square attic windows with iron wreaths around them, and the iron pineapples, a symbol of hospitality, on the newel posts of some stoops.

On Tenth Avenue, look also for the Empire Diner, an Art Deco diner car, and to the north, the massive London Terrace complex, built in 1930 and once one of the largest apartment buildings in the world, with its own swimming pool and doormen dressed as London bobbies.

It's a remarkable contrast: just a block or two from the freight terminals, the slaughterhouses, and the piers, Moore's carefully planned neighborhood of churches and townhouses has survived nearly two centuries.

deeper.title: Who Wrote The Night Before Christmas?
deeper.text:
You heard that some scholars doubt Clement Clarke Moore wrote A Visit from St. Nicholas. Here's the case, and the case against it.

The poem first appeared on December 23rd, 1823, in a small newspaper in Troy, New York, with no author's name. How it got there is unclear. One story says a family friend who had heard it at the Moores' sent it in. It was reprinted year after year, still anonymous. Moore's name was attached to it in a collection of poems in 1837, and in 1844 he included it in a book of his own poetry.

But the family of another New Yorker, Henry Livingston Junior, a farmer, surveyor and occasional poet from the Hudson Valley, insisted that he had written it, and had recited it to his own children years before it was published. Livingston had died in 1828, and his family's claim came years later, with no manuscript to back it up.

In 2000, a professor named Don Foster, famous for identifying anonymous authors from their writing style, took up the Livingston case. He argued that the poem's bouncy, cheerful rhythm matched Livingston's other light verse, and didn't sound like Moore, a serious scholar. He also pointed to the reindeer. In the first printing, two of them were named Dunder and Blixem, Dutch words for thunder and lightning. Livingston, who had Dutch roots, knew the language. Moore did not. Later versions changed the names to Donder and Blitzen.

Moore's defenders answered back. They pointed out that Moore wrote playful verse too, that he claimed the poem openly while people who could have contradicted him were still alive, and that parts of the Livingston family story had been shown to be wrong.

No one can prove it either way. The poem that helped create the American Santa Claus has an author on the plaque, and a question mark in the footnotes.

deeper.title: Captain Clarke's Chelsea
deeper.text:
Why is this neighborhood named after a district of London? Because of an old soldier, and the place where old soldiers retired.

In the middle of the 1700s, a retired British officer named Thomas Clarke bought farmland here, on the Hudson, a few miles north of the little city. He named his estate Chelsea, after the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London, the grand home for retired and wounded soldiers founded in the late 1600s, where veterans in scarlet coats still live today.

Clarke's daughter, Charity, married a young clergyman named Benjamin Moore, and their son, born in 1779, was Clement Clarke Moore. Clement inherited the estate from his mother in 1813, and he's the one who later divided it into the house lots you see around you.

Clement's father had his own place in history. Benjamin Moore became the Episcopal bishop of New York, and president of Columbia College. In July 1804, he was called to the bedside of Alexander Hamilton, who had been mortally wounded in his duel with Aaron Burr. Hamilton asked for holy communion. Moore hesitated, because the church condemned dueling. Only after Hamilton assured him that he repented of his part in the duel, and bore no ill will toward Burr, did the bishop give him the sacrament. Hamilton died on the afternoon of July 12th, the day after the duel.

So the name of this neighborhood carries a chain of stories: a veterans' home in London, an old soldier's farm, a bishop at a famous deathbed, and a scholar who may or may not have written the most famous Christmas poem in America.

deeper.title: The Seminary Close
deeper.text:
Behind the fence and brick walls of the General Theological Seminary is one of the most peaceful spaces in Manhattan, a quadrangle of lawns and trees that the seminary calls the Close.

The oldest building here is the West Building, a plain stone building from 1836, one of the earliest Gothic Revival buildings in the city. It had a twin, the East Building, from the 1820s, which was later torn down. These modest stone buildings were the seminary's first home on Clement Clarke Moore's land.

Most of what you see came later. Beginning in the 1880s, under an ambitious dean, Eugene Augustus Hoffman, the seminary hired the architect Charles Coolidge Haight to build a whole campus in the English collegiate Gothic style, with red brick, stone trim, pointed windows and a chapel with a tall tower. The idea was to give New York a little piece of Oxford, a college built around a green.

Look for the Chapel of the Good Shepherd, with its tower rising over the middle of the block. Notice, too, how the buildings turn inward, toward the lawn, rather than out toward the street. That's deliberate. A seminary was meant to be a retreat from the world, even in the middle of a city.

In recent decades, the seminary has struggled with money, like many religious schools, and has sold or leased some of its property. But the Close remains. Peek through the gates, and you'll see Chelsea as Moore's generation imagined it: quiet, green and dignified, a few blocks from the freight yards.

stops.title: West Chelsea Galleries & the Starrett-Lehigh Building
stops.text:
You're in West Chelsea, near Eleventh Avenue and West 26th Street. The blocks around you, roughly between Tenth and Eleventh Avenues from 18th to 28th Streets, contain one of the densest concentrations of art galleries in the world, hundreds of them, many in former garages and warehouses.

Galleries began moving here from SoHo in the late 1980s and 1990s, as SoHo's rents rose. The Dia Art Foundation opened an exhibition space on West 22nd Street in 1987, and big dealers followed. Garages, with their high ceilings, large open spaces, and freight doors, were perfect for showing large contemporary works. Today, galleries like Gagosian, David Zwirner, and Pace operate huge spaces here, and Thursday evenings, when many shows open, the sidewalks fill with art lovers.

Now look at the massive building that fills the block between 26th and 27th Streets, along Eleventh Avenue, with continuous horizontal bands of windows wrapping around its rounded corners. This is the Starrett-Lehigh Building, completed in 1931, and it's one of the great industrial buildings of the twentieth century.

It was built as a joint venture between the Starrett construction family and the Lehigh Valley Railroad. The railroad had a freight yard here, and the building was designed so freight trains could enter the ground floor on tracks. Even more remarkable, trucks could drive into enormous elevators and be lifted directly to any of the upper floors, then drive right up to the tenants' doors. It was essentially a vertical freight yard.

Its architecture is equally striking. Instead of a traditional facade with vertical columns, the building has cantilevered concrete floors with ribbons of steel windows running continuously around it. It was celebrated by the Museum of Modern Art in an early exhibition on modern architecture as an example of the new International Style.

Like 111 Eighth Avenue, it later found new life with creative companies. Martha Stewart's media company had offices here, as have photographers, fashion companies, and tech startups. The interior's huge windows offer some of the best Hudson River views in the city.

deeper.title: Following the Art to Chelsea
deeper.text:
You heard that the galleries came here from SoHo. One dealer's story shows how that happened.

In October 1968, Paula Cooper opened a gallery in a loft on Prince Street, the first gallery in what would become SoHo. Her first show was a benefit for a student group protesting the Vietnam War. Over the next decades she championed Minimalist and conceptual artists, and SoHo grew into the center of the contemporary art world.

By the 1990s, SoHo had become a shopping district. Rents had soared, and the big open lofts that artists and dealers loved were turning into boutiques. Cooper looked west, to Chelsea's garages and warehouses, which were cheap, enormous, and a long walk from anywhere. In 1995 she bought a building on West Twenty-First Street, and in 1996 she opened there, in a soaring space that people compared to a cathedral. Other major dealers made the same move around the same time, and within a few years, Chelsea had replaced SoHo.

The galleries here are free and open to anyone, usually Tuesday through Saturday. Don't be shy about walking in. The people at the front desk may look forbidding, but you're welcome to look, and many will gladly tell you about the work. Try walking one of the gallery blocks, between Tenth and Eleventh Avenues in the low Twenties, and ducking into whatever catches your eye. You might find a single huge sculpture filling a former garage, a quiet room of drawings, or something you can't quite explain.

The art world keeps moving. As rents here have climbed, some galleries have moved again, to the Lower East Side or to Tribeca. But for now, these blocks remain one of the greatest free art museums in the world, spread across hundreds of storefronts.

deeper.title: A Freight Yard in the Sky
deeper.text:
The name Starrett-Lehigh joins a family of builders and a railroad, and the building tells the story of a partnership that didn't last.

The Lehigh Valley Railroad, which carried coal and freight from Pennsylvania, had no tracks into Manhattan. Like other railroads, it stopped at the New Jersey shore. So freight cars from its yard in Jersey City were loaded onto car floats, long barges with rails on their decks, and towed across the Hudson to its freight terminal here, where they were rolled ashore.

In 1930, the railroad joined with the Starrett family's real estate company to replace that old terminal with something new: a building where trains could pull in on the ground floor, and trucks could ride elevators to any of the nineteen floors above. The builders were Starrett Brothers and Eken, the same firm that was putting up the Empire State Building at the very same time. The designers were two brothers, Russell and Walter Cory, engineers who had studied at night at Cooper Union, working with the architect Yasuo Matsui.

The timing was terrible. The building opened in the depths of the Depression, when few businesses could afford to expand. William Starrett, one of the family's leading builders, died in 1932, and the railroad bought out the building, but by 1933 it was losing money. In 1944 the railroad gave up on it, and in 1966 the tracks were taken out.

The truck elevators, though, kept running, and in recent years they have even carried food trucks up into the building, like their freight-hauling ancestors.

So look up at those ribbons of windows and imagine freight cars floating across the river, rolling off the barges and into the ground floor of a skyscraper.

deeper.title: Look Closer: Trees and Stones
deeper.text:
Walk over to West Twenty-Second Street, between Tenth and Eleventh Avenues, and look at the sidewalk. Beside many of the street trees stands a tall, narrow column of dark stone, like a small standing stone from some ancient site. It's a work of art, and part of a much bigger one.

The German artist Joseph Beuys began a project called 7000 Oaks in 1982, at a great art exhibition in the city of Kassel. He had seven thousand basalt stones dumped in a huge pile in front of the museum there, and announced that each stone would be moved only when a tree was planted beside it. Over the next five years, as the trees went in around the city, the pile shrank. The project was finished in 1987, the year after Beuys died. He saw it as social sculpture: an artwork made by a whole community, and a way of greening a city.

In 1988, the Dia Art Foundation, whose building on this street you heard about, brought the idea to New York, planting five trees with basalt stones outside its doors. In 1996, Dia added more, along this block. Today there are dozens of pairs here, though construction has sometimes forced a few of the stones to be taken away for a while.

Look at how the trees and stones change together over time. The stones stay the same. The trees keep growing, until one day they'll tower over their stone companions. That contrast was the point.

There's one more connection worth knowing. In 2003, Dia opened a huge museum up the Hudson, in the town of Beacon, in a former factory where the National Biscuit Company once printed its boxes. So a trail of art and crackers runs from these blocks all the way up the river.

stops.title: Hudson Yards & the Vessel
stops.text:
End your walk at Hudson Yards, the cluster of glass towers rising at the northern end of the High Line, around West 33rd Street.

The towers you see are built on a platform over an active rail yard. Beneath your feet, the Long Island Rail Road stores commuter trains between rush hours. For decades, the yard was an enormous hole on the far west side of Manhattan. Plans to cover it went back to the 1950s. In the 2000s, the city tried to build a football stadium here for the New York Jets, as part of a bid for the 2012 Olympics. That plan collapsed. Instead, the city rezoned the area, and the developers Related Companies and Oxford Properties built Hudson Yards, which opened its first phase in 2019.

To build it, engineers drilled hundreds of caissons down to bedrock between the rail tracks and built a giant platform over the yard while trains continued to run. It is often described as the largest private real estate development in American history. The city also extended the 7 subway line to a new station here, which opened in 2015.

The towers house offices for companies including financial firms, media companies, and tech companies, as well as a shopping mall, apartments, and a hotel. Look up at 30 Hudson Yards, the tallest tower, which has an outdoor observation deck called Edge, jutting out from the building in a triangular point at about eleven hundred feet. It's one of the highest outdoor observation decks in the Western Hemisphere.

In the central plaza, you'll see the Vessel, a honeycomb-like structure of interlocking staircases, designed by Thomas Heatherwick, the designer of Little Island. It has about one hundred fifty four flights of stairs and was meant to be climbed. Access has been restricted at times for safety reasons, with added barriers on the upper levels.

Next to it, the building with the giant movable outer shell, on rails, is The Shed, a cultural center that can expand its size by rolling its shell outward over the adjacent plaza.

Hudson Yards has been controversial. Critics have called it a playground for the rich, and debated the tax incentives the city provided to support it. Admirers point to the engineering achievement and the economic activity it brought to a former rail yard. Either way, it represents the latest chapter of the west side's transformation, from freight trains and piers to the most expensive real estate in America, all in about a century.

deeper.title: The Stadium That Wasn't
deeper.text:
You heard that the city once planned a football stadium on this site. The fight over it was one of the fiercest in modern New York politics.

In the early 2000s, Mayor Michael Bloomberg and his deputy mayor, Dan Doctoroff, wanted to bring the Olympic Games to New York in 2012. The centerpiece was to be a stadium over the rail yards, built for the New York Jets, who played their home games in New Jersey. It would host the Olympics first, and then the Jets, with hundreds of millions of dollars of public money for the platform and the roof, including three hundred million dollars from the state.

The opposition was fierce. Many West Side residents didn't want a stadium in their neighborhood, and many critics thought the money should go elsewhere. The most determined opponent was Cablevision, the company that owned Madison Square Garden, a few blocks east, which feared the competition. It fought the stadium hard, and even made its own bid for the rail yards.

In March 2005, the transit authority, which owned the yards, chose the Jets' bid. The last hurdle was an obscure state board, the Public Authorities Control Board, where three officials each held a veto: the governor, the leader of the State Senate, and the speaker of the Assembly. On June 6th, 2005, the representatives of the Senate leader, Joseph Bruno, and the Assembly speaker, Sheldon Silver, declined to vote yes, and the stadium was dead.

A month later, the International Olympic Committee chose London for 2012. The Jets eventually built a new stadium in New Jersey, together with the Giants. And the city turned to a different plan for the yards: rezone the area, extend the subway, and let developers build the towers you see now.

Some people still wonder what this place would be like with a stadium in it. Others are glad it never happened. Either way, the land where it would have stood is now some of the most expensive real estate in the country.

deeper.title: The Subway That Came to Meet It
deeper.text:
You heard that the city extended the 7 train to a new station here. That station is one of the deepest in the subway system, and its story says a lot about how Hudson Yards was built.

Before the extension, the far West Side was a long walk from the nearest subway. Developers wouldn't build big towers here without one. So the city made an unusual bet. Instead of waiting for state and federal money, it paid for the extension itself, about two and a half billion dollars, by selling bonds through a new agency, the Hudson Yards Infrastructure Corporation. The bonds were to be paid back with future tax revenue from the buildings the subway would attract. In other words, the city borrowed against a neighborhood that didn't exist yet.

Tunnel boring machines dug a mile and a half of new tunnel from Times Square. The new station opened in September 2015, the first completely new station in the subway system since 1989, about a hundred and twenty five feet below the street.

To get people up and down from that depth, the station was given something new to the New York subway: two inclined elevators, which ride up and down at an angle alongside the escalators. They also caused trouble. Problems with the inclined elevators and the fire safety systems helped delay the station's opening by almost two years.

When you ride the long escalators down, notice the curved ceiling and the mosaics and the sheer depth of the place. Then remember what it represents: a subway built before the neighborhood, on the promise that a neighborhood would come. This time, it did.

deeper.title: The Shed, a Building on Wheels
deeper.text:
Look at the building next to the Vessel, the one with the quilted, puffy outer shell. That's The Shed, and part of it moves.

The Shed was designed by Diller Scofidio and Renfro, one of the firms behind the High Line, working with the Rockwell Group. It opened in 2019 as an arts center for every kind of performance and exhibition. Its fixed base building holds galleries and theaters. But its outer shell, a steel framework more than a hundred feet tall, sits on giant wheels, each six feet across, running on rails.

When the shell rolls out over the plaza next door, it creates a huge enclosed hall, about seventeen thousand square feet, for concerts and big events. When it rolls back, the plaza becomes open public space again. The shell weighs about eight million pounds, yet it travels the length of the plaza in about five minutes, moving at a quarter of a mile an hour. The engineers borrowed the technology from the giant gantry cranes that load and unload ships at container ports, a fitting choice on a waterfront where freight once ruled.

The shell's skin is made of a tough, clear plastic called ETFE, puffed into cushions like a quilt. It's far lighter than glass and lets daylight in.

The building is named for Michael Bloomberg, whose philanthropy helped pay for it. It's the Bloomberg Building. Next door, the honeycomb of stairs called the Vessel took the opposite approach: less a building than a giant sculpture you can climb.

Together, they say something about this whole neighborhood: built on top of a working rail yard, borrowing tools from the docks and the railroads, and still, at heart, a piece of the industrial West Side.

overview:
The far west side of lower Manhattan, from the Meatpacking District up through Chelsea to Hudson Yards, was for most of its history the city's back of house. This was where the goods came in.

Along the Hudson River, a continuous wall of piers handled ocean liners and freighters. Behind them ran the freight railroad tracks of the New York Central, which carried meat, milk, produce, and manufactured goods into the city. At first, the trains ran at street level down Tenth and Eleventh Avenues, so dangerous to pedestrians that Tenth Avenue was nicknamed Death Avenue, and the railroad employed men on horseback called West Side Cowboys to ride ahead of the trains waving red flags. In the 1930s the tracks were lifted onto an elevated viaduct that ran directly into the warehouses and factories. Today that viaduct is the High Line.

The warehouses and factories along the line included some of the great names in American industry. The National Biscuit Company, Nabisco, baked crackers and cookies here, including the first Oreo. Massive freight terminals were built so trucks and trains could deliver directly to upper floors. In the Meatpacking District, hundreds of slaughterhouses and packing plants processed meat for the city.

Inland, Chelsea itself has a gentler history. The name comes from an estate owned in the 1700s by Captain Thomas Clarke, who named it after the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London. His grandson, Clement Clarke Moore, developed the estate into a neighborhood of elegant rowhouses in the 1830s and 40s. In the late nineteenth century, West 23rd Street was the center of the American theater, and later an early center of the film industry.

After World War Two, shipping moved to container ports in New Jersey, trucks replaced trains, and industry left Manhattan. The piers rotted. The High Line was abandoned. The Meatpacking District became a mix of the remaining meat businesses and late night clubs. Then, starting in the 1990s, art galleries began moving to West Chelsea from SoHo, followed by restaurants, boutiques, and luxury condos.
