The High Line reopened as a park in 2009 and became one of the most influential urban design projects of the century, copied in cities around the world. And at the north end, Hudson Yards rose on a platform built over an active rail yard.

This is also, as it happens, one of the main centers of the tech industry in New York. Google has a cluster of buildings here, and much of the neighborhood's transformation has been driven by companies that wanted big, open, industrial floors for their offices. As you walk, you'll see how buildings designed for freight trains and meat hooks became homes for software engineers.

title: East Village
blurb: Peter Cooper and Lincoln, CBGB and punk, Little Germany's tragedy, the Yiddish Rialto, and Loisaida's gardens.

stops.title: Cooper Union & Astor Place
stops.text:
You're at Astor Place, the busy intersection where Lafayette Street, Fourth Avenue, the Bowery, and Eighth Street converge.

Start with the large brownstone building on the triangular block to the south. This is the Foundation Building of the Cooper Union, completed in 1859. It was founded by Peter Cooper, one of the most remarkable figures in American industrial history. Cooper had very little formal schooling, but he became a successful inventor and industrialist. He built the Tom Thumb, one of the first American-built steam locomotives, in 1830. He ran glue factories and ironworks, made rolled iron beams used in early fireproof buildings, and was a major backer of the first transatlantic telegraph cable. He even patented a gelatin dessert, decades before Jell-O.

Cooper wanted to give working people the education he never had. He founded Cooper Union to provide free education in science, engineering, and art, open to men and women, regardless of race or religion, which was radical for the time. For most of its history, tuition was free for all students.

Fun detail: Cooper was so convinced that the passenger elevator would soon be practical that he had a round shaft built into the Foundation Building, before a working elevator design existed. He assumed elevators would be cylindrical. Today, an elevator runs in that shaft.

The building's Great Hall, in the basement, is one of the most historically important rooms in America. On February twenty-seventh, 1860, a little-known Illinois lawyer named Abraham Lincoln gave a speech there arguing against the expansion of slavery into the western territories. The speech was carefully reasoned and widely reprinted, and it helped make Lincoln a serious contender for the Republican nomination for president. A photograph taken by Mathew Brady the same day became one of his most famous portraits. Lincoln later reportedly said that Brady and the Cooper Union speech made him president. The Great Hall has hosted presidents, suffragists, and civil rights leaders ever since.

Now look at the big black cube balanced on one corner in the middle of the plaza. That's Alamo, a sculpture by Tony Rosenthal, installed in 1967. If you push it, it spins.

The plaza's name honors John Jacob Astor, a German immigrant who made a fortune in the fur trade and then invested it in Manhattan real estate, becoming the richest man in America. Near here stood the Astor Opera House, site of the Astor Place Riot of 1849. The riot began as a rivalry between two actors, the American Edwin Forrest and the Englishman William Charles Macready, but it became a violent clash between working-class nativists and the upper-class patrons of the opera house. Militia troops fired into the crowd, killing over twenty people.

Across Lafayette Street, the large Italianate brownstone building is the Public Theater. It was originally the Astor Library, founded with a bequest from John Jacob Astor and one of the first free public libraries in the city. Its collection later became part of the New York Public Library. In the 1960s, the producer Joseph Papp saved the building from demolition and turned it into the Public Theater. Papp also founded Shakespeare in the Park. The Public premiered the musical Hair in 1967, A Chorus Line in 1975, and Hamilton in 2015, all of which went on to Broadway.

deeper.title: Right Makes Might
deeper.text:
You heard that Lincoln's speech in the Great Hall helped make him president. Here is how it happened. The invitation was to speak at Henry Ward Beecher's church in Brooklyn. Only when Lincoln reached New York did he learn that a club of young Republicans had taken charge of the evening and moved it here, to Peter Cooper's brand new hall. His fee was two hundred dollars.

Lincoln knew that eastern audiences thought of him as a western stump speaker, a rail splitter with funny stories. So he told no stories at all. He had spent weeks in the state library in Springfield reading old congressional records, and he built the speech on one question: what did the men who wrote the Constitution believe about slavery in the western territories? Of the thirty-nine who signed it, he showed, twenty-three had later acted on that very question, in Congress or elsewhere, and twenty-one of them, a majority of all thirty-nine, had acted as if Congress had every right to keep slavery out. The founders, he argued, had treated slavery as an evil to be contained, and Republicans stood exactly where the founders stood.

About fifteen hundred people came. Some remembered the tall, awkward man in a badly wrinkled new suit, and a high voice that put them off at first, until the argument took hold. He ended with a line people still quote: let us have faith that right makes might, and in that faith, let us, to the end, dare to do our duty as we understand it.

The next morning, New York papers printed the whole speech. Lincoln went on to speak across New England, partly so he could visit his son Robert at school in New Hampshire. Less than three months later, the Republican Party nominated him for president.

deeper.title: Voices in the Great Hall
deeper.text:
Lincoln was only the beginning. Before they were elected, Ulysses Grant, Grover Cleveland, William Howard Taft, Theodore Roosevelt and Barack Obama all spoke from this stage. So did Frederick Douglass, and the suffrage leaders Susan B. Anthony and Victoria Woodhull.

In 1867, a young humorist from the West named Mark Twain gave his first New York lecture here, about the Sandwich Islands, as Hawaii was then called. He wrote afterward that the night was a failure and a success at once. In 1870, the hall filled for Red Cloud, the Lakota leader who had forced the army to abandon its forts along the Bozeman Trail. Through an interpreter, he told New Yorkers that his people had been handed papers to sign that no one honestly explained, and asked the East to help them get fair treatment.

And on the night of November twenty-second, 1909, the hall was packed with young garment workers, most of them immigrant women from the tenements to the south. For hours they listened to union leaders, Samuel Gompers among them, debate whether to call a general strike of the shirtwaist makers. Then a twenty-three-year-old worker named Clara Lemlich, who had recently been beaten on a picket line, asked for the floor. Speaking in Yiddish, she said she had no more patience for talk, and moved that a general strike be declared now. The hall erupted. The chairman asked the crowd to raise their right hands and swear an old oath: if I turn traitor to the cause I now pledge, may this hand wither from the arm I now raise.

Within days, some twenty thousand workers walked out, in what became known as the Uprising of the Twenty Thousand. By February, nearly every shop had signed a union contract. One that held out was the Triangle Waist Company, on Washington Place. A year later, it burned.

deeper.title: The Shakespeare Riot
deeper.text:
You heard that the Astor Place Riot began as a feud between two actors. It had been simmering for years. When the American star Edwin Forrest toured Britain in the 1840s, he was hissed in London and blamed his English rival, William Charles Macready. Soon after, Forrest stood up in a theater in Edinburgh and loudly hissed Macready's Hamlet. To his fans back home, Forrest was the voice of a rough young democracy, and Macready was the darling of the snobs.

The Astor Opera House, just west of here, was built for those snobs. It even had a dress code. So when Macready came to play Macbeth there in May 1849, the Bowery's working men took it personally. On the first night, the gallery pelted him with eggs and even chairs, and the play had to stop. Macready meant to sail home. But forty-seven prominent New Yorkers, Washington Irving and the young Herman Melville among them, signed an open letter begging him to stay, and promising that order would be kept.

The letter only made things worse. Handbills went up around the city asking: working men, shall Americans or English rule in this city? On May tenth, while Macready finished Macbeth under police guard, thousands outside hurled paving stones at the building. The Seventh Regiment was called out, and when the stones kept coming, the soldiers fired into the crowd. At least twenty-two people died. Macready slipped out in disguise and left the city.

One of the men convicted of stirring up the mob was a writer named Edward Judson, better known as Ned Buntline. He served a year on Blackwell's Island. Twenty years later he found a better use for his gift for spectacle: he made a young army scout named William Cody the hero of his dime novels, and turned him into Buffalo Bill.

deeper.title: Look Closer: Columns and Beavers
deeper.text:
Two details nearby are easy to walk past.

First, find the row of tall marble columns on the west side of Lafayette Street, facing the Public Theater. This is Colonnade Row, four survivors of a terrace of nine grand houses finished around 1833 and named La Grange Terrace, after the Marquis de Lafayette's country estate in France. Behind one continuous screen of Corinthian columns, each family had its own house, so the whole row read as a single palace. Members of the Astor family lived here, and so did Warren Delano, grandfather of Franklin Delano Roosevelt. The marble is said to have been cut by prisoners at Sing Sing. The other five houses were torn down long ago, and the survivors are grimy and patched, but squint and you can see one of the grandest addresses in the New York of Andrew Jackson's day.

Second, go down into the Astor Place subway station and look along the platform walls. Every so often you'll find a glazed terra cotta plaque of a beaver. The station opened in 1904 on the city's first subway line, and its designers chose the beaver as a nod to the fur trade that made John Jacob Astor rich. More than a century later, the beavers are still there.

When you come back up, look at the little cast iron and glass pavilion over the uptown entrance. It looks like 1904, but it's a replica, built in 1985 from old photographs of the kiosks that once stood over subway stairs all over the city.

stops.title: CBGB & the Merchant's House
stops.text:
You're on the Bowery, at 315 Bowery, near Bleecker Street. In 1973, a club owner named Hilly Kristal opened a bar here called CBGB, which stood for Country, Bluegrass, and Blues, the kind of music he planned to book. That's not what happened.

In the 1970s, the Bowery was still skid row, lined with flophouses, and CBGB was a narrow, dingy room with a long bar and a tiny stage. Kristal had a policy that bands had to play their own original music. A group of young musicians began playing there, and between about 1974 and 1977, CBGB became the birthplace of American punk rock and new wave. The Ramones played their early shows here, short, fast, loud songs that stripped rock and roll to its basics. So did Patti Smith, Television, Blondie, and the Talking Heads. These bands sounded nothing alike, but they shared a stripped-down, do-it-yourself aesthetic that changed popular music.

CBGB's bathrooms were legendarily filthy, and its awning, with its white letters on a dark background, became an iconic image, endlessly reproduced on T-shirts. The club closed in 2006 after a rent dispute, and the space later became a high-end clothing store, which preserved some of the graffiti-covered walls.

Now walk a couple of blocks west to East Fourth Street, between the Bowery and Lafayette Street, and look for a red brick house with a Greek Revival doorway at number 29. This is the Merchant's House Museum, and it's a time capsule from an entirely different world.

Built in 1832, it was bought in 1835 by Seabury Tredwell, a wealthy hardware merchant. At that time, this street was one of the most fashionable addresses in the city. The Tredwell family lived here for almost a century. The youngest daughter, Gertrude Tredwell, was born in the house and lived there until she died in 1933. As the neighborhood changed around her, she kept the house and furnishings almost exactly as they had been. A relative turned it into a museum in 1936.

It's one of very few nineteenth-century family homes in New York preserved with original furniture, clothing, and belongings intact. It's also said to be among the most haunted houses in Manhattan: staff and visitors have reported sightings of Gertrude Tredwell. The museum offers candlelit ghost tours around Halloween. It's a reminder that before the Bowery was skid row, and before it was punk, it was the edge of an elegant residential neighborhood.

deeper.title: Sunday Nights on the Bowery
deeper.text:
The full name on Hilly Kristal's awning was longer than CBGB. It read C B G B and O M F U G, for Country, Bluegrass, Blues and Other Music For Uplifting Gormandizers, a gormandizer being someone with a large appetite.

The other music arrived in the spring of 1974. A young band called Television, with the guitarists Tom Verlaine and Richard Lloyd, needed somewhere to play, and their manager, Terry Ork, kept pushing Kristal to let them in. Kristal finally gave them Sunday nights, his slowest of the week. By the band's own account, their first Sunday was March thirty-first, 1974. They brought their friends, the friends brought theirs, and the narrow room found its purpose. That August, four young men from Queens in leather jackets and torn jeans, all calling themselves Ramone, played there for the first time.

Kristal ran the club for more than thirty years, through punk and the hardcore years that followed, until a long fight with the landlord closed it. The last show, on October fifteenth, 2006, belonged to Patti Smith. She played for more than three hours and ended with her song Elegie, reading out the names of musicians and friends who had died. Kristal himself died the next summer.

Before you leave, walk a few steps north to the corner of East Second Street and look up, way up. The street sign there reads Joey Ramone Place, named in 2003 for the band's singer, who had died two years earlier. It became the most stolen street sign in New York, so in 2010 the city raised it to about twenty feet above the sidewalk. Marky Ramone, the band's drummer, joked that now you'd have to be a basketball player to see it.

deeper.title: Monk at the Five Spot
deeper.text:
Before punk, the Bowery had jazz. Just to the north, at number 5 Cooper Square, stood a plain workingman's bar called the Five Spot Café, run by the Termini brothers, Joe and Iggy. In the mid-1950s they started booking jazz, and painters and poets from the cheap lofts nearby made it their hangout.

In the summer of 1957, Thelonious Monk began a run there that lasted about six months. Monk had spent years barely able to work in New York, after the police took away the cabaret card that nightclub performers then needed. Now he had a steady stage, and a new tenor saxophonist, John Coltrane, who had just kicked heroin. Night after night, Coltrane worked his way through Monk's strange, angular tunes, and other musicians came to listen. Coltrane said later that if you lost track of where Monk was going, you'd feel as if you'd stepped into an empty elevator shaft.

In November 1959, the Five Spot introduced New York to Ornette Coleman, whose quartet played without any set pattern of chords. Critics and musicians packed the room to argue over whether it was genius or noise. That same year, the poet Frank O'Hara wrote The Day Lady Died on the day Billie Holiday died. The poem ends here, with the memory of a night at the Five Spot when she whispered a song along the keyboard to her pianist, Mal Waldron, and everyone, O'Hara included, stopped breathing.

In the early 1960s the club moved a few blocks north to St. Mark's Place, and it closed later that decade. The original building is gone, but for a few years this was one of the most important rooms in jazz.

deeper.title: Four Women on the Fourth Floor
deeper.text:
The Tredwells were not alone in their house on Fourth Street. Climb to the top floor of the museum and you reach two small rooms under the roof where the family's servants slept. The state census of 1855 lists four of them, all women, all born in Ireland.

They had come in the years of the Great Famine, when about a million Irish people died and more than a million left. By the 1850s, roughly one New Yorker in four had been born in Ireland, and for young Irish women the most common work was domestic service: cooking, carrying coal and water up and down the stairs, scrubbing, washing and sewing. A bell at the top of the stairs could summon them at any hour. The museum considers these rooms the oldest intact place in New York City where Irish immigrants are known to have lived.

The house itself survived on a string of near misses. By the 1960s it was crumbling, and the blocks around it had filled with factories and warehouses. When New York passed its landmarks law in 1965, after the outcry over the demolition of the old Pennsylvania Station, this house was among the first buildings protected, and the very first in Manhattan. In 1981 its interior became a landmark too, one of a small number of interiors in the city with that protection. In recent years, its defenders have fought construction next door that they fear could crack its old walls.

stops.title: McSorley's & Little Ukraine
stops.text:
You're on East Seventh Street, between Second and Third Avenues. Look for McSorley's Old Ale House, at number 15, with its sawdust floor and dark wood interior. McSorley's claims to date from 1854, which would make it one of the oldest continuously operating bars in New York, though some historians think it opened a bit later. Its motto is: Be good or be gone.

McSorley's serves only two kinds of beer, light and dark, and you order them two mugs at a time. The walls are covered with a dense layer of old photographs, newspaper clippings, and memorabilia, much of it untouched for over a century. Above the bar hang wishbones, said to have been left by young men going off to fight in World War One, intended to be collected when they returned. The ones still hanging belonged to those who didn't come back.

For most of its history, McSorley's banned women. It finally admitted them in 1970, after two lawyers from the National Organization for Women sued and won, and New York City passed a law banning sex discrimination in public places. Even then, it didn't have a women's restroom until 1986.

Now look east along Seventh Street, toward Second Avenue. This stretch is the heart of Little Ukraine. Ukrainians settled here starting in the late nineteenth century, and a larger wave arrived after World War Two, many of them people displaced by the war and fleeing Soviet rule. Look for St. George Ukrainian Catholic Church, with its large dome, on Seventh Street. Every year, its parish holds a Ukrainian festival.

At the corner of Second Avenue and Ninth Street, look for Veselka, a Ukrainian restaurant open since 1954, famous for its pierogi, borscht, and blintzes, and open nearly around the clock. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Veselka became a gathering place for the community and raised money for relief efforts. The Ukrainian Museum, on East Sixth Street, holds a fine collection of folk art, including painted Easter eggs called pysanky.

Next door to Veselka, just south on Second Avenue, is the Ukrainian National Home, for decades a gathering place for the community. Watch, too, for the occasional blue and yellow flag in windows. The community has been shrinking for decades, but it remains visible here.

deeper.title: The Woman Who Owned a Men's Bar
deeper.text:
McSorley's founder, John McSorley, was an Irish immigrant remembered as Old John. After he died, his son Bill kept the saloon almost exactly as his father had left it, which is one reason the walls look the way they do. The painter John Sloan drank here and painted the bar several times, starting in 1912. The poet E. E. Cummings wrote a poem that opens with him sitting in McSorley's while it snows outside. And in 1940, Joseph Mitchell wrote a long, loving portrait of the place for The New Yorker, called The Old House at Home, after the name the saloon carried in its early days.

In 1936, Bill McSorley sold the bar to one of his regulars, a retired policeman named Daniel O'Connell. Within a few years O'Connell died and left it to his daughter, Dorothy O'Connell Kirwan. So for decades, the most famous men-only bar in New York belonged to a woman.

She had promised her father that she would not disturb the customers, and as the story is told, she kept her word, coming in only on Sundays, when the bar was closed, or stopping at the door to raise a glass when a round was on the house. The bartenders ran the place, the old rules held, and the sawdust stayed on the floor.

When women were finally let in, in 1970, the walls did not change, and neither did the beer. But remember, as you look around, that for decades the keeper of New York's most famous men's bar was a woman, honoring a promise to stay outside it.

deeper.title: Lincoln's Ale and Houdini's Handcuffs
deeper.text:
A bar this old collects legends the way its walls collect dust, and McSorley's is happy to share them.

The biggest is that Abraham Lincoln stopped in for an ale after his speech at Cooper Union, a few blocks away, in February 1860. It makes a good story, but there is no record that he ever set foot inside, and Lincoln barely drank at all.

Then there are the handcuffs. Look for a pair fastened to the bar, and another hanging higher up. Harry Houdini, the story goes, was a regular around the turn of the twentieth century, and left a pair of his cuffs behind. Which pair, if either, is a matter of barroom debate, since one has been found to carry a serial number from after Houdini's death. Some regulars add that if you see a cat sitting in the window, it is Houdini, back for a visit.

You heard that the wishbones over the bar were hung by young men leaving for the First World War. That too is the bar's own story, passed down rather than written down. What is certain is that each generation of owners has left them where they hung.

Legends like these do a job. They tie a working man's saloon to the great names of the city, and they give every regular something to tell a newcomer. Listen at the bar long enough and someone will tell you one of them as gospel.

deeper.title: Taras Shevchenko Place
deeper.text:
Look for the short lane beside St. George's church, running between Sixth and Seventh Streets. Its sign reads Taras Shevchenko Place. Until 1978 it was Hall Place, a forgettable alley. That spring, as the parish dedicated its new domed church, Mayor Ed Koch signed a law renaming the lane for the man Ukrainians consider their national poet.

Taras Shevchenko was born in 1814 a serf, the property of a landowner in central Ukraine. He had a gift for drawing, and his owner took him to Saint Petersburg, where artists noticed him. In 1838 they bought his freedom, raising the money by raffling off a portrait painted by Karl Bryullov. Two years later Shevchenko published a book of poems called Kobzar, named for the wandering minstrels of the Ukrainian countryside. Writing in the language of peasants, which the Russian Empire treated as a mere dialect, he helped turn it into a literary language.

His poems mourned his country's bondage, and the czar's government punished him for them. In 1847 he was sent into exile as a common soldier on the edge of the Kazakh steppe, and forbidden to write or paint. He kept writing anyway, in tiny notebooks he hid in the tops of his boots. He was freed after ten years, and died in 1861, just as the czar was proclaiming the end of serfdom.

Ukrainian exiles, including the ones who rebuilt this neighborhood after the Second World War, carried his portrait and his poems with them. Look for his face in Ukrainian shops and churches. You'll also find him on monuments from Kyiv to Washington.

stops.title: St. Mark's Place
stops.text:
You're on St. Mark's Place, the stretch of Eighth Street between Third Avenue and Avenue A. It's probably the most famous street in the East Village.

It started out respectable. In the 1830s, the street was lined with fine Federal-style houses. Look for number 4 St. Mark's Place, the Hamilton-Holly House, built in 1831. Colonel Alexander Hamilton Junior, the son of the Alexander Hamilton buried at Trinity Church, lived there with his sister Eliza for a time.

By the late nineteenth century, the street was part of Little Germany, lined with German clubs and halls. At 19 to 25 St. Mark's Place stood the Arlington Hall, and later a Polish social hall called the Polski Dom Narodowy. In 1966, Andy Warhol rented the space for his multimedia show, the Exploding Plastic Inevitable, featuring the Velvet Underground and Nico, with light shows, film projections, and dancing. The building later became a nightclub called the Electric Circus, one of the first psychedelic discotheques.

In the late 1960s, St. Mark's Place was the East Coast capital of the hippie counterculture, packed with head shops, poster stores, and young runaways. In the 1970s and 80s it became the main drag of punk. The clothing store Trash and Vaudeville, which outfitted punk and rock musicians for decades, was a fixture of the street. Its owners have said that the Ramones, Debbie Harry, and many others shopped there.

Near Avenue A, look for the pair of tenement buildings at 96 and 98 St. Mark's Place. Their facade appears on the cover of Led Zeppelin's 1975 album Physical Graffiti, with the windows cut out on the album cover. The Rolling Stones also filmed their 1981 music video for Waiting on a Friend in front of these buildings.

In recent decades, St. Mark's Place became known for something else: Japanese food. Starting in the 1980s, a cluster of Japanese restaurants, izakayas, and shops opened on and around the street, giving the area the nickname Little Tokyo.

The famous Gem Spa newsstand, at the corner of St. Mark's Place and Second Avenue, sold what many considered the best egg cream in the city for decades. An egg cream, by the way, contains neither egg nor cream: it's chocolate syrup, milk, and seltzer. Gem Spa closed in 2020, another casualty of the neighborhood's changing economics.

deeper.title: Number 77
deeper.text:
Walk east toward Avenue A and look for number 77. Two very different men passed through its doors.

In the winter of 1917, its basement held the offices of Novy Mir, The New World, a Russian-language socialist paper for the city's immigrant radicals. One of its editors was Nikolai Bukharin, later a leader of Soviet Russia. That January a new writer joined them, just deported from France and Spain: Leon Trotsky. Trotsky lived with his family in the Bronx, but he spent his days here, writing fierce articles against the First World War and speaking in halls around the neighborhood. In March came the news that the czar had fallen. Within weeks Trotsky sailed for Russia, and by the end of the year he and Bukharin were helping lead a revolution.

Thirty-six years later, the poet W. H. Auden moved into an apartment upstairs. A plaque by the door says he lived here from 1953 to 1972. By then Auden was one of the most celebrated poets in the English language, and friends remembered his apartment as cold, cluttered and run down, with books and papers everywhere and pipes that froze in winter. He kept a famously strict schedule, working through the morning and serving cocktails at a set hour. He stayed through the arrival of the hippies, and watched the street change around him for almost twenty years. He left New York in 1972, and died the following year.

So the same doorway saw a revolutionary planning to overturn an empire, and a poet who wrote some of the century's most famous lines about love, grief and the city. St. Mark's Place has always had room for both.

deeper.title: Look Closer: Two Old Houses
deeper.text:
Two buildings on this street hold its whole history in their walls.

First, between Second and Third Avenues, find number 12, with its ornate front. High on the facade, in raised letters, is its original German name, which translates as the German-American Shooting Society. It was built in 1888 and 1889 as the clubhouse of a marksmanship club of about fourteen hundred members, organized into two dozen companies, who met here between their shooting contests. Look for the society's emblem and its German motto, which means unity makes strength. The members sold the building in 1920, as Little Germany emptied out, and the city made it a landmark in 2001. It is one of the few buildings left that still announces Kleindeutschland in its own language.

Then go back to number 4, the Hamilton-Holly House you heard about, built in 1831 for an age of carriages and calling cards. For about forty years, until 2016, it was the home of Trash and Vaudeville, the punk and rock clothing store whose racks of leather and studs dressed musicians from all over the neighborhood. Picture Alexander Hamilton's son climbing that stoop, and then the crowd that climbed it a hundred and forty years later.

As you walk the rest of the street, read it the same way. Look above the shop signs, at the cornices, the window frames and the old carved names, and you'll see a nineteenth-century street still standing behind the twenty-first.

deeper.title: Who Invented the Egg Cream?
deeper.text:
You heard that an egg cream contains neither egg nor cream. So where did the name come from? Nobody knows, and New Yorkers have argued about it for generations.

The most famous story involves a candy store owner named Louis Auster, who sold egg creams at his shop near Second Avenue and Seventh Street, a block from here, around the turn of the twentieth century. His family says he invented the drink, made his own chocolate syrup in secret, and turned down a fortune from a big ice cream chain that wanted the formula. The last batch of that syrup, they say, was made in the 1970s. The sociologist Daniel Bell credited someone else, a candy store man known as Uncle Hymie, on Second Avenue near Eighth Street. Brooklyn has its own claimants.

As for the name, take your pick. Some say egg comes from the Yiddish word echt, meaning genuine, so an egg cream was the real thing. Some say customers asked for a chocolate A cream, made with grade A milk, and the A became egg. Others think the name simply made a cheap drink sound rich. The dullest explanation may be the right one. Dictionary researchers have found nineteenth-century drinks called egg creams that really did contain eggs and cream, and the name may have stuck after the ingredients changed.

What is not in dispute is the method: a tall glass, a little cold milk, a hard blast of seltzer to raise a foam, and chocolate syrup stirred in. The classic syrup is Fox's U-bet, made in Brooklyn. Order one, and you are drinking an argument that is more than a century old.

stops.title: St. Mark's Church in-the-Bowery
stops.text:
At the corner of Second Avenue and East 10th Street, set back from the street in a small churchyard, stands St. Mark's Church in-the-Bowery. It is one of the oldest churches in New York.

This land was part of Peter Stuyvesant's farm. Stuyvesant, the peg-legged director-general of New Amsterdam who surrendered the colony to the English in 1664, built a family chapel here in the 1660s. He was buried in a vault beneath that chapel in 1672. The current church was built on the same site in 1799, making it among the oldest church buildings in Manhattan, second only to St. Paul's Chapel. The steeple was added in the 1820s, and the cast iron portico in the 1850s. Stuyvesant's remains are still in the vault beneath the church, and there's a bust of him in the churchyard. Some say his ghost walks the grounds, tapping his wooden leg.

Notice that the church doesn't line up with the street grid. It's oriented to Stuyvesant Street, a diagonal street just to the west, which follows an old road through the Stuyvesant farm. Stuyvesant Street is one of the only streets in Manhattan that runs true east-west, as opposed to the grid, which is tilted about twenty nine degrees. It's lined with historic houses, including the Stuyvesant-Fish House, built in 1804, and the charming Renwick Triangle, a group of townhouses designed in the 1860s.

In the twentieth century, St. Mark's became one of the most artistically adventurous churches in the city. In the 1920s, its rector hosted dancers, poets, and the architect Frank Lloyd Wright, who designed a tower for the property that was never built. Since 1966, the church has been home to the Poetry Project, where poets like Allen Ginsberg, Patti Smith, and many others have read their work. It also hosts experimental dance and theater.

In 1978, the church was badly damaged by fire. It was restored with the help of neighborhood volunteers, many of them young people trained in construction skills as part of the restoration. A reminder that in this neighborhood, even a two-hundred-year-old church is part of the creative scene.

deeper.title: The Merchant Prince's Missing Bones
deeper.text:
In the spring of 1876, one of the richest men in America, Alexander Turney Stewart, was laid in his family's vault in this churchyard. Stewart was an Irish immigrant who had built a dry goods shop into the first great American department store, first the Marble Palace on Broadway at Chambers Street, then the even bigger Iron Palace, a few blocks west of here on Broadway at Tenth Street.

On the morning of November seventh, 1878, the church's sexton noticed fresh earth over the Stewart vault. Someone had dug down in the night, broken open the coffin and carried off the body.

The theft was real, and it made headlines around the world. Letters arrived demanding a ransom, at one point reported as a quarter of a million dollars, and the executor of the estate, Judge Henry Hilton, refused to pay. Detectives chased false leads for years. What came next is the part that has never been proved. According to the story told ever since, Stewart's widow, Cornelia, quietly made her own deal and paid about twenty thousand dollars, and one night, on a lonely country road, a bag of bones was handed over. The remains were said to have been placed in the Cathedral of the Incarnation in Garden City, on Long Island, the planned town Stewart had founded, where his widow built the cathedral in his memory.

No one has ever shown that the bones were really his, or even that the exchange took place. No one was convicted of the theft. Somewhere, perhaps, Alexander Stewart is still missing.

deeper.title: Stuyvesant's Pear Tree
deeper.text:
Walk over to Third Avenue and up to Thirteenth Street, and look for a small tablet on the northeast corner. It marks the spot where, for more than two centuries, a single pear tree grew.

According to tradition, Peter Stuyvesant brought the tree from Holland in 1647, the year he arrived to take charge of New Amsterdam, and planted it on his farm. The farm became the city, but the tree stayed. As the street grid crept north and Third Avenue was cut through, the old pear tree survived at the corner, and New Yorkers came to see it as a living link to the Dutch colony. It was said to bear fruit almost to the end.

The end came in 1867. A section of its trunk was saved, and it is now in the collection of the New-York Historical Society.

In 1890, the Holland Society, whose members descend from the colony's early Dutch settlers, put up a bronze tablet that reads: On this corner grew Petrus Stuyvesant's pear tree. The tablet later went missing from the corner for decades, and was put back in 2005. A couple of years before that, a new pear tree was planted at the corner in memory of the old one.

It is a small thing to look for, but think of what it means. A tree planted by the last Dutch governor of New Amsterdam was still putting out blossoms every spring while horse cars rolled down Third Avenue and soldiers came home from the Civil War. For more than half of New York's history, you could have picked a pear from Peter Stuyvesant's garden.

deeper.title: Look Closer: The Churchyard's Company
deeper.text:
Before you leave, take a slow walk around the churchyard and the street beside it.

Look for the bronze bust of Peter Stuyvesant. It was a gift in 1915 from Queen Wilhelmina and the government of the Netherlands, made by the Dutch sculptor Toon Dupuis, and given, its inscription says, to the people of New York in trust of this church.

Stuyvesant has company. Daniel Tompkins, governor of New York and vice president under James Monroe, is buried here, a good reason to remember him before you reach the park that carries his name. Commodore Matthew Perry, who forced Japan to open its ports to American ships in the 1850s, was laid in a vault here too, though his body was later moved to Rhode Island.

At the front gate, on either side, stands a sculpture of a Native American man, one called Inspiration and the other Aspiration. They are by Solon Borglum, who grew up on the western frontier and spent his career portraying cowboys and Native Americans. His brother Gutzon led the carving of Mount Rushmore.

Finally, cross to Stuyvesant Street, the diagonal street beside the church, and find number 21, a Federal-style brick house built around 1804 for Peter Stuyvesant's great-great-granddaughter Elizabeth and her husband, Nicholas Fish. Their son, born here in 1808, was named Hamilton, after his father's friend Alexander Hamilton. Hamilton Fish grew up to be governor of New York, a senator, and secretary of state under Ulysses Grant. Today the house belongs to Cooper Union, and the college's president lives in it.

stops.title: The Yiddish Rialto
stops.text:
Walk north along Second Avenue to East 12th Street. In the early twentieth century, the stretch of Second Avenue from Houston Street to about 14th Street was the Yiddish Rialto, the center of Yiddish theater in America and, arguably, in the world.

At its height, in the 1910s and 1920s, there were more than a dozen Yiddish theaters in the area, presenting everything from melodramas and musical comedies to serious adaptations of Shakespeare and Ibsen in Yiddish. Audiences of immigrant workers packed the theaters, cheered and booed, and treated stars like royalty. Some great performers began here. The actor Paul Muni started in Yiddish theater before becoming a Hollywood star. Molly Picon became a beloved comedic star. Boris Thomashefsky and Jacob Adler were among the great actor-managers of the era. Jacob Adler's daughter, Stella Adler, later became one of the most influential acting teachers in America, teaching Marlon Brando and many others.

Look at the theater at the corner of Second Avenue and 12th Street. It's now a movie theater, the Village East by Angelika, but it was built in 1926 as the Yiddish Art Theatre, commissioned by the businessman Louis Jaffe for the actor-director Maurice Schwartz. Its interior features an extravagant Moorish-style ceiling with a giant Star of David. If you go in to see a movie, look up.

A few blocks south, at the corner of Second Avenue and 10th Street, look down at the sidewalk for small stars with names on them. This is the Yiddish Walk of Fame, honoring stars of the Yiddish stage. For decades it was in front of the Second Avenue Deli, a famous kosher deli that operated here from 1954 until 2006, before moving uptown.

Yiddish theater declined as immigration was cut off after 1924, as the children of immigrants assimilated and moved away, and as movies and radio took over. The Holocaust destroyed the European Yiddish-speaking world that sustained it. But its influence on American entertainment is enormous: many of the comedians, actors, songwriters, and producers who shaped Broadway, Hollywood, and television came out of this world.

deeper.title: The Jewish King Lear
deeper.text:
The Yiddish stage made its own royalty, and the greatest of them was Jacob Adler. Born in Odessa, he reached New York after years of touring, tall and commanding, and his fans called him the Great Eagle, since adler means eagle.

In 1892, a Russian-born writer named Jacob Gordin wrote a play for him called The Jewish King Lear. Gordin moved Shakespeare's story to a prosperous Jewish family in nineteenth-century Russia, borrowing too from Turgenev's King Lear of the Steppes: a proud father divides his fortune among his daughters and is cast out by those he trusted. Adler's performance was a sensation, and the play became his signature, revived again and again. It also marked a turning point. Yiddish theater had leaned on improvised clowning and melodrama, and Gordin insisted that actors speak the lines as written and play real people. Some historians date the golden age of Yiddish theater in New York from that production.

Stars like Adler and his rival Boris Thomashefsky, whose grandson is the conductor Michael Tilson Thomas, had fans so devoted that they formed clubs, called patriots, to cheer their favorite and jeer the competition.

A stroke ended Adler's career in 1920, and he died in 1926. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported that fifty thousand people attended his funeral. His children carried the name on. Luther Adler acted on Broadway and in Hollywood, and Jacob's daughter Stella became the acting teacher you heard about, who passed the passion of the Yiddish stage on to generations of American actors.

deeper.title: The Thirty-Dollar Song
deeper.text:
In 1932, the composer Sholom Secunda and the lyricist Jacob Jacobs wrote a love song for a Yiddish musical comedy called I Would If I Could. The show is long forgotten, but one song from it is not: Bei Mir Bistu Shein, which means, roughly, to me you're beautiful.

Secunda, a trained composer who wrote for the Second Avenue stage for decades, sold the rights to a small Brooklyn publisher of Yiddish music for thirty dollars, and split the money with Jacobs. For a song from a Yiddish operetta, it seemed a fair price.

Then the song escaped from Second Avenue. The songwriter Sammy Cahn told the story that he first heard it at the Apollo Theater in Harlem, sung in Yiddish by two Black performers, Johnnie and George, to an audience that went wild for it. Others claimed they had found it first. Either way, Cahn and Saul Chaplin wrote English lyrics, and in November 1937 three young sisters from Minnesota, the Andrews Sisters, recorded it, with the title spelled the German way. It became the most popular song in America the following year, and launched their career. The money went to the publishers and the record companies, not to the men who wrote it.

In 1961 the copyright ran out and the rights came back to Secunda and Jacobs, who at last earned something from their song. By then, millions of people who had never heard of the Yiddish Rialto had sung along to a tune born a few blocks from here.

deeper.title: The Yiddish Algonquin
deeper.text:
After the curtain came down on Second Avenue, the actors went out to eat, and for more than forty years the place to go was the Café Royal, at the corner of Second Avenue and Twelfth Street.

From 1908 until 1952, the Royal was the living room of the Yiddish world. Actors, playwrights, poets, critics and producers argued over coffee and cookies, made deals, settled feuds and started new ones. The journalist and poet Judd Teller called it the Yiddish writers' Algonquin and the Yiddish actors' Sardi's. The playwright Hy Kraft based a 1942 Broadway comedy, Café Crown, on it.

Two years after the Royal closed, the Second Avenue Deli opened a couple of blocks south, at Tenth Street, and took up its role. Its founder, Abe Lebewohl, an immigrant who arrived after the Second World War, built it into an institution famous for pastrami, chopped liver and matzo ball soup. He loved the Yiddish theater, and in the 1980s he set the stars of the Yiddish Walk of Fame into the sidewalk outside his door.

On March fourth, 1996, Lebewohl was shot and killed while taking the day's receipts to the bank. The crime has never been solved. His family kept the deli going, and when it lost its lease, they moved it uptown. The stars stayed behind in the Second Avenue sidewalk, worn down by the shoes of everyone who has walked over them since.

stops.title: Tompkins Square Park & the General Slocum
stops.text:
You're in Tompkins Square Park, between Avenues A and B and 7th and 10th Streets. It has been the center stage of the neighborhood's dramas for over a century and a half.

In the nineteenth century, the park was the heart of Little Germany. It was also a gathering place for protests. In January 1874, in the depths of an economic depression, thousands of unemployed workers gathered here to demand public works jobs. Police charged the crowd on horseback, beating demonstrators indiscriminately. The Tompkins Square Riot became a landmark event in American labor history. One young man who was there, a cigar maker named Samuel Gompers, later founded the American Federation of Labor. He said the experience taught him the importance of practical, disciplined organizing.

Now look for a small marble fountain near the north side of the park, showing a boy and a girl looking out to sea. This is the General Slocum memorial, and it marks one of the worst disasters in New York history.

On June fifteenth, 1904, the members of St. Mark's Evangelical Lutheran Church, a German congregation on East Sixth Street, chartered a paddle-wheel steamboat called the General Slocum for their annual Sunday school picnic. More than thirteen hundred people boarded, most of them women and children, since the men were at work. As the boat steamed up the East River, a fire broke out. The crew was poorly trained, the life preservers were rotten and useless, and the fire hoses were rotten too. The captain kept steaming forward instead of beaching the boat immediately. More than a thousand people died, burned or drowned, within sight of shore.

It was the deadliest single-day disaster in New York City's history until September eleventh, 2001. The tragedy devastated Little Germany. So many families lost wives and children that many survivors couldn't bear to stay. The German community, which had already begun migrating uptown, largely moved away to Yorkville on the Upper East Side.

The park has other stories. Under one of the large elms, look for a plaque. In 1966, the Indian spiritual teacher A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada held a public chanting session under this tree, and this is often considered the founding moment of the Hare Krishna movement in America. The jazz saxophonist Charlie Parker lived in a townhouse facing the park on Avenue B in the early 1950s, and a jazz festival is held here in his honor every summer.

In 1988, the park was the scene of another riot, when police tried to enforce a curfew to clear out homeless encampments, and clashed violently with protesters. The park was closed for a renovation in 1991 and reopened in 1992. It's now a lively, much-loved neighborhood park, with a famous dog run, one of the first in the city.

deeper.title: The Island at the End of the Voyage
deeper.text:
You heard that the General Slocum's captain kept steaming forward instead of turning for shore. He was heading for North Brother Island, a small island in the East River off the Bronx.

The island held Riverside Hospital, the city's hospital for contagious diseases, and as the burning boat bore down on it, the hospital's staff ran to the water. Nurses, doctors, orderlies and even patients waded in and formed human chains, pulling the living and the dead from the river. The boat finally grounded about twenty-five feet from the island's shore.

A few years later, the island received its most famous patient. Mary Mallon was an Irish-born cook and a healthy carrier of typhoid fever, who had passed the disease to the families she cooked for. In 1907 she was taken to North Brother Island and held there against her will. She was released in 1910 on the promise that she would never cook again, broke it, and in 1915 was sent back. She spent the rest of her life on the island, and died there in 1938. The newspapers called her Typhoid Mary.

The hospital closed in the 1940s. The island later housed veterans and then a drug treatment program for teenagers, and by the 1960s it was abandoned. Its buildings are slowly collapsing into the trees, and the public is not allowed to land. Today it is a bird sanctuary, and for some years it held one of the largest colonies of nesting herons in the city.

deeper.title: No Ordinary Criminal
deeper.text:
After the General Slocum burned, New York wanted someone to blame, and there was plenty of blame to go around. The boat had passed a federal inspection only weeks before. Investigators found its cork life preservers so old that they crumbled to dust, and they found that the company making new ones had hidden iron bars inside some of them to bring them up to the legal weight. The cork company's managers were indicted, and so were the steamboat company's officers and the inspectors. None of them was convicted.

In the end, only one man went to prison: the captain, William Van Schaick. In 1906 a federal jury found him guilty of criminal negligence, for failing to train his crew and keep the boat ready for fire. The judge told him, you are no ordinary criminal, I must make an example of you, and gave him the maximum sentence, ten years. He served about three and a half years in Sing Sing. President Theodore Roosevelt refused to pardon him, but in December 1912, President William Howard Taft did.

The disaster did change the rules. A federal commission blamed careless inspection as well as the owners, and the government tightened its requirements for life preservers, lifeboats and fire drills on passenger steamboats.

Many of the victims were buried together at the Lutheran cemetery in Middle Village, in Queens, where a monument honors the dead who were never identified. And the fountain here, with its two children gazing out to sea, was put up two years after the fire, a place for a neighborhood that had lost so many to remember them.

deeper.title: Look Closer: Hebe's Fountain
deeper.text:
Look for a little temple of four columns sheltering a drinking fountain. Above the columns, read the four words carved on its sides: Faith, Hope, Charity and Temperance. This is the Temperance Fountain, put up in 1888, and it was meant to save souls one sip at a time.

It was the gift of Henry Cogswell, a San Francisco dentist who made his fortune in the Gold Rush years and spent it on drinking fountains. His idea was simple: if a man could get a free drink of cold water on the street, he might walk past the saloon. He once pledged to build one fountain for every hundred saloons in San Francisco. Here, he worked with a local group called the Moderation Society, formed to fight drunkenness on the Lower East Side.

On top stands Hebe, the cupbearer of the Greek gods, modeled on a famous marble by the Danish sculptor Bertel Thorvaldsen. The original figure was zinc. By the 1980s the fountain was covered in graffiti and someone had sawed off Hebe's hands, and in 1992 she was replaced with the bronze you see now.

Not everyone loved Cogswell's gifts. Brooklyn tore out the fountain he gave it. In San Francisco, on New Year's 1894, a band of young men who considered his statue of himself an eyesore threw a rope around it and pulled it down. One of them was Gelett Burgess, soon to be famous for a little poem that begins, I never saw a purple cow.

deeper.title: The Name on the Park
deeper.text:
The park is named for Daniel D. Tompkins, and he deserves to be better remembered.

Tompkins was elected governor of New York in 1807, while still in his early thirties. During the War of 1812, when the federal government was slow to pay, he borrowed money on his own name to raise and pay the militia that defended New York harbor. After the war, neither the state legislature nor Congress would fully repay him, and he spent years fighting accusations over his accounts.

He is also the governor who finished off slavery in New York. A law passed in 1799 had promised freedom only to children born after that year, and only once they were grown. In 1817, at Tompkins's urging, the legislature set a final date: on July fourth, 1827, slavery in New York would end. When the day came, many Black New Yorkers held their celebrations on July fifth instead, to avoid trouble from white crowds on the holiday.

That same year, 1817, Tompkins became vice president under James Monroe, and served two terms. By the end his health and his fortune were both ruined. He died in 1825, three months after leaving office, in the Staten Island village he had founded and named Tompkinsville. He was fifty years old.

He is buried in the churchyard of St. Mark's in-the-Bowery, a few blocks from here. The square was named for him in the decade after his death, and it has spent nearly two centuries living up to his restless, embattled name.

stops.title: Loisaida & the Nuyorican Poets Cafe
stops.text:
End your walk in Alphabet City, near Avenue C and East Third Street. Look up at the street signs: on Avenue C, you'll see a second name, Loisaida Avenue. Loisaida is a Spanglish pronunciation of Lower East Side, popularized by Puerto Rican residents and artists in the 1970s.

Puerto Ricans began arriving in New York in large numbers after World War Two, many in the so-called Great Migration of the 1950s, when cheap airfares made the journey possible. They came for factory jobs and settled in East Harlem, the South Bronx, Brooklyn, and here. By the 1970s, much of Alphabet City was Puerto Rican.

Those were brutal years. The city was nearly bankrupt, landlords abandoned buildings or set them on fire for insurance money, and the city took ownership of thousands of abandoned properties. Drugs and crime were rampant. But residents fought back. Community activists organized to rehabilitate buildings through sweat equity, doing the work themselves in exchange for ownership. And they turned rubble-strewn lots into community gardens.

The community garden movement has deep roots here. In 1973, an artist named Liz Christy and a group called the Green Guerillas began throwing seed bombs, balloons filled with seeds and fertilizer, over fences into vacant lots. They planted a garden at the corner of the Bowery and Houston Street, now the Liz Christy Community Garden, considered the first community garden in New York City. Dozens of others followed in Alphabet City. Look for gardens like La Plaza Cultural, at Avenue C and East 9th Street. In the late 1990s, Mayor Rudy Giuliani tried to auction off many garden lots for development, provoking huge protests. Many gardens were saved.

At 236 East Third Street, between Avenues B and C, is the Nuyorican Poets Cafe. Founded in 1973 by the poet and professor Miguel Algarín, along with the playwright Miguel Piñero and others, it began as an informal gathering in Algarín's living room. The term Nuyorican refers to New Yorkers of Puerto Rican descent, and the café became a home for their poetry, music, and theater. In the 1990s, it became famous for its poetry slams, competitive performance poetry that helped launch the spoken word movement nationally. Piñero's play Short Eyes, written about his experiences in prison, was a major success and was nominated for Tony Awards.

In the 1990s, the musical Rent was set in this neighborhood, in the world of artists, squatters, and people living with HIV. Today, Alphabet City has gentrified dramatically, but the murals, gardens, and casitas, small wooden houses built in community gardens in the style of rural Puerto Rico, preserve the memory of Loisaida.

deeper.title: The Poet Who Named Loisaida
deeper.text:
Start with the map. Manhattan bulges out to the east here, so when the planners laid out the street grid in 1811, they added four avenues east of First Avenue and gave them letters, A, B, C and D. That is where the nickname Alphabet City comes from.

The name Loisaida came later, and it came from a poet. Bittman Rivas, known to everyone as Bimbo, came to New York from Puerto Rico and made his life here as a poet, playwright, actor, teacher and community organizer. In 1974 he wrote a poem called Loisaida, in a mix of English and Spanish, about the neighborhood he loved. The word took the English name, Lower East Side, and spelled it the way his Puerto Rican neighbors said it. Some people give a share of the credit to his friend and fellow organizer, Chino Garcia.

The word spread because it named something real. In the 1970s, as landlords abandoned buildings and the city cut services, residents began rebuilding the neighborhood themselves, with sweat equity, community gardens and cultural centers, and Loisaida became their banner. It went up on murals and posters, and into the names of community groups.

Eventually it reached the street signs, when Avenue C was given the second name Loisaida Avenue. Bimbo Rivas died in 1992. Every year, the Loisaida Festival fills the avenue with music, food and dancing, and the word he wrote down in a poem is still how many people here name their home.

deeper.title: Domes on the Empty Lots
deeper.text:
In the 1960s, two young men who had come up through the neighborhood's street gangs, Carlos Chino Garcia and Angelo Gonzalez, helped start an antipoverty group with a name that borrowed from President Johnson's programs: the Real Great Society. In 1968 the group hosted a lecture by Buckminster Fuller, the inventor famous for the geodesic dome, a shelter built from a lattice of triangles that is light, cheap and astonishingly strong. Some of the young men in the audience decided to build domes themselves.

In 1970, six of them formed a new group and named it with the first letters of their first names: Chino, Humberto, Angelo, Roy, Anthony and Sal. That spells CHARAS. Fuller's associate, Michael Ben-Eli, came down to teach them solid geometry and spherical trigonometry. They worked out the math, cut and joined the struts, and raised their first dome on a vacant lot beneath the Manhattan Bridge. A photographer named Syeus Mottel followed them for months, and his 1973 book, CHARAS: The Improbable Dome Builders, carried an introduction by Fuller himself.

In 1979 CHARAS leased an abandoned school, the old Public School 64 on East Ninth Street between Avenues B and C, and turned it into El Bohío, named for the thatched huts of the Puerto Rican countryside. For two decades it held a theater, studios, classes and meeting rooms for the neighborhood. Then, in 1998, the city auctioned the building to a developer who had given money to Mayor Giuliani's campaigns, and at the end of 2001 CHARAS was evicted. The empty school, its murals painted over, became a symbol of everything the neighborhood felt it had lost, and the fight over its future went on for years.

deeper.title: Scatter My Ashes
deeper.text:
Miguel Piñero, one of the founders of the Nuyorican Poets Cafe, lived the life he wrote about. He was born in Puerto Rico in 1946 and brought to the Lower East Side as a small child. He grew up poor, ran with gangs, used heroin, and was in and out of jail. In the early 1970s, serving time at Sing Sing for armed robbery, he joined a prison theater workshop, and there he wrote Short Eyes, a raw drama set in a house of detention, about what happens when a man accused of molesting a child is thrown in among the other inmates.

The play opened in a church, moved to the Public Theater with Joseph Papp's help, and then to Lincoln Center. In 1974 it won the New York Drama Critics' Circle Award for best American play. Piñero was suddenly famous. He wrote for television, acted in films and in shows like Miami Vice, usually as a criminal, and kept writing poems. He never escaped his addictions.

In one poem he asked for one last thing: after he had climbed up on a tenement sky, as he put it, he wanted his ashes scattered through the Lower East Side. He died in June 1988, at forty-one. His friend Miguel Algarín led a procession through the neighborhood, and they did as he had asked, scattering his ashes along the streets he had written about.

Another poet of the Cafe's early days, Pedro Pietri, wrote Puerto Rican Obituary, a long poem about workers who spent their lives chasing a dream that never arrived. In 2001, Benjamin Bratt played Piñero in a film about his life. But the Cafe itself, still filling up on poetry nights, may be the memorial Piñero would have liked best.

overview:
For a long time, the East Village wasn't called the East Village at all. It was simply the northern part of the Lower East Side. The name was invented in the 1960s, partly by real estate agents hoping to attach some of Greenwich Village's bohemian glamour to cheaper tenement apartments to the east. The marketing worked, perhaps too well: within a few years, the neighborhood had become the center of the hippie counterculture, and later of punk rock.

But the history goes much deeper. In the seventeenth century, this was the farm, or bouwerij, of Peter Stuyvesant, the last Dutch director-general of New Amsterdam. His family held the land for generations, and a few traces of their estate survive in diagonal streets and an old church.

In the nineteenth century, the area became the heart of Kleindeutschland, Little Germany, one of the largest German-speaking communities in the world outside of Berlin and Vienna. It was a neighborhood of beer halls, bakeries, singing societies, gymnastics clubs called Turnvereine, and Lutheran and Catholic churches. It was also a hotbed of labor organizing and socialist politics.

As the Germans moved out in the early twentieth century, Eastern European Jews, Ukrainians, Poles, and Italians moved in. Second Avenue became the Yiddish Rialto, the center of a thriving Yiddish theater scene. After World War Two, Ukrainian refugees built a community around Seventh Street, and Puerto Rican families settled in the area east of Avenue A, known as Alphabet City, or in Spanglish, Loisaida.

Then came the artists and the counterculture. In the 1950s and 60s, Beat poets, jazz musicians, and abstract painters moved into cheap apartments here. In the 1960s, St. Mark's Place became the East Coast counterpart to San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury. In the 1970s, the CBGB club on the Bowery launched punk rock. In the 1980s, the neighborhood was the center of a vibrant art and music scene, but it also suffered from drugs, abandoned buildings, arson, and the AIDS crisis. In the 1990s and 2000s, it gentrified rapidly.

As you walk, notice the layers: German names carved on old buildings, Ukrainian churches, Yiddish theater history, Puerto Rican murals and community gardens, punk landmarks, and new luxury buildings, all mixed together.

title: Union Square, Flatiron & Gramercy
blurb: Protests and Tammany Hall, Ladies' Mile department stores, Teddy Roosevelt's birthplace, the Flatiron, and Tin Pan Alley.

stops.title: Union Square
stops.text:
You're in Union Square. The name doesn't refer to labor unions, though it would be fitting. It comes from the union, or junction, of two major roads: Broadway and the old Bowery Road, which met here.

In the nineteenth century, this was a fashionable residential square, and then, as commerce moved in, a center of theaters, hotels, and luxury retail. Tiffany and Company, for example, had its flagship store on the west side of the square from 1870 to 1906, in a cast iron building that still stands. Tiffany was founded downtown in 1837 by Charles Lewis Tiffany as a stationery and fancy goods store, and became the most prestigious jeweler in America. The company followed its customers north, from lower Broadway to Union Square, and later to Fifth Avenue.

Union Square's real identity, though, is as New York's great stage for protest. On September fifth, 1882, about ten thousand workers marched from City Hall to Union Square in what is considered the first Labor Day parade in the United States. In the following decades, socialists, anarchists, suffragists, and labor unions rallied here. In 1927, crowds gathered here to protest the execution of Sacco and Vanzetti, two Italian anarchists convicted of murder in a widely criticized trial. After September eleventh, 2001, the square became a spontaneous memorial, filled with candles and handwritten messages. It remains the go-to place for protests in the city.

Look at the equestrian statue of George Washington at the south end. Sculpted by Henry Kirke Brown, it was dedicated in 1856, and it's one of the oldest public sculptures in New York.

On the east side of the square, at the corner of 17th Street, look for the neo-Georgian building with a peaked roof. This was the last home of Tammany Hall, the Democratic political machine that dominated New York politics for more than a century. Tammany provided jobs, favors, and help to immigrants in exchange for votes, and its bosses, including William Tweed, became synonymous with corruption. Tammany moved into this building in 1929. Its power faded in the following decades, and today the building houses offices and shops.

At the south side of the square, above the stores, you might see a giant digital display. Originally an art installation called Metronome, it was reprogrammed in 2020 as the Climate Clock, counting down the time left to limit global warming.

On the west side, at 33 Union Square West, the Decker Building, with its Moorish-style details, was where Andy Warhol moved his studio, The Factory, in 1968. In June of that year, the radical feminist writer Valerie Solanas shot Warhol there. He survived, but barely.

On Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays, the square hosts the Union Square Greenmarket, founded in 1976, which helped start the farmers' market movement in New York. Some of the city's top chefs shop here.

deeper.title: The First Labor Day
deeper.text:
You heard that the first Labor Day parade marched to Union Square on September fifth, 1882. Notice the day of the week: it was a Tuesday, an ordinary working day. The ten thousand or so workers who marched up Broadway from City Hall had to take the day off on their own, and many of them gave up a day's pay to do it.

The parade was organized by the Central Labor Union, an alliance of the city's unions. Who first thought of it is still argued about, and the argument has a comic twist: the two leading candidates had almost the same name. One was Matthew Maguire, a machinist who was the union's secretary. The other was Peter McGuire, a carpenter who helped found the national carpenters' union and later the American Federation of Labor. The federal Department of Labor lays out both claims, and notes that more recent research seems to favor the machinist.

The idea spread. Other cities held parades, states made the day a legal holiday, and in 1894 Congress made the first Monday in September a national one. Most of the rest of the world honors workers on the first of May instead, a date tied to the strikes for an eight-hour day, and the Haymarket affair, in Chicago in 1886.

Union Square kept its role. On March sixth, 1930, in the first winter of the Great Depression, tens of thousands of people filled the square for a Communist-led rally of the unemployed. When part of the crowd set off to march on City Hall without a permit, police on foot and on horseback charged into it with nightsticks. When you see a protest here today, you are watching one of the oldest traditions in the city.

deeper.title: Tiffany's Blue Box
deeper.text:
You heard that Tiffany had its flagship on the west side of the square from 1870. Charles Lewis Tiffany had a gift for publicity as sharp as his eye for jewels.

In 1858, when the first telegraph cable was laid across the Atlantic, New York went wild with celebration. Tiffany bought up leftover cable, cut it into short lengths, bound the pieces with brass bands, and sold them as souvenirs, each with a certificate. The cable itself stopped working within weeks, but the souvenirs helped make Tiffany a household name. During the Civil War, the store supplied the Union Army, including handsome presentation swords for its officers.

In 1878, Tiffany bought one of the largest yellow diamonds ever found, from the new mines at Kimberley in South Africa. It weighed two hundred and eighty-seven carats in the rough, and was cut down to about a hundred and twenty-eight. The Tiffany Diamond has been the company's showpiece ever since, and Audrey Hepburn wore it in publicity photographs for Breakfast at Tiffany's.

The famous color goes back even further. Since 1845, Tiffany has published a catalog called the Blue Book, and its robin's egg blue, on covers, boxes and bags, became one of the most recognizable colors in commerce. A New York newspaper reported in 1906 that there was one thing Tiffany would not sell you at any price: an empty box. You could only get one with something inside.

deeper.title: The Tammany Tiger
deeper.text:
You heard that Tammany Hall ended its days in the building on the east side of the square. It began in the 1780s as a social and patriotic club, the Society of Saint Tammany, named for Tamanend, a Lenape chief remembered for his wisdom and for making peace with William Penn. Its members borrowed Native American titles: their leaders were sachems, and their meeting hall was the Wigwam.

The tiger came later, and it came from an enemy. William Tweed got his start as foreman of a volunteer fire company, Americus Engine Company Number Six, known as Big Six, whose emblem was a snarling tiger. In 1871, the cartoonist Thomas Nast turned that tiger against him, drawing Tammany as a beast loose in a Roman arena, mauling the Republic, while Boss Tweed watched from the emperor's box. Tammany, unashamed, made the tiger its symbol.

No one explained the system better than George Washington Plunkitt, a Tammany district leader who held court at a shoeshine stand in the county courthouse. A reporter, William Riordon, wrote down his talks and published them in 1905. Plunkitt drew a line between dishonest graft, like shaking down gamblers and saloon keepers, and what he called honest graft: learning ahead of time where the city planned a new park or bridge, buying the land cheap, and selling it to the city at a profit. He summed up his career in a line that has never been forgotten: I seen my opportunities and I took 'em.

By the time Tammany moved here in 1929, its days were numbered. Fiorello La Guardia, mayor from 1934 to 1945, cut the machine off from city jobs, and in 1963 a young Greenwich Village lawyer named Ed Koch beat the last great Tammany boss, Carmine DeSapio, in a race for district leader.

deeper.title: Look Closer: The Square's Statues
deeper.text:
You heard about George Washington, on horseback at the south end. His sculptor, Henry Kirke Brown, also made the Abraham Lincoln at the north end, put up a few years after Lincoln's assassination. Lincoln didn't start there. He first stood at the southwest corner of the square, and was moved when the park was rebuilt.

His old corner now belongs to Mahatma Gandhi, striding along with his staff. The statue was dedicated on October second, 1986, Gandhi's birthday, and its sponsors chose Union Square for its long history of nonviolent protest.

Look for the Marquis de Lafayette, the young French nobleman who crossed the Atlantic to fight beside Washington, shown offering his heart and his sword to the American cause. He is the work of Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, who designed the Statue of Liberty. France gave him to New York to thank the city for its help to Paris during the siege of 1870 and 1871, and he was unveiled in 1876, in the very years Bartholdi was at work on Liberty.

Then find the tall flagpole rising from a massive bronze base. It was made for the hundred and fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, in 1926, and its base carries the Declaration's entire text. The Tammany Society paid for it, as a memorial to Charles Francis Murphy, the boss who had led the machine for more than twenty years.

Washington is the oldest of them all. He has watched nearly every rally, march and protest this square has seen.

stops.title: Ladies' Mile
stops.text:
You're on Broadway, around 18th to 20th Streets. Look around at the grand buildings on both sides, many with cast iron facades, mansard roofs, and huge plate-glass windows at street level. These were department stores, and this was Ladies' Mile.

From about the 1860s to the early 1900s, the area along Broadway, Fifth Avenue, and especially Sixth Avenue between roughly 14th and 23rd Streets was the premier shopping district in America. The department store was essentially invented in this period, and some of the most important American retailers had their flagships here: Lord and Taylor, Arnold Constable, B. Altman, Siegel-Cooper, and R. H. Macy and Company, which was on Sixth Avenue at 14th Street before moving to Herald Square in 1902.

Department stores changed American life. They offered fixed prices instead of haggling. They displayed huge varieties of goods under one roof. They offered amenities like restaurants, restrooms, reading rooms, and delivery. And critically, they created one of the first public spaces where middle-class women could go alone, without male chaperones, and spend the day. That's why the area was called Ladies' Mile.

Look for the Lord and Taylor building at Broadway and 20th Street, completed in 1870, with its cast iron facade and corner tower. Lord and Taylor was founded in 1826 and became one of the oldest department stores in the country, before closing its last stores in 2021. Over on Sixth Avenue, look for the massive Siegel-Cooper building, between 18th and 19th Streets, completed in 1896. It was one of the largest stores in the world. It featured a fountain under its central atrium with a statue of the Republic, and the phrase Meet me at the fountain became a common way for New Yorkers to arrange meetings.

The El, the elevated railway along Sixth Avenue, brought shoppers right to the store doors. But by the early 1900s, the stores began following their wealthy customers north, to Herald Square and Fifth Avenue in Midtown. The buildings were taken over by manufacturers and wholesalers. In 1989, the area was designated the Ladies' Mile Historic District, and in recent decades, retail has returned, with big-box stores and chains filling the old palaces.

The ABC Carpet and Home store on Broadway at 19th Street occupies a building originally built for W. and J. Sloane, a high-end furniture and carpet firm. The interior, crammed with antiques and rugs, still gives a hint of the old department store atmosphere.

deeper.title: The Woman Who Ran Macy's
deeper.text:
You heard that Macy's started out on Sixth Avenue at Fourteenth Street, at the southern edge of Ladies' Mile. You can hear about Rowland Macy himself, the Nantucket whaler, on the Midtown walk. This is the story of the person who ran his store.

Margaret Getchell was a distant cousin of Macy's, also from Nantucket. Around 1860, not yet twenty, she came to work at his new store in New York, keeping the books and handling the cash. She was quick with figures and even quicker at running things, and in 1866 Macy made her superintendent of the whole business, in charge of nearly two hundred employees and the store's daily operations. That freed him to sail to Europe on buying trips. Macy's has called her the first woman promoted to an executive position in American retailing.

She is credited with starting an early mail-order business, so customers could shop from home. In 1869 she married a Macy's colleague, Abiel LaForge, and the next year she stepped down to raise a family. She died in 1880, at only thirty-eight.

The Fourteenth Street store kept growing until it filled much of its block. Macy's says it was the first department store to decorate its windows for Christmas, in 1874, with porcelain dolls posed in scenes from Uncle Tom's Cabin. Macy died in 1877, and the store later passed to the Straus family, who carried the red star north to Herald Square in 1902.

deeper.title: Cash Girls and the White List
deeper.text:
Behind the counters of Ladies' Mile was a world the shoppers rarely saw. Saleswomen stood on their feet for long days, often in hot, stuffy rooms. And running between the counters were the cash girls and cash boys, children as young as ten, who carried each customer's money to the cashier's desk and brought back the change, whenever a clerk called out, Cash!

In 1890, the reformer Jacob Riis wrote that cash girls in New York stores earned about a dollar seventy-five a week, for days that in the busy season stretched to sixteen hours, and that girls fainted on the job.

A group of New York women decided to use the one power they had over the stores: their own shopping. At the start of the 1890s, with the reformer Josephine Shaw Lowell as president, they founded the Consumers' League of New York, and drew up a White List, a published list of stores that paid fair wages, kept reasonable hours, and provided decent, sanitary working conditions. Shoppers were urged to buy only from stores on the list, and in time about forty stores made it.

It was an early version of an idea that is still with us: that where you shop is a political act. Wire carriers and pneumatic tubes eventually replaced the cash children, and state laws began to limit how long women and children could work in stores. In 1910, the league hired a young social worker named Frances Perkins to run its New York office. She went on to become secretary of labor under Franklin Roosevelt, the first woman in a president's cabinet.

deeper.title: Birds on the Hats
deeper.text:
In February 1886, a young ornithologist named Frank Chapman went bird watching in the uptown shopping district, which in those days meant streets like these. He wasn't looking at the trees. He was looking at women's hats.

On two late afternoon walks, Chapman counted about seven hundred hats, and five hundred and forty-two of them were decorated with feathers, wings or whole stuffed birds. Among them he identified about forty native species, many of them common songbirds. He published his tally in the magazine Forest and Stream.

The milliners of Ladies' Mile were at the heart of the fashion. Plume hunters were wiping out colonies of egrets and herons in Florida, shooting the adults in breeding season, when their plumes were finest, and leaving the chicks to starve.

Chapman's count became ammunition for a new movement.
