In 1896, two Boston women, Harriet Hemenway and her cousin Minna Hall, held teas to persuade their friends to give up feathered hats, and founded the Massachusetts Audubon Society. Other states followed. In 1900 Congress passed the Lacey Act, which banned shipping illegally killed birds across state lines, and in 1903 Theodore Roosevelt, born just around the corner from here, created the first federal bird reservation, at Pelican Island in Florida.

Chapman spent more than half a century at the American Museum of Natural History, and in 1900 he proposed a new holiday tradition. Instead of competing to shoot as many birds as possible on Christmas Day, as hunters then did, people should go out and count them. The Christmas Bird Count still takes place every winter.

stops.title: Theodore Roosevelt's Birthplace
stops.text:
At 28 East 20th Street, between Broadway and Park Avenue South, look for a brownstone with a flag. This is the Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace National Historic Site.

Theodore Roosevelt was born here on October twenty-seventh, 1858, into a wealthy old New York family of Dutch descent. His father, Theodore Senior, was a glass importer, banker, and philanthropist who helped found the American Museum of Natural History and the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Young Theodore was a sickly, asthmatic child, and he famously built up his strength through intense exercise, including in a home gymnasium his father had built for him on the porch.

Roosevelt lived here until he was fourteen. He went on to become a state legislator, New York City police commissioner, assistant secretary of the Navy, leader of the Rough Riders in the Spanish-American War, governor of New York, vice president, and, after the assassination of William McKinley in 1901, president of the United States. At forty-two, he was the youngest person ever to become president. As president, he was a trustbuster, breaking up corporate monopolies, including the Northern Securities railroad trust organized by J. P. Morgan. He was a conservationist who protected huge areas of public land, and he won the Nobel Peace Prize for mediating an end to the Russo-Japanese War.

Here's a twist: this is not the original house. The original was demolished in 1916 to make way for a commercial building. After Roosevelt died in 1919, his family and supporters bought the site and rebuilt the house as a replica, with Roosevelt's sister and widow helping to recreate the interiors from memory and photographs. Many of the furnishings inside are original to the family. The reconstruction was designed by Theodate Pope Riddle, one of the first women licensed as an architect in the United States. It opened in 1923.

The museum is run by the National Park Service, and tours of the rooms are free. It's a strange and interesting artifact: a historically accurate reconstruction of a house from the 1860s, built in the 1920s, and now itself almost a century old.

deeper.title: The Boy Who Brought Home a Seal
deeper.text:
When Theodore was seven or eight, walking up Broadway, he passed a market and saw a dead seal laid out on a slab. He was spellbound. As long as the seal was there, he came back day after day to study it, and he measured it as best he could with a folding pocket ruler. He never got the seal, but he did get its skull, and with two of his cousins he made it the first specimen of what the boys grandly called the Roosevelt Museum of Natural History.

The museum grew, specimen by specimen, with whatever a determined boy could collect and preserve. For his fourteenth birthday, his father gave him lessons in taxidermy from John G. Bell, a taxidermist who had once traveled with John James Audubon. That same year, Theodore got his first pair of glasses, and discovered how much of the world a nearsighted boy had been missing. He later wrote that he had no idea how beautiful the world was until he got those spectacles.

That winter, on a family trip up the Nile, he spent the voyage shooting and preparing birds for his collection.

The boy naturalist became the president who protected more American land than any before him, in national forests, bird reservations and national monuments. Some of the birds he collected as a teenager survive to this day in museum collections.

deeper.title: Roosevelt's Midnight Rambles
deeper.text:
In 1895, at thirty-six, Roosevelt became president of the city's board of police commissioners, in charge of a department that a state investigation had just exposed as deeply corrupt. He decided to see for himself what his patrolmen did at night.

With the journalist Jacob Riis as his guide, the commissioner walked the streets in the small hours, checking on the men on their beats. They found officers asleep, chatting in saloons, or simply gone, and some were summoned to headquarters the next morning to face the commissioner himself. The newspapers loved it, and cartoonists drew Roosevelt as little more than a pair of glasses and a mouthful of teeth.

Riis had his own reasons. As a penniless young immigrant, he had once spent a night in one of the city's police station lodging houses, filthy rooms where the homeless were allowed to sleep, and there, he later wrote, a policeman killed the little stray dog that had been his only companion. He showed Roosevelt the lodging houses, and soon afterward Roosevelt shut them down.

Not every crusade went so well. Roosevelt insisted on enforcing the state law that closed saloons on Sundays, the one day most working men had free, and it made him enemies across the city, especially among German New Yorkers who loved their Sunday beer gardens. He held the job for about two years before leaving for Washington as assistant secretary of the Navy.

deeper.title: Teddy's Bear
deeper.text:
In November 1902, President Roosevelt went bear hunting in Mississippi, at the invitation of the state's governor. The other hunters found bears. He didn't. So his guide, Holt Collier, a renowned bear hunter who had been born into slavery, cornered a big black bear with his dogs, lassoed it, and tied it to a tree for the president to shoot. Roosevelt refused. It wasn't sporting. The cuddly version stops there. In most accounts, the bear had already been badly hurt, and Roosevelt had it put out of its misery.

A cartoonist at the Washington Post, Clifford Berryman, drew the scene on November sixteenth, under the title Drawing the Line in Mississippi: the president turning away from a frightened bear. In later cartoons the bear got smaller and cuter, and became a regular companion of the cartoon president.

In Brooklyn, a shopkeeper named Morris Michtom saw the cartoon. He and his wife, Rose, made stuffed toy bears and put them in their window with a sign that read Teddy's bears. The family always said he wrote to the White House and got the president's permission to use his name. The bears sold so well that the Michtoms went on to found the Ideal Novelty and Toy Company, one of the biggest toy makers in the country.

At almost the same moment, in Germany, Richard Steiff of the Steiff toy company designed a jointed stuffed bear of his own, and collectors still argue over who came first. One more irony: Roosevelt is said to have disliked the nickname Teddy. The bears made sure it stuck.

stops.title: Gramercy Park
stops.text:
You're at Gramercy Park, between 20th and 21st Streets and Park Avenue South and Third Avenue. Notice something unusual: the park is surrounded by a tall iron fence, and the gates are locked.

Gramercy Park is one of the very few private parks left in New York. It was created in 1831 by a lawyer and developer named Samuel Ruggles, who bought a marshy farm here, drained it, and laid out sixty-six lots around a private park. Owners of the lots surrounding the park were given keys, and the right to use the park was written into the property deeds. To this day, only residents of the buildings facing the park have access, and keys are tightly controlled. The locks are changed each year. Hotel guests at the Gramercy Park Hotel have sometimes been given access, and once a year, on Christmas Eve, the park is traditionally opened to the public for a few hours.

The name Gramercy is thought to come from a Dutch name for the marshy area, possibly Krom Moerasje, meaning little crooked swamp, and a creek that ran through it.

Look around at the historic buildings surrounding the park. On the south side, at 15 Gramercy Park South, is the National Arts Club, housed in a Victorian Gothic mansion that once belonged to Samuel J. Tilden. Tilden was the governor of New York who helped bring down Boss Tweed, and he ran for president in 1876, winning the popular vote but losing in the Electoral College after a disputed deal. According to a long-told story, Tilden, fearful of his political enemies, had a secret tunnel built from his house to escape to 19th Street. The mansion's facade, renovated by Calvert Vaux, features carved portraits of writers like Shakespeare, Goethe, and Dante.

Next door, at number 16, is The Players, a private club founded in 1888 by the actor Edwin Booth, one of the greatest Shakespearean actors of the nineteenth century. Booth was also the brother of John Wilkes Booth, the man who assassinated Abraham Lincoln. Edwin was devastated by his brother's crime and withdrew from the stage for months. Stanford White redesigned the building for the club. Booth lived in an apartment on the top floor, and his room has been preserved as it was when he died in 1893. Look for the statue in the center of the park: it's Edwin Booth, as Hamlet.

A short walk east, at Irving Place and 18th Street, is Pete's Tavern, which claims to be the oldest continuously operating bar in New York, open since 1864, and to have stayed open during Prohibition disguised as a flower shop. The writer O. Henry lived nearby and, according to the bar, wrote his famous Christmas story The Gift of the Magi in one of its booths.

deeper.title: A Booth Saves a Lincoln
deeper.text:
You heard that Edwin Booth was the brother of Lincoln's assassin. There is a stranger story about him, and the witness was a Lincoln.

During the Civil War, the president's son Robert was traveling from New York to Washington. On the crowded platform at the Jersey City station, passengers pressed toward the sleeping car as the train began to move, and Robert was twisted off his feet and slipped into the gap between the platform and the car. A hand seized his coat collar and pulled him back to safety. He turned to thank his rescuer, and knew him at once. It was Edwin Booth, whose face was famous.

Robert told the story himself, many years later, in a letter published in The Century Magazine. Booth learned whose life he had saved from his friend Adam Badeau, an officer on General Grant's staff, who wrote to tell him.

There is one more strange scene. On November twenty-fifth, 1864, Edwin and his brothers Junius and John Wilkes appeared on stage together for the only time, in Julius Caesar at the Winter Garden Theatre on Broadway, a benefit to raise money for a statue of Shakespeare in Central Park, the one that stands on the Mall today. Edwin played Brutus, the noble assassin. John Wilkes played Mark Antony. That same night, Confederate agents tried to set New York on fire, starting blazes in a string of hotels, one of them right next door to the theater. When the fire bells rang, Edwin stepped to the footlights and calmed the audience, and the play went on.

Less than five months later, John Wilkes Booth shot Robert's father at Ford's Theatre.

deeper.title: Tilden's Library
deeper.text:
You heard that Samuel Tilden won the popular vote for president in 1876 and lost the White House anyway. He lost it by a single electoral vote. He spent his last years among his books, here and at Greystone, his estate in Yonkers, and when he died in 1886, unmarried and childless, he left the bulk of his fortune to found a free library and reading room for the people of New York.

His relatives had other plans. A nephew sued, other relatives joined in, and they attacked the clause of the will that created the library trust. The case dragged on for years, and the courts largely sided with the family. In the end, only part of the fortune, roughly two million dollars by most accounts, reached the library trust.

That wasn't enough to build a great library. But New York had two other libraries that were struggling: the Astor Library, in the building on Lafayette Street that is now the Public Theater, and the Lenox Library on Fifth Avenue. In 1895 the three joined forces as the New York Public Library, whose great marble building on Fifth Avenue you can visit on the Midtown walk.

So a disappointed candidate's last wish, half broken by his own family, helped create one of the great libraries of the world.

deeper.title: The Four Million
deeper.text:
From 1903 to 1907, an apartment at 55 Irving Place, a short walk south of the park, was home to one of the most popular writers in America. He signed his stories O. Henry. His real name was William Sydney Porter, and he arrived in New York with a past: he had served three years in an Ohio prison for embezzling from a bank in Austin, Texas, where he had worked as a teller. It was in prison that he began publishing stories under his new name.

In New York he wrote at a furious pace, for a time a story a week for the Sunday edition of the New York World, about shopgirls, clerks, waiters, swindlers and lonely people in rented rooms.

In 1906 he collected some of them in a book called The Four Million. The title was a jab at Ward McAllister, the society arbiter who had declared that only about four hundred people in New York really mattered, the number, it was said, who could fit in Caroline Astor's ballroom. O. Henry's answer was that all four million New Yorkers were worth a story.

The book included The Gift of the Magi, the tale of a poor young couple, Jim and Della, who each sell their most precious possession to buy the other a Christmas present. She sells her long hair to buy a chain for his watch, and he sells his watch to buy combs for her hair. As you heard, Pete's Tavern claims he wrote it there, and it points to its second booth.

O. Henry drank too much and spent faster than he earned, and he died in 1910, at forty-seven.

deeper.title: Look Closer: Lamps, Knights and a Witch
deeper.text:
Walk around the park and look at the houses. Several have stories on their doorsteps.

On the west side, numbers 3 and 4 share a lacy cast iron porch, usually credited to the architect Alexander Jackson Davis. In front of number 4, look for a pair of tall lamps. This was the home of James Harper, one of the brothers who founded the publishing house Harper and Brothers, and mayor of New York in the 1840s. By an old custom, said to go back to Dutch New Amsterdam, a pair of lamps marked the mayor's home. Harper's lamps are still here, though the custom faded after Gracie Mansion became the mayor's official residence in 1942.

On the east side, look at number 36, a white terra cotta apartment house in the Gothic style, finished around 1910 to a design by James Riely Gordon. Two knights in armor stand guard at its door.

Next door, number 34, finished in 1883, is often described as the first cooperative apartment building in New York, where residents owned shares in the building instead of renting. Its residents have included the actor James Cagney, and Margaret Hamilton, who played the Wicked Witch of the West in The Wizard of Oz.

Like the other buildings around the park, these come with the most coveted perk in the neighborhood: a key to the gate.

stops.title: The Flatiron Building
stops.text:
You're looking at one of the most famous buildings in the world, the Flatiron Building, at the intersection of Broadway, Fifth Avenue, and 23rd Street.

When it was completed in 1902, it was officially named the Fuller Building, after the George A. Fuller Company, a pioneering Chicago construction firm that built it as its New York headquarters. But New Yorkers immediately nicknamed it the Flatiron, because its triangular shape resembled a clothes iron. The building fills a narrow triangular lot created where Broadway crosses Fifth Avenue on a diagonal. At its narrowest point, the tip, it's only about six and a half feet wide.

The architect was Daniel Burnham of Chicago, one of the great figures of American architecture. He had led the design of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago. He's famous for the phrase, Make no little plans; they have no magic to stir men's blood. The Flatiron is a steel-frame skyscraper, but Burnham clad it in limestone and terracotta, with elaborate decoration inspired by the Italian Renaissance. The facade is divided like a classical column, with a base, a shaft, and a capital.

When it opened, many people thought it would blow over. The intersection does create strong wind gusts, and there's a well-known story that in the early 1900s, men would gather on 23rd Street to watch the wind lift women's skirts. When police shooed them away, it was called giving them the twenty-three skidoo. Etymologists aren't sure this story is the true origin of the phrase, but it's a good one.

The building became a favorite subject for photographers and painters. Alfred Stieglitz and Edward Steichen both made famous photographs of it, in fog and twilight, which helped establish photography as a fine art. Stieglitz said it looked like a ship moving forward.

In the 1990s, the area around the building was nicknamed Silicon Alley, as internet startups moved into the neighborhood's old loft buildings. The Flatiron itself was home to the publishing company Macmillan for decades. More recently, the building was emptied for a long renovation, and plans have been announced to convert much of it into residences.

The best view is from the small plaza at the north tip, where you can see its prow cutting through the city like the bow of a ship.

deeper.title: The Cowcatcher
deeper.text:
Walk to the north tip of the Flatiron and look at the bottom of the prow. The building's sharp edge doesn't come all the way down to the sidewalk. A low, one-story shop pokes out in front of it, like the cowcatcher on the front of a locomotive, and that is exactly what New Yorkers called it.

It wasn't part of the original design. Harry Black, the head of the Fuller Company, wanted every square foot of rentable space he could get on his expensive lot, and he insisted on a storefront at the tip. Burnham objected. Black won, and the space was leased to United Cigar Stores.

You heard that the Flatiron is a steel-frame skyscraper. On this lot, that frame was everything. The building rises twenty-two stories, about two hundred and eighty-five feet, and the steel skeleton carries the weight, so the stone and terra cotta walls are a covering rather than a support. A traditional masonry building this tall would have needed enormously thick walls at the bottom, and on a triangle that narrows to about six and a half feet, the tip would have been nearly solid. Steel let the prow stay hollow, and full of offices.

Those offices at the prow are the most famous rooms in the building, narrow wedges with windows on both sides, looking out over Madison Square and up two of the most famous avenues in the world. Once you notice the cowcatcher, though, you will never see the Flatiron quite the same way again.

deeper.title: The Flatiron in Snow and Mist
deeper.text:
You heard that Alfred Stieglitz and Edward Steichen made famous photographs of the Flatiron. Here is how.

In the winter of 1903, on a day of heavy snow, Stieglitz set up his camera in Madison Square, across the street, and framed the new building behind the forked trunk of a snow-covered tree. Years later he recalled that the building had seemed to move toward him like the bow of a monster ocean steamer. He published the photograph in his magazine, Camera Work.

Steichen's version came a year or so later, at twilight, with a horse-drawn cab and the dark branches of a tree in front of the building. He printed the negative in layers of tinted gum over platinum, so each print came out a different color. Three of them, each in a different tone, are now at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, a gift from Stieglitz in 1933.

The two men led a movement called the Photo-Secession, which argued that a photograph could be a work of art, as personal as a painting. In 1905 they opened a small gallery a short walk up Fifth Avenue, at number 291, known simply as 291. Besides photographs, it gave many Americans their first look at modern art from Europe: drawings by Rodin, work by Matisse, and in 1911, Picasso. In 1916, Stieglitz showed the drawings of a young artist named Georgia O'Keeffe, whom he later married.

deeper.title: Toyland on Fifth Avenue
deeper.text:
From the Flatiron's tip, look north across Twenty-third Street at the big building on the west side of Fifth Avenue, number 200. For most of the twentieth century, this was the capital of the American toy business.

The site had been the Fifth Avenue Hotel, until it was torn down in 1908. The office building that replaced it filled with toy companies, and it became the heart of the annual Toy Fair, which had begun in 1903 with fewer than ten companies showing their wares, Lionel electric trains among them. Every winter, buyers from stores all over the country came to see what children would be asking for the following Christmas, in showrooms that spread into a second building on Broadway, joined to this one in 1967 by a bridge high above the street.

Some of the most famous toys in the world made their debuts at Toy Fair. In 1959, a California toy company introduced a teenage fashion doll there. Her name was Barbie.

In the 2000s the toy companies moved out, the building was sold and remade, and the fair moved to the Javits Center on the far West Side. Today the old Toy Center holds Eataly, the Italian food hall, and the corporate offices of Tiffany and Company. When you pass its doors, picture the buyers who once crowded in each winter to see what American children would want next.

stops.title: Madison Square Park & the Met Life Tower
stops.text:
You're in Madison Square Park, across from the Flatiron Building. In the second half of the nineteenth century, Madison Square was the most fashionable place in New York.

The park was surrounded by grand hotels, like the Fifth Avenue Hotel, where presidents stayed and political deals were made, and by mansions. Delmonico's opened a restaurant on the square. In the 1870s and 80s, the raised right arm and torch of the Statue of Liberty was displayed in this park for several years, part of a fundraising campaign to pay for the statue's pedestal. Visitors paid to climb up inside the torch.

Look across Madison Avenue, at the northeast corner of the park. On that site stood the original Madison Square Garden. The second Garden, designed by Stanford White and opened in 1890, was one of the grandest entertainment buildings in the country, with a tall tower modeled on the Giralda in Seville, topped by a gilded statue of Diana by Augustus Saint-Gaudens. On June twenty-fifth, 1906, Stanford White was shot dead in the rooftop theater of the Garden by Harry Kendall Thaw, a deranged millionaire who was obsessed with his wife, Evelyn Nesbit, a famous model and showgirl with whom White had had a relationship. The trial was called the trial of the century. The Garden was demolished in 1925, and the name moved uptown. On the site now stands the New York Life Insurance Building, by Cass Gilbert, completed in 1928, with its golden pyramid roof.

Now look at the tall white tower on the east side of the park, at Madison Avenue and 24th Street, with a giant clock and a gold cupola. This is the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company Tower, completed in 1909. Modeled on the Campanile of St. Mark's in Venice, it was the tallest building in the world until the Woolworth Building surpassed it in 1913. Each of its four clock faces is about twenty-six feet across. Met Life was one of the giants of the insurance industry, selling small policies to working-class families, and its headquarters here were a symbol of its dominance.

The park has a few more stories. Baseball's early history is linked to this area: the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club was organized near here in 1845 by players who had been playing on open lots around Madison Square, and its rules became the basis of modern baseball. At the northwest corner of the park, a granite obelisk marks the grave of General William Worth, a hero of the Mexican-American War, who is actually buried underneath it.

And finally, look for the Shake Shack in the park. It started in 2001 as a hot dog cart run by the restaurateur Danny Meyer, as part of an art project in the park. The cart was so popular that he opened a permanent kiosk in 2004. Shake Shack is now a publicly traded company with hundreds of locations around the world.

deeper.title: The Arm in the Park
deeper.text:
You heard that the Statue of Liberty's arm and torch stood in this park. They had already been on tour. Bartholdi's workshop in Paris finished the arm first, and shipped it to Philadelphia for the Centennial Exhibition of 1876, the great fair for a hundred years of American independence. It arrived months after the fair opened, but visitors still paid to climb up inside it to the balcony around the torch. The arm alone is about forty-two feet long, and the index finger is eight feet.

After the fair, the arm came here, to the northwest corner of Madison Square, and stayed until 1882, to drum up money for the pedestal. France was paying for the statue, but Americans were expected to pay for its base, and they were in no hurry. In 1882 the arm went back to France, to be joined to the rest of the statue. It took Joseph Pulitzer's newspaper campaign of 1885 to pay for the pedestal, and the statue was dedicated in October 1886.

The torch had a hard life after that. In 1916, German saboteurs blew up a munitions depot on Black Tom Island, across the harbor in New Jersey, and flying debris damaged the arm. The torch has been closed to visitors ever since. That same year, the sculptor Gutzon Borglum, who later carved Mount Rushmore, cut windows into the torch's copper flame and fitted them with amber glass, so it could glow from within. The windows leaked every time it rained, and for decades the water damaged the arm.

During the restoration for the statue's hundredth birthday, the old torch came down, and in 1986 a new one went up, its flame covered in gold leaf. The original, the one that once rose out of this park, is now on display in the Statue of Liberty Museum on Liberty Island.

deeper.title: The Trial of the Century
deeper.text:
You heard that Harry Thaw shot Stanford White on the roof of Madison Square Garden in June 1906. What followed filled the newspapers for years.

At the center of it was Evelyn Nesbit. She had come to New York as a teenage model and chorus girl, and White, more than thirty years older, pursued her when she was sixteen. In his apartment on Twenty-fourth Street there was a red velvet swing, and the girl on the red velvet swing became the most famous phrase of the scandal.

Thaw, the unstable heir to a Pittsburgh railroad fortune, married Nesbit in 1905, and his jealousy of White became an obsession. At his first trial, in 1907, Nesbit testified that White had drugged and assaulted her when she was sixteen, and the whole country hung on her words. The jury deadlocked. At the second trial, in 1908, Thaw's lawyers argued that he was insane, and the jury agreed: not guilty by reason of insanity. He was sent to the state hospital for the criminally insane at Matteawan.

His family's money kept working for him. In 1913 he escaped from Matteawan and fled to Canada, and was brought back. In 1915 a jury declared him sane, and he walked free.

Nesbit spent the rest of her long life trying to escape one night in 1906. She danced in vaudeville, acted in silent films, and struggled with poverty and addiction. In 1955 she served as an adviser on a Hollywood film about her own story, The Girl in the Red Velvet Swing, with Joan Collins playing her. She died in 1967.

deeper.title: The Light That Never Fails
deeper.text:
You heard that Met Life sold small policies to working-class families. It was called industrial insurance. For a few cents a week, collected door to door by an agent, a family could make sure there would be money for a funeral, and a little to live on, if the breadwinner died. Millions of families signed up, and their nickels and dimes paid for the tower on the east side of the park. For decades, the company used the tower as its symbol.

Its most remarkable idea came in 1909. At the suggestion of Lillian Wald, the founder of the Henry Street Settlement on the Lower East Side, Met Life began sending visiting nurses into the homes of sick policyholders, free of charge. It began with Henry Street nurses in Manhattan and grew into a service across the country that lasted more than forty years. The company argued that it was good business, too: healthier policyholders lived longer and kept paying their premiums.

Now look across Twenty-fourth Street, at the massive limestone building just north of the tower. It was meant to be the base of a skyscraper of up to a hundred stories. The Great Depression stopped it at about thirty. What you see is the stump of a tower that never was, and on its ground floor is the restaurant Eleven Madison Park.

deeper.title: Look Closer: Madison Square's Bronze Men
deeper.text:
Madison Square Park is full of statues, and three of them repay a closer look.

At the north end, find Admiral David Farragut, standing as if on the deck of his ship. Farragut was the Union admiral who, in 1864, led his fleet through the mines, then called torpedoes, at the mouth of Mobile Bay, with an order remembered as: damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead. The statue, unveiled in 1881, was the first major work of the young sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens, and its curving stone base, with figures and lettering that seem to flow like water, was a collaboration with his friend Stanford White, then a young architect. It made Saint-Gaudens famous, and began a partnership with White that lasted until White's death across the street.

At the southwest corner sits William Seward, Lincoln's secretary of state and the man who later bought Alaska. For generations, New Yorkers have told a story that the sculptor saved money by putting Seward's head on a body made for a statue of Lincoln. It is a good story, but no one has found evidence that it is true.

And at the southeast corner stands Roscoe Conkling, one of the most powerful senators of the Gilded Age. In March 1888, during the great blizzard that buried New York, Conkling set out on foot from his law office on Wall Street, heading uptown. The walk took about three hours, through deep drifts and a howling wind, and by most accounts he nearly collapsed in the snow around Union Square before he reached shelter. He died a few weeks later. His friends wanted his statue in Union Square, near where he fell. The park commissioners said no, and he ended up here.

stops.title: Tin Pan Alley
stops.text:
End your walk on West 28th Street, between Broadway and Sixth Avenue. On the north side of the street, look for a row of modest nineteenth-century brick buildings. This block is Tin Pan Alley, the birthplace of the American popular music industry.

From around the 1890s to the early 1900s, dozens of sheet music publishers had offices on this block. Before recorded music became widespread, the music business ran on sheet music. Families bought printed music to play on their parlor pianos, and a hit song could sell millions of copies. Publishers employed songwriters to write hits and song pluggers, piano players who demonstrated songs for customers, vaudeville performers, and bandleaders.

According to legend, the name Tin Pan Alley came from a journalist who wrote that the sound of dozens of pianos playing different songs at once, through open windows, sounded like people banging on tin pans.

The songs that came out of Tin Pan Alley shaped American culture. Composers and lyricists associated with this world include Irving Berlin, who wrote Alexander's Ragtime Band, God Bless America, and White Christmas; George Gershwin, who worked as a song plugger as a teenager; Scott Joplin, who lived in New York for a time; and many others. Songs like Take Me Out to the Ball Game and Give My Regards to Broadway came from this era and this industry.

Tin Pan Alley was also a place where Black composers and performers, Jewish immigrants, and others found a way into American popular culture, often against the odds. African American composers like James Weldon Johnson, his brother J. Rosamond Johnson, and Bob Cole wrote hit songs for the Tin Pan Alley publishers.

The music business followed the theaters uptown, toward Times Square, and later to the Brill Building at Broadway and 49th Street, where songwriters wrote many of the pop hits of the 1950s and 60s. In 2019, several buildings on this block were designated as New York City landmarks, after preservationists fought to save them.

Look around, too, at the flower shops nearby. Sixth Avenue and 28th Street is the heart of the city's Flower District, where wholesalers sell flowers and plants to florists. Early in the morning, the sidewalks are filled with greenery.

As you leave, imagine the sound of dozens of pianos drifting out of these windows, each one playing a different song, all hoping to be the next big hit.

deeper.title: Irving Berlin's Black Keys
deeper.text:
You heard that Irving Berlin came out of the Tin Pan Alley world. He never learned to read music. Israel Beilin was born in the Russian Empire in 1888 and came to New York with his family when he was five. His father, a cantor, died when Israel was thirteen, and before long the boy left home to make his own way, singing for pennies on street corners and in saloons. He found work as a singing waiter at the Pelham Café on Pell Street in Chinatown, making up parodies and new songs for the customers.

In 1907 he wrote the words for his first published song, Marie from Sunny Italy. As the story is usually told, the printer got his name wrong, and the sheet music credited I. Berlin. He kept it.

Berlin taught himself the piano, but he played almost entirely in one key, F sharp, which lies mostly on the black keys. Once he was successful, he had special pianos built with a lever that shifted the whole keyboard, so he could keep playing on the black keys while the music came out in whatever key he chose. Musical secretaries wrote down what he played and sang.

In 1911, Alexander's Ragtime Band made him a star. He went on to write around fifteen hundred songs, among them Blue Skies, Puttin' On the Ritz, Cheek to Cheek, Easter Parade and There's No Business Like Show Business. The composer Jerome Kern said that Irving Berlin had no place in American music. He was American music. Berlin lived to be a hundred and one.

deeper.title: Who Named the Alley?
deeper.text:
You heard the legend that a journalist gave Tin Pan Alley its name. The usual suspect is Monroe Rosenfeld, a songwriter and newspaperman who knew this block well. As the story goes, around the turn of the twentieth century, Rosenfeld visited the office of the composer and publisher Harry Von Tilzer, who liked to weave strips of paper through his piano strings to give them a tinny, banjo-like sound. Rosenfeld said it sounded like a tin pan, and when he wrote about the street, the name stuck.

That's the legend. The article in which Rosenfeld supposedly coined the phrase has never been found, and others say tin pan was simply slang for a battered, tinny piano, a name that may have been around before anyone wrote it down.

Harry Von Tilzer deserves a story of his own. He was born Aaron Gumbinsky, and as a teenager he took his mother's maiden name, Tilzer, and added a Von to make it sound grander. He wrote hundreds of songs, including A Bird in a Gilded Cage and Wait Till the Sun Shines, Nellie. His brother Albert wrote the music for Take Me Out to the Ball Game, though by most accounts neither Albert nor the lyricist, Jack Norworth, had ever been to a baseball game when they wrote it.

Whatever its origin, the name outlived the block. By the 1920s, Tin Pan Alley meant the whole American popular song business, wherever it happened to be.

deeper.title: The Song Pluggers
deeper.text:
You heard that publishers hired song pluggers to demonstrate their songs. The job went far beyond the office piano. Pluggers sang at the sheet music counters of department stores and five-and-dime stores, and wherever a crowd gathered. The young George Gershwin left high school at fifteen to plug songs for the publisher Jerome Remick, for fifteen dollars a week, pounding a piano for hours a day. Publishers also paid popular singers, in cash, gifts or a share of the royalties, to put their songs into their acts, an early form of what radio would later call payola.

The song that showed how much money there was in the business was After the Ball, a sentimental waltz by Charles K. Harris of Milwaukee. Harris published it himself, a popular singer put it into a hit musical comedy, and it went on to sell millions of copies, an unheard-of number at the time. After that, everyone wanted a piece of the trade, and publishers crowded onto this street, close to the theaters and the vaudeville booking offices.

For years, though, songwriters were paid only for printed music. When a restaurant orchestra played their song, they got nothing. In 1914, the composer Victor Herbert joined other songwriters and publishers to found ASCAP, the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers, to collect fees for public performance. Herbert sued Shanley's, a Times Square restaurant whose musicians had performed his song Sweethearts. The restaurant argued that diners paid for the food, not the music. In 1917, the Supreme Court sided with Herbert. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that if music did not pay, it would be given up. The fees that restaurants, stores and radio stations pay for the music they play trace back to that decision.

overview:
In the second half of the nineteenth century, the center of New York was not Midtown and not Wall Street. It was the stretch of Broadway and Fifth Avenue between 14th and 34th Streets. This was where fashionable New Yorkers shopped, dined, went to the theater, and lived.

The story of this area is the story of the city's relentless northward march. As commerce pushed up from lower Manhattan, wealthy families kept moving north to stay ahead of it. In the 1830s and 40s, they built mansions around Union Square and Gramercy Park. By the 1850s and 60s, Madison Square, at 23rd Street, was the most fashionable address in the city, surrounded by luxury hotels and mansions. Then the shops followed. In the 1870s and 80s, a stretch of Broadway and Sixth Avenue became known as Ladies' Mile, lined with enormous department stores that catered to middle- and upper-class women. Theaters clustered around Union Square and Madison Square. Restaurants like Delmonico's moved uptown to be near their clientele.

By the early 1900s, the fashionable crowd had moved on again, to upper Fifth Avenue and Midtown, and the department stores followed them to Herald Square and Fifth Avenue. The neighborhood shifted to light manufacturing, toy companies, publishing houses, and photography studios. The area around the Flatiron Building became the center of the toy industry, with an annual toy fair. Later, in the 1990s, the neighborhood got a new identity as Silicon Alley, the hub of New York's first internet startup boom, with companies like DoubleClick, which Google later acquired.

This walk takes you through some of the most important buildings in the history of American architecture and commerce: the Flatiron, which helped define the skyscraper; the Metropolitan Life Tower; the grand cast iron and stone palaces of Ladies' Mile; and the private, gated Gramercy Park, which still requires a key to enter. Along the way, you'll hear about Tammany Hall, Theodore Roosevelt, Andy Warhol, and the birth of the American popular song.

title: Midtown: Empire State to Grand Central
blurb: The Empire State, Macy's, the Garment District, Bryant Park, Times Square, Grand Central, and the Chrysler Building.

stops.title: The Empire State Building
stops.text:
You're at Fifth Avenue and 34th Street, at the base of the Empire State Building.

Before the skyscraper, this site held the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel, born of a family feud. In the 1890s, William Waldorf Astor built the Waldorf Hotel here, next to the mansion of his aunt, Caroline Astor, the queen of New York society. It was partly an act of spite. Her son, John Jacob Astor the Fourth, responded by building an even taller hotel, the Astoria, next door. The two hotels were then joined into the Waldorf-Astoria, the most luxurious hotel in the city. When the hotel moved to Park Avenue in 1931, the old one was demolished. By the way, John Jacob Astor the Fourth died on the Titanic in 1912. He was among the wealthiest people aboard.

The Empire State Building was the project of John J. Raskob, a financier and former executive of General Motors and DuPont, and Al Smith, the former governor of New York who had just lost the 1928 presidential election. Raskob was reportedly in a competition with Walter Chrysler, of the rival automaker, who was building the Chrysler Building a few blocks away.

The design, by the firm Shreve, Lamb and Harmon, was simple and efficient, and construction was astonishingly fast. Steel went up at a rate of about four and a half stories per week. The building opened on May first, 1931, after about thirteen and a half months of construction. President Herbert Hoover pressed a button in Washington to turn on the lights.

At one thousand two hundred fifty feet to its roof, it was the tallest building in the world, a title it held for nearly forty years. But it opened at the worst possible moment, in the depths of the Great Depression. For years, much of its office space was empty, and New Yorkers nicknamed it the Empty State Building. The observation deck's ticket sales helped keep it afloat.

The spire on top was originally meant to be a mooring mast for dirigibles, the airships. The idea was that passengers would disembark onto a gangplank eighty-six floors up. A couple of attempts were made, but high winds made it impractical and dangerous, and the idea was abandoned.

In 1933, the building became a movie star, when King Kong climbed to its top. On July twenty-eighth, 1945, an Army B-25 bomber, flying in heavy fog, crashed into the 79th floor, killing fourteen people. An elevator operator, Betty Lou Oliver, survived a fall of about seventy-five stories in an elevator whose cables had been damaged, which remains one of the most famous survival stories in the building's history.

The Art Deco lobby is one of the city's finest, with a ceiling mural of gears and planets in gold leaf and an image of the building itself in aluminum relief.

deeper.title: Al Smith's Consolation Prize
deeper.text:
You heard that Al Smith had just lost the 1928 presidential election when he took on this building. The two facts are connected.

Smith, the Lower East Side boy you may have heard about at Foley Square, had become a four-term governor of New York and, in 1928, the Democratic nominee for president. His campaign chairman was John J. Raskob. Smith was buried in a landslide by Herbert Hoover, after a campaign full of attacks on his religion, and he came home without a job. Raskob and his longtime partner, Pierre du Pont, gave him one: president of the company building the tallest tower in the world. Smith was its public face, the handshakes and the speeches. On opening day, two of his grandchildren cut the ribbon, and it was Hoover, the man who had beaten him, who pressed the button in Washington to switch on the lights.

Now a story, told later and probably polished in the retelling. Raskob is said to have pulled a thick pencil from a drawer, stood it on its end, and asked the architect, William Lamb, Bill, how high can you make it so that it won't fall down? True or not, the building does look a little like a pencil.

Smith's politics took a turn in this tower's early years. He had urged Franklin Roosevelt to run for governor in 1928, but he turned bitterly against the New Deal. In 1934, Raskob and the du Pont family helped found the American Liberty League to fight it, and Smith became one of its loudest voices, attacking his old ally's program in a famous speech in 1936. That fall, Roosevelt was reelected in one of the biggest landslides in American history.

Smith died in 1944. His name lives on in the Al Smith Dinner, a Catholic charity dinner held each fall, where in many election years both presidential candidates have shown up in white tie to roast each other, and themselves.

deeper.title: The Men on the Beams
deeper.text:
You heard the steel went up at about four and a half stories a week. Here are some of the men who put it there.

In 1930, the builders hired Lewis Hine to photograph the work. Hine was a former schoolteacher who had spent years photographing children at work in mills, mines and factories for the National Child Labor Committee, pictures that helped build the case for child labor laws. Now he turned his camera on the men building the tallest tower in the world, and he went up on the steel with them. His best-known picture from the job, called Icarus, shows a young ironworker swinging from a cable with the city far below. Hine later gathered many of these images in a book called Men at Work, a tribute to the skill and nerve of working people.

His pictures show how a riveting gang worked. One man heated the rivets in a small coal forge until they glowed, then tossed them with tongs to a catcher, who caught them in a tin can. Two more men set each rivet in its hole and hammered it home.

A sizable share of the ironworkers were Mohawk men from Kahnawake, near Montreal. Their tradition in high steel went back to the 1880s, when a railroad bridge was built across the Saint Lawrence River onto their land, and the bridge company hired young Mohawk men, who proved superb on the beams. Outsiders liked to say that Mohawks had no fear of heights. The ironworkers themselves have always said that's a myth: they feel it like anyone else, and work anyway. Generations of them commuted to New York for the big jobs, and their sons and grandsons later helped raise the World Trade Center.

The building came in ahead of schedule and under budget, helped by the Depression, which had pushed down the cost of labor and materials. Officially, five workers died during construction. Rumors at the time put the toll much higher, but the official count remains five.

deeper.title: Oscar of the Waldorf
deeper.text:
You heard about the Waldorf-Astoria, the grand hotel that stood here before the skyscraper. Its most famous employee wasn't a chef.

Oscar Tschirky was a Swiss immigrant who started working in New York restaurants as a teenager, and when the Waldorf opened in 1893, he became its maître d'hôtel, the man who ran the dining rooms. He knew every regular's name, table and tastes, and the whole city came to know him simply as Oscar of the Waldorf. He stayed with the hotel for about half a century, and moved with it to Park Avenue in 1931.

His most famous creation is a salad. According to the usual story, Oscar introduced it at a grand charity ball at the hotel in 1896, and it appeared in a cookbook he published that same year. The original Waldorf salad was very simple: diced apples and celery, bound with good mayonnaise. The walnuts came later, added by other cooks, and stuck.

The Waldorf turns up in another food story you may have heard at Delmonico's, in the Financial District. In one version of the origin of eggs Benedict, a stockbroker with a hangover ordered toast, poached eggs, bacon and hollandaise at the Waldorf in 1894, and Oscar liked the idea enough to put a version of it on the menu. Like most famous food stories, it was told decades after the fact.

Oscar's real art was hospitality, and the hotel was built for it. A long corridor joined the two halves of the Waldorf-Astoria, and well-dressed New Yorkers paraded up and down it to see and be seen. It's said to have been nicknamed Peacock Alley, and the new Waldorf on Park Avenue named a restaurant after it.

So as you look up at the Empire State Building, picture the dining rooms that stood here first, where a waiter from Switzerland decided what society ate, and gave America a salad that's still on menus a hundred and thirty years later.

stops.title: Herald Square & Macy's
stops.text:
You're at Herald Square, where Broadway crosses Sixth Avenue at 34th Street. The square takes its name from the New York Herald, a newspaper whose headquarters, designed by Stanford White, once stood here. Look for the bronze monument at the north end of the square, with a figure of Minerva and two bell ringers with hammers who strike a bell every hour. The ringers are nicknamed Stuff and Guff. The monument honors James Gordon Bennett Senior and Junior, the publishers of the Herald. It was the younger Bennett who sent the reporter Henry Morton Stanley to Africa to find the missionary David Livingstone, producing the famous line, Doctor Livingstone, I presume?

The giant store on the south side of 34th Street is Macy's. Rowland Hussey Macy, a former whaler from Nantucket, opened a dry goods store on Sixth Avenue at 14th Street in 1858, after several failed retail ventures. The company's red star logo is said to come from a tattoo Macy got while at sea. Macy's was innovative: it used fixed prices, sold goods for cash only, and advertised aggressively.

Later, Macy's was taken over by the Straus family, Isidor and Nathan Straus, who had run its china and glassware department. Isidor Straus and his wife Ida died together on the Titanic in 1912, after Ida reportedly refused to get into a lifeboat without him. Under the Strauses, Macy's moved here in 1902 and built what it advertised as the World's Largest Store.

Now look at the corner of Broadway and 34th Street. You'll notice a small, narrow building, covered in giant advertising signs, wedged into the corner of the Macy's block. Macy's doesn't own it. When Macy's was assembling the land for its store, an agent working for a rival, Henry Siegel of the Siegel-Cooper store, bought this corner lot first, hoping to force Macy's to buy it at an outrageous price, or to block its access to the corner. Macy's refused, and built around it. The holdout building still stands, and Macy's has rented its exterior for its own advertising.

Macy's had a fierce rivalry with Gimbels, a department store that stood a block away. The rivalry was so famous that it appears in the 1947 film Miracle on 34th Street, in which the Macy's Santa Claus sends customers to Gimbels if Macy's doesn't have what they want. Gimbels closed in 1987.

Macy's also gave the city one of its biggest traditions: the Thanksgiving Day Parade, first held in 1924. Its famous giant balloons were introduced in 1927. The parade ends right here, in front of the store.

deeper.title: The Owl-Mad Publisher
deeper.text:
You heard that James Gordon Bennett Junior sent Henry Morton Stanley to find Livingstone. Here's the man himself.

Bennett inherited the Herald from his father, who had founded it and made it one of the best-selling papers in the country. The son was rich, reckless and impossible. In 1877, he was engaged to a young woman from a prominent New York family. On New Year's Day, he turned up at her family's party drunk and behaved so badly that the engagement was off. The story told for a century is that he relieved himself in the fireplace, but that part may be legend. Her brother, Frederick May, went after Bennett, and within days, the two men met for a duel at a remote spot in Delaware called Slaughter Gap. Shots were fired, nobody was hurt, and Bennett soon left for Europe.

He spent most of the rest of his life in France, running the Herald by cable, and in 1887 he founded a Paris edition, which lived on for more than a century as the International Herald Tribune. He paid for adventures as well as news. Besides Stanley's expedition, he backed an attempt to reach the North Pole aboard a ship called the Jeannette, which was crushed by the Arctic ice in 1881. Its captain and many of its crew died. He also put up trophies for races in cars, balloons and airplanes, and the Gordon Bennett balloon race is still flown today.

And he loved owls. He kept live ones, and when Stanford White designed the Herald building here, Bennett had a row of bronze owls set along its roof, with electric eyes that flashed at night. Look at the monument: two of those owls are still perched on it. Bennett even planned a tomb in the shape of a giant owl, about a hundred and twenty-five feet tall, to be designed by White. It was never built. White was shot dead in 1906, as you may have heard at Madison Square, and Bennett died in France in 1918.

deeper.title: Where the Movies Began
deeper.text:
Stand in front of Macy's and picture a music hall. Before the store was built, part of this block held Koster and Bial's Music Hall, a popular variety house, with singers, dancers, acrobats and comics. On the night of April 23rd, 1896, the bill ended with something new.

After the live acts, the lights went down, and a projector threw moving pictures onto a large screen: six short films, each lasting about a minute. Thomas Edison's company had been selling peep-show machines, where one person at a time bent over a box to watch a tiny film. This was different. A whole audience sat in the dark and watched the same images together, larger than life. Others had projected films before, but this was the show that caught on, and the night is often remembered as the start of the movie business in America.

The machine was billed as Edison's Vitascope. In fact, it was mostly the work of a young inventor named Thomas Armat. The businessmen who bought the rights thought Edison's name would sell more tickets, and Edison agreed to manufacture it and take the credit. He was in the audience that night.

The program included dancers, a comic boxing match and waves breaking on a beach in England, a sight that seemed astonishing on a screen.

Koster and Bial's closed in 1901 to make way for Macy's. Look for a plaque on the Macy's building marking the spot. Within a decade, storefront movie theaters called nickelodeons were spreading across the city, and the music halls that had launched the movies were losing their audiences to them.

deeper.title: Balloons Over Broadway
deeper.text:
You heard the giant balloons joined the Thanksgiving parade in 1927. They came from a puppeteer.

Tony Sarg was a marionette maker who also designed Macy's holiday window displays, filled with moving puppets that drew crowds to the glass. For the 1927 parade, he came up with huge figures filled with air, and worked with the Goodyear tire and rubber company to build them. The first star was Felix the Cat, the most famous cartoon character of the day. Sarg is said to have called his creations upside-down marionettes: instead of hanging from strings, they floated above the street, held down by handlers walking below.

Those first balloons were awkward, and handlers sometimes propped them up on poles. For 1928, Sarg switched to helium, and Macy's tried a stunt. At the end of the parade, the balloons were let go, to drift away over the city. They were built to leak slowly and come down somewhere days later, and each carried a return address. Macy's offered a reward of a hundred dollars to anyone who brought one back. It didn't go smoothly. By one account, of the first five released, two came down in the water, and a third was torn to shreds by neighbors fighting over it. The aviator Clarence Chamberlin, famous for flying across the Atlantic, once snagged a balloon in midair with his plane. The releases ended in the early 1930s.

The first parade, in 1924, had no balloons at all. It had floats, bands and live animals borrowed from the Central Park Zoo. Within a few years, the balloons had taken the animals' place.

Today, the balloons are still designed and built in Macy's own studio, and the night before the parade, crowds come to watch them being inflated near the American Museum of Natural History, a show of its own.

stops.title: The Garment District
stops.text:
You're on Seventh Avenue, around 39th Street. Look at the street signs: this stretch of Seventh Avenue is also called Fashion Avenue. Look down: in the sidewalk, you may find bronze plaques of the Fashion Walk of Fame, honoring American designers. And look at the corner of Seventh Avenue and 39th Street, where a giant sculpture of a needle threading a button stands, along with an information kiosk.

You're in the Garment District, roughly between Fifth and Ninth Avenues, from about 34th to 42nd Streets. For much of the twentieth century, this was the center of the American clothing industry. In the early 1900s, the industry was concentrated in the tenement sweatshops of the Lower East Side. After the Triangle fire and new safety laws, and as the industry grew, manufacturers moved into new loft buildings here, built in the 1920s. Those tall, setback buildings were designed for garment production, with big windows for light and large open floors for rows of sewing machines.

By the 1950s, this district was producing a large majority of the women's clothing made in the United States, and the industry employed hundreds of thousands of workers in New York. The streets were jammed with trucks and with workers pushing rolling racks of clothing from factories to showrooms. Many of the workers were Jewish and Italian immigrants and their children, and later Puerto Rican, Chinese, Dominican, and other immigrants. The industry was heavily unionized, and the International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union was one of the most powerful unions in the city.

Look for the statue of a garment worker at a sewing machine, a bronze sculpture by Judith Weller, at 555 Seventh Avenue. It honors the many immigrant workers, especially Jewish workers, who built the industry.

Beginning in the 1960s and accelerating in the 1980s and 90s, most garment manufacturing moved overseas, to Asia and Latin America, where labor was cheaper. The number of garment jobs in New York collapsed. The district's buildings were gradually converted to offices, showrooms, hotels, and tech companies.

Still, New York remains a fashion capital, the home of major designers, fashion magazines, and New York Fashion Week. Nearby schools, including the Fashion Institute of Technology on 27th Street and Parsons School of Design, train designers from around the world. And you'll still find a few fabric stores, button shops, and trimming suppliers on the side streets, especially around 38th and 39th Streets, where designers come to buy materials.

deeper.title: Shall We Save New York?
deeper.text:
You heard the garment industry moved into this district in the 1920s. It didn't simply drift here. It was pushed.

In the early 1900s, as the industry outgrew the Lower East Side, many shops moved into new loft buildings along lower Fifth Avenue and the streets around it, and they kept creeping north. At lunchtime and at the end of the day, thousands of garment workers poured onto the sidewalks of Fifth Avenue, which the avenue's fashionable stores considered their own. The merchants decided the crowds were bad for business.

On March 5th, 1916, the Fifth Avenue Association, the merchants' organization, ran advertisements in the city's newspapers under the headline, Shall We Save New York? The ads warned that the loft factories were swallowing the shopping district, and the merchants pledged to stop buying from manufacturers who stayed in the area around them. The campaign fed into the zoning law the city passed that same year, the first comprehensive one in the country. Besides shaping the skyscrapers, as you may have heard at the start of this tour, the law divided the city into districts for homes, for business and for industry, and helped keep new factories away from the shopping blocks.

So the garment makers moved west, to the blocks beyond Sixth Avenue, which included much of the old Tenderloin, a district of saloons, dance halls and brothels. Developers put up tall new loft buildings for them, and by 1924, the lofts reached all the way to Ninth Avenue. A new garment center rose here, close to Penn Station and the department stores of Herald Square, but out of sight of Fifth Avenue's customers.

It's an early example of how zoning could be used not just for light and air, but to decide who belongs where.

deeper.title: Pins and Needles
deeper.text:
You heard that the International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union was one of the most powerful unions in the city. In 1937, it also produced a Broadway hit.

The union ran education and culture programs for its members: classes, choruses, sports teams and drama groups. It took over a small theater, renamed it the Labor Stage, and asked a young songwriter, Harold Rome, to write a musical revue. The cast was made up of union members, garment workers who rehearsed after work: cutters, basters and sewing machine operators. The show was called Pins and Needles.

It opened on November 27th, 1937, and the opening number set the tone: Sing Me a Song with Social Significance. The sketches and songs poked fun at bosses, at dictators abroad and at politicians at home. Critics liked it, and audiences kept coming.

In March 1938, the cast performed at the White House for President and Eleanor Roosevelt. The show was rewritten again and again to keep up with the news, moved to a larger Broadway house, the Windsor Theatre, in 1939, and closed in June 1940 after one thousand one hundred and eight performances, one of the longest runs Broadway had seen up to then.

The union kept singing. Decades later, as garment jobs were moving overseas, its television commercials showed workers singing Look for the Union Label, urging shoppers to buy clothes made by union members in America. By then the union was fighting a losing battle against cheaper imports. But for a few years in the 1930s, the people who worked these sewing machines were the toast of Broadway.

deeper.title: Press Week
deeper.text:
You heard that New York is home to Fashion Week. It began with a publicist and a war.

Before the Second World War, American fashion took its cues from Paris. Manufacturers on Seventh Avenue sent buyers to the Paris collections and copied what they saw, and most American designers worked anonymously, their names hidden behind the manufacturers' labels. Then, in 1940, Germany occupied Paris, and the flow of French fashion stopped.

Eleanor Lambert saw an opening. She was a publicist who had worked with artists before turning to fashion, and she already ran the International Best-Dressed List, the annual ranking of the world's most stylish people. In 1943, she staged what she called Press Week: a series of shows of American designers' collections, at the Plaza Hotel, for fashion editors from newspapers across the country. To make sure they came, she paid for their travel. The editors went home and wrote about American designers by name, many of them for the first time. Press Week is the ancestor of today's New York Fashion Week.

Lambert spent the rest of her long life promoting American fashion. In the early 1940s, she helped create the Coty awards for American designers, and in 1962, she founded the Council of Fashion Designers of America, which still gives the industry's top American awards. The council also credits her as the force behind the Metropolitan Museum's Costume Institute benefit, today's Met Gala, and behind the Battle of Versailles, a fashion show at the palace in 1973 where, by most accounts, the Americans stole the show from the French.

In the 1990s, the shows gathered under big white tents in Bryant Park, the next stop on this walk, until they moved to Lincoln Center in 2010. Lambert kept working into her late nineties and died in 2003, at the age of one hundred.

stops.title: Bryant Park & the New York Public Library
stops.text:
You're in Bryant Park, behind the New York Public Library, between Fifth and Sixth Avenues and 40th and 42nd Streets.

In the nineteenth century, the site of the library held the Croton Distributing Reservoir, completed in 1842. It was part of the Croton Aqueduct system, which brought clean water to the city from the Croton River, forty miles north, transforming public health in New York. The reservoir was surrounded by massive Egyptian-style stone walls, and New Yorkers strolled along a promenade on top of them, looking down at the water.

Next to the reservoir, on the site of today's park, New York hosted its first world's fair in 1853, housed in a giant iron-and-glass building called the Crystal Palace, inspired by the one in London. It was here, in 1854, that Elisha Otis demonstrated his safety elevator by cutting the rope. The Crystal Palace burned down in 1858.

The library, built over the old reservoir, opened in 1911. It was designed by Carrère and Hastings, and it's a masterpiece of Beaux-Arts architecture. The library was created by combining two private libraries, those of John Jacob Astor and James Lenox, with a large bequest from Samuel Tilden, the former governor you heard about at Gramercy Park. In front, on Fifth Avenue, are the famous marble lions. In the 1930s, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia named them Patience and Fortitude, the qualities he said New Yorkers would need to survive the Depression.

If you can, go inside and see the Rose Main Reading Room on the third floor, nearly two blocks long, with a painted ceiling of clouds.

As for the park, it's named for William Cullen Bryant, a poet and longtime editor of the New York Evening Post, who campaigned for the creation of Central Park. By the 1970s, Bryant Park was a notorious haven for drug dealers and was considered dangerous. In the 1980s, a private nonprofit, the Bryant Park Restoration Corporation, led by Daniel Biederman, took over its management. It was redesigned with open sightlines, movable chairs, and food kiosks, and reopened in 1992. Its turnaround became a model for business improvement districts and public-private park management around the world. Today, it hosts an ice rink in winter, outdoor movies in summer, and some of the best people watching in the city.

Before you leave, look at the black and gold tower on 40th Street, facing the park. That's the American Radiator Building, completed in 1924 and designed by Raymond Hood. It was built for the American Radiator Company, which made heating equipment, and the black brick and gold top were meant to evoke glowing coals. Georgia O'Keeffe painted it at night. It's now a hotel.

deeper.title: Reservoir Square's Lost Wonders
deeper.text:
You heard about the Crystal Palace, the iron and glass hall built here for New York's world's fair in 1853. Just across 42nd Street, the fair had a rival attraction.

It was the Latting Observatory, a wooden tower about three hundred and fifteen feet tall, put up by a promoter who guessed, correctly, that fairgoers would pay to look down on the city. For three years, it was the tallest structure in New York, taller than the spire of Trinity Church. From the top, visitors could look out over farms, rocky lots and shanties to both rivers. But the fair lost money, the crowds faded, and in 1856, the tower burned.

The Crystal Palace lasted two years longer. It was supposed to be fireproof, a building of iron and glass, but it had plenty of wood in its floors and fittings, and it was full of exhibits. On October 5th, 1858, a fire broke out inside and spread with terrible speed. By one account, the whole building was gone in about forty minutes, its great dome collapsing into the flames. The cause was never settled.

For years afterward, the open ground beside the reservoir was known as Reservoir Square. It was renamed for William Cullen Bryant in 1884, a few years after his death, and when the reservoir came down to make way for the library, the park began to take the shape you see now.

So as you sit here, picture the view in 1853: a glass palace glittering in the sun, a wooden tower rising beside it, and the massive stone walls of the reservoir, at what was then the northern edge of the city.

deeper.title: The Orphans of Fifth Avenue
deeper.text:
Walk toward Fifth Avenue and look a couple of blocks north. In 1863, on Fifth Avenue between 43rd and 44th Streets, stood the Colored Orphan Asylum, a home and school for Black children. It had been founded in 1836 by two Quaker women, and by the time of the Civil War, it was home to more than two hundred children.

That July, the federal government began drafting men for the Union army. The law let a man buy his way out for three hundred dollars, a sum far beyond most working men, and anger at the draft exploded into one of the deadliest riots in American history. For four days, mobs, many of them poor Irish immigrants, attacked draft offices, police, the homes of abolitionists and, above all, Black New Yorkers, who were beaten and murdered in the streets.

On the first day, July 13th, a huge crowd surrounded the orphanage. The staff gathered the children, two hundred and thirty-three of them, and led them out a back door as rioters broke in the front, looted the building and set it on fire. The children were taken to shelter, and the building burned to the ground.

The asylum never came back to Fifth Avenue. It rebuilt uptown, first in Harlem and later in Riverdale, in the Bronx, and in 1944, it became the Riverdale Children's Association, carrying on its work with children under a new name.

It's hard to picture a mob burning an orphanage on this stretch of Fifth Avenue today. But the attack became one of the defining images of the draft riots, a reminder that the Civil War was fought in New York's own streets too.

deeper.title: Under the Lawn
deeper.text:
Look at the lawn in front of you. Beneath it, and beneath the paths and the people, are the library's book stacks.

By the 1980s, the library had run out of room, and there was no space to expand on Fifth Avenue. So during the park's restoration, the lawn was dug up, and workers excavated a vast underground storage space, about thirty feet deep. The park was then rebuilt on top of it. The first level of the new stacks opened in 1991. A second, deeper level was fitted out years later and opened in the 2010s as the Milstein Research Stacks. Together, they hold millions of volumes, kept at the cool, steady temperature and humidity that old paper needs.

Down there, the books aren't shelved by subject, as they are in most libraries. They're shelved by size, which packs far more of them into the same space, and the library keeps track of exactly where each one sits.

When a reader in the Rose Main Reading Room asks for a book from the stacks, it rides up through the building on a book train, a system of small cars that run along tracks and climb between the stacks and the reading rooms. The current train went into service in 2016, replacing an older conveyor.

So the people lounging on this lawn are sitting on top of one of the great research collections in the world. In this park, the grass is a roof.

deeper.title: Look Closer: The Lions and the Fountains
deeper.text:
If you walk around to the library's Fifth Avenue steps, take a closer look at the two marble lions. You heard Mayor La Guardia named them Patience and Fortitude. They'd had other names before.

The lions were modeled by the sculptor Edward Clark Potter and carved by the Piccirilli Brothers, a family of Italian-born stone carvers who worked in the Bronx, from pink Tennessee marble. They were unveiled in May 1911, when the library opened. New Yorkers soon nicknamed them Lady Astor and Lord Lenox, after the library's founders, even though both lions have manes. Patience sits on the south side, to your left as you face the building, and Fortitude on the north. In December, they wear holiday wreaths.

Now look on either side of the entrance, at the two fountains set into the wall, by Frederick MacMonnies, the sculptor of the winged figures on the Washington Square Arch. One is Truth, a man seated on a sphinx, the symbol of mystery. The other is Beauty, a woman riding Pegasus, the winged horse. For about thirty years, the fountains sat dry, until a restoration in 2015 got the water flowing again.

Then look up, above the columns, at the six figures by the sculptor Paul Wayland Bartlett. They represent History, Drama, Poetry, Religion, Romance and Philosophy, a short list of what you'll find inside.

stops.title: Times Square
stops.text:
You're in Times Square, at the junction of Broadway and Seventh Avenue, between 42nd and 47th Streets.

Until 1904, this was Longacre Square, a district of carriage makers and horse stables. Then the New York Times moved into a new tower at 42nd Street, the narrow building at the south end of the square, now called One Times Square. The Times's publisher, Adolph Ochs, persuaded the city to rename the square after his newspaper. The same year, the first subway line opened, with a station right here.

To celebrate the new building, the Times hosted a New Year's Eve celebration with fireworks on December thirty-first, 1904. A few years later, when fireworks were banned, the paper lowered an illuminated ball from the building's flagpole at midnight. The first ball drop was on New Year's Eve, 1907, and it's happened almost every year since. The Times itself moved out of the tower in 1913, but the name stuck. In 1928, the building installed a news ticker that ran headlines around the building in lights, the famous zipper.

By the 1920s, the area was the center of the American theater, with dozens of Broadway theaters on the side streets. Electric advertising signs turned Broadway into the Great White Way. Advertisers competed to create the most spectacular displays. Look up at the giant screens around you. Zoning rules actually require buildings in Times Square to have large, illuminated signs. It's one of the only places in the world where flashy advertising is legally mandatory.

After World War Two, Times Square declined. By the 1970s, 42nd Street was lined with pornographic theaters, peep shows, and drug dealers, and it became a national symbol of urban decay. In the 1990s, the city and state launched an aggressive redevelopment. A key moment came in 1997, when the Walt Disney Company restored the historic New Amsterdam Theatre on 42nd Street, signaling that big corporations were willing to invest here. Within a few years, the area was transformed into a family-friendly district of chain stores, restaurants, and tourist attractions. Some New Yorkers mourn the old grit; most are glad to be rid of it.

In 2009, under Mayor Michael Bloomberg and his transportation commissioner, Janette Sadik-Khan, the city closed parts of Broadway to cars and created pedestrian plazas. The experiment was so popular it was made permanent.

At the north end of the square, look for the red glass steps, which sit atop the TKTS booth, where you can buy discounted same-day theater tickets, and the statue of Father Francis Duffy, the chaplain of the Fighting 69th regiment in World War One. Behind him is a statue of George M. Cohan, the composer of Give My Regards to Broadway.

deeper.title: The Smoke Ring Sign
deeper.text:
You heard that advertisers competed here to build the most spectacular signs. For a quarter of a century, the most famous one blew smoke rings.

It was the sign for Camel cigarettes, on the side of the Hotel Claridge, on Broadway, and it went up around 1941. It was the work of Douglas Leigh, a sign man who specialized in what the trade called spectaculars: signs that didn't just show a picture, but did something. This one showed a giant face, and about every four seconds, a perfect ring of what looked like smoke puffed from its mouth and drifted out over the crowd. It was really steam, pushed out in rings by a piston and a diaphragm behind the sign, a little like a drum being struck.

The face changed with the times. During the Second World War, it was a man in uniform, and over the years, others took his place. But the rings kept coming, day and night, until 1966, when the sign came down. A few years later, cigarette ads were banned from American television, though tobacco signs hung on in Times Square for decades.

Look around you at the screens that flicker and move. The idea that a sign should perform, not just sit there, runs straight from the smoking face to them.

deeper.title: Father Duffy's War
deeper.text:
You heard about the statue of Father Francis Duffy at the north end of the square. Here's who he was.

Duffy was born in 1871 in Cobourg, Ontario, in Canada, came to New York as a young man, and became a Catholic priest. When the United States entered the First World War, he went to France as chaplain of the 69th, New York's famous Irish regiment, which the army renamed the 165th Infantry. It was part of the Rainbow Division, so called because it drew units from states across the country. The regiment fought through some of the worst battles of 1918, and Duffy went with the men into the front lines, tending the wounded and burying the dead. He came home one of the most decorated chaplains in the army.

Two other men of the regiment became famous. One was William Donovan, a battalion commander nicknamed Wild Bill, who in the next war led the country's spy agency, the Office of Strategic Services. The other was the poet Joyce Kilmer, the author of Trees, who had transferred into the 69th with Duffy's help. Kilmer was killed in July 1918. When Duffy published his memoir, Father Duffy's Story, in 1919, it included a historical appendix by Kilmer.

After the war, Duffy served as pastor of Holy Cross Church, a few blocks west on 42nd Street, until he died in 1932. The statue, by Charles Keck, was dedicated in 1937, and two years later, this end of the square was named Father Duffy Square. In 1940, Hollywood told the regiment's story in the film The Fighting 69th, with Pat O'Brien as Father Duffy and James Cagney as a fictional soldier.

deeper.title: The City's Front Yard
deeper.text:
Times Square is where New York comes to celebrate the New Year. It's also where the city comes to hear big news together.

On November 7th, 1918, a wire service, the United Press, sent out a report from France that Germany had signed an armistice. It wasn't true, but nobody knew that yet. Across the country, offices emptied, whistles blew and crowds filled the streets. In New York, so much paper rained down from office windows that the wire service was reportedly made to pay for the cleanup. Four days later, on November 11th, the real armistice was signed, and the city celebrated all over again.

On August 14th, 1945, the crowds came for the end of the Second World War. People packed the square, reading the news ticker that wrapped around the Times tower, and when word of Japan's surrender came that evening, the square erupted.
