That day, the photographer Alfred Eisenstaedt caught a sailor bending a woman in a white uniform backward into a kiss. Published in Life magazine, it became one of the best-known photographs of the century. For decades, many people claimed to be the couple. Most researchers now identify them as George Mendonsa, a sailor on leave, and Greta Zimmer Friedman, a dental assistant who had come to America as a teenage refugee from Austria. They were strangers. Years later, Friedman said it wasn't her choice and it wasn't romantic: he simply grabbed her. The picture looks different once you know that.

deeper.title: The Knickerbocker Door
deeper.text:
Under your feet is the oldest stretch of the subway, and a door to a hotel.

You heard that the first subway line opened in 1904 with a station here. It ran up the East Side to Grand Central, turned west under 42nd Street, and then headed north under Broadway. In 1918, the line was split in two and each half was extended, creating the separate East Side and West Side lines riders use today. The short crosstown piece under 42nd Street was left over, and it became the shuttle, running back and forth between Times Square and Grand Central. When you ride it, you're on the tracks of the original 1904 subway.

Now look at the southeast corner of 42nd Street and Broadway, at the red-brick building with the steep mansard roof. It opened in 1906 as the Knickerbocker Hotel, built by John Jacob Astor the Fourth, whom you may have heard about at the Empire State Building, and it was the first luxury hotel of the new Times Square. The tenor Enrico Caruso lived there, and on Armistice Day in 1918, he is said to have come to his window and led the crowd below in the Star-Spangled Banner. The hotel bar had a famous mural by Maxfield Parrish of Old King Cole. When the hotel closed, around 1920, the mural moved, and it now hangs in the King Cole Bar of the Saint Regis, another Astor hotel, on 55th Street.

The Knickerbocker had its own entrance from the subway. If you ride the shuttle, look on its Times Square platform for an old doorway with the word Knickerbocker above it. The building has been a hotel again since 2015, but that door no longer opens for guests.

stops.title: Shubert Alley & the Theater District
stops.text:
Walk west to Shubert Alley, a private pedestrian alley running between 44th and 45th Streets, just west of Broadway.

The alley is named for the Shubert brothers, Lee, Sam, and Jacob, three immigrants from Lithuania who grew up poor in Syracuse, New York, and built the largest theater empire in America. At their peak, the Shuberts owned, operated, or booked a huge number of theaters across the country. The Shubert Organization, headquartered in the Shubert Theatre building next to the alley, still owns more Broadway theaters than anyone else.

Shubert Alley was created as a fire exit for the theaters on either side. It became a gathering place for actors, who would wait here hoping to be noticed by producers, since casting offices were nearby. Today, the walls are covered with posters for current shows.

The theaters around you, on 44th, 45th, and nearby streets, are the heart of Broadway. Broadway is technically not the street, but a designation for about forty professional theaters, each with at least five hundred seats, mostly located between 41st and 54th Streets. Many date from the 1910s and 1920s, the golden age of theater construction. The Shubert Theatre, next to the alley, opened in 1913, and was home to A Chorus Line for its fifteen-year run. The Booth Theatre, on the other side, is named after Edwin Booth, the actor whose club you may have visited at Gramercy Park.

On West 44th Street, look for Sardi's, the restaurant famous for the caricatures of Broadway stars covering its walls. It's been a gathering place for theater people since the 1920s, and for decades, opening night casts would gather there to wait for the reviews in the morning papers.

Broadway is a big business. In a typical recent season, it has drawn more than twelve million attendees and grossed over a billion and a half dollars, with tourists making up the majority of the audience. Shows are high-risk investments: most lose money, but a hit, like The Phantom of the Opera, which ran for thirty-five years at the Majestic Theatre on 44th Street, or The Lion King, can earn billions over its life.

If you have time, the stretch of West 44th and 45th Streets between Broadway and Eighth Avenue is the best place to see a cluster of historic theater facades, marquees, and stage doors, where crowds gather after shows to get autographs.

deeper.title: The Brothers Who Took On the Syndicate
deeper.text:
You heard that the Shubert brothers built the largest theater empire in America. They built it by going to war.

At the turn of the century, the theater business was controlled by a combine called the Theatrical Syndicate, formed in 1896 by six men and led by the producers Marc Klaw and Abraham Erlanger. The Syndicate controlled the bookings of first-class theaters across the country. If a producer or a star wanted to tour, they played Syndicate houses on Syndicate terms, or they didn't play the big towns at all. Even the great French actress Sarah Bernhardt, touring America without the Syndicate, famously played some of her dates in a circus tent.

The Shuberts started out managing theaters in Syracuse and came to New York around 1900, leasing theaters and producing shows. Then, in 1905, Sam, the brothers' leader, died after a train wreck. According to the family's account, when Lee went to Erlanger to confirm a deal Sam had made, Erlanger refused, saying he wouldn't honor an agreement with a dead man. Lee and his younger brother, Jacob, known as J.J., set out to break the Syndicate.

They did it by building and buying theaters, in New York and in cities across the country, until stars and producers had somewhere else to go. Within about a decade, the Syndicate's grip was broken. But the Shuberts became what they had fought. They grew so dominant that in the 1950s, the federal government took them to court under the antitrust laws, and they had to sell off some of their theaters.

Lee and J.J. were famously difficult, and they quarreled with each other for decades. But between them, they ran the business for half a century.

deeper.title: The Tapes Behind A Chorus Line
deeper.text:
You heard that A Chorus Line ran for fifteen years at the Shubert Theatre, right next to the alley. It began with a tape recorder.

At midnight on January 26th, 1974, the director and choreographer Michael Bennett gathered twenty-two Broadway dancers in a studio. They were gypsies, as chorus dancers call themselves, the performers who move from show to show without their names ever going up in lights. Bennett turned on a tape recorder and asked them to talk about their lives: how they started dancing, their families, their fears, what they'd do when they couldn't dance anymore. The session went on through the night, and there were more sessions afterward.

Those tapes became the raw material for the show. The characters on stage, dancers auditioning for a few places in a chorus line and telling their stories to an unseen director, were built largely from the real stories on the tapes, and several of the dancers who had been in the room ended up in the cast, playing versions of themselves.

The show was developed downtown at Joseph Papp's Public Theater, which borrowed about one point six million dollars to produce it. It opened there in April 1975, became the hottest ticket in town, and moved here to the Shubert that July. It won the Pulitzer Prize for drama and nine Tony Awards, and when it closed in April 1990, after six thousand one hundred and thirty-seven performances, it was the longest-running show in Broadway history, a record it held until Cats passed it in 1997.

For the Public Theater, it was a gold mine: its share came to more than thirty-eight million dollars. The dancers had signed away the rights to their stories for a dollar each, and later received a small share of the royalties. Some of them felt they had given away far more than they got.

deeper.title: Ghost Lights and the Bishop of Broadway
deeper.text:
Theaters are full of superstitions, and Broadway has its share of ghosts. These are stories, and they're told here as stories.

Start with the ghost light. When a theater goes dark for the night, the last person out leaves a single bare bulb burning on a stand in the middle of the stage. There's a practical reason: a pitch-black stage is dangerous, and someone could walk off the edge into the orchestra pit. But theater people will also tell you the light is there for the ghosts, so they can perform when nobody's watching, or so they don't make mischief in the dark.

Now Broadway's most famous ghost. A short walk east on 44th Street, on the far side of Broadway, is the Belasco Theatre, built in 1907 and renamed in 1910 for its owner, David Belasco, a producer and director known for astonishingly realistic stage sets. He was a showman offstage too. He dressed in a dark suit with a clerical collar, and people called him the Bishop of Broadway. He kept a lavish private apartment upstairs in the theater.

Belasco died in 1931, but according to the stories, he never left. Actors and staff reported a figure in clerical dress watching from his old box, and it was said that if he appeared on an opening night, the show would be a hit. Some also reported a mysterious woman in blue. The sightings are said to have stopped around 1970, about when a famously nude revue moved into the theater, which, the joke goes, was more than the old man could take.

Nobody has ever proven any of it. But if you pass the Belasco late at night, glance up at the windows.

stops.title: Grand Central Terminal
stops.text:
You're at Grand Central Terminal, at 42nd Street and Park Avenue. Go inside, if you can, and stand in the Main Concourse.

The terminal was built by the New York Central Railroad, the Vanderbilt family's railroad empire. The first Grand Central opened here in 1871. In those days, steam locomotives ran down Park Avenue, through an open trench and a smoky tunnel. In January 1902, two trains collided in the smoke-filled tunnel, killing seventeen people. Public outrage led to a law banning steam locomotives in Manhattan.

The railroad's chief engineer, William Wilgus, came up with a brilliant plan. He proposed electrifying the trains, and since electric trains don't produce smoke, the tracks could be put underground and covered over. Then the railroad could sell the air rights above the tracks to developers. The new terminal, with two levels of underground tracks, opened in 1913. It was designed by the architects Reed and Stem and Warren and Wetmore. The covered tracks became Park Avenue, and the blocks above them were developed into hotels, apartments, and office buildings, a district called Terminal City. The sale of air rights helped pay for the whole project. It was one of the great real estate deals in history.

Look up at the ceiling of the Main Concourse: a turquoise sky with gold constellations of the zodiac. The constellations are painted backward, as if you're looking down at the sky from outside. Some say it was a mistake; others say it's a view from the heavens. Look also for a small dark patch near one corner. During restoration in the 1990s, workers left one area uncleaned, to show how dark the ceiling had become, mostly from decades of tobacco smoke.

At the center of the concourse is the four-faced clock on top of the information booth. Its faces are made of opal, and it's often said to be worth millions of dollars.

Grand Central's survival is a landmark story. In 1963, the Pennsylvania Railroad demolished the original Penn Station, a magnificent Beaux-Arts building, to build Madison Square Garden. The loss shocked the city and led to the creation of the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission in 1965. In the late 1960s, Grand Central's owners planned to build an office tower on top of the terminal. The city refused, and with support from Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and other prominent New Yorkers, the case went to the Supreme Court. In 1978, in Penn Central Transportation Company versus New York City, the court upheld the city's right to protect landmarks, a decision that has shaped historic preservation across the country.

Downstairs, near the Oyster Bar, look for the Whispering Gallery, a low tiled archway where you can whisper into one corner and someone standing diagonally opposite can hear you clearly.

deeper.title: The Commodore
deeper.text:
You heard that the first Grand Central was opened by Cornelius Vanderbilt in 1871. Everyone called him the Commodore, and he earned the title on the water.

Vanderbilt was born on Staten Island in 1794. As the family story goes, at sixteen he borrowed a hundred dollars from his mother to buy a sailboat, and ferried passengers and freight across the harbor. He was tireless and tough, and by his twenties he was captaining a steamboat called the Bellona, between New Jersey and New York, for an owner named Thomas Gibbons.

There was a catch. New York State had given a monopoly on steamboats in its waters to Robert Livingston and Robert Fulton, and Gibbons was running his boats in defiance of it. For years, Vanderbilt dodged the officers who came aboard to serve him with court papers, reportedly hiding in a secret compartment. The fight went to the Supreme Court, and in 1824, in Gibbons versus Ogden, the court ruled that trade between the states was for Congress to regulate, and the monopoly fell. It's still one of the most important cases on the power of the federal government, and it opened the waters to competition.

Vanderbilt built his own fleet of steamships and became one of the richest men in America. Then, late in life, he switched to railroads and took control of the New York Central. When he died in 1877, he was worth about a hundred million dollars, and he left nearly all of it to his son William. His biggest gift was a million dollars to found a university in Nashville, which was named for him: Vanderbilt University.

deeper.title: Look Closer: Mercury, the Clock and the Acorns
deeper.text:
Step outside onto 42nd Street, and look up at the top of the terminal's front.

The sculpture group crowning the building is the Glory of Commerce, by the French sculptor Jules-Félix Coutan. In the middle stands Mercury, the Roman god of commerce and travelers, in his winged helmet. On one side is Hercules, though some say it's Vulcan, the god of the forge, and on the other is Minerva, the goddess of wisdom. Together, they're about forty-eight feet high and weigh some fifteen hundred tons. They were unveiled in 1914, a year after the terminal opened.

Just below Mercury is a clock thirteen feet across, made with glass from Tiffany. It's often called the largest piece of Tiffany glass in the world.

Below that, above the viaduct that carries Park Avenue traffic around the building, stands the bronze statue of Cornelius Vanderbilt. You may have heard in SoHo how it came here in 1929 from his old freight depot.

Now look for a smaller detail, and you'll find it everywhere: acorns and oak leaves, carved into the stone and worked into the metal, inside and out. The acorn was a Vanderbilt family emblem, a reminder of the old saying, great oaks from little acorns grow, a fitting motto for a fortune that, by family tradition, started with one small boat. Once you start spotting them, you won't stop.

deeper.title: Guastavino's Vaults
deeper.text:
You heard about the Whispering Gallery, downstairs near the Oyster Bar. Look closely at what it's made of.

The low arches there, and the vaulted ceiling of the Oyster Bar beyond, are built of thin terracotta tiles laid in a herringbone pattern. This is Guastavino tile, named for a Spanish builder, Rafael Guastavino, and his son, also named Rafael, who came to New York from Spain in the 1880s. They brought with them an old Mediterranean way of building, the tile vault, with deep roots in the region of Valencia: several layers of thin tiles set in fast-drying mortar, which can span wide spaces, needs little support while it's being built, and won't burn. In a city terrified of fire, that was a powerful selling point. In 1889, they founded the Guastavino Fireproof Construction Company.

Their vaults are all over New York. You may have heard about the tiles in the old City Hall subway station. They also built the great vaulted ceiling of the registry room at Ellis Island, where millions of immigrants were processed, after an explosion in 1916 damaged the old roof. When the room was restored decades later, only seventeen of its nearly thirty thousand tiles had to be replaced. And they built the vaults under the Queensboro Bridge, at 59th Street.

The Oyster Bar opened in 1913, a few weeks after the terminal, under those tiles. As for the whispering, the curved tile surfaces carry sound along the arch from one corner to the opposite one. Nobody is sure whether the effect was planned, or whether the builders simply discovered it once the vault was up.

deeper.title: Track 61
deeper.text:
Somewhere north of here, beneath Park Avenue, is a platform that has become one of New York's favorite secrets.

When the railroad buried its tracks, its train yards stretched for blocks under Park Avenue, and new buildings went up on top of them. When the new Waldorf-Astoria opened in 1931, on Park Avenue at 49th Street, it sat above part of the yards. A siding there, known as Track 61, had a platform and a freight elevator big enough to carry a car up into the hotel.

The legend says this was a secret presidential entrance. Franklin Roosevelt, who used a wheelchair and worked hard to hide it from the public, is said to have arrived in his own armored railroad car, had his automobile driven off the train and onto the elevator, and gone straight up into the Waldorf without anyone seeing him. And down on the platform, the story goes, his armored car still waits.

Here's what's documented. Roosevelt did use the siding, on October 21st, 1944, during his last campaign, arriving by train beneath the hotel. The rest is mostly myth. The old railroad car that has sat on the track for years is a baggage car, not Roosevelt's, and there's no evidence of a regular secret commute.

The legend survives because the place is real and the story is almost true. Track 61 is still down there, closed to the public, under the traffic of Park Avenue.

stops.title: The Chrysler Building
stops.text:
End your walk at Lexington Avenue and 42nd Street, looking up at the Chrysler Building, which many people consider the most beautiful skyscraper in the world.

It was built for Walter Chrysler, a former railroad mechanic who had founded the Chrysler Corporation in 1925, which quickly became one of the big three American automakers. Chrysler paid for the building himself, rather than with company money, so that his children would inherit it. The architect was William Van Alen.

The building was at the center of the great race for the sky in 1929 and 1930. Van Alen's former partner, H. Craig Severance, was designing 40 Wall Street, and the two buildings were competing to be the tallest in the world. When 40 Wall Street seemed to have won, Van Alen revealed his secret. A steel spire, called the vertex, had been assembled in pieces inside the building's dome. In October 1929, it was raised through the top and bolted into place in about ninety minutes. The Chrysler Building rose to one thousand forty-six feet, the tallest in the world, and the first structure to exceed one thousand feet. It held the title for less than a year, until the Empire State Building opened.

Look at the details. The stainless steel crown has rows of triangular windows in a sunburst pattern. Near the top, at the setbacks, are gleaming steel gargoyles shaped like eagle heads, and lower down, ornaments modeled on Chrysler radiator caps and hubcaps, along with a frieze of stylized car wheels. It's a temple to the automobile.

If it's open, step into the lobby, which is clad in red Moroccan marble, with a ceiling mural by Edward Trumbull showing transportation and human endeavor, and elevator doors with elaborate wood inlays.

Before you go, look east along 42nd Street. At 220 East 42nd Street is the Daily News Building, designed by Raymond Hood and completed in 1930, home of the tabloid New York Daily News, once the highest-circulation newspaper in America. Its lobby has a giant rotating globe. In the 1978 film Superman, the building appeared as the Daily Planet.

At the end of 42nd Street, along the East River, is the United Nations headquarters, built on land that once held slaughterhouses. John D. Rockefeller Junior bought the land and donated it to the United Nations in 1946. The Secretariat Building, completed in 1952, was among the first glass curtain wall skyscrapers in New York.

From railroads and department stores, to newspapers, cars, and the world's diplomats, the businesses that built Midtown are all written into its skyline.

deeper.title: Walter Chrysler's Locomobile
deeper.text:
You heard that Walter Chrysler started out as a railroad mechanic. In a way, he never stopped being one.

Chrysler grew up in a railroad town in Kansas, the son of a locomotive engineer, and apprenticed as a machinist in the railroad shops, where, like many apprentices, he made his own tools. He moved from railroad to railroad, rising to manage locomotive works. In 1908, at an auto show in Chicago, he fell for a car, a Locomobile, that cost far more than he could afford. He put in his savings, borrowed the rest, and bought it.

Then he did something odd. He hardly drove it. For about three months, he took the car apart, studied every piece, and put it back together, again and again, until he understood exactly how it worked. That car was his education in the automobile business.

In 1912, he left the railroads, taking a big cut in pay, to run production at Buick, in Michigan, and he made its factories some of the most efficient in the industry. He became Buick's president, left General Motors a rich man, and was hired to rescue struggling carmakers, which led him to found his own company.

When his tower opened, he put his past on display. By one account, the tools he'd made as an apprentice were shown in a glass case near the observation floor, high in the building. And from 1930, three floors near the top held the Cloud Club, a private lunch club where executives ate high above the city.

Chrysler died in 1940, at sixty-five. The building that carries his name was paid for with his own money, a monument to a mechanic who never trusted a machine he hadn't taken apart himself.

deeper.title: The Architect Who Lost His Fee
deeper.text:
You heard how William Van Alen won the race for the sky with a spire hidden inside his building. His reward was a lawsuit.

Van Alen had trained in New York and in Paris, at the École des Beaux-Arts, and he had a reputation as a daring designer. But he never signed a contract with Walter Chrysler. When the building was finished, he asked for the usual architect's fee of the day, six percent of the construction cost, which came to roughly eight hundred and forty thousand dollars. Chrysler refused to pay, and attacked Van Alen's character. Van Alen took him to court, and won.

The victory cost him. Clients were wary of an architect who had sued a famous millionaire, and the Depression had stopped most new building anyway. Van Alen never landed another major commission.

He did get one more famous moment. On January 23rd, 1931, the Society of Beaux-Arts Architects held its costume ball at the Hotel Astor, and several of the city's leading architects came dressed as their own buildings. A well-known photograph shows them lined up like a little skyline. Van Alen is dressed as the Chrysler Building, with its crown on his head, towering over the rest. William Lamb, one of the architects of the Empire State Building, came dressed as his tower, the one that would take Van Alen's title only a few months later. Others came as clubs and office buildings.

Look up at the crown again. It has outlived the lawsuit, the Depression and the loss of the height record. In the end, it's Van Alen's crown, not his fee, that people remember.

deeper.title: Who Owns the Ground?
deeper.text:
Here's a question most people never ask about a skyscraper: who owns the ground under it?

For the Chrysler Building, the answer is a college: Cooper Union, the school founded by Peter Cooper that you may have heard about in the East Village. Cooper Union has owned this land since 1902. Walter Chrysler built his tower on it under a long-term lease, and every owner of the building since then has paid the college rent for the ground beneath it.

There's more. Because Cooper Union is a nonprofit, the land is exempt from property taxes, so the building's owners pay the college an amount equal to what the taxes would be, by one recent account more than twenty million dollars a year. For a college that offered every student a free education for more than a century, the land under this tower has been a lifeline.

It has also made owning the building a roller coaster. In 2008, an investment fund from Abu Dhabi paid eight hundred million dollars for most of the tower. But the ground rent was set to jump, and between 2017 and 2018, it rose from about seven point eight million dollars a year to thirty-two and a half million, with more increases scheduled. With rent like that, the building was worth far less. In 2019, it sold for about a hundred and fifty million dollars, a fraction of what it had fetched eleven years earlier.

The new owners struggled too. In 2024, after they fell more than twenty million dollars behind on the rent, Cooper Union moved to end the lease, and after a court fight, the college took the building back. It has since been looking for a new partner to run it.

So one of the most admired skyscrapers in the world is, in a sense, a college's endowment, with a stainless steel crown on top.

overview:
Midtown Manhattan is the densest concentration of office space in the United States, and arguably the most recognizable urban landscape on Earth. Hundreds of thousands of people commute into these few square miles every workday. But for much of the nineteenth century, this area was on the outskirts of the city, a patchwork of farms, rocky outcrops, squatters' shanties, and institutions that wanted to be out of the way, like reservoirs, cattle yards, and rail yards.

The great transformation came at the turn of the twentieth century, driven by transportation. In 1871, Cornelius Vanderbilt opened the first Grand Central at 42nd Street, consolidating his railroads in one terminal. In 1904, the first subway line opened, running up the east side to Grand Central, across 42nd Street to Times Square, and up the west side. In 1910, the Pennsylvania Railroad opened Penn Station at 34th Street, connecting Manhattan by tunnel to New Jersey and Long Island. In 1913, the new Grand Central Terminal opened. Suddenly, Midtown was the most accessible place in the region.

Business followed. Department stores moved to Herald Square and Fifth Avenue. Theaters moved to Times Square. The garment industry moved to the West Thirties. Corporations built headquarters along 42nd Street and Park Avenue. In the late 1920s, during an extraordinary boom, Midtown became the site of a race for the sky, producing the Chrysler Building and the Empire State Building within a year of each other.

The look of Midtown was shaped by one law in particular. In 1916, after the massive Equitable Building downtown blocked light and air from its neighbors, New York passed the first comprehensive zoning law in the country. It required buildings to step back as they rose, so that light could reach the street. This produced the wedding-cake setbacks that define Art Deco skyscrapers, including the Empire State Building. As you walk, look up at the towers and you'll notice those setbacks everywhere.

On this walk, you'll see icons of American commerce, the department store, the corporate skyscraper, the advertising sign, and the train terminal, and you'll hear about the people who built them, the companies that paid for them, and the controversies that shaped them.

title: Rockefeller Center, Park Avenue & Fifth Avenue
blurb: Rockefeller Center, St. Patrick's, MoMA, Park Avenue's glass towers, Gilded Age Fifth Avenue, the Plaza, and Carnegie Hall.

stops.title: Rockefeller Center
stops.text:
You're at Rockefeller Plaza, between Fifth and Sixth Avenues and 48th to 51st Streets, the heart of Rockefeller Center.

The story begins in 1928. John D. Rockefeller Junior, the son of the Standard Oil founder, agreed to lease land here from Columbia University to build a new home for the Metropolitan Opera. Then the stock market crashed in 1929, and the opera pulled out. Rockefeller was stuck with a long-term lease on a large swath of Midtown real estate. Rather than walk away, he decided to build a commercial development on his own, with his own money. Construction began in 1930 and continued through the Depression, employing tens of thousands of workers when jobs were scarce.

The result, completed in the late 1930s, was fourteen Art Deco buildings, organized around plazas, gardens, and a private street, Rockefeller Plaza. It was one of the first developments to combine offices, shops, restaurants, theaters, and public space in a coherent design, and it's been a model for urban developments around the world ever since.

The centerpiece is 30 Rockefeller Plaza, the tall, slender limestone tower. It was originally the RCA Building, headquarters of the Radio Corporation of America, which owned NBC. NBC has broadcast from here since 1933, and shows like Saturday Night Live and The Tonight Show have been produced inside. The building was later renamed for General Electric, and then for Comcast, which now owns NBC.

During construction, in 1932, a photographer captured eleven ironworkers eating lunch on a steel beam high above the city, their legs dangling over the void. The image, Lunch atop a Skyscraper, became one of the most famous photographs of the twentieth century. It was taken on this building.

The center has a famous art controversy. Rockefeller commissioned the Mexican muralist Diego Rivera to paint a mural in the lobby of the RCA Building. Rivera, a communist, included a portrait of Vladimir Lenin. Rockefeller asked him to remove it. Rivera refused. The mural was covered and, in 1934, destroyed. Rivera later recreated it in Mexico City.

Look down into the sunken plaza, where the ice rink is in winter, and the gilded statue of Prometheus by Paul Manship, bringing fire to humanity. The famous Christmas tree tradition began in 1931, when construction workers set up a small tree on the site. It became official in 1933.

On Fifth Avenue, in front of the International Building, is the giant bronze statue of Atlas holding the heavens, by Lee Lawrie and Rene Chambellan. And at Sixth Avenue and 50th Street is Radio City Music Hall, opened in 1932, the largest indoor theater in the world at the time and home of the Rockettes.

deeper.title: The Garden Under the Plaza
deeper.text:
You heard that John D. Rockefeller Junior leased this land from Columbia University. How did a university come to own a slice of Midtown? The answer is a garden.

In 1801, when this was open country far north of the city, a doctor named David Hosack bought about twenty acres here and planted the Elgin Botanic Garden, the first public botanical garden in the United States. Hosack taught botany and medicine, and he's remembered for another reason too: he was the doctor who attended Alexander Hamilton after his duel with Aaron Burr in 1804. At Elgin, he grew a great variety of plants, native and foreign, with greenhouses for tender species, so that medical students could learn to recognize the plants their medicines came from.

The garden was expensive, and Hosack couldn't keep paying for it. In 1810, he sold it to New York State. In 1814, the state handed the land to Columbia, in place of money it had promised the college. The garden faded, and as the city grew north, the land became valuable beyond anyone's imagining. By the 1920s, it was covered with brownstones, and when the opera plan came along, Columbia was the landlord.

Columbia kept the land through the building of Rockefeller Center and for half a century afterward. In 1985, it finally sold the ground under the center for four hundred million dollars.

So the next time you walk among the flower beds of the Channel Gardens, remember that long before there was a Rockefeller Center, this ground was a garden.

deeper.title: Who Were the Men on the Beam?
deeper.text:
You heard about Lunch atop a Skyscraper, the photograph of eleven ironworkers eating lunch on a beam high above the city. It's one of the most famous pictures ever taken in New York, and almost everything about it is a mystery.

Start with how it happened. The usual date is September 20th, 1932, when the building's frame was nearing the top. The beam was real, and so was the drop, but the moment is believed to have been arranged. Rockefeller Center was trying to rent office space in the depths of the Depression, and it ran its own publicity operation, with photographers on hand to show off the project.

Then, who took it. The picture is most often credited to Charles Ebbets, who did publicity photography for the center. But other photographers were up on the steel that day too, and nobody can say for certain whose shutter clicked.

And who's in it. Over the years, many families have looked at those faces and recognized a father, an uncle or a grandfather. In 2012, an Irish documentary followed claims that two of them came from the west of Ireland, and Native American families have claimed others. Most of the eleven have never been identified for certain, and that may be part of the picture's power. They aren't famous men. They're the men who built the city.

deeper.title: Look Closer: Wisdom and the Channel
deeper.text:
Stand in front of 30 Rockefeller Plaza and look up over the main entrance. The bearded figure leaning out of the clouds, holding a giant compass, is Wisdom, carved by the sculptor Lee Lawrie, who also made the Atlas on Fifth Avenue. He's measuring out the universe, and the panels on either side, called Light and Sound, suit a building made for radio. Below him runs a line from the book of Isaiah: Wisdom and knowledge shall be the stability of thy times. It was a hopeful thing to carve over a door in the depths of the Depression.

Now turn toward Fifth Avenue and walk through the gardens that slope down to the plaza. They're called the Channel Gardens, and the name is a little joke. On one side stands La Maison Française, built for French businesses, and on the other, the British Empire Building. Between France and Britain lies a channel, and so does this one. Look above their doors for the gilded reliefs celebrating each country.

The center was built with an art program unlike any other commercial development of its time. Dozens of artists made murals, mosaics, sculpture and metalwork for its buildings. Look up as you walk, at the doorways, the lobbies and the tops of the walls, and you'll find gods, workers, airplanes, radio waves and planets, a whole Depression-era vision of the modern world in stone and metal.

deeper.title: The Showplace of the Nation
deeper.text:
You heard that Radio City Music Hall opened in 1932 as the largest indoor theater in the world. It was the dream of one showman, Samuel Rothafel, known to everyone as Roxy.

Roxy had made his name running grand movie palaces, and he promised this one would top them all. It opened on December 27th, 1932, with an enormous stage show, a parade of acts that included the dancer Martha Graham and the comic dancer Ray Bolger, later the Scarecrow in The Wizard of Oz. More than a hundred thousand people asked for tickets to the opening, for a hall with about six thousand seats. Within two weeks, the hall was showing movies too, and for more than four decades, it paired first-run films with lavish stage shows.

Its most famous performers came from Saint Louis. In 1925, a choreographer named Russell Markert put together a precision dance troupe called the Missouri Rockets, every dancer kicking in perfect unison. Roxy brought them to New York, where they became the Roxyettes, and when he opened the Music Hall, he brought them with him. In 1934, they became the Rockettes. Their eye-high kicks in a long straight line, and their Christmas show, have made them one of the city's great traditions.

Step inside if you can, to see the great auditorium with its sunburst of arches, and the Art Deco lounges and furniture by the designer Donald Deskey. In 1978, when the hall was in danger of closing, a public campaign saved it, and its interior was named a city landmark.

stops.title: St. Patrick's Cathedral
stops.text:
Across Fifth Avenue from Atlas is St. Patrick's Cathedral, the largest Gothic Revival Catholic cathedral in the United States.

When construction began in 1858, this site was far north of the city's center, and critics mocked the decision to build a cathedral out in the countryside. They called it Hughes's Folly, after Archbishop John Hughes, who pushed the project forward. Hughes was a formidable figure, an Irish immigrant nicknamed Dagger John because of the cross he drew next to his signature and because of his combative defense of Catholics against nativist attacks. Building a grand cathedral on Fifth Avenue was a statement that Irish Catholics, despised by many Protestant New Yorkers, had arrived. The project was funded by wealthy donors and by the small contributions of tens of thousands of working-class Irish immigrants.

Construction was interrupted by the Civil War, and the cathedral was finally dedicated in 1879. Its twin spires, which rise about three hundred thirty feet, were added in 1888. The architect was James Renwick Junior, who also designed Grace Church downtown and the Smithsonian Castle in Washington.

Inside, look for the great rose window, the bronze doors, and the Lady Chapel behind the altar. Beneath the altar is a crypt where past archbishops of New York are buried, along with Pierre Toussaint, the formerly enslaved Haitian philanthropist you may have heard about at Old St. Patrick's on the Lower East Side, who is the only layperson buried there.

The cathedral underwent a major restoration in the 2010s that cleaned the marble exterior, which had been blackened by pollution, back to its bright white.

Notice the dialogue between the cathedral and Rockefeller Center across the street. The Atlas statue faces the cathedral directly, holding up the heavens. Whether that was meant as a symbol of human ambition facing faith, or simply a coincidence of planning, it's become one of the most photographed juxtapositions in New York.

Next to the cathedral, on Fifth Avenue between 49th and 50th Streets, is Saks Fifth Avenue, which opened its flagship here in 1924. It was one of the first major department stores on upper Fifth Avenue, helping to cement the avenue's transformation from mansions to luxury retail.

deeper.title: Look Closer: The Red Hats
deeper.text:
Go inside, and look for something hanging high overhead: wide, flat red hats with long tassels. They're galeros, the hats once given to cardinals of the Catholic Church, and each one here belonged to a cardinal archbishop of New York.

The tradition goes back centuries. When a cardinal died, his red hat was hung from the ceiling of his cathedral, above his tomb, and left there. It was said that it would hang until it rotted and fell, a reminder that all earthly glory passes away. In the late 1960s, as part of a reform of the church's ceremonies, the Vatican stopped giving out the galero altogether.

Four hang here. The oldest belonged to John McCloskey, who in 1875 became the first American named a cardinal. The others belonged to his successors John Farley, Patrick Hayes and Francis Spellman, the powerful archbishop who led New York's Catholics from 1939 to 1967. During the cathedral's restoration in the 2010s, the old silk hats were taken down, carefully conserved and hung back up, which isn't quite the tradition, but saved them from falling to dust.

Beneath the altar, in the crypt you heard about, these cardinals lie with other archbishops of New York. So when you look up at the hats, you're looking at the cathedral's own history: an immigrant church that built this place, and the men who led it as it rose to power in the city.

deeper.title: A Ceiling That Was Meant to Be Temporary
deeper.text:
You heard that construction began in 1858. The cathedral didn't open until 1879, with work halted for years during the Civil War, and money was short the whole way. The evidence is over your head.

James Renwick designed the cathedral in the manner of the great Gothic cathedrals of Europe, with pointed arches, ribbed vaults and soaring piers, all clad in white marble outside. In a true medieval cathedral, the vaulted ceiling is stone. Stone vaults are enormously heavy, and they push outward on the walls, which is why medieval builders added flying buttresses, the stone arms that brace the walls from outside. Renwick planned a masonry ceiling too. But the money wasn't there, so the vault you see overhead was built as a lighter, cheaper ceiling of plaster on wood and lath, meant as a stopgap.

The stopgap became permanent. And because a plaster vault weighs so little, the cathedral could do without the great flying buttresses that brace the stone vaults of Europe's cathedrals.

The restoration in the 2010s took on that old ceiling. Workers raised scaffolding to the vaults, repaired the cracks, and kept the plaster fixed to its original timber laths.

So St. Patrick's is a little like the city that built it: a grand European idea, put up by an immigrant community on a budget, and made to last anyway.

deeper.title: The Bishop on Television
deeper.text:
In the early 1950s, one of the most popular stars on American television was a Catholic bishop who preached here.

Fulton Sheen was an auxiliary bishop of New York, a gifted speaker with piercing eyes, a flowing cape and a showman's timing. In 1952, he began a weekly television program called Life Is Worth Living. There was no choir and no altar, just Sheen in a study with a blackboard, talking for half an hour about love, fear, communism and the meaning of suffering, with jokes thrown in. He was scheduled on Tuesday nights against the biggest star on television, the comedian Milton Berle, and few expected him to last. Instead, he drew millions of viewers of every faith, won an Emmy as television's most outstanding personality, and in accepting it, is said to have thanked his writers: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.

Sheen later became bishop of Rochester, and then an archbishop. When he died in 1979, he was buried in the crypt beneath the altar here, among the archbishops of New York. But he had grown up in Peoria, Illinois, and the diocese there, which was leading the effort to have him declared a saint, wanted his body. After years of legal fighting, with his family taking Peoria's side, the Archdiocese of New York gave way, and in June 2019, his remains were moved to the cathedral in Peoria.

So for forty years, the crypt beneath this altar held one of the first stars of television.

stops.title: MoMA & Paley Park
stops.text:
Walk to West 53rd Street, between Fifth and Sixth Avenues. Here you'll find the Museum of Modern Art.

MoMA was founded in 1929 by three wealthy women: Abby Aldrich Rockefeller, the wife of John D. Rockefeller Junior, and her friends Lillie P. Bliss and Mary Quinn Sullivan. At the time, established museums like the Met were reluctant to collect contemporary art. The founders wanted a museum dedicated to the art of their own time. It opened nine days after the stock market crash, in rented rooms in an office building. Its first director, Alfred Barr, was just twenty-seven years old. His vision, that a museum should show modern painting alongside photography, film, industrial design, and architecture, was revolutionary.

The museum moved to 53rd Street in 1939, into a modernist building designed by Philip Goodwin and Edward Durell Stone. It's been expanded many times since, most recently in 2004 by the Japanese architect Yoshio Taniguchi and in 2019 by Diller Scofidio and Renfro, the firm behind the High Line. Its collection includes Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night, Pablo Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, Claude Monet's Water Lilies, Andy Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans, and much more. Its design collection includes everything from a helicopter to the original emoji set.

Now walk east, to East 53rd Street between Fifth and Madison Avenues, and look for a small park with a waterfall. This is Paley Park, a tiny vest-pocket park opened in 1967. It was created by William S. Paley, the founder of CBS, in memory of his father, on the site of the famous Stork Club, a nightclub where celebrities and gossip columnists gathered in the mid-century.

Paley Park is only about forty-two by one hundred feet, but it's considered one of the most perfect small urban spaces in the world. The twenty-foot waterfall at the back drowns out traffic noise. Honey locust trees provide dappled shade. Movable chairs let people sit wherever they like. The urbanist William H. Whyte studied this park and others like it in the 1970s, filming how people used public spaces, and found that small, well-designed spaces with seating, water, food, and trees could attract heavy use. His findings shaped the city's plaza rules and later the redesign of Bryant Park.

CBS's own headquarters, a dark granite tower nicknamed Black Rock, designed by Eero Saarinen and completed in 1965, stands a block west, at Sixth Avenue and 52nd Street.

deeper.title: The Stork Club
deeper.text:
You heard that Paley Park stands on the site of the Stork Club. For more than three decades, it was the most famous nightclub in America.

It was run by Sherman Billingsley, an Oklahoman who had been a bootlegger, and it began as a speakeasy during Prohibition. In 1934, it moved to this block of 53rd Street and became the place where movie stars, socialites, politicians and writers all wanted to be seen. Getting in was the game. A doorman decided who passed the gold chain at the entrance, and the inner room, the Cub Room, had its own gatekeeper, nicknamed Saint Peter.

The club's most powerful regular was Walter Winchell, the gossip columnist and radio broadcaster, followed by tens of millions of Americans. He held court at Table 50 in the Cub Room, and a mention in his column could make or break a career. Billingsley and Winchell made each other famous.

Then, in October 1951, the singer and dancer Josephine Baker, an American star who lived in France, came in with friends, ordered dinner, and by her account waited about an hour for food that never came. She was sure she was being refused service because she was Black. Winchell had been in the room, and Baker publicly accused him of doing nothing. Winchell said he had left before the trouble began, and turned on her in his column. The NAACP picketed the club, and the quarrel played out in the newspapers for months.

The club's glamour faded in the years that followed. It closed in 1965, the building was torn down, and the site became the little park where you can sit today.

deeper.title: The Fire at the Museum
deeper.text:
On April 15th, 1958, the Museum of Modern Art caught fire.

Workers were renovating on the second floor, and a fire broke out among their materials, by the most common account from a workman's cigarette. Thick smoke poured up through the building. On the floor above hung a major exhibition of the paintings of Georges Seurat, including one of the most famous pictures in the world, A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, lent by the Art Institute of Chicago. Paintings were rushed to safety, and La Grande Jatte ended up next door in the Whitney Museum, which then stood beside the Modern. It came through undamaged, but it was the first time Chicago had ever lent the painting, and it hasn't traveled since.

One workman died, and more than two dozen people, many of them firefighters, were hurt. The greatest loss to the collection was a painting. In 1955, the museum had bought one of Claude Monet's huge late paintings of water lilies, about eighteen feet long. It was destroyed. A smaller Monet came out scorched, looking, as one writer later put it, like a toasted marshmallow. The museum's conservators worked on it for three years before declaring it beyond repair.

The museum didn't give up on Monet. Soon afterward, it bought another of his enormous water lily paintings in Paris, a triptych of three panels that together stretch more than forty feet. That's the painting you'll usually find in the galleries today, one of the most popular in the museum. If you stand in front of it, you're looking at the museum's answer to the fire.

deeper.title: Look Closer: Two Gardens
deeper.text:
Two of the best outdoor rooms in Midtown are a block apart, and they're related.

The first is behind the museum: the Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, named for one of the museum's founders. It was designed by the architect Philip Johnson, who also ran the museum's architecture department, with the landscape architect James Fanning, and it opened in 1953. Johnson laid it out like an open-air room, paved in marble, with pools of water, trees, and sculptures set against the sky and the surrounding towers. In 1964, he enlarged it, working with the landscape firm Zion and Breen. If you go in, notice how the walls, the water and the trees make you forget the street outside.

The second is Paley Park, which opened three years later, designed by the same landscape firm, led by Robert Zion. You can feel the family resemblance: a small room cut off from the city, with water, a canopy of trees, and chairs you can move. Zion was a champion of what came to be called pocket parks, tiny parks tucked between buildings, and this one became the model for them.

What both gardens understand is that a city space doesn't have to be big. It needs walls to hold you, something to look at, the sound of water, shade, and a place to sit. Those are simple ingredients, and they're why these two small gardens are still full on a sunny day, more than half a century later.

stops.title: Park Avenue: Lever House & the Seagram Building
stops.text:
You're on Park Avenue, around 52nd and 53rd Streets. Remember that Park Avenue exists because the railroad tracks going into Grand Central were covered over. In the 1910s and 20s, this stretch was lined with elegant apartment buildings. After World War Two, corporations replaced them with glass towers. Two buildings, across the avenue from each other, started that transformation.

On the west side, at 390 Park Avenue, look for a green glass tower that rises from a low horizontal base lifted on columns. This is Lever House, completed in 1952. It was designed by Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore, Owings and Merrill for the Lever Brothers company, the British soap maker that produced brands like Lifebuoy and Lux, and is now part of Unilever. The company wanted a building that looked clean, like its products. Lever House was among the first glass curtain-wall office buildings in New York, and it was revolutionary: instead of filling its lot, it left most of the ground open, with a courtyard and a slim tower. Its glass was even cleaned by a gondola that moved along the facade, which was itself a marketing statement.

Across the avenue, at 375 Park Avenue, is the Seagram Building, completed in 1958. It was the headquarters of Joseph E. Seagram and Sons, the Canadian whiskey distiller. The founder's daughter, Phyllis Lambert, a young architecture student, persuaded her father to hire Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, the German modernist master. Mies designed a dark bronze and glass tower set back from the street behind a granite plaza with two reflecting pools. He used bronze I-beams on the exterior, purely for visual effect, to express the steel structure inside. It was enormously expensive, and enormously influential. The Seagram Building became the template for countless corporate towers around the world.

Its plaza inspired a change in the city's zoning law in 1961, which gave developers extra height if they provided public plazas. Not all of those plazas turned out as well as Seagram's.

Inside the Seagram Building, the restaurant space designed by Philip Johnson housed the Four Seasons, where the power lunch is said to have been invented.

Now look south along Park Avenue, toward 47th Street, at the massive new tower at 270 Park Avenue. This is the new global headquarters of JPMorgan Chase, completed in the mid-2020s. To build it, the bank demolished the previous fifty-two-story tower on the site, the former Union Carbide Building, making it the tallest building ever intentionally demolished. JPMorgan Chase's history, as you may have heard on the Financial District tour, includes J. P. Morgan's bank and Aaron Burr's Manhattan Company. Its new tower is a sign that, for the biggest banks, Midtown, not Wall Street, is now the center of gravity.

Also on Park Avenue, at 49th Street, is the Waldorf Astoria, the Art Deco hotel that opened in 1931 after the old one was demolished for the Empire State Building. For decades, it was where presidents stayed in New York.

deeper.title: No, No, No, No, No
deeper.text:
You heard that Phyllis Lambert persuaded her father to hire Mies van der Rohe. Here's how she did it.

In 1954, Lambert was twenty-seven and living in Paris when she saw the design her father, Samuel Bronfman, the head of Seagram, had in mind for the company's new headquarters on Park Avenue, a conventional tower by a commercial firm. She was appalled. She sat down and wrote him an eight-page letter, and by her own account, it began with the words No, no, no, no, no. The rest was a passionate argument that a company's building is a public statement that will stand for generations, and that Seagram should build something great.

Her father did something unusual. Instead of brushing her off, he put her in charge of finding a new architect. She came back to New York and spent weeks meeting the leading architects of the day, with advice from Philip Johnson, and chose Mies, then in his late sixties and working in Chicago. Johnson joined him on the project, designing interiors including the Four Seasons restaurant.

Lambert didn't stop there. She went on to study architecture herself and became an architect, a preservationist and a fierce critic of careless development. In 1979, she founded the Canadian Centre for Architecture in Montreal, one of the world's great architecture museums.

The Seagram Building turned out to be what she had promised her father: a landmark copied around the world, and a reminder of what one stubborn letter can do.

deeper.title: The Paintings That Never Hung
deeper.text:
The Four Seasons restaurant, inside the Seagram Building, was meant to be a complete work of modern design: Mies's building, Philip Johnson's rooms, and on the walls, paintings by one of the greatest living painters.

Around 1958, Mark Rothko accepted a commission to paint a series of large murals for the restaurant. He threw himself into the work, producing dozens of dark, brooding canvases in deep maroons and blacks. But he had doubts. He told a writer he met on a ship to Europe that he had taken the job with strictly malicious intentions, hoping to paint something that would ruin the appetite of every rich diner who ever ate in that room.

Then he went to dinner at the restaurant himself. By most accounts, the expensive, showy atmosphere confirmed his fears, and he decided that his paintings would never hang there. He withdrew from the commission and kept the murals. Years later, he gave nine of them to the Tate in London, on condition that they hang together in a room of their own. They arrived in London on the same day in 1970 that Rothko died in New York.

The restaurant got along without him. For decades, a different masterpiece hung in its corridor: a huge stage curtain painted by Pablo Picasso for a ballet, Le Tricorne. In 2014, after a dispute with the building's owner, the curtain was moved to the New-York Historical Society.

The Four Seasons left the building in 2016, and its famous rooms have since been taken over by new restaurants. But the story of the Rothkos is a reminder that some art refuses to be decoration.

deeper.title: The Woman Behind the Glass
deeper.text:
You heard that Lever House was designed by Gordon Bunshaft of Skidmore, Owings and Merrill. For decades, his was the only name most people knew. Working beside him was Natalie de Blois.

De Blois was one of very few women in American architecture when she joined the firm in the 1940s, and she rose to become one of its senior designers. On Lever House, she worked closely with Bunshaft, and colleagues and historians have since credited her with a large share of the design. But when the building opened in 1952 and the praise poured in, it went to Bunshaft and the firm. That was how big firms worked in those days, and it was doubly true for a woman.

She went on to help design other corporate towers of the era, including the Pepsi-Cola Building, a few blocks up Park Avenue, and, by most accounts, the Union Carbide Building, the tower at 270 Park Avenue you heard was torn down for JPMorgan Chase. Later she taught architecture in Texas and spoke out for women in the profession, and she has slowly been written back into the story.

Lever House itself had to fight to survive. Its low base and open courtyard used only a fraction of what the zoning allowed, which made it a tempting target for a bigger tower. Preservationists rallied, and in 1982, when the building was barely thirty years old, the city named it a landmark. It's still here, still green glass, still showing how much a building can give back to the street.

deeper.title: Trees for the Sons
deeper.text:
Look at the planted islands running down the middle of Park Avenue. They gave the avenue its name.

This was once Fourth Avenue, and for much of the nineteenth century, its northern stretch was a railroad right-of-way, with trains running through an open cut and tunnels. As the tracks were covered over, the avenue got landscaped medians on top, and with them a grander name: Park Avenue. Over time, the name spread south along the old Fourth Avenue, all the way down to Union Square, and the medians became some of the most carefully tended strips of green in the city, with tulips in spring.

Every December, the medians get something else: a long line of Christmas trees, lit for almost fifty blocks. The tradition began in 1945. After the Second World War, a group of Park Avenue mothers arranged for lighted fir trees along the avenue, in memory of the sons the war had taken. The trees came back the next year, and they've come back ever since.

Today, about a hundred and twenty trees are shipped down from Nova Scotia each year, and the lights are switched on at a ceremony at the Brick Presbyterian Church, uptown on Park Avenue. Most people walking past in December think they're just decorations. They began as a memorial.

stops.title: Gilded Age Fifth Avenue
stops.text:
You're at Fifth Avenue and 57th Street, the most famous luxury shopping intersection in America.

Imagine this corner in the 1890s. On the west side of Fifth Avenue, from 57th to 58th Street, stood the largest private house ever built in New York City, the mansion of Cornelius Vanderbilt the Second, the grandson of the Commodore. It was a French château with well over one hundred rooms, and it took up the whole block front. Vanderbilt family mansions lined Fifth Avenue for blocks to the south. This was the heart of the Gilded Age.

By 1926, the Vanderbilt mansion was demolished. Its site became the department store Bergdorf Goodman, founded by Herman Bergdorf, a tailor, and Edwin Goodman, which moved here in 1928. Bergdorf's is still one of the most exclusive department stores in the world. The mansion's grand iron gates were saved, and today they stand at the entrance to the Conservatory Garden in Central Park.

On the southeast corner of 57th Street is Tiffany and Company's flagship store, which opened here in 1940. Above the entrance, look for the statue of Atlas holding a clock, which was moved here from the company's earlier stores. In the 1961 film Breakfast at Tiffany's, Audrey Hepburn ate a pastry while gazing into these windows. The store underwent a major renovation in the early 2020s.

Walk back a few blocks south, to Fifth Avenue and 52nd Street, and look for an Italian Renaissance mansion of pale stone, home to the Cartier jewelry store. Here's one of the best stories in New York real estate. The mansion was built for Morton Plant, a railroad and steamship magnate. By 1917, the neighborhood was going commercial, and Plant wanted out. Meanwhile, Pierre Cartier, the French jeweler, wanted a Fifth Avenue store. Plant's wife, Maisie, admired a double strand of natural pearls Cartier had. At the time, natural pearls were extraordinarily valuable, before cultured pearls became widespread. So they made a trade: the mansion, plus a small sum of cash, for the pearl necklace. Cartier got its New York flagship, which it still occupies. A few decades later, after cultured pearls had flooded the market, the necklace sold at auction for a small fraction of its former value. The house turned out to be the better deal.

Up and down this stretch, flagship stores for luxury brands occupy some of the most expensive retail space in the world. Upper Fifth Avenue's rents regularly rank among the highest anywhere.

deeper.title: Alva's Ball
deeper.text:
You heard that Vanderbilt family mansions lined Fifth Avenue for blocks south of here. The most famous party ever thrown in one of them was a social coup.

In the early 1880s, the Vanderbilts were among the richest people in America, but old New York society looked down on them as new money, descendants of a rough ferry captain. Society's gatekeeper was Caroline Astor, known simply as the Mrs. Astor, and her circle, the one later nicknamed the Four Hundred, as you may have heard at Gramercy Park, kept the Vanderbilts out.

Alva Vanderbilt, the wife of the Commodore's grandson William Kissam Vanderbilt, set out to change that. She had a new château built on Fifth Avenue at 52nd Street, designed by Richard Morris Hunt, and on March 26th, 1883, she threw a costume ball to show it off, for more than a thousand guests. Society talked of nothing else for weeks. Guests came as kings, queens and figures from history, and Alva's sister-in-law came dressed as Electric Light.

Now the story, as it's usually told, and it may have been polished. Mrs. Astor's daughter, Carrie, was dying to go, and had been rehearsing a dance for the ball with her friends. But no invitation came. Alva let it be known that she couldn't invite someone whose mother had never paid a call on her. So Mrs. Astor swallowed her pride, had her carriage driven to Alva's door, and left her calling card. The invitation arrived the next day.

Whether or not it happened just that way, the ball worked. The Vanderbilts were in. Alva's château is long gone, but her ambitions were just getting started.

deeper.title: The Duke and the Dollar Princess
deeper.text:
A few blocks south, at Fifth Avenue and 53rd Street, stands Saint Thomas Church. In 1895, in the church that stood on that corner before the present one, Alva Vanderbilt married off her daughter.

Consuelo Vanderbilt was eighteen, and in love with an American. Alva had other plans. In the Gilded Age, rich American families married their daughters to European aristocrats: the families gained titles, and the aristocrats gained fortunes to prop up their estates. The brides were called dollar princesses. Alva chose the ninth Duke of Marlborough, who needed money for Blenheim Palace. Consuelo resisted, and by her own later account, her mother kept her shut away and pressured her until she gave in. On November 6th, 1895, she married the duke there, reportedly in tears, while crowds jammed Fifth Avenue to watch. Her father settled a fortune in railroad stock on the marriage.

The marriage was miserable. The couple separated and later divorced, and when the marriage came before a church court for annulment in 1926, Alva testified that she had forced her daughter into it.

Alva, meanwhile, had become a different person. Earlier in 1895, she had divorced William Vanderbilt, a scandal in itself, and she soon married Oliver Belmont. After his death in 1908, she poured her energy and money into the fight for women's votes. In 1909, she founded the Political Equality Association, and as you may have heard on the Lower East Side, she backed the striking shirtwaist makers that winter. Later, she bankrolled the most militant wing of the suffrage movement, the National Woman's Party, and served as its president.

The mother who forced her daughter into a loveless marriage ended her life as a champion of women's independence. History doesn't always run in a straight line.

deeper.title: The Hope Diamond in the Mail
deeper.text:
Look for the Harry Winston salon, at Fifth Avenue and 56th Street. The jeweler who founded it once sent the most famous diamond in the world through the mail.

Harry Winston rose from his father's small jewelry shop to become known as the king of diamonds, trading in many of the world's great stones. In 1949, he bought the Hope Diamond, a deep blue stone of about forty-five carats, along with the rest of the jewels of the Washington socialite Evalyn Walsh McLean, its last private owner. For years, he took it on tour to charity events. Then he decided it belonged to the public, and gave it to the Smithsonian Institution.

How do you deliver a priceless diamond to Washington? Winston put it in a box, wrapped it in plain brown paper, and sent it by registered first-class mail. The postage came to two dollars and forty-four cents, plus a hundred and forty-two dollars and eighty-five cents to insure it for a million dollars. It rode to Washington in a mail car on the train, and a letter carrier delivered it to the museum on November 10th, 1958. The Smithsonian still has the wrapping paper, stamps and all.

The Hope Diamond comes with a legend: that it carries a curse. Its owners did include a French king who lost his head and a socialite whose family suffered terrible losses. But the curse story seems to have been largely spread by jewelers and newspapers to make the stone more intriguing, and it may have helped sell it. Winston owned it for nearly a decade and lived a long and prosperous life.

Today, the diamond is one of the most visited museum objects in the world, and it got there for the price of a postage stamp.

stops.title: The Plaza Hotel & Grand Army Plaza
stops.text:
You're at Grand Army Plaza, at Fifth Avenue and 59th Street, the southeast corner of Central Park.

The grand, château-style building facing the park is the Plaza Hotel. It opened in 1907, designed by Henry Janeway Hardenbergh, who also designed the Dakota apartment building on the Upper West Side. It was built to be the most luxurious hotel in the world, and the Vanderbilts and other wealthy families took up residence there.

The Plaza has played a starring role in countless stories. Kay Thompson's Eloise books, published starting in 1955, featured a mischievous six-year-old girl who lives at the Plaza; a portrait of Eloise hangs in the hotel. In 1964, the Beatles stayed here on their first visit to America. In 1966, the writer Truman Capote held his Black and White Ball in the hotel's ballroom, a masked party considered by many to be the social event of the century.

The Plaza has a place in financial history too. In September 1985, finance ministers and central bankers from the United States, Japan, West Germany, France, and the United Kingdom met at the Plaza and agreed to coordinate interventions in currency markets to bring down the value of the US dollar, which had risen sharply. The agreement, the Plaza Accord, worked. The dollar fell dramatically over the following two years. Many economists link the resulting rise of the Japanese yen to Japan's asset bubble in the late 1980s and its collapse into a long stagnation.

In the plaza in front of the hotel is the Pulitzer Fountain, with a statue of Pomona, the Roman goddess of abundance, funded by a bequest from the newspaper publisher Joseph Pulitzer. North of it, at the park's corner, is a gleaming gilded statue of General William Tecumseh Sherman on horseback, led by a winged figure of Victory, by Augustus Saint-Gaudens, completed in 1903. It's considered one of the finest equestrian statues in America.

Across Fifth Avenue is the General Motors Building, a white marble tower completed in 1968. In front of it is a glass cube, the entrance to Apple's Fifth Avenue store, opened in 2006. The store is underground, open around the clock, and the cube has become one of the most photographed retail designs in the world.

For decades, the GM Building was also home to the toy store FAO Schwarz, founded in 1862 and famous for the giant floor piano played in the 1988 film Big. The store closed here in 2015 and has since reopened at Rockefeller Center.

deeper.title: Look Closer: The Woman Leading Sherman
deeper.text:
You heard that the gilded statue of General Sherman, by Augustus Saint-Gaudens, is considered one of the finest equestrian statues in America. Look at the figure walking ahead of his horse.

She's Victory, striding forward with a palm branch in one hand and her other arm raised, wings spread, leading Sherman on. Saint-Gaudens worked on the monument for more than a decade. He had Sherman himself sit for a portrait bust in 1888, and the general's lean, weathered face came from those sittings. The horse was modeled by another sculptor, Alexander Phimister Proctor, a specialist in animals. Look down at its hooves: one of them treads on a branch of Georgia pine, a reminder of Sherman's march through Georgia to the sea.

For Victory, the sculptor's principal model was Hettie Anderson, a Black woman who was one of the most sought-after artists' models in New York in the 1890s. She posed for Saint-Gaudens over several years, and her face and figure shaped one of the most admired allegories in American sculpture. It's often said that she also posed for the figure of Liberty on the gold twenty-dollar coin that Saint-Gaudens designed a few years later, though that's harder to pin down. For a long time, her name was left out of the story, and only recently has she been given her due.

Think about the pairing for a moment. Sherman's armies helped bring an end to slavery. Leading him in bronze and gold, at the corner of Central Park, is the likeness of a Black woman.

The monument was shown in Paris at the World's Fair of 1900 before it was unveiled here in 1903. Its bright gilding has divided people almost from the start. Some find it glorious, others gaudy, and each time it's been regilded, the argument has started all over again.

deeper.title: The Fountain of Abundance
deeper.text:
You heard that the fountain in front of the Plaza was paid for by a bequest from Joseph Pulitzer. Its making was haunted by a death.

Pulitzer, whose newspaper campaign paid for the Statue of Liberty's pedestal, as you may have heard near City Hall, died in 1911 and left money in his will for a fountain at this corner of Central Park, in the spirit of the great fountains of Paris. The design went to Thomas Hastings, of Carrère and Hastings, the architects of the New York Public Library, who drew a series of stone basins stepping down toward the plaza. For the figure on top, the commission went to Karl Bitter, a Vienna-born sculptor who had become one of the busiest in New York. You may have seen his bronze doors at Trinity Church.

Bitter chose Pomona, the Roman goddess of abundance, with a basket of fruit in her arms. In April 1915, he had just finished the plaster model when he was struck by a car and killed. He was forty-seven.

His widow and Hastings chose another sculptor, Isidore Konti, to carry the figure through to bronze, working with Bitter's young assistant, Karl Gruppe, and the fountain was dedicated in 1916. In the 1930s, Gruppe led the parks department's campaign to restore the city's neglected monuments, cleaning and repairing statues all over town.

So the goddess of abundance at the edge of the park is a collaboration across a death: Bitter's model, finished by his colleagues, in a fountain paid for by a newspaperman's will.

deeper.title: Zelda in the Fountain
deeper.text:
Here's a story New Yorkers love to tell about the Pulitzer Fountain. It may even be true.

In 1920, F. Scott Fitzgerald published his first novel, This Side of Paradise, became famous almost overnight, and married Zelda Sayre of Montgomery, Alabama, in the rectory of St. Patrick's Cathedral, down Fifth Avenue. The two of them became the golden couple of the Jazz Age, and they lived the part: riding on the roofs of taxis, dancing on tables, getting asked to leave hotels. And according to legend, one night Zelda, fully dressed, jumped into the fountain in front of the Plaza, with Scott perhaps right behind her.

Did it happen? Nobody has pinned it down. Other versions put Zelda's famous plunge in the fountain at Union Square or in Washington Square Park, and in her hometown, people tell a similar story about a fountain there. It's exactly the kind of thing Zelda might have done, and exactly the kind of story people tell about the Fitzgeralds whether or not it happened. So file it under legend.

What's certain is that the Plaza meant something to Scott. The couple stayed here, and in The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, the novel's great confrontation takes place in a sweltering suite at the Plaza, where Tom Buchanan finally faces down Gatsby over Daisy. In the middle of the quarrel, the narrator, Nick Carraway, realizes that it's his thirtieth birthday. If you've read the book, look up at the windows and picture that hot afternoon.

stops.title: Carnegie Hall & Billionaires' Row
stops.text:
End your walk at Seventh Avenue and 57th Street, outside Carnegie Hall.

Carnegie Hall was built by Andrew Carnegie, the Scottish-born steel magnate who was one of the richest men in history, and who later gave away most of his fortune, funding more than two thousand five hundred public libraries around the world. He built the hall at the urging of a young conductor, Walter Damrosch, and his wife Louise, who was a member of the Oratorio Society. It opened in 1891, with the Russian composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky conducting on opening night. Its acoustics are considered among the best in the world. Everyone from Gustav Mahler to Benny Goodman, Judy Garland, and the Beatles has performed here.

In the 1950s, Carnegie Hall faced demolition after the New York Philharmonic decided to move to the new Lincoln Center. The violinist Isaac Stern led a campaign to save it, and in 1960, the city bought it. The main auditorium is now named for Stern.

There's an old joke: a tourist stops a musician on 57th Street and asks, How do you get to Carnegie Hall? The musician answers, Practice, practice, practice.

Now look up and around you, along 57th Street. You're on Billionaires' Row, a cluster of super-tall, super-slender luxury residential towers built since the 2010s, mostly along 57th Street at the south edge of Central Park. They include One57, Central Park Tower, the tallest residential building in the world, and, just east of here, 111 West 57th Street, often called the Steinway Tower. It's one of the most slender skyscrapers in the world, with a width-to-height ratio of about one to twenty-four. It incorporates the historic Steinway Hall, built in 1925 as the showroom of Steinway and Sons, the piano company founded by the German immigrant Henry Steinway in 1853, whose pianos are used by most of the world's concert pianists.

These towers were made possible by new engineering techniques and by developers buying up the unused air rights of neighboring buildings, allowing them to build much taller than would otherwise be allowed. Their apartments have sold for tens of millions of dollars, and some for over one hundred million. Critics point out that many are owned by international buyers as investments and sit empty much of the year, and that the towers cast long shadows across Central Park.

It's a fitting place to end: a nineteenth-century concert hall built by a steel baron, a twentieth-century piano showroom, and twenty-first-century towers for the global rich, side by side on the same block. On 57th Street, wealth keeps finding new ways to show itself.

deeper.title: Jazz Comes to Carnegie Hall
deeper.text:
You heard that everyone from Mahler to Benny Goodman has played here. Goodman's night is the famous one. But he wasn't the first to bring this kind of music here.

On May 2nd, 1912, James Reese Europe led his Clef Club Orchestra onto this stage for a Concert of Negro Music, a benefit for the Music School Settlement for Colored People. Europe was a Black bandleader and composer who had organized the Clef Club, a union and booking agency for Black musicians in New York. His orchestra had more than a hundred players, with banjos, mandolins and pianos, and it played to a sold-out hall with a racially mixed audience. Whether you call the music jazz or the ragtime that came just before it, it was the first time that sound filled this hall. Europe went on to lead the band of the 369th Infantry, the Harlem Hellfighters, in the First World War, carrying the new American music to France.

Twenty-six years later, on January 16th, 1938, Benny Goodman, the King of Swing, brought his band here. Swing was dance music, played in ballrooms and clubs, and many people thought it had no place in a concert hall. Goodman's musicians included the Black pianist Teddy Wilson and vibraphonist Lionel Hampton, at a time when most bands were segregated, and he brought in guests from Count Basie's and Duke Ellington's bands. Before the concert, asked how long an intermission he wanted, Goodman is said to have answered: I don't know. How long does Toscanini take? When the band tore into Sing, Sing, Sing, the hall went wild.

The recording of that night, released years later, became one of the best-selling jazz albums ever made. Five years later, Duke Ellington premiered his long jazz symphony, Black, Brown and Beige, on this stage. Jazz has had a home at Carnegie Hall ever since.

deeper.title: The Studios Upstairs
deeper.text:
Look up above the hall. For more than a century, the building's upper floors were full of artists.

A few years after the hall opened, two towers of studios were added, finished in the 1890s, with big windows and skylights for working artists. They became one of the great creative addresses in New York. Over the years, the tenants included painters, sculptors, dancers, singers, actors, teachers and photographers.
