Marlon Brando lived in one as a young actor. Leonard Bernstein lived in another early in his career, before he became the most famous conductor in America. Students climbed the stairs for lessons, while the stars performed down below.

The best-known of the last tenants was Bill Cunningham, the photographer who for decades rode his bicycle around Manhattan photographing what people actually wore on the street, for the New York Times. He lived and worked in a tiny studio here, crammed with filing cabinets full of negatives, for about sixty years.

In 2010, Carnegie Hall moved out its remaining residents to turn the towers into rehearsal rooms, classrooms and offices for its education programs. Some of the longtime tenants fought it, and the papers wrote about the end of a bohemian era. Today, young musicians practice where the artists once lived, which seems only fitting in a building where the answer to the old joke is practice.

deeper.title: Music Hall, Founded by Andrew Carnegie
deeper.text:
Look above the entrance arches, and you'll find words carved in stone: Music Hall, founded by Andrew Carnegie. That was the building's first name.

Its architect, William Tuthill, was not a famous one. He was in his thirties, a gifted amateur cellist who sat with Carnegie on the board of the Oratorio Society, and before he drew the hall, he toured Europe to study the concert halls most admired for their sound. Many people credit his musician's ear for the acoustics you heard about.

When the hall opened in May 1891, it was simply the Music Hall. The opening was a five-day festival. On the first night, after a speech by the Episcopal bishop of New York, Walter Damrosch conducted the orchestra, and then one of the most famous composers in the world stepped onto the stage: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, who had come from Russia to conduct his own music. Two days later, on his fifty-first birthday, he conducted his Third Suite.

Tchaikovsky kept a diary of his American trip. It's full of wonder at the city and the warmth of its people, and full of homesickness too. He wrote that he seemed to be far more famous in America than in Europe. And he could be blunt: sitting through a long choral work by Berlioz on opening night, he found it tedious until the very end.

The plain name didn't last. The hall's board persuaded a reluctant Carnegie to let them use his. The story goes that to European performers, a music hall meant a place for comic songs and variety acts, not symphonies. By the mid-1890s, the Music Hall had become Carnegie Hall, though the old name is still carved over the door.

Its rooms have since taken on other names, many of them for donors, and the main auditorium is named for Isaac Stern, the violinist who saved the building. But to musicians around the world, the whole place is simply Carnegie, the hall every young performer dreams of playing.

overview:
This walk covers the stretch of Midtown that has long been the showroom of American wealth and corporate power: Fifth Avenue, Park Avenue, and 57th Street.

In the second half of the nineteenth century, as the rich moved north from Madison Square, Fifth Avenue between about 50th and 70th Streets became a canyon of mansions. The Vanderbilts alone built a string of enormous houses along the avenue, each trying to outdo the others, in French château and Italian Renaissance styles. This was the Gilded Age, the era of railroad, oil, and steel fortunes, and Fifth Avenue was its main street.

Within a few decades, the mansions were gone. Rising property taxes, the income tax introduced in 1913, the cost of servants, and the relentless pressure of commerce made them impractical. Families sold them to developers and moved into apartments on the Upper East Side. Department stores and luxury retailers took over Fifth Avenue: Saks, Bergdorf Goodman, Tiffany, Cartier. Office buildings rose around them.

Then came Rockefeller Center, built in the 1930s during the Great Depression, a city within a city that became the model for the modern mixed-use urban development. After World War Two, Park Avenue, which had been lined with elegant apartment buildings, was transformed into a corridor of glass corporate headquarters, starting with Lever House and the Seagram Building, two of the most influential skyscrapers ever built. In recent years, the newest form of wealth display has appeared along 57th Street: super-tall, super-thin residential towers for the global ultra-rich, known as Billionaires' Row.

As you walk, notice how each era expressed wealth differently: Gilded Age mansions with marble and ornament; the Art Deco optimism of Rockefeller Center; the cool, minimalist glass of mid-century corporate modernism; and the needle-thin towers of today. Every one of them was built to impress you.

title: Central Park: The Southern Park
blurb: Olmsted and Vaux's masterpiece, from the Pond and the Dairy to the Mall, Bethesda Fountain, Bow Bridge, and Strawberry Fields.

stops.title: The Pond & Gapstow Bridge
stops.text:
You're at the southeast corner of Central Park, near Fifth Avenue and 60th Street, beside the body of water called the Pond.

Olmsted and Vaux designed the park's entrances carefully. They wanted visitors to leave the city behind within a few steps. Here, the path descends from the busy street to the water's edge, and the noise of the city begins to fade. Notice how the Pond curves out of sight, so you can't see its full extent. This was a classic technique of English landscape design: hide the edges, and the space feels larger and more mysterious.

Look for the arched stone bridge over the northern neck of the Pond. That's Gapstow Bridge. The current stone bridge dates from 1896, replacing an earlier, more ornate wooden and iron bridge by Jacob Wrey Mould. It's one of the most photographed spots in the park, because of the view south, with the towers of Midtown, including the Plaza Hotel and the needle-thin towers of Billionaires' Row, rising above the trees. It's a perfect demonstration of the park's central contrast: wild nature, framed by the city.

On the peninsula jutting into the Pond is the Hallett Nature Sanctuary, a small woodland that was closed to the public for decades to serve as a bird sanctuary. It's now open on a limited schedule. It's named after George Hallett, an amateur birder and conservationist.

In winter, the Pond and the rink beyond it fill with skaters. In the nineteenth century, ice skating was hugely popular in the park, and it was one of the first activities that brought huge crowds to Central Park, even before construction was complete. Skating was also one of the few activities in Victorian New York where men and women could socialize relatively freely.

The park was the first major landscaped public park in America, and when it opened, there was a lot of debate about how people should behave in it. The park's early rules were strict: no walking on the grass in many areas, no picnics, no ball playing for adults, and no commercial vehicles. Over time, as the park became more democratic, those rules loosened.

stops.title: The Arsenal & the Zoo
stops.text:
Walk north along the eastern side of the park, near 64th Street and Fifth Avenue.

The brick building with the corner towers that looks like a fortress is the Arsenal. It was built between 1847 and 1851, before the park existed, as a storehouse for New York State's munitions. It's one of only two buildings in the park that predate the park itself. Later, it served as a museum, a weather station, and a police precinct, and the American Museum of Natural History got its start here in the 1870s, before its building on the Upper West Side was completed. Today, it's the headquarters of the city's Parks Department. If you peek in, the lobby has murals from the 1930s, painted as part of a Depression-era federal arts program.

The Central Park Zoo, next to the Arsenal, began informally in the 1860s, when New Yorkers started donating animals to the park: a bear, a swan, monkeys, and others. They were kept around the Arsenal in what became known as the menagerie. In 1934, Robert Moses built a formal zoo with brick buildings and cages. By the 1980s, it was outdated, and the Wildlife Conservation Society, which runs the Bronx Zoo, redesigned it with naturalistic habitats. It reopened in 1988. Look for the sea lion pool in the center, and the penguins and snow leopards.

At the north end of the zoo, look up at the Delacorte Musical Clock, an archway topped by a clock and bronze animals: a bear with a tambourine, a hippo with a violin, a goat with pipes, a kangaroo with horns, and others. Every half hour, they rotate around the clock while it plays nursery rhymes. The clock was a gift from the publisher George Delacorte, who founded Dell Publishing, and installed in 1965. Delacorte, a philanthropist, also funded the Delacorte Theater, home of Shakespeare in the Park, and the Alice in Wonderland sculpture near the Conservatory Water.

Nearby is the Tisch Children's Zoo. And a little to the north is the Conservatory Water, where people race model sailboats on summer weekends, a scene immortalized in the children's book Stuart Little by E. B. White.

stops.title: The Dairy & the Carousel
stops.text:
Walk west into the park to a small Gothic building with a steep roof and a wooden porch with ornate gingerbread trim. This is the Dairy, built in 1870 and designed by Calvert Vaux.

The Dairy was part of Olmsted and Vaux's vision for the Children's District, the southern part of the park that was meant to be especially for families. It served a practical purpose. In the mid-nineteenth century, milk in New York was dangerous. Much of it came from cows kept in filthy city stables next to breweries and fed on distillery waste, called swill. Swill milk was blamed for the deaths of thousands of children every year. At the Dairy, families could buy fresh, safe milk from cows grazing in the country. There were even cows grazing on the lawn nearby. Today the Dairy serves as a visitor center and gift shop.

A short walk west is the Carousel, one of the largest carousels in the United States. There's been a carousel in this spot since 1871. The first one was powered by a horse or mule walking in circles in a pit underneath it. The current carousel, with its colorful hand-carved horses, was built in 1908 by the carvers Solomon Stein and Harry Goldstein, Russian Jewish immigrants who were among the master carvers of Coney Island-style carousels. It originally stood at an amusement park in Coney Island and was moved here in 1951 after an earlier carousel burned.

Nearby, look for the Chess and Checkers House, a small building where you can borrow game pieces and play at outdoor tables. Chess hustlers have long been a fixture in New York parks.

And down the hill to the south is the Wollman Rink, which opened in 1950 with money from the philanthropist Kate Wollman. In winter it's one of the most famous skating rinks in the world, with the skyline of Central Park South rising above it.

stops.title: Sheep Meadow
stops.text:
You're at the edge of Sheep Meadow, a vast, open lawn of about fifteen acres between roughly 66th and 69th Streets. On a sunny weekend, it's covered with sunbathers, picnickers, and people reading. It's a designated quiet zone: no ball games, no loud music, no dogs.

Olmsted and Vaux designed this meadow as a large open pastoral space, something rare and precious in a dense city. They wanted people to experience the expansiveness of rolling countryside, with a long view toward the trees and the sky. The original plan actually called it the Parade Ground, but Olmsted resisted using it for military drills.

And it really did have sheep. From the 1860s to 1934, a flock of purebred sheep grazed here, tended by a shepherd who lived in a building called the Sheepfold. The sheep kept the grass trimmed and added to the pastoral illusion. Twice a day, the shepherd would stop traffic on the West Drive to lead the flock across. In 1934, Robert Moses removed the sheep, sending them to Prospect Park in Brooklyn, and converted the Sheepfold into a restaurant. That restaurant is Tavern on the Green, at the western edge of the park near 67th Street.

In the 1960s and 70s, Sheep Meadow became a gathering place for the counterculture, with Be-Ins, protests against the Vietnam War, and concerts. Heavy use turned it into a dust bowl. In 1980, it was one of the first major restoration projects of the new Central Park Conservancy, which reseeded it and introduced rules to protect it, including closing it in winter and when the ground is wet.

Look south, over the lawn, at the skyline of Central Park South and Billionaires' Row. The tall, thin towers you see were designed to exploit this view. It's often said that the view of Central Park is the most valuable view in real estate.

stops.title: The Mall & Literary Walk
stops.text:
You're at the southern end of the Mall, the wide, straight promenade lined with towering elm trees that runs from about 66th to 72nd Streets.

The Mall is the only formal, straight-line feature in Olmsted and Vaux's design. Everything else in the park curves and meanders. But they believed that a great urban park needed one grand promenade, a place where people of all classes could stroll, see and be seen. In the nineteenth century, it was the most fashionable place in the park, where people paraded in their finest clothes on Sunday afternoons.

Look up at the trees. These are American elms, and the Mall has one of the largest and finest remaining stands of American elms in North America. Elms were once the most common street tree in America, until Dutch elm disease, a fungus spread by beetles, killed most of them in the twentieth century. Central Park's elms survived, thanks partly to the park's relative isolation and careful monitoring by the Conservancy. Their branches arch overhead like the vaulted ceiling of a cathedral.

At the southern end of the Mall, look for the statues of writers. This section is called the Literary Walk. You'll find William Shakespeare, the Scottish poets Robert Burns and Sir Walter Scott, and the American poet Fitz-Greene Halleck. There's also a statue of Christopher Columbus. Olmsted and Vaux didn't want statues in their park, which they saw as a landscape, not a museum. But public pressure to honor famous figures was intense, and statues were installed anyway, mostly here in the southern part of the park.

At the northern end of the Mall, look for the Naumburg Bandshell, a limestone bandshell built in 1923, a gift of the banker Elkan Naumburg. Free concerts have been held here for a century, and the area in front of it was the site of political rallies and the funerals of famous figures. Nearby, on summer weekends, you'll often find roller skaters dancing to music, a tradition that dates back to the 1970s.

Before you leave, notice the people around you. The Mall still does what its designers intended: everyone is here, from tourists and joggers to musicians, families, and old men on benches.

stops.title: Bethesda Terrace & Fountain
stops.text:
At the northern end of the Mall, walk down the grand staircase, or through the arcade beneath the road, to Bethesda Terrace.

Look up as you pass through the arcade. The ceiling is covered in about sixteen thousand ornate encaustic tiles made by the English company Minton. They were designed by Jacob Wrey Mould, Vaux's collaborator, who also designed much of the decorative carving on the terrace. After decades of neglect, the tiles were removed, stored, and restored, and reinstalled in 2007. It's one of the most beautiful spaces in the park, and the acoustics make it a favorite spot for musicians.

On the terrace, look closely at the stone carvings on the staircases. They depict birds, plants, and animals representing the seasons and times of day.

At the center of the terrace is the Bethesda Fountain, topped by a bronze statue called the Angel of the Waters, by the sculptor Emma Stebbins. Unveiled in 1873, it was the first public sculpture in New York City commissioned from a woman. The angel refers to the Gospel of John, in which an angel stirs the waters of the Pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem, giving them healing powers. The symbolism had a local meaning: the fountain celebrated the Croton Aqueduct, which in 1842 had brought clean water to New York for the first time, dramatically reducing diseases like cholera. Pure water, in other words, was New York's healing angel.

There's another layer. Emma Stebbins was in a long-term relationship with the actress Charlotte Cushman, and the fountain has become meaningful to the LGBTQ community. It appears prominently in Tony Kushner's play Angels in America, which ends at this fountain.

Bethesda Terrace was designed as the heart of the park, the place where the formal Mall meets the wild landscape. Stand at the fountain and look north across the Lake toward the Ramble's woods, and you'll see the composition Olmsted and Vaux intended: the architecture gives way to nature. In the 1970s, the fountain was dry, covered in graffiti, and a center of drug dealing. It was among the first places the Conservancy restored, and it's now one of the most beloved spots in the city.

stops.title: Bow Bridge & the Lake
stops.text:
Walk west along the Lake to Bow Bridge, the graceful cast iron bridge arching across the water.

Completed in 1862, Bow Bridge was designed by Calvert Vaux and Jacob Wrey Mould. Its name comes from its shape, like the curve of an archer's bow. It's about sixty feet long, with a decorative railing of interlocking circles and planters. It's one of the oldest cast iron bridges in America, and probably the most romantic spot in the park. It has appeared in many films, and countless marriage proposals have happened on it.

The bridge connects Cherry Hill and the Bethesda area to the Ramble, the wild woodland on the north shore of the Lake. That contrast is deliberate. Crossing Bow Bridge, you move from the formal, social part of the park to the wild, solitary part.

The Lake itself is entirely artificial, created from a swamp. It covers about twenty acres. In the nineteenth century, it was the main skating spot in the park, and in winter, tens of thousands of skaters would flock here. When the ice was thick enough to be safe, the park raised a red ball on a flagpole, and streetcars would display a similar signal, letting New Yorkers across the city know that skating was open. The Lake is no longer used for skating, now that there are rinks.

In summer, you can rent rowboats at the Loeb Boathouse, on the east side of the Lake, where there's also a restaurant. Rowing on the Lake has been a popular activity since the 1860s. In the nineteenth century, the park also had gondolas, and even a gondolier imported from Venice.

Look around at the trees and the skyline beyond. From the middle of the bridge, the towers of the Upper West Side, including the twin-towered San Remo and the Dakota, rise above the trees, perfectly framed by the park's landscape.

Just west of the bridge is Cherry Hill, a raised plaza with a small fountain. Originally it was a turnaround for carriages, and the fountain was a watering trough for horses.

stops.title: Strawberry Fields
stops.text:
End your walk at Strawberry Fields, a teardrop-shaped garden on the western edge of the park, near West 72nd Street.

This is a memorial to John Lennon. On the evening of December eighth, 1980, Lennon was shot and killed outside the Dakota, the apartment building where he lived with Yoko Ono, just across Central Park West from here. He was forty years old. The killing devastated fans around the world, and on the following Sunday, hundreds of thousands of people gathered in Central Park for ten minutes of silence.

Yoko Ono, who continued to live at the Dakota, worked with the city to create a memorial in the park. Strawberry Fields, named after the Beatles song Strawberry Fields Forever, was dedicated in 1985, on what would have been Lennon's forty-fifth birthday. It was designed by the landscape architect Bruce Kelly. Ono invited countries around the world to contribute plants, and many did.

At the center of the garden, look for the black and white mosaic with a single word: Imagine. The mosaic was a gift from the city of Naples, Italy, and it's modeled on ancient Roman mosaics. On any given day, you'll find flowers left on it, often arranged into a peace sign, and musicians playing Beatles songs. On December eighth and on Lennon's birthday, October ninth, crowds gather here to sing.

The area is designated a quiet zone, meant for contemplation, though it's often busy with visitors.

Look across the street at the Dakota, the dark, gabled building with its own fortress-like entrance. You'll hear more about it on the Upper West Side tour. It's one of the most famous apartment buildings in the world.

This is a good place to reflect on the park as a whole. Olmsted and Vaux designed Central Park as a place of escape and renewal. More than a century later, it's become something they couldn't have foreseen: the city's collective memory, a place where New Yorkers come to celebrate, protest, mourn, and remember.

overview:
Central Park looks natural. It isn't. Almost every rock outcrop, lake, meadow, and hill you see was planned, sculpted, and planted by people. It's one of the largest and most ambitious works of landscape design ever made, and it's been copied in cities all over the world.

By the 1840s, New York was growing fast and had almost no public green space. The 1811 grid plan had allotted very little land to parks, on the theory that the rivers on either side would give residents fresh air. Wealthy New Yorkers, who had seen the great public parks of London and Paris, began to argue that a world-class city needed a great park. The poet and editor William Cullen Bryant and the landscape designer Andrew Jackson Downing were among the leading advocates. In 1853, the state legislature authorized the city to acquire the land, and the park was eventually expanded to its current size of about eight hundred forty acres, stretching from 59th Street to 110th Street, and from Fifth Avenue to Central Park West.

The land wasn't empty. It was rocky, swampy, and considered poor for building, but it was home to about sixteen hundred people, including Irish and German immigrants who raised pigs and goats, and a community of African American property owners called Seneca Village. All were removed through eminent domain. You'll hear more about Seneca Village on the northern Central Park tour.

In 1857, the park's commissioners held a design competition. The winning entry, called the Greensward Plan, came from two men: Frederick Law Olmsted, a journalist, farmer, and failed businessman who had never designed a park, and Calvert Vaux, a young English-born architect. Their vision was a pastoral escape from the city, a sequence of carefully composed scenes, meadows, woods, water, and rocky outcrops, meant to feel like an unspoiled landscape. They believed the park could improve the health and spirit of all New Yorkers, rich and poor alike, and offer a democratic space where all classes could mix.

Building it was a colossal undertaking. Over roughly fifteen years, thousands of workers blasted rock with more gunpowder than was used at the Battle of Gettysburg, according to a frequently repeated claim, moved millions of cubic yards of earth and stone, planted hundreds of thousands of trees and shrubs, and built bridges, arches, and buildings. One of the cleverest features was the design for traffic. Olmsted and Vaux sunk four transverse roads below the level of the park, so that crosstown traffic would pass through without disturbing the landscape. And they separated carriage drives, bridle paths, and footpaths, using bridges and arches so they rarely crossed.

The park declined badly in the mid-twentieth century, and by the 1970s it was covered in graffiti, its lawns were dust bowls, and many considered it dangerous. In 1980, the Central Park Conservancy, a private nonprofit, was founded to restore it, and it now manages the park in partnership with the city.

This tour covers the southern half, the more formal and heavily visited part of the park.

title: Central Park: The Ramble to Harlem Meer
blurb: The Ramble's woods, Belvedere Castle, the Great Lawn, a 3,500-year-old obelisk, Seneca Village, the Reservoir, the North Woods, and the Conservatory Garden.

stops.title: The Ramble
stops.text:
You're in the Ramble, about thirty-six acres of woodland just north of the Lake, roughly between 73rd and 79th Streets.

Olmsted called it a wild garden. It was designed to feel like a natural forest, with winding paths, rocky outcrops, a small stream called the Gill, and dense trees and shrubs. But it's as carefully designed as any part of the park. The stream is artificial and fed by city water. The rocks were placed. The paths were laid out to disorient you, so that you lose your sense of the city around you. It's very easy to get lost in the Ramble, and that's exactly the point.

The Ramble is one of the best birding spots in North America. Central Park sits on the Atlantic Flyway, a major migration route for birds traveling between South and Central America and Canada. For migrating birds flying over a vast expanse of concrete, Central Park looks like an oasis, and they drop in to rest and feed. More than two hundred species of birds have been recorded in the park. In the spring and fall migration seasons, especially May, the Ramble fills with warblers, thrushes, tanagers, and orioles, and with birders carrying binoculars. Look for small feeders near the Azalea Pond in winter.

The park's most famous birds, though, have lived in the surrounding city. In the 1990s, a red-tailed hawk nicknamed Pale Male built a nest on the facade of a luxury apartment building on Fifth Avenue, overlooking the park, and he and his mates raised chicks there for years. When the building's co-op board removed the nest in 2004, birders protested, and the nest was eventually allowed to be rebuilt. More recently, a Eurasian eagle-owl named Flaco, who escaped from the Central Park Zoo in 2023, became a city celebrity during the year he lived free in the park and around Manhattan.

In the twentieth century, the Ramble also became known as a gathering place for gay men, who found privacy in its winding paths during an era when gay life was largely hidden. It's part of the park's history that is now openly acknowledged.

stops.title: Belvedere Castle & Turtle Pond
stops.text:
Climb up to Belvedere Castle, the small stone castle perched on Vista Rock, the second highest natural point in the park.

Calvert Vaux and Jacob Wrey Mould designed it, and it was completed in 1869. It's a folly, an ornamental building with no real defensive purpose, a fantasy castle designed to be seen from a distance as a romantic focal point. The name Belvedere means beautiful view in Italian, and from the castle's terraces, you get one of the best views in the park, over Turtle Pond, the Great Lawn, and the surrounding skyline.

Originally, the castle had open windows and no doors. It was meant as a lookout, not a building. In 1919, the United States Weather Bureau set up a station here, and the castle was enclosed. Today, automated instruments here and nearby measure the official weather for Central Park, which is often cited in weather reports as the weather for New York City. When you hear on the news that Central Park got six inches of snow, those measurements come from instruments here and nearby.

By the 1970s, the castle had been vandalized and was in ruins. It was restored in the 1980s, and again in 2019. It now houses a visitor center with nature exhibits for children.

Below the castle is Turtle Pond, which, as its name suggests, is home to many turtles, mostly red-eared sliders, many of them abandoned pets. Look for them basking on rocks and logs on sunny days. The pond is what's left of the old Lower Reservoir, which was drained in the 1930s.

West of the pond is the Delacorte Theater, the open-air amphitheater that has been home to Shakespeare in the Park since 1962. The producer Joseph Papp began staging free Shakespeare in the 1950s, and fought Robert Moses, who wanted to charge admission. Papp won, and the theater was built with funding from George Delacorte. Performances are still free, and people line up for hours, sometimes overnight, for tickets. Stars like Meryl Streep, Al Pacino, and Denzel Washington have performed here.

Next to the theater is the Shakespeare Garden, planted with flowers and plants mentioned in Shakespeare's plays and poems.

stops.title: The Great Lawn
stops.text:
North of the castle and Turtle Pond is the Great Lawn, a vast oval field of about fifty-five acres, with baseball diamonds and broad lawns.

It wasn't originally a lawn at all. In Olmsted and Vaux's plan, this space was occupied by the Lower Reservoir, a rectangular reservoir built in the 1840s as part of the Croton water system, which predated the park and was incorporated into it. By the 1930s, the reservoir was no longer needed and was drained.

While it sat empty during the Great Depression, homeless New Yorkers built a shantytown in the empty reservoir bed. They called it Hooverville, or Hoover Valley, after President Herbert Hoover, whom they blamed for the Depression. Shacks were made of scrap wood, cardboard, and tin, and some residents, unemployed bricklayers and carpenters, built surprisingly substantial structures. Hoovervilles sprang up all over the country, but this one, in the middle of the richest city in America, was a powerful symbol. The camp was cleared in 1933, and the reservoir bed was filled in to create the Great Lawn.

Since then, the Great Lawn has been the site of some of the largest gatherings in American history. In September 1981, Simon and Garfunkel reunited for a free concert here, drawing about half a million people. In June 1982, about a million people gathered here for a rally against nuclear weapons, one of the largest political demonstrations in American history. Pope John Paul the Second celebrated mass here in 1995, and in 1997, Garth Brooks drew an enormous crowd for a free concert.

All those crowds took a toll. By the 1990s, the Great Lawn was a dust bowl. The Conservancy rebuilt it in the late 1990s with new drainage, irrigation, and soil, and now closes it during wet weather and in winter to protect the grass. Big concerts are mostly gone, but the New York Philharmonic and the Metropolitan Opera still hold free summer performances here.

Look around at the skyline framing the lawn: the towers of Fifth Avenue to the east, and Central Park West to the west, rise just above the trees, like walls around a giant room.

stops.title: Cleopatra's Needle
stops.text:
On a small hill just east of the Great Lawn, behind the Metropolitan Museum of Art, stands the oldest man-made object in Central Park, and one of the oldest outdoor monuments anywhere in the Americas: a granite obelisk nicknamed Cleopatra's Needle.

It has nothing to do with Cleopatra. It was carved around 1450 BC, more than a thousand years before Cleopatra's time, for the Egyptian pharaoh Thutmose the Third, and erected at the temple city of Heliopolis. Look for the hieroglyphics carved on its sides, though they're badly weathered on some faces. Around 12 BC, the Romans moved it to Alexandria, where it stood outside a temple built by Cleopatra in honor of Julius Caesar, or Mark Antony, depending on the source. That's how it got its nickname.

In the 1870s, the ruler of Egypt, Khedive Ismail Pasha, offered the obelisk to the United States as a gift, hoping to win friendship and support. A similar obelisk had gone to London. The cost of moving it, more than one hundred thousand dollars, was paid by William Henry Vanderbilt, the son of the Commodore. A Navy officer named Henry Gorringe engineered the move. The obelisk, about seventy feet tall and weighing over two hundred tons, was lowered, loaded into the hold of a steamship through a hole cut in its hull, shipped across the Atlantic, floated to the Hudson River, and hauled across Manhattan on a special railway over several months. It was erected here in January 1881, with a Masonic ceremony attended by thousands.

New York's climate, with its freeze-thaw cycles and air pollution, has been much harder on the stone than three thousand years in Egypt. Some of the hieroglyphics have eroded significantly since it arrived.

Look at the base, at the corners. You'll see bronze crabs. They're replicas of crabs the Romans placed under the obelisk to support it when they moved it to Alexandria. The originals are in the Met.

Speaking of which, the massive building next to you is the back of the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Look for the glass wall of the Sackler Wing. Inside, visible through the glass, is the Temple of Dendur, an Egyptian temple built around 15 BC, given to the United States by Egypt in the 1960s, in gratitude for American help in saving monuments threatened by the Aswan High Dam. So here, two ancient Egyptian monuments face each other across a park in Manhattan.

stops.title: Seneca Village
stops.text:
Walk west across the park to the area near West 85th Street, near Central Park West. Here, between roughly 82nd and 89th Streets, stood Seneca Village.

In 1825, a young African American shoeshiner named Andrew Williams bought three lots of land here from a white landowner named John Whitehead. Other Black New Yorkers followed, buying lots of their own. At that time, slavery had not yet been fully abolished in New York State; final emancipation came in 1827. Seneca Village was one of the first communities of African American property owners in New York.

Owning property mattered for another reason. In 1821, New York State had changed its voting laws, eliminating property requirements for white men, but requiring Black men to own at least two hundred and fifty dollars in property to vote. In Seneca Village, many Black residents met that threshold. Property ownership was a path to political rights.

By the 1850s, Seneca Village had about two hundred twenty-five residents, mostly African American, along with Irish and German immigrants. It had three churches, including an African Methodist Episcopal Zion church, a school, and cemeteries. Residents worked as laborers, servants, cooks, and in various trades. It was a stable, settled community, far from the crowded neighborhoods downtown.

In 1857, the city took the land by eminent domain to build Central Park. Residents were compensated, though many contested the amounts as inadequate. The village was destroyed. Newspapers of the time sometimes described the area's residents dismissively, calling their homes shanties, which helped justify the removal. Where the residents went is largely unknown.

For more than a century, Seneca Village was mostly forgotten. In the 1990s, historians began to recover its story, and in 2011, archaeologists excavated the site, finding foundations of houses and thousands of artifacts, including household items like ceramics, a toothbrush, and a child's shoe. In recent years, the Conservancy has installed signs and a display here explaining the history.

As you stand here, look at the landscape around you: the gentle slope, the rocks, the playground nearby. It's a reminder that the park's pastoral beauty was built on top of a real community, with real homes and families.

stops.title: The Reservoir
stops.text:
Climb to the Reservoir, the vast body of water covering much of the park between 86th and 96th Streets. Officially, it's the Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis Reservoir.

It was built between 1858 and 1862, as part of the Croton water system, to hold water from the Croton Aqueduct. It covers about one hundred six acres, and holds about a billion gallons of water. Olmsted and Vaux had to design the park around it, and its huge size is one reason the park is so narrow in places.

For more than a century, it was part of the city's water supply. In 1993, it was decommissioned, after a newer system of underground water tunnels made it obsolete. The water you see today is no longer for drinking.

Running around it is a track of about one point six miles, one of the most famous running paths in the world. Joggers have used it since the jogging craze of the 1970s, and on a nice morning, it's packed with runners. Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, who lived on Fifth Avenue facing the park, was a regular jogger here, and after her death in 1994, the reservoir was renamed in her honor. She was also a passionate advocate for the city's landmarks and was instrumental in saving Grand Central Terminal.

Look around: the view across the water is one of the most spectacular in the city, especially at sunrise or sunset, with the skylines of the Upper East and Upper West Sides on either side, and Midtown's towers to the south. The open water also attracts birds, especially in winter, when ducks, geese, gulls, and grebes gather here.

Look for the old gatehouses on the north and south ends of the Reservoir. These stone buildings housed the machinery that controlled the flow of water. Along the reservoir's edges, notice the beautiful iron fences. They were replaced in the 2000s with replicas of the original 1920s designs.

North of the Reservoir lies the North Meadow, a large area with baseball and soccer fields, and the Central Park Tennis Center, where New Yorkers have played tennis for decades.

stops.title: The North Woods & the Blockhouse
stops.text:
Walk to the northern end of the park, into the North Woods, around 102nd to 106th Streets on the west side.

Olmsted and Vaux designed this area to evoke the Adirondack Mountains of upstate New York. It's the most rugged part of the park, with steep slopes, rocky outcrops, and dense woods. Through it runs the Loch, Scottish for lake, a stream that flows through a ravine, over small waterfalls, into the Harlem Meer. The stream is artificial; its water comes from the city supply. But the effect is strikingly real. Standing in the ravine, it's easy to forget you're in Manhattan.

Look for the stone arches that carry paths and roads over the ravine. The Glen Span Arch, at the western entrance to the ravine, is a rustic stone arch. And the Huddlestone Arch, near the east end, is made of huge, rough boulders, some weighing many tons, held together only by gravity, without any mortar.

Now climb to the top of the rocky hill at the northwest corner of the North Woods, near 109th Street. Here you'll find the Blockhouse, a small stone fort and the oldest structure in Central Park.

It was built in 1814, during the War of 1812. The British had burned Washington, D.C., that August, and New Yorkers feared a British invasion from the north, by way of the Harlem River. Volunteers built a line of fortifications across upper Manhattan, including this blockhouse, on high ground overlooking the approaches to the city. The British never came. The blockhouse never saw combat. Olmsted and Vaux kept it as a picturesque ruin. Today it's an empty stone shell, but its walls and gun ports are still visible.

This area also saw action in the Revolutionary War. In 1776, after the Battle of Brooklyn, George Washington's army retreated north through Manhattan. The British later built fortifications in this area, near a tavern called McGown's Pass Tavern, which stood on a hill near the east side of the park, overlooking the old Post Road. The steep ridge here made it a strategic chokepoint.

stops.title: Harlem Meer & the Conservatory Garden
stops.text:
End your walk on the east side of the park, at the Harlem Meer and the Conservatory Garden.

The Harlem Meer is an eleven-acre lake in the park's northeast corner. Meer is the Dutch word for lake, a nod to the Dutch village of Haarlem that stood nearby in the colonial era. The Meer was dredged and restored in the 1990s and is now stocked with fish for catch-and-release fishing. On its north shore is the Dana Discovery Center, a visitor center. On the south side, look for the newly rebuilt pool and rink complex, which has reopened the shoreline to the public.

Now walk to Fifth Avenue at about 105th Street, and look for an ornate wrought iron gate. These are the Vanderbilt Gates, which once stood at the entrance to the Cornelius Vanderbilt the Second mansion on Fifth Avenue at 58th Street, which you may have heard about on the Fifth Avenue tour. They were made in Paris in 1894. When the mansion was demolished, the gates were donated to the city, and they were installed here in 1939.

Walk through the gates into the Conservatory Garden, the only formal garden in Central Park. It's six acres, divided into three sections, each in a different style. The central garden, in the Italian style, has a large lawn surrounded by hedges and an iron pergola covered with wisteria. The north garden, in the French style, has concentric beds of flowers around a fountain called the Untermyer Fountain, with three dancing maidens. The south garden, in the English style, has lush perennial borders and a small pool with a statue of two children, inspired by the characters in Frances Hodgson Burnett's novel The Secret Garden.

The garden's name comes from a large glass conservatory that stood here from 1899 to 1934, when it was demolished. Robert Moses then created the formal garden, which opened in 1937. By the 1970s, it had fallen into disrepair. It was restored in the 1980s and is now one of the most beautiful and peaceful places in the city. It's a popular spot for wedding photos.

It's a fitting end for a walk through the park. Olmsted and Vaux designed Central Park to give people of all classes access to beauty, peace, and nature. Here, in the northern end, near Harlem and East Harlem, that vision is as alive as ever.

overview:
The northern two-thirds of Central Park are quieter, wilder, and less visited than the southern end, and many New Yorkers consider them the best part of the park.

Olmsted and Vaux designed the park as a sequence of moods. The south end, near the city's busiest streets, has the more formal and social features: the Mall, the Dairy, the Carousel, the zoo. As you move north, the landscape becomes more rugged and more pastoral. The Ramble, north of the Lake, is a dense, winding woodland. Above it, at Vista Rock, Belvedere Castle overlooks the park. Beyond that are the great open lawns and the Reservoir. And in the far north, above 100th Street, the North Woods were designed to evoke the Adirondack Mountains, with a ravine, a stream, and waterfalls.

The northern section also holds the park's deepest history. During the Revolutionary War, British and Hessian troops built fortifications on the high ground near the northern end, and during the War of 1812, Americans built a blockhouse there that still stands, the oldest structure in the park. And on the west side, between about 82nd and 89th Streets, there once stood Seneca Village, a community of African American property owners, along with Irish and German immigrants, that was destroyed to build the park.

The north end of the park was also slower to be completed, and for much of the twentieth century it was less maintained and less safe than the south end. In the 1970s and 80s, much of it was overgrown and neglected. The restoration of the north end by the Central Park Conservancy, beginning in the 1980s and continuing to this day, has been one of its biggest achievements. Projects completed in recent years include a rebuilt Lasker Rink and pool area near the Harlem Meer, reconnecting the park's landscape to the water.

This tour starts in the Ramble, just north of the Lake, and ends at the Conservatory Garden on Fifth Avenue at 105th Street. It's a long walk, a little over two miles if you take a direct path, so feel free to take it in pieces.

title: Upper East Side & Museum Mile
blurb: Gilded Age mansions turned museums, the Met and the Guggenheim, Carnegie's house, German Yorkville, and Gracie Mansion.

stops.title: The Park Avenue Armory
stops.text:
You're at Park Avenue and 66th Street, in front of a massive brick building that looks like a medieval fortress, with towers and crenellations. This is the Park Avenue Armory, completed in 1880 as the headquarters of the Seventh Regiment of the New York State Militia.

The Seventh Regiment was nicknamed the Silk Stocking Regiment, because so many of its members came from New York's wealthiest families. It was a social club as well as a military unit. It also had a practical role: in the nineteenth century, the city's militia was used to put down riots and labor disturbances, including the deadly Draft Riots of 1863. Armories built in this era often had fortress-like designs, reflecting the fears of the wealthy that the city's working classes might rise up.

The building was paid for not by the government but by the members themselves, and they spared no expense. The interior rooms were designed by some of the most celebrated designers of the era, including Louis Comfort Tiffany, the son of the jeweler, and Stanford White. The Veterans Room, designed by Tiffany's firm, is a masterpiece of the Aesthetic Movement, with dark wood, metalwork, and stained glass.

Behind the front building is the drill hall, a vast iron-trussed space of about fifty-five thousand square feet, one of the largest unobstructed interior spaces in New York. It was modeled on the great train sheds of the era. The regiment drilled here, and it was also used for sporting events and exhibitions.

In the 2000s, a nonprofit took over the building and turned it into a cultural center. The drill hall now hosts large-scale art installations, theater, music, and performances that couldn't fit anywhere else, along with the famous Winter Show, an antiques fair.

Look around the neighborhood, too. Just north is Hunter College, a public college founded in 1870 as a teacher-training school for women. Along Park Avenue, look at the elegant apartment buildings, mostly built in the 1910s and 20s, many designed by the architect Rosario Candela, whose buildings are considered among the most desirable in the city.

stops.title: The Frick Collection
stops.text:
At Fifth Avenue and 70th Street, facing Central Park, stands a low, elegant mansion of limestone set back behind a garden. This is the Frick Collection.

It was built between 1912 and 1914 as the home of Henry Clay Frick, designed by Thomas Hastings of Carrère and Hastings, the architects of the New York Public Library. Frick was one of the most ruthless industrialists of the Gilded Age. He made his fortune producing coke, a fuel used in steelmaking, in western Pennsylvania, and became the chairman of Carnegie Steel, Andrew Carnegie's company. In 1892, during a strike at the Homestead steel works near Pittsburgh, Frick brought in hundreds of armed Pinkerton agents. A battle broke out between the strikers and the Pinkertons, and people were killed on both sides. The state militia then occupied the town, and the strike was broken. Weeks later, an anarchist named Alexander Berkman burst into Frick's office, shot him twice and stabbed him. Frick survived, and reportedly returned to work within about a week.

Frick and Carnegie eventually had a bitter falling out. Frick moved to New York, and built his mansion a few blocks north of Carnegie's. Some say he wanted to make Carnegie's house look like a miner's shack.

Frick spent his later years collecting European art, and he intended from the beginning that his house and collection would become a museum after his death. He died in 1919, and the museum opened in 1935. The Frick has an extraordinary collection, including works by Vermeer, Rembrandt, Holbein, Goya, Titian, and Turner, displayed as they would have been in a private home, among furniture and decorative objects. Many visitors find it the most intimate and beautiful museum in the city.

The Frick underwent a major renovation and expansion in the early 2020s, opening up the second floor of the mansion, where the family's private rooms were, for the first time. During the renovation, the collection was displayed temporarily in the Breuer building on Madison Avenue, the former home of the Whitney Museum.

stops.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
stops.text:
You're on Fifth Avenue at 82nd Street, at the foot of the famous steps of the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

The Met was founded in 1870 by a group of businessmen, financiers, artists, and civic leaders, including Theodore Roosevelt Senior, who wanted New York to have an art museum to rival the great museums of Europe. Its first home was in a building on Fifth Avenue downtown. In 1880, it moved into a red brick Gothic building inside Central Park, designed by Calvert Vaux and Jacob Wrey Mould. That original building is now buried within the museum; part of its brick facade is visible inside, in the Lehman Wing.

The grand Beaux-Arts facade you see on Fifth Avenue was designed by Richard Morris Hunt and completed in 1902, after his death, by his son. Look up at the tops of the paired columns. Above them, there are large rough blocks of stone. They were intended to be carved into sculptures representing great periods of art, but the money ran out, and they've been left uncarved for more than a century.

Today, the Met is the largest art museum in the Americas, with a collection of around one and a half million objects spanning five thousand years. Its galleries include Egyptian art, including the Temple of Dendur; European paintings, including works by Rembrandt, Vermeer, and Van Gogh; an American Wing, with entire period rooms; arms and armor; and much more. The museum's annual fundraising gala, the Met Gala, held each May for the Costume Institute, has become one of the biggest celebrity events in the world.

The steps themselves are one of the great public spaces in the city. People sit here to eat lunch, meet friends, watch street performers, and people-watch. In the beloved 1967 children's novel From the Mixed-Up Files of Mrs. Basil E. Frankweiler, two children run away from home and secretly live inside the Met, sleeping in an antique bed and bathing in a fountain.

If you go to the roof garden in the warmer months, you'll get a spectacular view over Central Park and the skyline.

stops.title: The Guggenheim & the Neue Galerie
stops.text:
Walk north along Fifth Avenue. At 86th Street, look for an elegant Beaux-Arts mansion on the corner, built in 1914 for the industrialist William Starr Miller and later home to Grace Vanderbilt. Today it's the Neue Galerie, a museum of early twentieth-century German and Austrian art and design, founded by the cosmetics heir Ronald Lauder and the art dealer Serge Sabarsky.

Its star is Gustav Klimt's 1907 portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer, the dazzling gold painting often called The Woman in Gold. The painting was seized by the Nazis from the Bloch-Bauer family in Vienna, and after the war it hung in an Austrian state museum for decades. Adele's niece, Maria Altmann, who had fled to the United States, fought a long legal battle and won its return in 2006. Lauder then bought it for a reported one hundred thirty-five million dollars, at the time a record price for a painting. Downstairs, Café Sabarsky serves Viennese coffee and pastries in an elegant, wood-paneled room.

Continue north to 89th Street, where you'll see one of the most famous buildings of the twentieth century: the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright.

Solomon Guggenheim came from a family that made an enormous fortune in mining and smelting, especially copper and silver. Advised by the artist Baroness Hilla von Rebay, he collected what they called non-objective art, abstract painting by artists like Wassily Kandinsky. In 1943, they commissioned Wright to design a museum for the collection. The project took sixteen years, through endless disputes with city officials, the museum's board, and Wright's own stubbornness. Wright died in April 1959, about six months before the museum opened that October.

The design is a radical departure from traditional museums. Instead of a series of rooms, it's a single continuous spiral ramp, coiling up around a central atrium, under a glass skylight. Visitors typically take an elevator to the top and walk down the ramp. Wright, who mostly despised cities, designed the building as a kind of organic shell, set apart from the grid of Manhattan. Some artists objected that the curved, sloping walls were terrible for displaying paintings. The building's admirers say the building is itself the greatest work of art in the collection.

Look at the building from across the street. Its white, inverted, stacked spirals widen as they rise. When it opened, critics compared it to a washing machine, an inverted cupcake, and a snail.

stops.title: Carnegie Hill: Andrew Carnegie's Mansion
stops.text:
At Fifth Avenue and 91st Street, look for a large red brick and limestone mansion set within a garden. This was the home of Andrew Carnegie, built between 1899 and 1902.

When Carnegie built here, this area was considered remote, and the land around his mansion was still partly empty and rocky, with shanties nearby. He chose it for the space and sunlight. He wanted a big garden, and he deliberately bought up surrounding lots to protect his light and air. The neighborhood around it came to be known as Carnegie Hill.

Carnegie, as you may have heard at Carnegie Hall, was born in Scotland in 1835, emigrated to Pittsburgh as a poor boy, and worked as a bobbin boy in a cotton mill and a telegraph messenger before rising in the railroad industry and then founding the steel company that made him one of the richest people in history. In 1901, he sold Carnegie Steel to J. P. Morgan, who combined it with other companies to form U.S. Steel, the first company in the world valued at over one billion dollars. Carnegie then devoted himself to giving his fortune away. In an essay called The Gospel of Wealth, he argued that the rich had a moral obligation to use their wealth for the public good, and that the man who dies rich dies disgraced.

Carnegie described the house as the most modest, plainest, and most roomy house in New York, though it had more than sixty rooms. It was one of the first private homes in the United States to have a structural steel frame, appropriately enough for a steel magnate, and it included an Otis passenger elevator and an early form of air conditioning and central heating.

Today, the mansion is home to the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, the only museum in the United States devoted entirely to historic and contemporary design. The museum was founded in 1897 by Sarah, Eleanor, and Amy Hewitt, the granddaughters of Peter Cooper, the founder of Cooper Union. Its collection includes everything from wallpaper and textiles to furniture, product design, and graphic design.

A block north, at 92nd Street, is the Jewish Museum, housed in the French Gothic mansion of the banker Felix Warburg, completed in 1908. The Warburgs were among the leading families of the German Jewish financial elite in New York, along with the Schiffs, the Loebs, and the Lehmans, a group sometimes called Our Crowd.

stops.title: Yorkville
stops.text:
Walk east to East 86th Street and Second Avenue. You're in Yorkville, the eastern part of the Upper East Side.

Starting in the late nineteenth century, Yorkville became a working-class immigrant neighborhood. After the General Slocum disaster in 1904, which you may have heard about on the East Village tour, many German families left the Lower East Side and resettled here. 86th Street became known as the German Broadway, lined with beer halls, cafés, bakeries, butchers, dance halls, and German-language theaters and movie houses. Hungarians, Czechs, Slovaks, and Irish also lived in the neighborhood, with their own churches and social clubs.

Yorkville also had a dark chapter. In the 1930s, the German American Bund, a pro-Nazi organization, was active here, holding rallies and parades along 86th Street. Its activities provoked counter-protests and violent confrontations. Its leader, Fritz Kuhn, was convicted of embezzling the group's funds in 1939, and the Bund collapsed after the United States entered World War Two.

A few traces of German Yorkville survive. Look for Schaller and Weber, a German butcher and grocer on Second Avenue, open since 1937, and its sausage shop next door. Glaser's Bake Shop, on First Avenue, operated from 1902 until 2018. There are still a few German restaurants nearby.

A few blocks north, between Second and Third Avenues and 90th to 93rd Streets, stood the Jacob Ruppert Brewery, one of the largest breweries in the country, makers of Knickerbocker beer. Jacob Ruppert Junior, the brewery's heir, used his fortune to buy the New York Yankees in 1915. He bought Babe Ruth from the Boston Red Sox in 1919 and built the original Yankee Stadium in 1923, turning the Yankees into the most successful franchise in American sports. The brewery closed in 1965 and was demolished. Apartment towers, named Ruppert Towers, now stand on the site.

Underneath Second Avenue runs the Second Avenue Subway. It was first proposed in the 1920s, and construction started and stopped several times over the decades. The first phase, from 63rd Street to 96th Street, finally opened on January first, 2017. The station at 86th Street has large, bright mosaic artworks by the artist Chuck Close. It's worth a peek.

stops.title: Gracie Mansion & Carl Schurz Park
stops.text:
End your walk at Carl Schurz Park, along the East River at the end of East 86th Street, and at Gracie Mansion, the official residence of the mayor of New York City.

Gracie Mansion was built in 1799 as a country house for Archibald Gracie, a Scottish-born merchant and shipping magnate. In his time, this was the countryside, far north of the city, and wealthy merchants built summer estates along the East River. Gracie entertained prominent guests here, including Alexander Hamilton, John Quincy Adams, and the future King Louis Philippe of France. Gracie lost his fortune in the economic turmoil around the War of 1812 and sold the house in 1823.

After passing through several owners, the city took over the property in 1896 and made it part of the park. For decades, it housed the Museum of the City of New York, and a concession stand. In 1942, at the urging of Robert Moses, it became the official residence of the mayor. Fiorello La Guardia was the first mayor to live here. Most mayors since have lived in the house, though Michael Bloomberg, who was a billionaire with his own townhouse, chose not to.

The park is named after Carl Schurz, a German revolutionary who fled to America after the failed revolutions of 1848 in Germany. He became a general in the Civil War, a United States senator from Missouri, Secretary of the Interior, and a journalist and reformer. He's credited with a famous version of the phrase My country, right or wrong: if right, to be kept right; and if wrong, to be set right. The park honored him because of the large German population in Yorkville. He lived nearby, at the end of his life.

Walk to the promenade along the river. Look out at the water. This stretch of the East River, where the river meets the Harlem River and Long Island Sound, is called Hell Gate, from the Dutch Hellegat. Its swirling currents and submerged rocks wrecked hundreds of ships. In the 1870s and 1880s, the Army Corps of Engineers undertook a huge project to clear the rocks. In 1885, they detonated about three hundred thousand pounds of explosives to blow up Flood Rock. It was one of the largest planned explosions in history before the atomic bomb, and it reportedly was felt as far away as Princeton, New Jersey.

Across the water, you'll see Roosevelt Island, Randall's Island, and Queens. From the promenade, you can watch boats and barges pass by, and the lights of the Triborough Bridge, now the Robert F. Kennedy Bridge, in the distance.

overview:
The Upper East Side has been, for more than a century, the most famous wealthy neighborhood in America. Its name is shorthand for old money, private schools, charity galas, and Park Avenue co-ops with famously selective boards.

It wasn't always that way. In the mid-nineteenth century, much of the area was rocky, rural land, dotted with farms, country estates along the East River, and shantytowns. The New York and Harlem Railroad ran up Fourth Avenue, now Park Avenue, in an open cut, belching smoke and noise. Elevated trains rumbled along Second and Third Avenues starting in the late 1870s, and the blocks near them filled with tenements for working-class immigrants: Germans, Irish, Hungarians, Czechs, and others.

The transformation came in two stages. First, after Central Park opened, the very rich began building mansions along Fifth Avenue facing the park, moving north from the Gilded Age mansions in the Fifties. By the early 1900s, Fifth Avenue from 59th Street to 96th Street was lined with palaces built by the families of the industrial age: steel, oil, railroads, banking, and tobacco. Second, after Grand Central's tracks were covered in the early twentieth century, Park Avenue became a grand boulevard, and luxury apartment buildings rose along it. The rich discovered that a large apartment with a doorman was much easier to run than a mansion with dozens of servants.

As the mansions became impractical, many of them were demolished, but many were converted into museums, consulates, schools, and cultural institutions. That's why Fifth Avenue along the park, from the Met at 82nd Street north to about 105th Street, has so many museums that it's called Museum Mile. Many of these museums are the former homes and private collections of the people who made the great American fortunes.

East of Lexington Avenue, the story is different. The area known as Yorkville was a working-class neighborhood of German, Hungarian, and Czech immigrants, with breweries, beer halls, and churches. Elevated trains kept it modest for decades. After the elevated trains were torn down in the 1940s and 50s, high-rise apartments replaced the tenements, and the neighborhood became more uniformly affluent. And at the far east, along the river, is Gracie Mansion, the official home of New York's mayor.

On this walk, you'll see how private wealth became public culture, and how a working-class immigrant neighborhood became part of the city's most famous zip codes.

title: Upper West Side
blurb: Columbus Circle, the lost neighborhood of San Juan Hill, the Dakota, the Ansonia, the Natural History Museum, Zabar's, and Riverside Park.

stops.title: Columbus Circle
stops.text:
You're at Columbus Circle, at the southwest corner of Central Park, where Broadway, Eighth Avenue, Central Park West, and 59th Street converge.

In the center of the circle, atop a tall granite column, stands a marble statue of Christopher Columbus by the Italian sculptor Gaetano Russo. It was erected in 1892, for the four hundredth anniversary of Columbus's first voyage, and was paid for by Italian Americans through a fundraising campaign led by the Italian-language newspaper Il Progresso. At the time, Italian immigrants faced intense discrimination, and Columbus was embraced as a symbol of Italian contributions to America. In recent years, the statue has been the subject of debate over how Columbus should be remembered, given his treatment of Indigenous people. A fun fact: Columbus Circle is the official point from which distances to and from New York City are measured on highway signs.

Look at the twin glass towers on the west side of the circle. This is the Deutsche Bank Center, formerly the Time Warner Center, completed in 2003, on the site of the old New York Coliseum, a convention hall built by Robert Moses. It houses offices, luxury condos, a hotel, restaurants, and Jazz at Lincoln Center's concert halls, with a window behind the stage overlooking Central Park.

On the south side of the circle, at 2 Columbus Circle, is a curious white marble building with round porthole-like openings at its base. It was designed by Edward Durell Stone and completed in 1964 as a museum for the collection of the A&P supermarket heir Huntington Hartford. Critics mocked it; the architecture critic Ada Louise Huxtable called it a die-cut Venetian palazzo on lollipops. It was controversially remodeled in the 2000s, and now houses the Museum of Arts and Design.

A block south, at Eighth Avenue and 57th Street, look for the Hearst Tower, a glass skyscraper with a distinctive diagonal grid pattern, rising from a six-story Art Deco stone base. William Randolph Hearst, the newspaper and magazine baron who built a media empire on sensational yellow journalism, commissioned the base in 1928 as the foundation for a skyscraper. The Depression halted the plan. Nearly eighty years later, in 2006, the Hearst Corporation finally completed the tower, designed by Norman Foster, rising from the old base. The company, publisher of magazines like Cosmopolitan and Esquire, still has its headquarters there.

stops.title: Lincoln Center & the Lost San Juan Hill
stops.text:
You're at Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts, between 62nd and 66th Streets, Columbus and Amsterdam Avenues. Walk into the main plaza and stand near the Revson Fountain.

Around you are three great halls. Straight ahead is the Metropolitan Opera House, with its five tall arched windows. Inside, visible through the windows, hang two enormous murals by Marc Chagall. To the left is the David H. Koch Theater, home of the New York City Ballet. To the right is David Geffen Hall, home of the New York Philharmonic. Nearby are the Juilliard School, the Vivian Beaumont Theater, the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts, and other institutions.

Lincoln Center was built between 1959 and the late 1960s, championed by John D. Rockefeller the Third and Robert Moses. It was the first major center of its kind in the world, bringing together opera, symphony, ballet, theater, and education in one complex. President Dwight Eisenhower broke ground in 1959.

But there's a story underneath the plaza. Before Lincoln Center, this area was a neighborhood called San Juan Hill. In the early twentieth century, it was one of the largest African American neighborhoods in Manhattan, before Harlem became the center of Black New York. Its name may refer to the Battle of San Juan Hill in the Spanish-American War, in which Black soldiers fought. San Juan Hill was a crowded neighborhood of tenements, with a vibrant musical culture. The stride pianist James P. Johnson lived and played here, and he said the dance the Charleston was inspired by the dances of Gullah dockworkers from South Carolina he saw in the neighborhood. The jazz pianist Thelonious Monk lived on West 63rd Street for decades. By the 1940s and 50s, the neighborhood was largely Black and Puerto Rican.

In the 1950s, the city declared the area a slum and cleared it as part of the Lincoln Square urban renewal project. Thousands of families were displaced. Before the buildings were demolished, the film crew for the 1961 movie version of West Side Story shot its opening scenes in the neighborhood's streets, a story about Puerto Rican and white gangs fighting over the very neighborhood that was about to be destroyed.

Lincoln Center has acknowledged this history in recent years with exhibitions and programs. As you look around this elegant plaza, it's worth remembering the neighborhood that was erased to make room for it.

stops.title: The Dakota
stops.text:
At Central Park West and 72nd Street stands the Dakota, one of the most famous apartment buildings in the world. Look at its steep roofs, gables, dormers, and towers, its yellow brick and sandstone, and its moat-like areaway surrounded by an iron fence.

The Dakota was completed in 1884, designed by Henry Janeway Hardenbergh, who later designed the Plaza Hotel. It was built by Edward Clark, the lawyer who was president of the Singer Manufacturing Company, the sewing machine giant. Clark had made a fortune from Singer and invested heavily in West Side real estate.

At the time, wealthy New Yorkers lived in private houses, and apartments were associated with tenements. Clark set out to create apartments luxurious enough to attract the rich. The Dakota had large apartments, some with as many as twenty rooms, with high ceilings, elaborate woodwork, and modern amenities, including central heating, its own electrical generating plant, and hydraulic elevators. Its interior courtyard was large enough for carriages to drive in.

A popular story says it was called the Dakota because it was so far uptown, so remote from the city, that it might as well have been in the Dakota Territory. Historians think it was more likely just part of Clark's fondness for western names; he also proposed renaming the West Side avenues after western states. But the story stuck.

The Dakota became a home for artists, musicians, and actors, including Leonard Bernstein, Lauren Bacall, Boris Karloff, Judy Garland, and Rudolf Nureyev. The building's co-op board is famously selective, and it reportedly turned down several celebrities who wanted to buy in. Its gloomy, Gothic exterior made it the setting for Roman Polanski's 1968 horror film Rosemary's Baby.

And, most famously, it was the home of John Lennon and Yoko Ono. On December eighth, 1980, Lennon was shot and killed just outside the building's entrance, the arched carriage gate on 72nd Street. Yoko Ono continued to live in the building for many years. The Strawberry Fields memorial in Central Park is just across the street.

Look up and down Central Park West. The avenue is lined with grand apartment buildings, many of them built in the 1920s and 30s, including the twin-towered San Remo at 74th Street and the Majestic and the Century, with their Art Deco towers. Their twin towers create one of the most recognizable skylines in the city, especially viewed from across the park.

stops.title: The Ansonia & Verdi Square
stops.text:
Walk west to Broadway and 73rd Street. Look up at the huge, ornate Beaux-Arts building with rounded corner towers, iron balconies, and a mansard roof. This is the Ansonia, completed in 1904, one of the grandest and strangest apartment hotels ever built.

Its developer was William Earl Dodge Stokes, a wealthy and eccentric heir to a copper and real estate fortune. He named it after his grandfather, Anson Greene Phelps, whose company, Phelps Dodge, became a mining giant. Stokes's ambitions were enormous. The Ansonia had hundreds of apartments, a grand lobby, Turkish baths, and one of the world's largest indoor swimming pools at the time. And on the roof, Stokes kept a small farm, with chickens, goats, ducks, and reportedly a small bear. He sold fresh eggs to residents at a discount. In the lobby, there was a fountain with live seals. The city's health department eventually shut down the farm.

The Ansonia's thick walls made it nearly soundproof, which attracted musicians and singers. The opera star Enrico Caruso, the composer Igor Stravinsky, the conductor Arturo Toscanini, and the singer Lily Pons all lived here at various times.

Baseball fans have a reason to visit too. Babe Ruth lived here in the early 1920s, after joining the Yankees. And in 1919, members of the Chicago White Sox reportedly met in a room at the Ansonia with gamblers to plan the fixing of the World Series, the infamous Black Sox scandal, in which eight players were banned from baseball for life.

In the 1970s, the building's basement was home to the Continental Baths, a gay bathhouse where Bette Midler got her start, singing for patrons with Barry Manilow accompanying her on piano. Later, the space became Plato's Retreat, a notorious swingers' club.

Just to the north is Verdi Square, a small triangular park with a statue of the Italian composer Giuseppe Verdi, surrounded by characters from his operas. In the 1960s and 70s, this park became notorious as Needle Park because of open drug use, and was the setting for the 1971 film The Panic in Needle Park, an early starring role for Al Pacino. Today, the park has been restored, and the neighborhood is a world away from those days.

Across Broadway, the subway station at 72nd Street has its original 1904 control house, a small Beaux-Arts building, the entrance to one of the first subway stations in the city.

stops.title: The American Museum of Natural History
stops.text:
You're on Central Park West, between 77th and 81st Streets, at the American Museum of Natural History, one of the largest natural history museums in the world.

It was founded in 1869 by the naturalist Albert Bickmore and a group of wealthy New Yorkers, including Theodore Roosevelt Senior. Its first home was in the Arsenal in Central Park. In 1877, it moved into its first building here, on what was then a rocky, rural site called Manhattan Square. Today, the museum complex is a patchwork of more than two dozen interconnected buildings, built over a century and a half, in different styles.

The main entrance on Central Park West is the Theodore Roosevelt Memorial, completed in 1936, honoring Theodore Roosevelt Junior, the former president, naturalist, and conservationist, who was a lifelong supporter of the museum. For decades, a bronze equestrian statue of Roosevelt flanked by an African man and a Native American man stood on the front steps. Critics argued that it portrayed the two men as subordinate, and it was removed in 2022. It's been relocated to North Dakota.

Inside, the museum is famous for its dinosaur halls, which hold one of the greatest collections of fossils in the world, including a Tyrannosaurus rex. Its dioramas of animals in their habitats, created in the early twentieth century, are masterpieces of naturalistic art. The Milstein Hall of Ocean Life features a life-size model of a blue whale, ninety-four feet long, suspended from the ceiling.

On the north side, on 81st Street, look at the giant glass cube enclosing a sphere. This is the Rose Center for Earth and Space, which opened in 2000, and houses the Hayden Planetarium. Shortly after it opened, its exhibits grouped Pluto with the Kuiper Belt objects, not with the planets, a decision that caused a public uproar, years before astronomers officially reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet in 2006. The planetarium's director, Neil deGrasse Tyson, became a celebrity partly through that controversy.

On the Columbus Avenue side, look for the newest addition, the Richard Gilder Center for Science, Education, and Innovation, which opened in 2023. Designed by Jeanne Gang's firm, Studio Gang, its flowing, cave-like atrium is inspired by natural canyons and geological formations.

Behind the museum, on Columbus Avenue, there's a popular Sunday flea and farmers' market.

stops.title: Zabar's & Upper Broadway
stops.text:
Walk to Broadway and 80th Street. Here, you'll find Zabar's, the most famous food store on the Upper West Side.

Zabar's was founded in 1934 by Louis and Lillian Zabar, Jewish immigrants from Ukraine, who started with a small counter selling smoked fish. They grew it into a sprawling gourmet store, now spread across a full block front. Inside, you'll find smoked fish, coffee, cheese, breads, and cooking equipment upstairs. The store is still run by the Zabar family. Its bright orange signs and shopping bags are an icon of the neighborhood.

Zabar's is part of the larger story of the Upper West Side's Jewish culture. After the subway opened in 1904, many Jewish families moved here from the Lower East Side and Harlem, and the West Side became one of the most important centers of Jewish life in America. The neighborhood is home to many synagogues, delis, and bakeries. Nearby on Broadway, H and H Bagels was a famous bagel shop for decades; Barney Greengrass, on Amsterdam Avenue at 86th Street, has been selling smoked fish and appetizing since 1908, calling itself The Sturgeon King.

Look up and down Broadway. Notice how wide it is, with a planted median down the middle. That's because the old Bloomingdale Road was widened into a grand boulevard in the 1860s and 70s, called the Boulevard, before it was renamed Broadway in 1899. The subway runs right underneath it.

At Broadway and 78th to 79th Streets, look for the Apthorp, a giant Italian Renaissance apartment building, completed in 1908, built by William Waldorf Astor, the same Astor who built the Waldorf Hotel. It has a large interior courtyard with gardens and fountains, and grand iron gates at its entrances. It was among the first and largest courtyard apartment buildings in the city, and it was the model for a style of luxury living that defined the Upper West Side: big, solid buildings with plenty of light and air.

The neighborhood was also home to the Thalia, a repertory cinema on West 95th Street, which appears in Annie Hall, and Symphony Space, which still hosts readings and concerts.

stops.title: Riverside Park & the Soldiers' and Sailors' Monument
stops.text:
End your walk in Riverside Park, at Riverside Drive and 89th Street, at the Soldiers' and Sailors' Monument.

Riverside Park stretches for about four miles along the Hudson, from 59th Street up to 158th Street. Frederick Law Olmsted, one of the designers of Central Park, designed the original park and Riverside Drive in the 1870s. The drive curves along the contours of the land, unlike the rigid street grid, and was designed for carriages, with views of the river and the New Jersey Palisades.

There was one big problem: the New York Central Railroad's tracks ran along the shore at the bottom of the park, with smoke, noise, and soot. In the 1930s, Robert Moses covered the tracks with a deck, extended the park on landfill, and built the Henry Hudson Parkway along the water, as part of the West Side Improvement Project. The rail line is still there, in a tunnel under the park, and is used today by Amtrak trains. Moses's project also created the 79th Street Rotunda and Boat Basin, where people still live year-round on houseboats.

The white marble monument in front of you, a circular temple of Corinthian columns, is the Soldiers' and Sailors' Memorial, completed in 1902 to honor the Union soldiers and sailors who fought in the Civil War. It was modeled on the ancient Choragic Monument of Lysicrates in Athens.

Look out over the river from the monument's terrace. The views of the Hudson and the New Jersey Palisades are among the best in the city, especially at sunset.

Riverside Drive is lined with handsome apartment buildings and a few surviving mansions. Some of its most famous residents included the newspaper publisher William Randolph Hearst, who lived in a vast apartment at the Clarendon, at Riverside Drive and 86th Street, which he expanded until it took up several floors, and the composer George Gershwin, who lived on Riverside Drive in the 1920s.

Up and down the park, look for other monuments: a statue of Joan of Arc at 93rd Street, a statue of Eleanor Roosevelt at 72nd Street, and a garden at 91st Street that featured prominently in the final scene of the 1998 film You've Got Mail. Riverside Park is less famous than Central Park, but many West Siders love it more: quieter, more local, and with a river view.

overview:
The Upper West Side developed later than the Upper East Side, and it has always had a different personality. If the East Side was old money and Society with a capital S, the West Side was intellectual, artistic, liberal, and a little bohemian.
