It's the neighborhood of musicians, writers, academics, psychoanalysts, and serious eaters, and the setting for countless novels and films, from West Side Story to When Harry Met Sally to You've Got Mail.

In the mid-nineteenth century, this area was mostly countryside, called Bloomingdale, from the Dutch Bloemendael, or valley of flowers. The old Bloomingdale Road, which followed a Native American trail, ran through it; it later became upper Broadway. There were country estates along the Hudson, farms, villages, and shantytowns, as well as institutions like the Bloomingdale Insane Asylum, which stood on the site of today's Columbia University.

Development was slow until transportation arrived. The Ninth Avenue elevated train reached the area in 1879. Developers began building rowhouses on the side streets, and a few ambitious apartment buildings, like the Dakota. But the real boom came with the first subway, the IRT, which opened in 1904 and ran up Broadway. Almost overnight, the West Side became accessible to the middle class, and giant apartment buildings rose along Broadway, Central Park West, West End Avenue, and Riverside Drive. Many of them were built for a new population: upwardly mobile, often Jewish families moving up from the Lower East Side and other parts of the city.

The neighborhood went through hard times in the mid-twentieth century. Many large apartments were cut up into single-room-occupancy hotels, and parts of the neighborhood were considered dangerous by the 1970s. Urban renewal projects demolished whole neighborhoods, most notably San Juan Hill, for Lincoln Center. Then, starting in the 1980s, the West Side gentrified dramatically. Today, it's one of the most expensive neighborhoods in the country, though it retains its reputation as a place of books, music, and lively street life.

On this walk, you'll explore some of the most famous apartment buildings in the world, great cultural institutions, and a few beloved food shops, and you'll end on the banks of the Hudson in Riverside Park.

title: Morningside Heights
blurb: The unfinished cathedral, Columbia and the birth of the atomic age, Riverside Church, and the man in Grant's Tomb.

stops.title: Morningside Park
stops.text:
You're at Morningside Park, the long, narrow park that runs along a steep cliff from 110th Street to 123rd Street, separating Morningside Heights above from Harlem below.

The park was designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, the designers of Central Park, in the 1870s and 80s. The cliff was too steep for buildings, so the city turned it into a park. Olmsted and Vaux designed it with a walkway along the top of the cliff, offering sweeping views east across Harlem, and paths and stairs winding down through rocky outcrops to the flatter area at the bottom.

For much of the twentieth century, the park was neglected, and it became known as dangerous. It also became a symbol of the divide between Columbia, at the top of the cliff, and Harlem, at the bottom.

That divide exploded in 1968. Columbia planned to build a new gymnasium in the park, on land leased from the city. The plan included a separate, smaller entrance on the Harlem side, at the bottom of the cliff, for community residents, while Columbia students would enter from the top. Critics called it Gym Crow, comparing it to the Jim Crow segregation laws of the South.

In April 1968, student protesters, led by groups including the Students for a Democratic Society and the Student Afro-American Society, occupied several campus buildings, including the president's office in Low Library. They protested the gym, and the university's ties to the Institute for Defense Analyses, a think tank doing research for the Vietnam War. After a week, the police stormed the buildings, arresting more than seven hundred people, with violence that injured many students and turned much of the campus against the administration. The university canceled the gym, and the protests became a turning point in the student movement of the 1960s.

Look for the pond and waterfall at the bottom of the park, near 113th Street. They were built on the site where gym construction had begun, as a kind of healing gesture. The park has been substantially restored since the 1990s and is now well used by both Columbia and Harlem residents.

stops.title: The Cathedral of St. John the Divine
stops.text:
At Amsterdam Avenue and 112th Street stands the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, the mother church of the Episcopal Diocese of New York, and one of the largest cathedrals in the world.

The cornerstone was laid on December twenty-seventh, 1892, the feast day of St. John. The original design, by the architects George Heins and Christopher Grant LaFarge, was in a Romanesque and Byzantine style. After Heins died in 1907, the church hired Ralph Adams Cram, the leading Gothic Revival architect in America, who redesigned the nave in a French Gothic style. That's why the building looks like a mix of styles. The eastern end, with its rounded arches, is from the original design. The long nave, with its pointed arches and soaring vault, is Cram's.

Construction has stopped and started many times, interrupted by two world wars, the Depression, and financial troubles. The cathedral has never been finished. Its towers on the west front are incomplete stumps, and the planned central tower was never built. New Yorkers nicknamed it St. John the Unfinished. In the 1980s, the cathedral ran a program training young people from Harlem in medieval stone carving, and they carved some of the statues on the west front portal. Look closely and you'll find some surprising details, including an apocalyptic scene with a recognizable depiction of the Manhattan skyline being destroyed.

Step inside, if you can. The nave is about six hundred feet long, longer than two football fields, and its vaulted ceiling rises over one hundred twenty feet. The cathedral regularly hosts concerts, art installations, and events, and every October, it holds a Blessing of the Animals for the Feast of St. Francis, in which people bring dogs, cats, birds, and even camels and elephants to be blessed.

In 2001, a fire badly damaged the north transept, which was home to the cathedral's gift shop. It took years to clean and restore.

Look for the peacocks. The cathedral keeps a few of them, and they roam the grounds. In the garden on the south side, look for the Peace Fountain, a large bronze sculpture by Greg Wyatt, depicting the struggle between good and evil, with the archangel Michael and a giant crab.

Across Amsterdam Avenue is the Hungarian Pastry Shop, a beloved café for Columbia students and faculty for decades, where writers have worked on dissertations, novels, and screenplays over endless cups of coffee.

stops.title: Columbia University
stops.text:
Walk to the main gate of Columbia University, at Broadway and 116th Street, and walk onto the College Walk.

Columbia was founded in 1754 as King's College, by royal charter from King George the Second. It's the oldest institution of higher learning in New York, and the fifth oldest in the country. Among its early students were Alexander Hamilton; John Jay, the first chief justice of the United States; Gouverneur Morris, who wrote the final draft of the Constitution; and Robert Livingston, who helped draft the Declaration of Independence. After the Revolution, it was renamed Columbia.

The college's first home was near City Hall Park. In 1857, it moved to Midtown, at 49th Street and Madison Avenue. In 1897, it moved here, to the former grounds of the Bloomingdale Asylum. The president of the university, Seth Low, hired the firm McKim, Mead and White to design the new campus, which was conceived as an academic city, inspired by Greek and Roman architecture.

At the center of the campus is Low Memorial Library, with its great dome and columned portico, completed in 1897 and named in honor of Seth Low's father, a merchant in the China trade. Low himself paid for it. It was the university's main library until 1934, when the larger Butler Library, across the quadrangle, opened. Look at Butler's facade: carved across the top are the names of great writers and thinkers from antiquity, including Homer, Herodotus, Sophocles, Plato, Aristotle, Demosthenes, Cicero, and Virgil.

On the steps of Low Library sits the bronze statue of Alma Mater, by Daniel Chester French, the sculptor of the Lincoln Memorial. Look closely in the folds of her robe for a small owl, a symbol of wisdom. Tradition says that the first freshman of each class to find it will become class valedictorian. During the 1968 protests, the statue was damaged by a bomb.

Columbia is also tied to modern finance. The Columbia Business School was where Benjamin Graham, the father of value investing, taught for decades, starting in the 1920s. His most famous student was Warren Buffett, who enrolled in 1950 after reading Graham's book The Intelligent Investor. Graham's classes, and his book Security Analysis, written with David Dodd, have shaped generations of investors.

stops.title: Pupin Hall & the Atomic Age
stops.text:
Walk to the northwest corner of the campus, near Broadway and 120th Street, and look for Pupin Hall, the physics building, a tall brick and limestone tower with a small observatory dome on the roof.

It's named for Michael Pupin, a Serbian immigrant who arrived in New York in 1874 with almost nothing, worked as a laborer, put himself through Columbia, and became a renowned physicist and inventor. His inventions, including loading coils that dramatically improved long-distance telephone lines, made him wealthy. AT&T bought the rights to his patent. His autobiography, From Immigrant to Inventor, won the Pulitzer Prize in 1924.

But Pupin Hall is famous for what happened in its basement in January 1939. Just weeks earlier, scientists in Germany had discovered that uranium atoms could be split, releasing energy, a process called nuclear fission. When the news reached the United States, physicists at Columbia, led by John Dunning, set out to confirm it. On January twenty-fifth, 1939, using a cyclotron, a particle accelerator, in the basement of Pupin Hall, Dunning's team observed fission, among the first such experiments carried out in the United States. The Italian physicist Enrico Fermi, who had just fled fascist Italy, came to Columbia and worked here on nuclear chain reactions.

Fermi and Leo Szilard, also at Columbia, conducted early research on the possibility of a nuclear chain reaction. Szilard drafted the famous letter that Albert Einstein signed in August 1939, warning President Franklin Roosevelt that Germany might build an atomic bomb, and urging the United States to start its own research.

When the United States launched its effort to build the bomb, the Army Corps of Engineers set up the Manhattan Engineer District, headquartered at first in an office building at 270 Broadway, near City Hall. That's why the program became known as the Manhattan Project. Much of the early research took place here at Columbia, before the work shifted to Chicago, Oak Ridge, Hanford, and Los Alamos.

Pupin Hall was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1965. The cyclotron was dismantled in 2008. Standing outside this ordinary-looking academic building, it's sobering to think that the atomic age began, in part, in its basement.

stops.title: Riverside Church
stops.text:
Walk west to Riverside Drive and 120th Street, to Riverside Church, with its massive Gothic tower rising over the Hudson.

The church was built by John D. Rockefeller Junior, the son of the Standard Oil founder, and completed in 1930. Rockefeller was a devout Baptist, and he wanted to create a great interdenominational church, open to all Christians. He chose as its minister Harry Emerson Fosdick, one of the most famous preachers of the era, a liberal Protestant who had been forced out of his previous pulpit for challenging fundamentalist doctrine.

The architecture was modeled largely on Chartres Cathedral in France, but the building has a steel frame, like a skyscraper. The tower is about three hundred ninety feet tall, and contains offices, classrooms, and meeting rooms, as well as the Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial Carillon, named for Rockefeller's mother. The carillon has seventy-four bells. Its largest bell, the bourdon, weighs about twenty tons, and is said to be the largest tuned carillon bell in the world. On Sundays, you can hear the bells ring across the neighborhood. You can sometimes take an elevator up the tower, for a tremendous view of the Hudson and upper Manhattan.

Riverside Church has been a center of progressive activism. On April fourth, 1967, exactly one year before his assassination, the Reverend Martin Luther King Junior delivered his speech Beyond Vietnam: A Time to Break Silence, from the pulpit here. In it, King publicly denounced the Vietnam War, calling the United States government the greatest purveyor of violence in the world today. The speech was condemned by much of the press and many of his allies at the time, and it marked a decisive shift in his public stance. In 1990, Nelson Mandela spoke here, just months after his release from prison in South Africa.

Many presidents, foreign leaders, and religious leaders have spoken here. The church has also been active in the anti-apartheid movement, the sanctuary movement for refugees, and LGBTQ rights.

Look at the west portal, which is modeled on the portal at Chartres, with carved figures of saints and prophets. Mixed in with the traditional figures are carvings of modern figures, including scientists and philosophers, including Albert Einstein. Einstein is said to be the only living person included when the carvings were made.

stops.title: Grant's Tomb
stops.text:
End your walk across the street, at Riverside Drive and 122nd Street, at the General Grant National Memorial, better known as Grant's Tomb.

Here's a trivia question made famous by Groucho Marx on his quiz show You Bet Your Life, who used it to make sure every contestant went home with a prize: Who is buried in Grant's Tomb? The technical answer is: nobody. Ulysses S. Grant and his wife Julia are not buried underground. Their sarcophagi rest in a crypt, above ground, inside the monument. They're entombed, not buried.

Ulysses S. Grant was the commanding general of the Union Army who won the Civil War, and he served two terms as president, from 1869 to 1877. After his presidency, he and Julia settled in New York, in a house on East 66th Street. And here's the part of Grant's story that many people don't know.

Grant's son, Ulysses Junior, known as Buck, had gone into business with a charming young Wall Street financier named Ferdinand Ward. Their firm, Grant and Ward, seemed to be wildly successful, and the former president invested nearly all his money in it and lent the firm his name. But Ward was running a fraud, borrowing against the same securities multiple times and paying old investors with new investors' money, a scheme that would today be called a Ponzi scheme. In May 1884, the firm collapsed, and the Grants were ruined. Grant was left nearly penniless. Ward went to prison.

That same year, Grant was diagnosed with throat cancer. Desperate to provide for his family, he began writing his memoirs. His friend Mark Twain offered him a generous publishing deal through Twain's own publishing company. Grant raced against death to finish, writing in great pain, and completed the manuscript just days before he died in July 1885. The Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant became a massive bestseller, earning his widow a fortune, and are still regarded as among the finest military memoirs ever written.

Grant had requested to be buried in New York, and around ninety thousand people contributed to build this tomb, which was completed in 1897. It was designed by John Duncan, and inspired by the ancient Mausoleum at Halicarnassus. It's the largest mausoleum in North America. More than a million people attended the dedication parade.

Look around the back and sides of the tomb, at the colorful, wavy mosaic benches. They were created in the 1970s by the artist Pedro Silva, with community volunteers, inspired by the work of Antoni Gaudí in Barcelona. The benches caused controversy, since some felt they didn't match the solemn monument, but they've become a beloved part of the site.

Look north along Riverside Drive. Nearby is a small, easily missed monument, the Amiable Child memorial, marking the grave of a five-year-old boy named St. Claire Pollock, who died in 1797 when this land was a private estate. It's one of the only private graves on public land in New York City.

overview:
Morningside Heights is a plateau high above Harlem, bounded by the cliffs of Morningside Park on the east and the Hudson River on the west. Around the turn of the twentieth century, it became home to so many major institutions, a university, a cathedral, seminaries, a hospital, and a monumental tomb, that it was nicknamed the Acropolis of America.

Before that, it was rural and isolated. In the colonial era, it was farmland. In September 1776, it was the site of the Battle of Harlem Heights, one of George Washington's few early successes in the New York campaign. After a string of defeats on Long Island and in lower Manhattan, Washington's troops fought the British to a standstill in the fields around what is now 120th Street and Broadway, near the Columbia campus. The victory was small, but it boosted the morale of an army that badly needed it.

In the nineteenth century, the plateau was dominated by the Bloomingdale Insane Asylum, a psychiatric hospital surrounded by gardens, and the Leake and Watts Orphan House. The asylum was considered progressive for its time, offering patients fresh air and landscaped grounds. When the city grew northward and land became valuable, those institutions moved out and new ones moved in. In the 1890s, Columbia University bought the asylum's land, the Episcopal Church began building a massive cathedral nearby, and General Grant's Tomb rose on Riverside Drive. The subway arrived in 1904, and the neighborhood filled with apartment buildings for professors, students, and middle-class families.

Morningside Heights has also been a place of conflict. Columbia's relationship with its Harlem neighbors has often been tense, as the university expanded, bought up buildings, and, in 1968, proposed building a gymnasium in Morningside Park, which triggered one of the most famous student uprisings in American history.

On this walk, you'll see one of the largest cathedrals in the world, which is still unfinished more than a century after construction began; the campus where the first nuclear fission experiment in the United States was carried out; a soaring Gothic church built by John D. Rockefeller Junior; and the tomb of Ulysses S. Grant, whose story ends with a financial scandal you won't expect.

title: Harlem
blurb: The Apollo, Hotel Theresa, the Harlem Renaissance, Marcus Garvey's Black Star Line, the Savoy, Strivers' Row, and Hamilton's Grange.

stops.title: Marcus Garvey Park
stops.text:
You're at Marcus Garvey Park, between 120th and 124th Streets, at Madison Avenue and Fifth Avenue. Originally called Mount Morris Park, it was renamed in 1973 for Marcus Garvey.

Garvey was a Jamaican-born activist who arrived in New York in 1916. He founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association, the UNIA, which became the largest mass movement of people of African descent in history, with chapters around the world and, by some estimates, millions of members and supporters. Garvey preached Black pride, self-reliance, and Pan-Africanism, the idea that people of African descent around the world shared a common destiny, and that Africa should be free of colonial rule. He held huge parades through Harlem, with uniformed marchers, and rallies at the UNIA's Liberty Hall on West 138th Street.

In 1919, Garvey launched the Black Star Line, a shipping company owned by Black shareholders, which would carry passengers and goods between America, the Caribbean, and Africa. It was a bold idea: an international business controlled by Black people, at a time when they were shut out of most industries. Tens of thousands of supporters bought shares, some for as little as five dollars. But the company was badly managed, bought old, unseaworthy ships, and collapsed within a few years. In 1923, Garvey was convicted of mail fraud related to the sale of Black Star Line stock, in a prosecution that many saw as politically motivated, encouraged by J. Edgar Hoover's Bureau of Investigation. He was imprisoned and then deported to Jamaica in 1927. His ideas, though, influenced generations of activists, from Malcolm X to the leaders of African independence movements.

Now look up at the rocky hill in the center of the park. On top stands the Harlem Fire Watchtower, a cast iron tower built in 1857. In the days before telephone alarms, watchmen stood here scanning the area for smoke, and rang the bell to call firefighters. It's the last surviving fire watchtower of its kind in the city. It was dismantled for restoration and reinstalled in 2019.

Around the park, look at the Mount Morris Park Historic District, with some of the most beautiful brownstones and townhouses in Harlem, built in the 1880s and 90s. A few blocks away, at 20 East 127th Street, is the townhouse where the poet Langston Hughes lived for the last twenty years of his life.

stops.title: 125th Street & the Apollo Theater
stops.text:
Walk west to 125th Street, Harlem's main commercial street, and look for the red and white vertical sign of the Apollo Theater, at 253 West 125th Street.

The building opened in 1914 as Hurtig and Seamon's New Burlesque Theater. Like many theaters in Harlem at the time, it was for white audiences only. In 1934, new owners reopened it as the Apollo Theater, presenting variety shows for Black audiences. It quickly became the most famous venue for Black performers in America.

Its most famous institution is Amateur Night, held on Wednesday nights since 1934. The audience is famously tough. If they like a performer, they cheer; if not, they boo, and a figure called the Executioner sweeps the performer off the stage. In November 1934, a seventeen-year-old girl named Ella Fitzgerald, who had planned to dance, lost her nerve and decided to sing instead. She won. It launched her career. Other performers who were discovered or got early breaks at the Apollo include Billie Holiday, Sarah Vaughan, James Brown, Gladys Knight, the Jackson Five, Stevie Wonder, Lauryn Hill, and many more.

Look for the Tree of Hope, a stump on the stage. It's a piece of an elm that once stood outside on Seventh Avenue, between the Lafayette Theatre and Connie's Inn. Performers rubbed the tree for luck. When it was cut down in the 1930s, a piece was saved and placed on the Apollo stage, and amateur performers still rub it for luck before they go on.

James Brown recorded his album Live at the Apollo here in October 1962. Released in 1963, it became one of the most celebrated live albums ever made.

Look along 125th Street. It's officially named Martin Luther King Junior Boulevard. Throughout the twentieth century, it was the commercial and political heart of Harlem, lined with stores, theaters, and restaurants. For decades, many of its stores were owned by white merchants who refused to hire Black workers. In the 1930s, Harlem activists launched the Don't Buy Where You Can't Work campaign, boycotting and picketing stores until they hired Black employees. The campaign was one of the first major direct-action civil rights campaigns in the North.

Since the 1990s, national chains have moved onto 125th Street, and in 2008, the city rezoned the street for taller buildings, changes that have been both welcomed and resented.

stops.title: The Hotel Theresa
stops.text:
Walk to the corner of 125th Street and Adam Clayton Powell Junior Boulevard, also known as Seventh Avenue. Look at the tall white terracotta building on the corner. This is the former Hotel Theresa.

When it opened in 1913, the Theresa was a hotel for white guests only, even as the neighborhood around it became predominantly Black. In 1940, under new ownership, it opened to Black guests and quickly became the most important Black hotel in the country. It was nicknamed the Waldorf of Harlem. At a time when most hotels in Midtown Manhattan wouldn't accept Black guests, the Theresa hosted Black celebrities, athletes, and musicians. Joe Louis, the heavyweight boxing champion, celebrated his victories here, with crowds filling the street below. Jimi Hendrix, Little Richard, Duke Ellington, Josephine Baker, and Dinah Washington stayed here.

In September 1960, the Theresa became the center of world attention. Fidel Castro, the new leader of Cuba, came to New York for a meeting of the United Nations General Assembly. After a dispute with his Midtown hotel, he moved his entire delegation to the Theresa in Harlem, a deliberate political statement. He was visited there by Malcolm X and by the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev, who came up to Harlem to meet him. Crowds gathered on the street outside. A few weeks later, the presidential candidate John F. Kennedy campaigned outside the Theresa.

Malcolm X later rented offices in the Theresa for his new Organization of Afro-American Unity, which he founded in 1964 after splitting from the Nation of Islam. In February 1965, Malcolm X was assassinated while giving a speech at the Audubon Ballroom in Washington Heights.

The hotel closed in 1966 and was converted into offices. Its distinctive white facade remains.

Across the street, the tall office tower is the Adam Clayton Powell Junior State Office Building, completed in the 1970s, on the site where Black activists had hoped to build a community center. Its construction led to protests and an occupation of the site in 1969. In front of it, look for the statue of Adam Clayton Powell Junior, whom you'll hear about at Abyssinian Baptist Church.

stops.title: The Schomburg Center
stops.text:
Walk north on Malcolm X Boulevard, also known as Lenox Avenue, to 135th Street. On the corner is the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, one of the world's leading research libraries devoted to the history and culture of people of African descent.

It began with the collection of Arturo Alfonso Schomburg, an Afro-Puerto Rican scholar and collector who arrived in New York in 1891. As a schoolboy in Puerto Rico, Schomburg had been told by a teacher that Black people had no history. He spent his life proving the teacher wrong, gathering books, manuscripts, art, and artifacts documenting the achievements of people of African descent. In 1926, the New York Public Library bought his collection, with funding from the Carnegie Corporation, and placed it here, in the 135th Street branch library. Schomburg later became the curator.

The library, and its neighborhood, became a hub of the Harlem Renaissance. Writers met, read, and debated at the library. The poet Countee Cullen and the writer Zora Neale Hurston were among the many who used its resources.

Step into the lobby and look down. Under the floor of the atrium, beneath a cosmogram, a circular design inspired by African and African American symbols, lie the ashes of the poet Langston Hughes. The design incorporates the words of his poem The Negro Speaks of Rivers, with rivers radiating out from the center. Hughes's interment here honors his deep connection to this library.

Langston Hughes was the leading poet of the Harlem Renaissance, and his poetry, with its jazz and blues rhythms and its portraits of everyday Black life, made him one of the most important American writers of the twentieth century. His poem Harlem, which asks what happens to a dream deferred, inspired the title of Lorraine Hansberry's play A Raisin in the Sun.

Across Lenox Avenue, look for Harlem Hospital, which has a series of murals painted in the 1930s by Black artists, including Charles Alston, as part of the Works Progress Administration. They were among the first government commissions given to Black artists, and they depict Black life, history, and medicine.

stops.title: Abyssinian Baptist Church
stops.text:
Walk to West 138th Street, between Lenox Avenue and Adam Clayton Powell Boulevard. Look for the Gothic stone church, Abyssinian Baptist Church, one of the oldest and most influential Black churches in the United States.

Its origins go back to 1808, in lower Manhattan. Black members of the First Baptist Church, along with some Ethiopian merchants and sailors visiting the city, were forced to sit in segregated seating. They walked out and founded their own congregation, naming it Abyssinian, after the old name for Ethiopia. The church moved several times, following its members uptown, and in 1923, it built this church in Harlem.

The church's most famous pastors were a father and son. Adam Clayton Powell Senior led the church from 1908 to 1937 and oversaw its move to Harlem. Under his leadership, it became one of the largest Protestant congregations in the country. His son, Adam Clayton Powell Junior, succeeded him as pastor and became one of the most important Black political figures in American history. In the 1930s, he led protests and boycotts, including the Don't Buy Where You Can't Work campaign. In 1944, he was elected to Congress, the first Black congressman from New York. In Congress, he became chairman of the powerful Education and Labor Committee, where he helped pass major legislation of the 1960s, including laws on minimum wage, education, and anti-poverty programs. He was also flamboyant, defiant, and controversial, and he was eventually expelled from Congress in 1967 over ethics charges, though the Supreme Court later ruled the expulsion unconstitutional.

Another historical connection: the German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, who later became famous for resisting the Nazis, spent a year in New York in 1930 and 1931, studying at Union Theological Seminary. He worshipped at Abyssinian and taught Sunday school here. He said that his experience in the Black church in Harlem shaped his theology, and his commitment to standing with the oppressed.

Today, Abyssinian's Sunday services, with their powerful gospel music, draw so many tourists that the church has had to set rules to make sure members have seats. If you go, dress respectfully and arrive early.

stops.title: The Savoy Ballroom & Lenox Avenue
stops.text:
Walk to Lenox Avenue between 140th and 141st Streets. Today, there's an apartment complex here. Look for a plaque marking the site of the Savoy Ballroom, which stood here from 1926 to 1958.

The Savoy took up an entire block front, with a dance floor that held thousands of people, and two bandstands at either end, so the music never stopped. It was nicknamed the Home of Happy Feet. Crucially, it was integrated: Black and white dancers danced together, at a time when that was rare and, in many places, illegal.

The Savoy is where the Lindy Hop was born, a fast, acrobatic swing dance that became a national craze. According to a widely told story, in 1928, a dancer named George Shorty Snowden was asked what the dance was called, and, thinking of Charles Lindbergh's recent solo flight across the Atlantic, called it the Lindy Hop. Dancers like Frankie Manning, who invented the first aerial moves, took the dance to new heights, literally.

The Savoy was also famous for its battles of the bands. The house band, led by the drummer Chick Webb, with a young Ella Fitzgerald as his singer, famously took on visiting bands. In a celebrated 1937 battle, Webb's band went up against Benny Goodman's orchestra, and many in the crowd thought Webb won.

A few blocks south, at the corner of Lenox Avenue and 142nd Street, stood the original Cotton Club. It was owned by gangsters, including Owney Madden, and it was a whites-only club, despite being in Harlem, featuring Black performers in shows that often played to racist stereotypes of the jungle and the plantation. It was nonetheless a launching pad for some of the greatest musicians of the era. Duke Ellington's orchestra played there from 1927 to 1931, broadcasting on the radio nationwide, which made Ellington famous. Cab Calloway, Lena Horne, and Ethel Waters also performed there.

Farther south, at West 118th Street, Minton's Playhouse, in the Hotel Cecil, was where in the early 1940s musicians including Thelonious Monk, Dizzy Gillespie, Charlie Parker, and Kenny Clarke jammed late at night and helped invent bebop, the fast, complex style that became the foundation of modern jazz.

And at Lenox Avenue and 126th Street, look for Sylvia's, opened in 1962 by Sylvia Woods, known as the Queen of Soul Food. It became a Harlem institution, visited by presidents, celebrities, and tourists from around the world.

stops.title: Strivers' Row
stops.text:
Walk west to West 138th and 139th Streets, between Adam Clayton Powell Junior Boulevard and Frederick Douglass Boulevard. These two blocks, officially the St. Nicholas Historic District, are known as Strivers' Row, and they're among the most beautiful residential blocks in New York.

They were built in 1891 to 1893 by a developer named David King, who hired three of the leading architectural firms of the day to design them, each with a distinct style. James Brown Lord designed the red brick Georgian houses on the south side of 138th Street. Bruce Price and Clarence Luce designed the yellow brick and limestone Colonial Revival houses on the north side of 138th and the south side of 139th. And McKim, Mead and White, the most prestigious firm in the country, designed the dark brick Italian Renaissance houses on the north side of 139th Street. Together, they form a rare example of a unified, planned development, with houses sharing rear alleys and service courts.

Look for the signs on the gateposts to the rear alleys, reading Walk your horses. The alleys were used for deliveries and for horses and carriages to reach the stables.

Originally, the houses were built for wealthy white families. But the houses were built just before an economic downturn, and as Harlem's population changed, they didn't sell well to white buyers. By 1919 and 1920, the houses were sold to African American buyers, many of them doctors, lawyers, musicians, and other professionals. The neighborhood got its nickname because it was seen as a place for ambitious, upwardly mobile Black Harlemites, strivers.

Residents over the years included the composer and bandleader W. C. Handy, known as the Father of the Blues; the bandleader Fletcher Henderson; and the surgeon Louis T. Wright, one of the first Black doctors on the staff of a New York City hospital.

Strivers' Row remains one of the most prestigious addresses in Harlem. As you walk along the blocks, notice how carefully the houses have been maintained, with their stoops, ironwork, and doorways. It's a reminder of the Black middle and upper class that has always been part of Harlem's story.

stops.title: Sugar Hill & Hamilton Grange
stops.text:
End your walk on the hill to the west, near St. Nicholas Park and West 141st Street. This is Hamilton Heights, and just to the north is Sugar Hill.

In St. Nicholas Park, look for a yellow Federal-style house with a porch. This is Hamilton Grange, the only house Alexander Hamilton ever owned. He built it in 1802 as a country retreat, on a thirty-two-acre estate, naming it after his father's ancestral home in Scotland. He only lived here for about two years before he was killed in his duel with Aaron Burr in 1804.

The house has moved twice. In 1889, as the neighborhood was developed, it was moved a short distance to make way for the street grid and squeezed between a church and an apartment building, on Convent Avenue. In 2008, the National Park Service moved it again, lifting the entire house over the church's portico and rolling it down the street to its current location in the park, closer to its original setting. Inside, you can see rooms restored to Hamilton's era. Tours are free.

Up the hill to the west is the campus of the City College of New York, with its striking Gothic buildings, built from dark Manhattan schist excavated during construction of the subway, and trimmed with white terracotta. City College was founded in 1847 as the Free Academy, offering free higher education to the children of the working class. For decades, it was called the Harvard of the proletariat, and it educated generations of immigrants and their children, including many future Nobel Prize winners.

Sugar Hill, the area north of here roughly between 145th and 155th Streets, got its name in the 1920s and 30s because it was where Harlem's sweet life was lived: the most prosperous and successful Black New Yorkers lived here. Two apartment buildings on Edgecombe Avenue became legendary. At 409 Edgecombe Avenue lived W. E. B. Du Bois, the civil rights leader and scholar; Thurgood Marshall, who argued Brown versus Board of Education and became the first Black Supreme Court justice; Walter White and Roy Wilkins, leaders of the NAACP; and many others. At 555 Edgecombe Avenue lived the actor and singer Paul Robeson, the bandleader Count Basie, and the boxer Joe Louis, among others.

Duke Ellington's famous theme song, Take the A Train, written by Billy Strayhorn in 1939, was about the subway line that took you to Sugar Hill.

overview:
Harlem is one of the most famous neighborhoods in the world, a name that stands for African American culture, music, politics, and creativity. But Harlem was not always Black, and the story of how it became the capital of Black America is one of the most interesting in New York history.

The Dutch founded the village of Nieuw Haarlem in 1658, named after the city of Haarlem in the Netherlands. For two centuries, Harlem was farmland and country estates, connected to the city by the old Post Road. In the late nineteenth century, elevated trains arrived, and developers built elegant brownstones and apartment buildings for middle- and upper-middle-class white families, many of them German and Jewish immigrants and their children. Harlem became a fashionable suburb within the city.

Then came a crash. Developers, anticipating the arrival of the first subway line along Lenox Avenue in 1904, built far more apartment buildings than the market could fill. Prices collapsed, and landlords were left with empty buildings. Enter Philip A. Payton Junior, a Black real estate entrepreneur, who founded the Afro-American Realty Company in 1904. Payton persuaded white landlords to rent their vacant buildings to Black tenants, who were desperate for decent housing, since they were confined to crowded, run-down neighborhoods like the Tenderloin and San Juan Hill. Payton's company leased and bought buildings, and Black New Yorkers began moving in. White residents resisted, sometimes forming associations to keep Black tenants out, but the movement was unstoppable. The Great Migration, the movement of millions of African Americans out of the rural South starting around 1915, along with immigration from the Caribbean, filled Harlem. By the 1920s, it was the largest Black urban community in the country.

The result was the Harlem Renaissance, a flowering of Black literature, music, art, and political thought in the 1920s and 30s. Writers like Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Claude McKay, and Countee Cullen; musicians like Duke Ellington, Louis Armstrong, Bessie Smith, and Fats Waller; and intellectuals like W. E. B. Du Bois and Alain Locke made Harlem a cultural capital.

Harlem's later history includes the Great Depression, which hit it hard; the political activism of Adam Clayton Powell Junior and Malcolm X; decades of disinvestment, crime, and abandonment in the 1970s and 80s; and, since the 1990s, a dramatic and contested wave of gentrification. Through it all, Harlem has remained a center of Black culture, faith, and politics.

As you walk, notice the remarkable architecture. Harlem has some of the finest rows of brownstones and townhouses in the city, built for wealthy white families who left long ago.

title: Washington Heights & Inwood
blurb: Washington's headquarters, the Audubon Ballroom, the High Bridge, the George Washington Bridge, the Cloisters, and Manhattan's last forest.

stops.title: Morris-Jumel Mansion
stops.text:
You're at the Morris-Jumel Mansion, at West 160th Street and Edgecombe Avenue, the oldest surviving house in Manhattan.

It was built in 1765 as a summer villa for Roger Morris, a British army officer, and his wife Mary Philipse, from one of the wealthiest families in the colony. It's in the Palladian style, with a grand columned portico, and it sat on a hilltop with views of both the Hudson and Harlem Rivers and all the way down to the harbor. When the Revolution came, the Morrises, who were loyalists, fled.

In September and October 1776, George Washington made the house his headquarters, during the weeks around the Battle of Harlem Heights. From here, he could watch British movements. After Washington left, the British and their Hessian allies used it as a headquarters too. After the war, in 1790, Washington returned for a dinner here with members of his cabinet, including John Adams, Thomas Jefferson, and Alexander Hamilton.

In 1810, the house was bought by Stephen Jumel, a wealthy French-born wine merchant, and his wife Eliza. Eliza Jumel was born into poverty in Rhode Island and rose to become one of the richest women in America. After Stephen died in 1832, Eliza married Aaron Burr, the former vice president who had killed Alexander Hamilton, in this house in 1833. She was in her late fifties; he was seventy-seven. The marriage quickly fell apart when Burr started speculating with her money. She filed for divorce, and the divorce was finalized on the very day Burr died, in 1836. Her divorce lawyer was Alexander Hamilton Junior, the son of the man Burr had killed.

Lin-Manuel Miranda was given permission to write here while working on Hamilton, and he reportedly wrote parts of the musical in Aaron Burr's bedroom.

As you leave, look across the street at Sylvan Terrace, a short cobblestone lane lined with two rows of small yellow wooden houses, built in 1882 as housing for working people. It looks like a village street from another century, because it is.

stops.title: The Audubon Ballroom
stops.text:
Walk to Broadway and West 165th Street, where you'll see a building with an ornate terracotta facade, with figures of Neptune and sea creatures, attached to a modern glass research building. This is the former Audubon Ballroom.

It was built in 1912 by William Fox, a Hungarian Jewish immigrant who had started out in the garment business and moved into the new business of movies. Fox built a chain of theaters, and later founded the Fox Film Corporation, which merged in 1935 to become Twentieth Century-Fox, one of the great Hollywood studios. The Audubon was a theater and ballroom, used for vaudeville, movies, dances, and meetings. Labor unions, political groups, and community organizations rented its ballroom.

On February twenty-first, 1965, Malcolm X was speaking to a meeting of his Organization of Afro-American Unity in the ballroom when he was shot and killed by several gunmen in front of his wife, Betty Shabazz, and their children. Three members of the Nation of Islam were convicted of the murder. In 2021, after a reinvestigation, two of the three men's convictions were vacated, after it emerged that authorities had withheld evidence. The case remains a subject of investigation and debate.

In the 1980s and 90s, Columbia University, which owned the building, planned to demolish it for a biomedical research center. Preservationists and activists protested, and in a compromise, part of the facade and ballroom were preserved and incorporated into the new research building. Today, the building houses the Malcolm X and Dr. Betty Shabazz Memorial and Educational Center, with a mural depicting Malcolm X's life.

The research building is part of the vast Columbia University Irving Medical Center and NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital complex, which opened here in 1928, as the first academic medical center in the world, combining a hospital, medical school, and research in one place.

A few blocks south, at 155th Street and Broadway, is the Trinity Church Cemetery and Mausoleum, the only active cemetery in Manhattan. John James Audubon, the naturalist and painter of The Birds of America, is buried there. He owned an estate, called Minnie's Land, along the Hudson in this neighborhood, which is why the Audubon name appears all over the area.

stops.title: The High Bridge
stops.text:
Walk east to Highbridge Park, near West 173rd Street and Amsterdam Avenue, at the edge of the cliff overlooking the Harlem River. Here you'll find the High Bridge, the oldest standing bridge in New York City.

The High Bridge was completed in 1848 as part of the Croton Aqueduct, the great water system you may have heard about at Bryant Park and Bethesda Fountain. Before the aqueduct, New Yorkers relied on wells and polluted cisterns, and epidemics of cholera and other diseases ravaged the city, while fires burned unchecked because there wasn't enough water. The Croton Aqueduct brought clean water from the Croton River in Westchester County, forty-one miles to the north, flowing entirely by gravity. The aqueduct had to cross the Harlem River, and engineers built this bridge, modeled on the arched aqueducts of ancient Rome, to carry the water pipes over it.

When it opened, the bridge was a sensation. A promenade on top became a favorite destination for New Yorkers on Sunday outings. It was the Victorian equivalent of the High Line.

In the 1920s, several of the original stone arches over the river were replaced with a single steel arch, to allow bigger ships to pass underneath. The bridge stopped carrying water in the mid-twentieth century, and it was closed to the public in the 1970s. After a long restoration, it reopened to pedestrians and cyclists in 2015, connecting Manhattan to the Bronx.

Next to the bridge on the Manhattan side stands the High Bridge Water Tower, an octagonal granite tower completed in 1872. It held water in a tank at the top to provide pressure to supply the growing neighborhoods on the high ground of northern Manhattan. Its design, with its bell tower, makes it look more like a church tower than a piece of infrastructure.

The Croton system set New York on the path to having one of the best municipal water supplies in the world. Today, the city's water comes mainly from reservoirs in the Catskill Mountains and the Delaware River watershed, upstate, and it's so clean that it's one of the few big city water systems in the United States that doesn't need to be filtered.

stops.title: The George Washington Bridge & the Little Red Lighthouse
stops.text:
Walk west to Fort Washington Park, along the Hudson, beneath the George Washington Bridge, near West 178th Street. Here you'll find a small red lighthouse right at the foot of the bridge.

Look up at the bridge. The George Washington Bridge opened in 1931, connecting Manhattan with Fort Lee, New Jersey. Its chief engineer was Othmar Ammann, a Swiss immigrant, who later designed the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge. When it opened, its main span, about thirty-five hundred feet, was nearly double the length of the previous record holder, an astonishing leap. The towers were originally meant to be covered in concrete and granite, but the Depression put a stop to that, and they were left as bare steel latticework. The Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier called it the most beautiful bridge in the world, praising the honesty of its exposed steel. A second, lower deck was added in 1962. Today, it's one of the busiest motor vehicle bridges in the world, carrying hundreds of thousands of vehicles a day.

Now look at the lighthouse. It's officially called the Jeffrey's Hook Lighthouse. It was built in 1880 at Sandy Hook, New Jersey, and moved here in 1921 to warn ships away from the rocky point. When the bridge was built, its bright lights made the lighthouse obsolete, and it was decommissioned in 1948. The Coast Guard planned to auction it off.

But the lighthouse had become famous. In 1942, a children's book called The Little Red Lighthouse and the Great Gray Bridge, by Hildegarde Swift and Lynd Ward, told the story of a little lighthouse that felt useless next to the giant bridge, until one foggy night, it saved a ship. Children who loved the book wrote letters and protested to save it, and in 1951, the Coast Guard gave the lighthouse to the city. It was restored and is occasionally open for tours.

High on the ridge above you, near 183rd Street and Fort Washington Avenue, is Bennett Park, the highest natural point in Manhattan, at about two hundred sixty-five feet above sea level. It's also where Fort Washington stood. You can still see the outline of the fort marked in the park. On November sixteenth, 1776, about eight thousand British and Hessian troops attacked the fort from several directions. It fell within hours. It was a devastating blow to the American cause, and it forced Washington into a long retreat across New Jersey.

stops.title: Fort Tryon Park & the Cloisters
stops.text:
Take the A train to 190th Street, or walk north, to Fort Tryon Park, one of the most beautiful parks in New York, perched on cliffs high above the Hudson. In the park is The Met Cloisters, a branch of the Metropolitan Museum of Art devoted to the art and architecture of medieval Europe.

The park and the museum were gifts of John D. Rockefeller Junior. In the 1910s and 20s, he bought up the land here, including the former estate of the industrialist C. K. G. Billings. He hired the Olmsted Brothers firm, run by the sons of Frederick Law Olmsted, to design a park, and gave it to the city, which opened it in 1935. Rockefeller also bought land across the Hudson, along the Palisades in New Jersey, and donated it to the public, to ensure that the view from the park would never be spoiled by development. It still hasn't been.

The museum began with the collection of an American sculptor named George Grey Barnard, who had gathered medieval sculptures and architectural fragments from ruined abbeys and churches in France. Rockefeller bought the collection in 1925 for the Met and funded a new building to house it. The Cloisters, which opened in 1938, was designed by the architect Charles Collens. It incorporates parts of five medieval cloisters, the covered walkways around a monastery's garden, from France and Spain, along with chapels, doorways, and windows, reassembled into a building that evokes a medieval monastery.

Inside, you'll find some of the greatest treasures of medieval art, including the Unicorn Tapestries, seven tapestries woven in the Netherlands around 1500, depicting the hunt for a unicorn. The gardens, planted with species that were grown in the Middle Ages, are especially beautiful in spring and summer.

The park takes its name from Fort Tryon, an American outpost that was captured by Hessian troops during the Battle of Fort Washington in 1776, and renamed by the British for William Tryon, the last British governor of New York. Near the park's entrance, look for Margaret Corbin Circle. Margaret Corbin fought here in that battle. Her husband was a gunner, and when he was killed, she took his place at the cannon and kept firing until she was seriously wounded. She later became the first woman in the United States to receive a military pension.

stops.title: Dyckman Farmhouse
stops.text:
Walk to Broadway and West 204th Street, where you'll find a small white clapboard and fieldstone farmhouse with a gambrel roof and a front porch, sitting on a little hill above the street. This is the Dyckman Farmhouse Museum, the last surviving Dutch colonial farmhouse in Manhattan.

The Dyckman family were among the early Dutch settlers of upper Manhattan. Jan Dyckman arrived in the 1660s, and the family farmed land here for generations, eventually owning hundreds of acres. During the Revolutionary War, British and Hessian troops occupied the area and burned the original Dyckman house. After the war, around 1784, William Dyckman built this farmhouse, in the Dutch colonial style, with fieldstone and brick walls, a steep roof, and a porch called a stoep, from which the New York word stoop comes.

The family lived here and farmed until the mid-nineteenth century. By the early twentieth century, the house was in poor condition, surrounded by new apartment buildings. In 1915, two Dyckman descendants, Mary Alice Dyckman Dean and Fannie Fredericka Dyckman Welch, bought the house, restored it, filled it with family furniture and heirlooms, and donated it to the city as a museum in 1916.

Look around the garden behind the house. There's a reconstruction of a hut used by Hessian soldiers during the British occupation, and a smokehouse. In this neighborhood of busy streets and apartment buildings, the farmhouse is a startling reminder that all of Manhattan was once countryside.

Inwood, the neighborhood around you, is one of the most residential and affordable parts of Manhattan, with a large Dominican population, and a mix of Irish and Jewish families who have been here for generations. The area along Dyckman Street, with its restaurants, bars, and music, comes alive on summer nights.

stops.title: Inwood Hill Park
stops.text:
End your walk in Inwood Hill Park, at the northern tip of Manhattan. Walk in from the entrance at Seaman Avenue and 207th Street, past the ballfields, to the salt marsh.

Inwood Hill Park contains the last natural forest and the last natural salt marsh in Manhattan. Unlike Central Park, which was entirely designed and rebuilt, much of the woods here were never cleared for farming or development. Some of the trees are very old. Walking the trails up the hill, among large tulip trees, oaks, and rock outcrops, you can get a sense of what the island looked like before Europeans arrived.

The Lenape lived and fished here for thousands of years. Archaeologists have found evidence of their camps, and on the hillside, you'll find rock shelters, natural caves formed by fallen boulders, which were used by the Lenape.

Near the salt marsh, look for a boulder with a plaque. This is Shorakkopoch Rock. It marks the spot where a giant tulip tree stood until 1938, when it died. Local tradition holds that this was where, in 1626, Peter Minuit of the Dutch West India Company bought Manhattan from the Lenape for trade goods worth sixty guilders, an amount that later writers calculated as twenty-four dollars. Historians doubt the story's details, including the location. And the Lenape likely understood the transaction very differently from the Dutch, as an agreement to share the land rather than a permanent sale. But it's the closest thing to a founding site Manhattan has.

Walk to the water's edge. The water to the north is Spuyten Duyvil Creek, which separates Manhattan from the Bronx. The name is Dutch, and its meaning is debated: it may mean in spite of the devil or spouting devil, referring to its strong currents. Look across the creek at the cliff on the Bronx side. You'll see a giant blue C painted on the rock. It was first painted in the 1950s by members of the Columbia University rowing team, who train on the river nearby, and it's been repainted many times since. Columbia's athletic facilities, including its football stadium, are just to the east.

Spanning the creek is the Henry Hudson Bridge, a steel arch bridge built by Robert Moses in 1936. According to tradition, somewhere near here in 1609, the explorer Henry Hudson, sailing for the Dutch East India Company, anchored his ship, the Half Moon, on his voyage up the river that now bears his name, looking for a passage to Asia.

You're standing about as far as you can get from Wall Street and still be in Manhattan, in the place where the island's story began.

overview:
North of Harlem, Manhattan narrows and rises. The island's spine becomes a ridge of rock, with cliffs dropping to the Hudson River on the west and the Harlem River on the east. This is Washington Heights, and at the very top of the island, Inwood. Many New Yorkers who live downtown have never been up here, which is a shame, because this part of Manhattan has some of the city's most dramatic landscapes and some of its deepest history.

The neighborhood's name comes from Fort Washington, a Revolutionary War fortification built on the highest ground in Manhattan in 1776. That November, the fort fell to the British in one of the worst American defeats of the war, and almost three thousand American soldiers were captured. Many died in the horrific conditions of British prison ships in Wallabout Bay, in Brooklyn. For the rest of the war, the British held all of Manhattan.

For most of the nineteenth century, the area remained rural, with farms and grand country estates. The naturalist John James Audubon had his estate here. Development came with the subway in the early 1900s, and apartment buildings filled the ridge. The neighborhood became home to successive waves of immigrants: Irish, then Greek, and in the 1930s and 40s, so many German Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi persecution that the area was nicknamed Frankfurt on the Hudson. The future Secretary of State Henry Kissinger grew up here, after his family fled Germany in 1938.

From the 1960s onward, Washington Heights became the center of the Dominican community in the United States. Today, it's often called Little Dominican Republic, and you'll hear Spanish and bachata everywhere, especially along St. Nicholas Avenue and 181st Street. Lin-Manuel Miranda, who grew up in nearby Inwood, set his musical In the Heights here, and he wrote parts of Hamilton in a historic house you'll visit on this walk.

This tour covers a long stretch, from 160th Street to the northern tip of Manhattan at about 218th Street. It's best done in pieces, using the A train or the 1 train, which run up the length of the neighborhood.

title: Brooklyn Bridge & DUMBO
blurb: The Roeblings' bridge, Washington's escape, Whitman's ferry, coffee and sugar warehouses, the invention of the cardboard box, and Squibb.

stops.title: The Brooklyn Bridge
stops.text:
You're on the Brooklyn Bridge. Look up at the massive granite towers with their Gothic arches, and the web of steel cables radiating from them.

The bridge was designed by John Augustus Roebling, a German immigrant engineer who had pioneered the manufacture of wire rope and built several suspension bridges. In 1869, while surveying the site, Roebling's foot was crushed by a ferry against the pilings at the Fulton Ferry landing. His toes were amputated, and he died of tetanus a few weeks later. He was sixty-three.

His son, Washington Roebling, a thirty-two-year-old Civil War veteran and engineer, took over. To build the towers' foundations, workers labored inside caissons, huge upside-down wooden boxes sunk to the river bottom, filled with compressed air to keep water out. As the caissons sank deeper, workers began suffering from a mysterious illness: crippling joint pain, paralysis, and sometimes death. They called it caisson disease. Today we know it as decompression sickness, or the bends, caused by nitrogen bubbles forming in the blood when people come out of high pressure too quickly. Several workers died. Washington Roebling himself was struck by it in 1872 and left partially paralyzed and in pain for the rest of his life.

Unable to visit the site, Roebling directed construction from his bedroom window in Brooklyn Heights, watching through a telescope. His wife, Emily Warren Roebling, became his link to the project. She learned higher mathematics, the strength of materials, and cable construction, and relayed his instructions to the engineers. Over time, she effectively became a manager of the project. On opening day, May twenty-fourth, 1883, she was given the honor of the first ride across the bridge, carrying a rooster as a symbol of victory. A plaque on the bridge honors her, along with her husband and father-in-law.

The bridge was an engineering marvel. Its main span, about sixteen hundred feet, was the longest in the world. It was the first suspension bridge to use steel wire for its cables. There was a scandal during construction: the contractor supplying the wire, J. Lloyd Haigh, was caught substituting defective wire. Some of it had already been woven into the cables. Roebling compensated by adding extra wires, and the bridge was built to be several times stronger than necessary, which is part of why it's still standing.

A week after it opened, on May thirtieth, a rumor that the bridge was collapsing caused a stampede on the crowded walkway, and twelve people were crushed to death. To prove the bridge was safe, in 1884, the showman P. T. Barnum led a parade of twenty-one elephants across it.

stops.title: Fulton Ferry Landing
stops.text:
You're at Fulton Ferry Landing, at the foot of Old Fulton Street, on the water just north of the Brooklyn Bridge. This was the gateway to Brooklyn for centuries.

Ferries crossed here as early as the 1600s, rowed or sailed across the treacherous East River. In 1814, Robert Fulton, the steamboat pioneer buried at Trinity Church, launched steam ferry service here. The street leading up the hill was renamed Fulton Street in his honor, and it became Brooklyn's main street.

This landing was also the site of one of the most important moments of the American Revolution. In August 1776, the British defeated George Washington's army at the Battle of Brooklyn, also called the Battle of Long Island, the largest battle of the war. Washington's army was trapped in Brooklyn Heights, with the British army in front and the East River behind. On the night of August twenty-ninth, Washington ordered a secret retreat. Using every boat they could find, soldiers from a Massachusetts regiment of fishermen and sailors from Marblehead, led by Colonel John Glover, ferried about nine thousand troops, with their supplies and artillery, across the river to Manhattan, in total silence, through the night. As dawn broke, a thick fog rolled in, hiding the last boats from the British. By the time the fog lifted, the entire army was gone. If the British had captured Washington's army that night, the Revolution might well have ended.

Walt Whitman, the great poet, was a Brooklyn man, and he rode this ferry constantly. In his poem Crossing Brooklyn Ferry, published in 1856, he imagined future generations making the same crossing, looking at the same river and sky, and he addressed them directly: Just as you feel when you look on the river and sky, so I felt. Whitman also worked as editor of the Brooklyn Daily Eagle, the newspaper whose former warehouse, the Eagle Warehouse, still stands just up Old Fulton Street, now converted to apartments.

Look around the landing. The barge moored nearby is Bargemusic, a floating concert hall that has hosted chamber music concerts since 1977. Nearby is the River Café, a celebrated restaurant opened in 1977, when this area was still desolate. And up the street are two of the most famous pizzerias in the city, which have long attracted lines of tourists.

stops.title: Empire Stores & Jane's Carousel
stops.text:
Walk north along the water into Brooklyn Bridge Park, to the long row of massive brick warehouses facing the river. These are the Empire Stores, built in two phases between 1869 and 1885.

In the nineteenth century, a warehouse was called a store, because it stored goods. Ships from around the world unloaded their cargoes here: coffee from Brazil, sugar from the Caribbean, jute, hides, and other goods. The thick brick walls and small windows kept goods safe and the temperature stable. Workers used iron shutters to protect the cargo, and you can still see some of them on the windows.

The waterfront here was dominated by coffee and sugar. One of the most important companies was Arbuckle Brothers, a coffee company founded in Pittsburgh. Arbuckle had a brilliant innovation: it sold coffee already roasted, sealed in one-pound paper packages, at a time when most people bought green coffee beans and roasted them at home. The coffee was coated with a glaze of sugar and egg to keep it fresh. Their brand, Ariosa, became so popular in the American West in the late nineteenth century that it was called the coffee that won the West. Arbuckle moved its operations to Brooklyn, along this waterfront, and also went into sugar refining, challenging the powerful sugar trust in a famous price war.

The Empire Stores sat empty for decades after the shipping industry declined. They were redeveloped in the 2010s into offices, shops, and restaurants, with a rooftop terrace.

Next door, the roofless brick ruin with arched openings is the Tobacco Warehouse, built in the 1870s and used to store tobacco during inspection. The roof was removed in the 1990s, and part of it is now home to St. Ann's Warehouse, a theater.

Now look at the glass box by the water. Inside is Jane's Carousel, a carousel built in 1922 by the Philadelphia Toboggan Company for an amusement park in Youngstown, Ohio. In 1984, Jane Walentas, an artist and the wife of the developer David Walentas, bought it at auction and spent more than two decades restoring it by hand, stripping away layers of paint to reveal the original colors of its forty-eight horses. In 2011, it reopened here, inside a transparent pavilion designed by the French architect Jean Nouvel. The carousel survived Hurricane Sandy in 2012, when the pavilion flooded but the carousel was undamaged, and photos of it lit up in the storm went viral.

stops.title: Robert Gair & the Invention of the Cardboard Box
stops.text:
Walk up to Washington Street, at Water Street, and turn to face the Manhattan Bridge. This is one of the most photographed views in New York: the narrow street framed by brick warehouses, with the Manhattan Bridge's tower filling the gap at the end, and the Empire State Building visible through the bridge's arch.

The buildings around you were once part of Gairville, the factory empire of Robert Gair, a Scottish immigrant who invented a product you've probably used today: the folding cardboard box.

Gair ran a business printing and making paper bags. In 1879, one of his workers made a mistake: a metal printing rule, used to crease paper, shifted, and it cut through a stack of paper bags instead of creasing them. Gair realized that he could use the same principle to cut and crease cardboard in one operation, producing flat, pre-cut boxes that could be folded into shape. Before this, boxes had to be cut and assembled by hand, slowly and expensively. Gair's machines could produce thousands quickly and cheaply.

The innovation transformed packaging. Gair's company became one of the largest producers of boxes in the world. One of his most important customers was the National Biscuit Company, Nabisco, which used Gair's boxes for its Uneeda Biscuits, the first crackers sold in sealed packages, which you may have heard about on the Chelsea tour. The cardboard box was essential to the rise of national brands, because it allowed companies to package, label, and ship products directly to consumers.

Gair bought and built more and more buildings in this area. They were among the first large reinforced concrete factory buildings in the city. Look for the building at 1 Main Street with a clock tower on top. That was one of Gair's buildings. Its clock tower penthouse, with enormous clock faces as windows, was converted into one of the most expensive apartments in Brooklyn.

The Gair company moved out in the 1920s, and the buildings were used by other manufacturers. Today, many of them house tech companies, design studios, and media firms. DUMBO is part of what the city has promoted as the Brooklyn Tech Triangle, along with the Navy Yard and Downtown Brooklyn. It's fitting that a neighborhood built on a packaging innovation is now full of startups trying to invent the next one.

stops.title: Squibb & the Watchtower
stops.text:
Walk south, under the Brooklyn Bridge, to the corner of Columbia Heights and Old Fulton Street, at the foot of Brooklyn Heights. Look up at the large buildings climbing the hillside above you.

For most of the twentieth century, these buildings were home to two very different organizations. The first was E. R. Squibb and Sons, the pharmaceutical company. Edward Robinson Squibb was a Navy doctor who was horrified by the poor quality of the medicines given to sailors. In 1858, he set up a laboratory here in Brooklyn to manufacture pure, standardized drugs, especially ether, an anesthetic, and chloroform. During the Civil War, his company supplied medicines to the Union army. Squibb was a crusader for drug quality and an early advocate of federal regulation of food and drugs. His company became one of the leading pharmaceutical companies in the country, and it's an ancestor of today's Bristol Myers Squibb.

The second organization was the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society, the headquarters of the Jehovah's Witnesses. The Witnesses moved their headquarters to Brooklyn in 1909, and over the decades, they bought many buildings in Brooklyn Heights and DUMBO, including the old Squibb buildings, for their offices, residences, and printing plants. They printed hundreds of millions of copies of their magazines, The Watchtower and Awake!, here, distributing them around the world. For decades, a giant red sign reading Watchtower, with the time and temperature, sat on top of one of the buildings, and it became a familiar sight for anyone crossing the Brooklyn Bridge.

In the 2010s, the Witnesses moved their headquarters to Warwick, in upstate New York, and sold their Brooklyn properties to developers for large sums. The Watchtower sign was taken down in 2017. The buildings have been converted into offices and apartments.

Up the hill, along Columbia Heights, is the beginning of Brooklyn Heights, America's first designated historic district, and the Brooklyn Heights Promenade, which you can explore on the Brooklyn Heights tour. It was from a house on Columbia Heights, near here, that Washington Roebling watched the Brooklyn Bridge being built through his telescope.

stops.title: Brooklyn Bridge Park & the Piers
stops.text:
End your walk on Pier 1 in Brooklyn Bridge Park, just south of the Brooklyn Bridge, on the water.

Look out at the view: the towers of lower Manhattan rising across the river, the Statue of Liberty in the harbor to the south, and the Brooklyn Bridge arching overhead. It's one of the best views in New York.

This waterfront was once among the busiest port areas in the world. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the New York Dock Company and other companies operated a continuous line of piers, warehouses, and rail yards along the Brooklyn shore, from here south to Red Hook. Brooklyn's docks handled a huge share of the cargo coming into the Port of New York. Thousands of longshoremen, many of them Irish and Italian immigrants, loaded and unloaded ships by hand. The work was brutal, and the docks were controlled by corrupt unions and organized crime, as dramatized in the 1954 film On the Waterfront.

Then came the shipping container. In 1956, a trucking entrepreneur named Malcolm McLean shipped containers from Port Newark, in New Jersey, on a converted tanker, launching the container revolution. Containers could be lifted by crane directly from ship to truck or train, eliminating most of the labor of loading and unloading. But they needed huge open spaces for stacking and handling, which Brooklyn's narrow piers didn't have. The shipping industry moved to the vast container terminals in New Jersey. By the 1980s, Brooklyn's piers were nearly abandoned.

In the 2000s, after years of community advocacy, the piers were transformed into Brooklyn Bridge Park, designed by the landscape architecture firm Michael Van Valkenburgh Associates. The park stretches about a mile and a half along the waterfront, from here to Atlantic Avenue. Each pier has a different use: lawns, playgrounds, sports fields, a salt marsh, and even a beach for kayaks. The park was designed to be financially self-sustaining: luxury apartment buildings and a hotel were built within its boundaries, and their fees pay for the park's maintenance, a model that has been both praised and criticized.

The park also uses salvaged materials. Look for benches made of wood from the old pier sheds, and parts of the old industrial waterfront incorporated into the design. Stand at the end of the pier and imagine this view a century ago, filled with ships, ferries, and barges.

overview:
Before the Brooklyn Bridge, Brooklyn was a separate city, and for much of the nineteenth century, it was the third largest city in the United States, after New York and Philadelphia. The only way to get to Manhattan was by boat. The ferry from the foot of Fulton Street was the main link, and the area around the ferry landing became the commercial heart of Brooklyn.

The waterfront north and south of the ferry developed into one of the busiest port districts in the world. Massive warehouses, called stores, lined the shore, holding coffee, sugar, tobacco, grain, and other goods unloaded from ships. Factories sprang up in the blocks behind them, making paper boxes, machinery, soap, and other products. The neighborhood that we now call DUMBO, for Down Under the Manhattan Bridge Overpass, was one of the great industrial districts of the country. Some of its businesses became household names. Others invented things you use every day without knowing where they came from.

Then came the bridges. The Brooklyn Bridge opened in 1883, followed by the Williamsburg Bridge in 1903 and the Manhattan Bridge in 1909. In 1898, Brooklyn voted, narrowly, to merge with New York, becoming one of its five boroughs. Many Brooklynites still call it the Great Mistake of 1898.

After World War Two, the waterfront declined. Container shipping moved the port to New Jersey, the warehouses emptied, and factories moved out. By the 1970s, the area under the Manhattan Bridge was a desolate industrial zone, with a few artists living illegally in the empty lofts. In 1978, residents coined the name DUMBO, reportedly on purpose to make it sound unappealing and keep developers away. It didn't work. A developer named David Walentas began buying buildings in the early 1980s, and over the following decades, he and others transformed DUMBO into one of the most expensive neighborhoods in New York, filled with tech companies, designers, and luxury apartments. Meanwhile, the piers along the water were transformed into Brooklyn Bridge Park.

This tour begins on the Brooklyn Bridge and ends in the park. If you're starting in Manhattan, walk across the bridge, and the first stop will play as you approach the first tower.

title: Brooklyn Heights & Atlantic Avenue
blurb: America's first suburb, the Promenade, Beecher's church, Capote and Hart Crane, Jackie Robinson's signing, Borough Hall, and the oldest subway tunnel.

stops.title: The Brooklyn Heights Promenade
stops.text:
You're on the Brooklyn Heights Promenade, a walkway running about a third of a mile along the edge of the bluff, from Remsen Street to Orange Street. The view across the East River to lower Manhattan, the Brooklyn Bridge, and the Statue of Liberty is one of the most famous in the world.

The Promenade exists because of a highway. In the 1940s, Robert Moses planned the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, and his original route ran right through the middle of Brooklyn Heights, which would have destroyed blocks of historic houses. The residents fought back. The compromise was ingenious. Instead of cutting through the neighborhood, the highway was built along the edge of the bluff, in a stack of three cantilevered levels. Two levels of highway traffic, one in each direction, are stacked on top of each other, and on top of the highway is the Promenade, which opened in 1950. It's a rare example of a highway built to fit a neighborhood, rather than the other way around.

That structure, known as the triple cantilever, is now around seventy-five years old and has been deteriorating, and its future has been the subject of a long, contentious debate over how to repair or replace it.

During the Revolutionary War, this bluff was strategically important. In August 1776, as the British closed in after the Battle of Brooklyn, George Washington held a council of war in a house that stood near here, the Four Chimneys, the home of Philip Livingston, a signer of the Declaration of Independence. It was there that Washington decided to retreat across the East River to Manhattan, the escape you can hear about at Fulton Ferry Landing.

Look across the river at the skyline. From here, you can trace the history of lower Manhattan, from the old church steeples to the skyscrapers of Wall Street, to One World Trade Center. Many New Yorkers watched the Twin Towers burn from this Promenade on September eleventh, 2001. Some residents of the Heights were among those killed, and the Promenade became a gathering place for vigils.

stops.title: Columbia Heights & Willow Street: Writers' Row
stops.text:
Walk north from the Promenade to Columbia Heights and Willow Street, where some of the most famous writers in American history have lived.

At 110 Columbia Heights, which no longer stands, Washington Roebling lived while he supervised the building of the Brooklyn Bridge from his window. In a remarkable coincidence, more than forty years later, the poet Hart Crane rented a room in the same building, and he discovered that it was the very room from which Roebling had watched the bridge. Crane, inspired, wrote his epic poem The Bridge, published in 1930, which uses the Brooklyn Bridge as a symbol of America.

Now walk to 70 Willow Street, a large yellow Greek Revival house built in the 1830s. In the 1950s and 60s, Truman Capote rented a basement apartment here, from a friend who owned the house. It was here that he wrote Breakfast at Tiffany's, published in 1958, and much of In Cold Blood, published in 1966. He described the neighborhood in an essay, A House on the Heights, which captures its atmosphere in the 1950s. The house sold in 2012 for a then-record price for a Brooklyn single-family home.

Other writers who lived in the Heights include Arthur Miller, who lived here in the years around Death of a Salesman; Norman Mailer, who wrote much of The Naked and the Dead while living in the Heights and later lived on Columbia Heights for decades; W. H. Auden and Carson McCullers, who shared a famous house on Middagh Street in the early 1940s with other artists, including the burlesque star Gypsy Rose Lee and the composer Benjamin Britten; and Marianne Moore, who lived in Fort Greene nearby. Thomas Wolfe lived here too.

Look around at the houses on Willow Street and the side streets. Notice the variety of styles, from early nineteenth century Federal houses, with their small dormers and simple doorways, to grand Italianate brownstones from the mid-1800s. At 155 to 159 Willow Street, look for three small Federal-style houses, among the oldest in the neighborhood. And on the corner of Willow and Middagh Streets, look for 24 Middagh Street, a charming wooden Federal house built in 1824, one of the oldest houses in the Heights.

stops.title: Plymouth Church
stops.text:
