Walk to Orange Street, between Hicks and Henry Streets, to Plymouth Church, a plain brick church with a courtyard and a bronze statue.

Plymouth Church was founded in 1847, and its first minister was Henry Ward Beecher, the most famous preacher in America in the mid-nineteenth century. Beecher came from a remarkable family. His father, Lyman Beecher, was a renowned preacher, and his sister was Harriet Beecher Stowe, the author of Uncle Tom's Cabin. Henry Ward Beecher was a passionate, theatrical speaker and an outspoken opponent of slavery. People came by ferry from Manhattan in such large crowds to hear him that the ferries were nicknamed Beecher Boats.

Beecher dramatized the evils of slavery by staging mock slave auctions in the church. Most famously, in 1860, he brought a young enslaved girl, nicknamed Pinky, before the congregation and asked them to contribute money to buy her freedom. The congregation filled the collection plates, and she was freed. The church is believed to have been a stop on the Underground Railroad, sheltering people escaping slavery in its basement, though documentation is limited.

Beecher also helped raise money to send rifles to anti-slavery settlers in Kansas, which were shipped in boxes labeled Bibles, and they were nicknamed Beecher's Bibles.

In February 1860, Abraham Lincoln attended a service here, just before his Cooper Union speech in Manhattan. The pew where he sat is marked.

Beecher's career was later tarnished by scandal. In 1874, his friend Theodore Tilton accused him of having an affair with Tilton's wife, Elizabeth. Tilton sued Beecher, and the trial in 1875 was a national sensation, covered by newspapers across the country. The jury couldn't reach a verdict, and Beecher remained in his pulpit, but his reputation never fully recovered.

In the courtyard, look for the bronze statue of Beecher by Gutzon Borglum, the sculptor who carved Mount Rushmore. It includes figures of two enslaved people at its base. On the wall nearby is a relief of Lincoln. Inside the church, there's a stained glass window commemorating Beecher, and a piece of Plymouth Rock in Massachusetts.

stops.title: Montague Street & Jackie Robinson
stops.text:
Walk south to Montague Street, the main commercial street of Brooklyn Heights, lined with shops, restaurants, and grand bank buildings.

Look for the building at 215 Montague Street. In the 1940s, this was the headquarters of the Brooklyn Dodgers baseball club. On August twenty-eighth, 1945, the Dodgers' president, Branch Rickey, met here with a young Black baseball player named Jackie Robinson. For three hours, Rickey questioned him and warned him about the abuse he would face as the first Black player in the major leagues. Rickey famously told him he was looking for a player with the guts not to fight back. Robinson agreed. He signed with the Dodgers organization, and on April fifteenth, 1947, he took the field at Ebbets Field, breaking baseball's color barrier. A plaque on the building marks the meeting.

Montague Street was also the financial center of Brooklyn. Look for the grand bank buildings near the corner of Clinton Street, like the former Brooklyn Trust Company building at 177 Montague Street, designed by York and Sawyer, the architects of the Federal Reserve Bank in Manhattan, and modeled on a Renaissance palazzo. Today, it's a Chase branch.

At the corner of Pierrepont and Clinton Streets, look for the elaborate red brick and terracotta building with busts on the facade. This is the Center for Brooklyn History, originally built in 1881 for the Long Island Historical Society, designed by George B. Post, the architect of the New York Stock Exchange. The busts on the facade depict famous figures, including Christopher Columbus, Benjamin Franklin, Shakespeare, Beethoven, and Michelangelo, and there's a Viking and a Native American representing Long Island's history. Inside, the library is one of the most beautiful historic reading rooms in New York.

Nearby, on Montague Street, the church of St. Ann and the Holy Trinity has some of the earliest figural stained glass windows made in America, from the 1840s.

The Heights has had many prominent residents in business, too. Charles Pratt, of the Astral Oil Company, whose story you'll hear on the Williamsburg and Greenpoint tour, built mansions nearby, on Clinton Avenue in Clinton Hill. And the neighborhood's banks, insurance companies, and law firms made Montague Street the Wall Street of Brooklyn.

stops.title: Borough Hall
stops.text:
Walk to Joralemon and Court Streets, to the white marble building with a columned portico and a cupola. This is Brooklyn Borough Hall, completed in 1848 as the City Hall of the City of Brooklyn.

Brooklyn was an independent city from 1834 to 1898. It grew rapidly, fed by ferries, the Navy Yard, the port, and industry, and by the 1890s it was the fourth largest city in the United States, with nearly a million people. Brooklyn had its own newspapers, its own museums, its own parks, and a strong civic identity.

In 1894, voters in New York, Brooklyn, and the surrounding towns voted on whether to consolidate into one city. In Brooklyn, the vote was extremely close: consolidation passed by only a few hundred votes, out of more than a hundred and twenty thousand. On January first, 1898, Greater New York was born, with five boroughs: Manhattan, Brooklyn, the Bronx, Queens, and Staten Island. This building became Borough Hall. Many Brooklynites resented the merger, which they called the Great Mistake. Some still do.

The building's design is Greek Revival. The cupola was added later, after a fire, in 1898. Today, it's the office of the Brooklyn Borough President. Notice the statue of Justice that was planned for the top but only installed in the 1980s, over a century after it was first designed.

Look around the plaza. Columbus Park, in front of Borough Hall, has a statue of Henry Ward Beecher, whom you may have heard about at Plymouth Church. To the north, the massive building with columns is the Brooklyn Municipal Building, and the large building to the east is the New York State Supreme Court. Downtown Brooklyn has been transformed since a rezoning in 2004, with dozens of residential towers, including the first skyscraper in Brooklyn to exceed one thousand feet, completed in the early 2020s.

Court Street, running south from here, leads into the neighborhoods of Cobble Hill and Carroll Gardens. A farmers' market is held in front of Borough Hall several days a week.

stops.title: Atlantic Avenue & the Secret Tunnel
stops.text:
End your walk on Atlantic Avenue, near Court Street.

Look along the street for the Middle Eastern shops, restaurants, and grocery stores. Starting in the late nineteenth century, immigrants from the Ottoman province of Syria, including what is now Lebanon, settled in lower Manhattan, in a neighborhood called Little Syria, on Washington Street. Most were Christians, and many were merchants, selling textiles and lace. When the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel construction and other projects destroyed much of Little Syria in the 1940s, many of these businesses moved here, to Atlantic Avenue. The most famous is Sahadi's, a grocery store that opened in Manhattan in 1895 and moved here in 1948. It's still run by the Sahadi family, selling dried fruits, nuts, spices, olives, and other foods.

Now here's a secret: beneath your feet is the oldest subway tunnel in the world. In 1844, the Long Island Rail Road built a tunnel under Atlantic Avenue, about half a mile long, from near the waterfront to about Boerum Place. It was the first railroad tunnel under a city street in the world. It was used for less than twenty years, closed in 1861, and sealed off. Over time, it was forgotten. Legends grew up around it: that it held the body of a murdered man, or an old steam locomotive, or the lost pages of John Wilkes Booth's diary. In 1980, a young engineering student named Bob Diamond, who had heard the stories, tracked down the tunnel, found a manhole under the street, crawled through it, and broke through a wall to discover it. He ran tours of the tunnel for years, until the city closed it in 2010. The tunnel is still there, sealed under the pavement.

A few blocks east, at Boerum Place and Schermerhorn Street, is the New York Transit Museum, housed in a decommissioned subway station from 1936. On its platforms, you can walk through a collection of historic subway cars, from early wooden cars to sleek cars from the 1960s. It's a fun place to end this walk, and a reminder of how transportation, from ferries to bridges to railroads and subways, shaped every part of Brooklyn.

overview:
Brooklyn Heights is often called America's first suburb. In the early nineteenth century, it was a bluff of farmland and estates above the East River, directly across from lower Manhattan. When steam ferry service began at Fulton Ferry in 1814, a merchant could live up here, in a quiet, leafy neighborhood with fresh air and a stunning view, and commute to his counting house on Wall Street in minutes. Real estate promoters advertised the neighborhood exactly that way, and the idea of commuting from a residential district to a business district was born.

The key figure was Hezekiah Pierrepont, a merchant who made his fortune in shipping and, notably, in gin. He owned the Anchor Gin distillery on the Brooklyn waterfront. Pierrepont bought up much of the land on the Heights, invested in the steam ferry, and divided his property into lots for townhouses. Other landowners followed. Several of the streets are named after the families who owned the land: Pierrepont, Remsen, Joralemon, Hicks, Middagh. Others are named for fruits: Orange, Pineapple, and Cranberry Streets. According to a long-told local story, an early resident, Lady Middagh, was annoyed by her neighbors naming streets after themselves, tore down their street signs, and replaced them with the names of fruits. The city eventually accepted her names.

Brooklyn Heights became one of the most beautiful residential neighborhoods in the country, with streets of Federal, Greek Revival, Gothic Revival, Italianate, and Romanesque townhouses. It was the home of prosperous merchants, ministers, and, later, writers and artists. In the twentieth century, as the wealthy moved elsewhere, many houses were split into rooming houses and apartments, and the neighborhood attracted writers drawn by cheap rents, beautiful streets, and views of Manhattan.

In the 1950s, the neighborhood fought to protect itself from Robert Moses's highway plans and from urban renewal, and in 1965, it became the first neighborhood protected as a historic district under New York City's new landmarks law. The south end of this walk takes you down to Atlantic Avenue, with its Middle Eastern shops and a remarkable secret beneath the street, and to Borough Hall, the old City Hall of the independent City of Brooklyn.

title: Navy Yard, Fort Greene & Downtown Brooklyn
blurb: Where the Arizona and Missouri were built, the Prison Ship Martyrs, brownstone Fort Greene, BAM, the old bank tower, and why the Dodgers left.

stops.title: The Brooklyn Navy Yard
stops.text:
You're at the Brooklyn Navy Yard, at Flushing Avenue and Carlton Avenue, outside Building 92, a brick building that serves as the yard's visitor center and museum.

The site sits on Wallabout Bay, a curve of the East River. During the Revolutionary War, the British anchored prison ships here, decaying old warships where they held American prisoners of war. Conditions were horrific: prisoners were crammed below decks, starved, and ravaged by disease. More than eleven thousand prisoners are believed to have died on these ships, more than died in all the battles of the Revolution combined. Their bodies were often buried in shallow graves along the shore, and for years afterward, bones washed up on the beach. You'll see their memorial in Fort Greene Park.

The federal government bought the site in 1801 and established the New York Navy Yard, commonly known as the Brooklyn Navy Yard. Over the following century and a half, it built and repaired many of the Navy's most important ships. The USS Maine, whose explosion in Havana harbor in 1898 helped spark the Spanish-American War, was built here. The battleship USS Arizona, sunk at Pearl Harbor on December seventh, 1941, was built here and launched in 1915. And the battleship USS Missouri, on whose deck Japan signed its surrender ending World War Two, in September 1945, was built here and launched in 1944.

During World War Two, the yard was a city of its own, with dry docks, foundries, machine shops, and cranes, and around seventy thousand workers, including thousands of women and African Americans who found industrial jobs here for the first time.

The Navy closed the yard in 1966, a devastating blow to Brooklyn. The city bought it and turned it into an industrial park. Today, it's home to hundreds of businesses employing thousands of people: manufacturers, artists, designers, and film studios, including Steiner Studios, one of the largest film and television production facilities on the East Coast. There's a rooftop farm, a distillery, and companies making everything from furniture to food. If you have time, Building 92's exhibits tell the yard's story, and tours of the yard are offered.

stops.title: Fort Greene Park & the Prison Ship Martyrs Monument
stops.text:
Walk south to Fort Greene Park, and climb to the top of the hill, where a tall Doric column rises from a broad granite stairway.

This hill was the site of Fort Putnam, built in 1776 under General Nathanael Greene, to defend Brooklyn against the British. It was rebuilt during the War of 1812 and renamed Fort Greene in his honor.

The park was among the first public parks in Brooklyn. The poet Walt Whitman, as editor of the Brooklyn Daily Eagle in the 1840s, campaigned for its creation, arguing that the working people of the crowded city needed open space. It was laid out in 1847, and then redesigned in 1867 by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, the designers of Central Park and Prospect Park.

The monument at the top is the Prison Ship Martyrs Monument, dedicated in 1908 to the more than eleven thousand American prisoners who died on British prison ships in Wallabout Bay during the Revolution, which you heard about at the Navy Yard. For decades, their remains, collected from the shore, were kept in various vaults. In 1873, they were placed in a crypt here, beneath the stairway. Then, the architects McKim, Mead and White designed this monument: a column about one hundred forty-nine feet tall, at the time among the tallest Doric columns in the world, topped by a bronze urn. President-elect William Howard Taft dedicated it in November 1908. The crypt is beneath the stairway, though it's not open to the public.

The prisoners on the ships came from all thirteen colonies and from many countries, including sailors captured on American privateers, and some were of African descent. Each year, a ceremony is held here to remember them.

From the top of the hill, look around at the view, and at the neighborhood of brownstones surrounding the park. On a clear day you can see the Manhattan skyline to the northwest.

stops.title: Fort Greene Brownstones
stops.text:
Walk to South Portland Avenue and South Oxford Street, between DeKalb and Lafayette Avenues, two of the most beautiful residential blocks in Brooklyn.

These rows of brownstones and Italianate townhouses were built mostly in the 1850s to 1870s, for prosperous merchants and professionals. Brownstone is a type of sandstone, quarried mostly in Connecticut and New Jersey, that was hugely popular in nineteenth-century New York. It was relatively cheap, easy to carve, and gave a sense of solid respectability. Most brownstone houses are actually brick buildings with a brownstone veneer on the front.

Fort Greene went through many changes. In the early twentieth century, as wealthier residents moved to newer neighborhoods, many houses were divided into rooming houses. After World War Two, Black families, many working at the Navy Yard, moved into the neighborhood. Fort Greene developed a strong Black middle-class community. The novelist Richard Wright wrote much of his landmark 1940 novel, Native Son, while living on Carlton Avenue, nearby.

In the 1980s and 90s, Fort Greene became the center of what was sometimes called a Black Bohemia or a Black Renaissance in Brooklyn. The filmmaker Spike Lee, who grew up in Fort Greene, set up his production company, 40 Acres and a Mule Filmworks, in a converted firehouse on DeKalb Avenue. His films, like She's Gotta Have It and Do the Right Thing, were rooted in Brooklyn. Writers, jazz musicians like Branford Marsalis, artists, and actors lived in the neighborhood.

Since the 2000s, Fort Greene has gentrified, and brownstones now sell for millions of dollars. The Black population has declined significantly, a change that's been the subject of much discussion, including Spike Lee's own outspoken criticism.

Look for the Lafayette Avenue Presbyterian Church, at Lafayette Avenue and South Oxford Street. It was founded in 1857 by abolitionists and was reportedly a stop on the Underground Railroad. Inside, there's a collection of Tiffany stained glass windows.

stops.title: BAM: The Brooklyn Academy of Music
stops.text:
Walk west on Lafayette Avenue to the Brooklyn Academy of Music, known as BAM, in the large building with a terracotta and brick facade on the corner of Ashland Place.

BAM was founded in 1861, making it one of the oldest performing arts centers in the United States. Its first building was in Brooklyn Heights, on Montague Street, but it burned down in 1903. The current building, the Peter Jay Sharp Building, opened in 1908. In its early years, BAM hosted the biggest names in the performing arts: the opera singer Enrico Caruso, the actress Sarah Bernhardt, the dancer Isadora Duncan, and the Metropolitan Opera, which performed here regularly.

Like much of Brooklyn, BAM declined in the mid-twentieth century. Its turnaround came in 1967, when Harvey Lichtenstein became its director. Lichtenstein transformed BAM into one of the world's leading centers for avant-garde and experimental performance. He brought companies and artists that were too daring for Manhattan's establishment venues. In 1983, he launched the Next Wave Festival, which showcased artists like the composer Philip Glass, the director Robert Wilson, the choreographers Merce Cunningham and Pina Bausch, and the performance artist Laurie Anderson. BAM became a destination, drawing audiences from Manhattan to Brooklyn at a time when few people crossed the river for culture.

BAM's growth has been an anchor for the Brooklyn Cultural District, which now includes theaters, galleries, and other institutions, and BAM itself has expanded with additional theaters and cinemas in the neighborhood.

Look around at the area. Mark Morris, the choreographer, built his dance center across the street. And the large modern buildings nearby are part of the district's growth, many with arts spaces on their lower floors.

stops.title: The Williamsburgh Savings Bank Tower
stops.text:
Look up at the tall tower with a gold-domed top and four large clock faces, at One Hanson Place, at the corner of Ashland Place and Flatbush Avenue. This is the Williamsburgh Savings Bank Tower, completed in 1929.

For eighty years, it was the tallest building in Brooklyn, at about five hundred twelve feet. It was built for the Williamsburgh Savings Bank, one of the largest savings banks in Brooklyn, a type of bank that held the deposits of working people and made mortgage loans. The tower was designed to be visible from all over Brooklyn, a symbol of the bank's strength and stability, completed just before the stock market crash.

Its four clock faces, each about twenty-seven feet across, were among the largest in the world when it was built. They became a landmark for generations of Brooklynites.

Step inside, if possible, to see the former banking hall, now an event space. It's one of the most spectacular interiors in Brooklyn, with soaring arches, mosaics, and marble. Its decoration is full of symbols of thrift, industry, and security, the virtues a savings bank wanted its depositors to associate with it.

For many decades, the upper floors of the tower were filled with dentists' offices. It's a piece of Brooklyn trivia: if you went to the dentist in Brooklyn in the mid-twentieth century, there's a good chance it was here. In the 2000s, the tower was converted to luxury condominiums. The banking hall became an event venue.

Next to the tower is the Atlantic Terminal, a hub for the Long Island Rail Road and nine subway lines. It's one of the busiest transit hubs in New York.

stops.title: Barclays Center & the Dodgers' Lost Stadium
stops.text:
Walk south across Flatbush Avenue to the corner of Atlantic and Flatbush Avenues, to the Barclays Center, the arena with the rusted steel skin and a giant oculus over its entrance plaza.

This intersection holds one of the great what-ifs of New York history. In the 1950s, the Brooklyn Dodgers were one of the most beloved teams in baseball. They played at Ebbets Field, in the Flatbush neighborhood, but it was small, aging, and lacked parking. The team's owner, Walter O'Malley, wanted to build a new, modern stadium, possibly a domed one, right here, at Atlantic and Flatbush, above the Long Island Rail Road terminal, where subway lines and commuter trains converged.

O'Malley needed the city's help to acquire the land. But Robert Moses, who controlled much of the city's development, refused to support a stadium here. He wanted the team to move to a site in Flushing Meadows, in Queens. O'Malley refused to move the team to Queens. Meanwhile, Los Angeles offered O'Malley a large tract of land for a new stadium. After the 1957 season, the Dodgers left Brooklyn for Los Angeles. Brooklynites felt betrayed. For many, O'Malley was the villain, though historians have argued that Moses deserves a large share of the blame. Ebbets Field was demolished in 1960 and replaced with apartment buildings. A few years later, the Mets began playing in Queens, in Shea Stadium, on the very site Moses had offered the Dodgers.

More than half a century later, major league sports finally came back to this corner. In 2012, the Barclays Center opened here, as part of a large and controversial development called Atlantic Yards, now called Pacific Park. It is home to the Brooklyn Nets basketball team, who moved from New Jersey, the first major professional sports team in Brooklyn since the Dodgers. The development involved the use of eminent domain to acquire property, and it led to years of protests and legal battles by neighborhood residents.

The arena's design, with its weathered steel exterior, was meant to evoke the borough's industrial heritage.

stops.title: Fulton Mall & Junior's
stops.text:
End your walk on Fulton Street, between Flatbush Avenue and Adams Street, in the pedestrian-friendly shopping area known as the Fulton Mall.

For most of the twentieth century, Fulton Street was Brooklyn's downtown, its equivalent of Herald Square, lined with department stores, movie palaces, and banks. The biggest department store was Abraham and Straus, known as A and S. It was founded in 1865 by Abraham Abraham, a Jewish merchant. In the 1890s, he brought in partners from the Straus family, the same family that ran Macy's. A and S became one of the largest department stores in the country, and its building at Fulton and Hoyt Streets became a landmark. In 1995, A and S was merged into Macy's, and the building became a Macy's store.

Fulton Street declined in the 1970s and 80s, as shoppers moved to the suburbs. In 1977, it was converted into a pedestrian and bus mall, and it became a busy shopping district for Black and Caribbean Brooklynites, known for its sneaker stores, hip-hop fashion, and music. It was celebrated in early hip-hop culture. Since the 2000s, it has gentrified, with national chains, new office buildings, and high-rise apartments.

Look for the Dime Savings Bank of Brooklyn building, on DeKalb Avenue, near Fulton Street, with its massive dome and columns, modeled on the Pantheon in Rome, completed in 1908. Look for the dimes incorporated into its decoration. Its banking hall has been preserved as part of a new residential tower, which became one of the tallest buildings in Brooklyn.

Finally, at the corner of Flatbush and DeKalb Avenues, look for Junior's, a restaurant that has been serving its famous cheesecake since 1950. It was founded by Harry Rosen, who named it after his two sons. Its cheesecake, rich and creamy, made with cream cheese, became famous across the country. Junior's survived a fire in 1981, rebuilt, and remains a Brooklyn icon.

A slice of cheesecake at Junior's is a fitting way to end a walk through Brooklyn's downtown.

overview:
This walk covers the neighborhoods just east of Downtown Brooklyn: the Brooklyn Navy Yard on the waterfront, the brownstone neighborhood of Fort Greene, and the commercial heart of the borough around Fulton Street and Atlantic Avenue.

For more than a century and a half, the Brooklyn Navy Yard was one of the most important shipyards in the United States. Ships built here fought in every American war from the War of 1812 to Vietnam. At its peak in World War Two, the yard employed around seventy thousand people working around the clock, making it one of the largest industrial employers in the country. The yard's workers, and the businesses that served them, filled the surrounding neighborhoods.

Fort Greene takes its name from a Revolutionary War fort, built in 1776 under the direction of General Nathanael Greene, as part of the defenses of Brooklyn. In the nineteenth century, the area developed into a neighborhood of handsome brownstones and townhouses for the merchants and professionals of the independent City of Brooklyn. In the twentieth century, it became one of the centers of Black middle-class life in Brooklyn, and in the 1980s and 90s, it was home to a creative renaissance of Black artists, filmmakers, musicians, and writers, including Spike Lee, whose film company is based here.

Downtown Brooklyn, around Fulton Street, Flatbush Avenue, and Atlantic Avenue, was the shopping and business center of Brooklyn, with department stores, banks, and theaters. Like downtowns across America, it declined in the mid-twentieth century. In recent decades, it has been transformed by a rezoning, new towers, and the Barclays Center arena.

There's also a story here about the most painful loss in Brooklyn's history: not a battle or a fire, but a baseball team. As you walk, you'll find out why the Brooklyn Dodgers left for Los Angeles, and what that has to do with the arena at the corner of Atlantic and Flatbush.

title: Williamsburg & Greenpoint
blurb: The Sugar Trust's refinery, Brewers' Row, Peter Luger, the hipster boom, Eberhard Faber pencils, Pratt's Astral Oil, and the USS Monitor.

stops.title: Domino Sugar & the Sugar Trust
stops.text:
You're at Domino Park, on the waterfront at Kent Avenue and South 3rd Street. Look at the massive brick building along the water, with the giant illuminated sign that reads Domino Sugar. This is the old Domino Sugar refinery.

The story starts with the Havemeyer family, German immigrants who began refining sugar in Manhattan in the early nineteenth century. In 1856, they built a refinery here in Williamsburg, on the waterfront, where ships could unload raw sugar from the Caribbean. After a fire, the main building was rebuilt in 1882, and it was then one of the largest sugar refineries in the world. By the late nineteenth century, the Williamsburg refineries were producing more than half of the sugar consumed in the United States.

Henry Osborne Havemeyer was the driving force behind one of the most powerful monopolies of the Gilded Age. In 1887, he organized the Sugar Refineries Company, combining most of the major refiners into a trust, which was later reorganized as the American Sugar Refining Company. By the early 1890s, it controlled the vast majority of the country's sugar refining. When the federal government sued, in a case known as United States versus E. C. Knight Company, the Supreme Court ruled in 1895 that the Sherman Antitrust Act didn't apply, because refining was manufacturing, not interstate commerce. The decision greatly weakened antitrust enforcement for years, until later cases, including the breakup of Standard Oil, restored it. In 1900, the company introduced the Domino brand, and it eventually renamed itself Domino Sugar.

The work inside was grueling and dangerous: workers labored in intense heat, and many were immigrants, first German and Irish, later Polish, Puerto Rican, and others. The refinery closed in 2004.

In 2014, before redevelopment began, the artist Kara Walker filled the building's vast, sticky interior with a giant sculpture made of sugar: a sphinx-like woman with the features of a stereotypical mammy figure, called A Subtlety, or the Marvelous Sugar Baby. It confronted the history of slavery in the Caribbean sugar plantations that produced the raw sugar refined here. More than a hundred thousand people came to see it.

The site has since been redeveloped by Two Trees Management, the same company that redeveloped DUMBO. The waterfront became Domino Park, which opened in 2018, designed by James Corner Field Operations, the firm behind the High Line. Look for the old cranes, gantries, and syrup tanks that were incorporated into the park's design, and for the walkway built from salvaged industrial pieces.

stops.title: Peter Luger & South Williamsburg
stops.text:
Walk to Broadway and Driggs Avenue, near the foot of the Williamsburg Bridge. Look for a plain brick building with a sign reading Peter Luger Steak House.

Peter Luger has been serving steaks here since 1887. It was founded as Carl Luger's Café, Billiards and Bowling Alley, in what was then a German neighborhood, near the ferry to Manhattan. Peter Luger was the owner; his nephew Carl was the chef. After Peter Luger's death, the restaurant declined. In 1950, it was bought at auction by Sol Forman, a businessman whose metalware factory was across the street, and who had eaten lunch there for years. His wife, Marsha, learned to select beef, and the family turned it into the most famous steakhouse in New York. Its porterhouse steak, dry-aged on the premises and served sizzling, is legendary. For many years it accepted only cash or its own house card.

Look up at the Williamsburg Bridge. As you may have heard on the Lower East Side tour, when it opened in 1903 it was the longest suspension bridge in the world. It transformed Williamsburg from a German neighborhood into a crowded, largely Jewish and Eastern European neighborhood almost overnight.

South of Broadway is South Williamsburg, home of a large Hasidic Jewish community, centered on the Satmar sect. The Satmar Hasidim came from the town of Satu Mare, in present-day Romania. Their leader, Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, survived the Holocaust and arrived in New York in 1946. He built a community here that has grown into tens of thousands of people. The community is very traditional, speaking Yiddish as its primary language, with distinctive dress: men in black coats and hats, with sidelocks, and women in modest dresses with head coverings. Walk along Lee Avenue, the main commercial street, and you'll see kosher shops, Yiddish signs, and bustling families.

The area to the east, along Broadway and the South Side, known as Los Sures, has been the heart of the Puerto Rican and Dominican community in Williamsburg since the 1950s. Community organizations here fought for affordable housing in the 1970s and 80s, when many buildings were abandoned.

stops.title: Brewers' Row & the Brooklyn Brewery
stops.text:
Walk north to North 11th Street, near Wythe Avenue, to the Brooklyn Brewery.

In the late nineteenth century, Brooklyn was one of the largest beer-producing places in America. German immigrants brought lager brewing with them, and by the 1890s, Brooklyn had several dozen breweries, concentrated in Williamsburg and Bushwick, in an area nicknamed Brewers' Row. Brands like Schaefer, Rheingold, Piels, and Trommer's were brewed here. The Schaefer brewery, on the Williamsburg waterfront along Kent Avenue, was one of the largest in the country. Its slogan, Schaefer is the one beer to have when you're having more than one, was famous in the mid-twentieth century.

Prohibition, from 1920 to 1933, closed many breweries. Those that survived faced competition after World War Two from national brewers like Anheuser-Busch, which could produce beer more cheaply in giant, modern breweries and advertise on national television. Brooklyn's breweries closed one after another. Schaefer and Rheingold, the last big ones, closed in 1976. For about a decade, there was no commercial brewing in Brooklyn.

Then, in 1988, two men founded the Brooklyn Brewery: Steve Hindy, a former Associated Press foreign correspondent who had learned home brewing from diplomats in the Middle East, and Tom Potter, a banker. They hired the brewmaster Bill Moeller, whose family had brewed beer in Germany, and they hired the famous graphic designer Milton Glaser, who created the I heart NY logo, to design their logo. The first beers were contract brewed upstate. In 1996, they opened their own brewery here, in a former ironworks. In 1994, they hired Garrett Oliver as brewmaster, and he became one of the most influential figures in American craft brewing.

The Brooklyn Brewery was one of the pioneers of the craft beer movement, and it helped revive Williamsburg's industrial waterfront. It has offered tours and tastings to visitors for years, and its connection to Williamsburg defines the brand.

Look around at the old brick factory and warehouse buildings nearby. Many of them have been converted to offices, shops, music venues, and condominiums.

stops.title: Bedford Avenue & Hipster Williamsburg
stops.text:
Walk to Bedford Avenue and North 7th Street, at the Bedford Avenue station on the L train, the first stop in Brooklyn coming from Manhattan.

In the 1970s and 80s, this area was a struggling industrial neighborhood, with Polish, Italian, and Puerto Rican working-class families and many empty factories. In the late 1980s and 1990s, artists began moving into the lofts, priced out of the East Village and SoHo. The L train put them just one stop from Manhattan. By the late 1990s, Williamsburg had a thriving underground art and music scene, with galleries, performance spaces, and illegal warehouse parties.

In the 2000s, Williamsburg became internationally famous. Bands like Yeah Yeah Yeahs, TV on the Radio, and Vampire Weekend were associated with the Brooklyn indie rock scene. Coffee shops, vintage clothing stores, and restaurants serving artisanal food opened along Bedford Avenue. The word hipster became almost synonymous with Williamsburg. Magazines and newspapers around the world wrote about it, and the neighborhood's aesthetic, beards, tattoos, flannel, craft beer, and pickles, was exported to cities everywhere.

Then the money came. In 2005, the city rezoned the Williamsburg and Greenpoint waterfront, allowing towers of up to forty stories on land that had been zoned for manufacturing. Glass towers rose along the river. Rents soared. Many of the artists who had made the neighborhood famous were priced out, moving farther east to Bushwick and beyond. Big brands arrived: Apple, Whole Foods, and luxury hotels opened stores and locations near Bedford Avenue.

Walk toward the river, to Marsha P. Johnson State Park, formerly East River State Park, named in 2020 for the transgender activist who was a central figure in the gay liberation movement. On weekends in warm months, it's the site of Smorgasburg, a giant outdoor food market, launched in 2011, with dozens of vendors.

From the waterfront, look across the river at the Manhattan skyline, from the Williamsburg Bridge to the Empire State Building. Every new tower on this side of the river was built to capture this view.

stops.title: McCarren Park & the Pool
stops.text:
Walk east to McCarren Park, at the border between Williamsburg and Greenpoint, around Bedford Avenue and Lorimer Street.

On the west side of the park, look for the large building with a grand arched entrance. This is McCarren Park Pool, one of eleven huge public swimming pools that opened in New York City in the summer of 1936, built by Robert Moses with funding from the federal Works Progress Administration during the Great Depression. The eleven pools were designed to bring recreation and relief to working-class neighborhoods during the heat of summer. McCarren Pool could hold nearly sixty-eight hundred swimmers at a time.

The pool was a beloved neighborhood institution for decades, but by the 1980s, it had deteriorated, and the city closed it in 1984. It sat empty for more than twenty years, a ruin surrounded by a fence. In the mid-2000s, while plans for its restoration were made, the empty pool became a concert venue, hosting free summer concerts by indie rock bands, as well as dodgeball leagues and other events, part of Williamsburg's emergence as a cultural destination. After a major restoration, the pool reopened for swimming in 2012. In winter, part of it becomes an ice skating rink.

Just east of the park, at North 12th Street and Driggs Avenue, look for the Russian Orthodox Cathedral of the Transfiguration of Our Lord, with its five green onion domes. It was built in the 1920s, and it's a reminder of the many Eastern European communities in North Brooklyn.

The park is named for Patrick McCarren, a state senator and Democratic political boss of Brooklyn in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Today, it's the backyard of the neighborhood, filled with soccer games, softball, runners, and people lounging on the grass.

stops.title: Greenpoint & the Eberhard Faber Pencil Factory
stops.text:
Walk north into Greenpoint, to the corner of Kent Street and Franklin Street, near the Greenpoint waterfront. Look at the buildings at Greenpoint Avenue and West Street, and on Kent Street. On the facade of one of them, look for decorative ornaments shaped like giant yellow pencils, along with stars.

These were the buildings of the Eberhard Faber Pencil Company. Eberhard Faber came from a German family that had been making pencils in Bavaria since the eighteenth century, and he came to New York in 1848 to represent the family business. In 1861, he opened a pencil factory in Manhattan. After it burned down in 1872, he moved the factory here to Greenpoint, and over the following decades the company expanded into a complex of buildings. Eberhard Faber became one of the largest pencil manufacturers in the country. Its Mongol pencil was one of the most popular pencils in America. The company also made erasers, rubber bands, and pens. The factory moved to Pennsylvania in 1956, and the buildings were converted to other uses. They're now protected as a historic district.

The pencil company was one of many factories in Greenpoint. Along with the five black arts, Greenpoint had shipbuilding, rope making, and sugar refining. The Union Porcelain Works, in Greenpoint, produced fine porcelain tableware in the nineteenth century, some of which is now in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum and the Brooklyn Museum.

Walk along Manhattan Avenue, Greenpoint's main shopping street, a few blocks to the east. For more than a century, Greenpoint has been the heart of the Polish community in New York, with Polish bakeries, butcher shops selling kielbasa, delis, churches, and restaurants. Polish immigrants came in waves, in the late nineteenth century, after World War Two, and again in the 1980s, when many fled the communist government's crackdown on the Solidarity movement. The Polish population has declined as younger generations have moved and new residents have arrived, but you'll still hear Polish spoken on the street.

Look also at the beautiful churches of Greenpoint, including St. Anthony of Padua, on Manhattan Avenue, with its tall spire, and St. Stanislaus Kostka, the Polish Catholic parish, which Pope John Paul the Second visited as a cardinal in 1969 and again in 1976.

stops.title: Charles Pratt's Astral Oil & the Monitor
stops.text:
Walk north along Franklin Street, to Franklin and India Streets.

In the nineteenth century, Greenpoint and the shore of Newtown Creek, just to the north, became one of the largest oil-refining centers in America. In 1867, Charles Pratt, a businessman who had made money in paint and oil, opened the Astral Oil Works on the creek. He produced kerosene, a fuel refined from petroleum, used for lighting lamps. Pratt's brand, Astral Oil, was known for its quality and safety, at a time when cheap kerosene often exploded. Its advertising slogan claimed that the holy lamps of Tibet were primed with Astral Oil.

In 1874, Pratt sold his company to John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil, becoming one of its leading partners and making a vast fortune. He used part of it to found the Pratt Institute, an art and engineering school in Clinton Hill, which opened in 1887 to train working people in practical skills. He also built the Astral Apartments, at 184 Franklin Street, completed in 1886, as model housing for his workers, with better light, air, and sanitation than typical tenements of the time. Look for it, a large, handsome brick building in the Queen Anne style.

The oil industry left a toxic legacy. In 1978, a Coast Guard helicopter patrol spotted an oil slick on Newtown Creek. Investigators discovered that over many decades, oil from refineries and storage facilities had leaked into the ground under Greenpoint. Estimates of the total ranged from seventeen to thirty million gallons, making it one of the largest oil spills in American history, larger than the Exxon Valdez spill. Cleanup has continued for decades, and Newtown Creek is now a federal Superfund site.

Now walk to the waterfront at the end of India Street, near the ferry pier. Just north of here, at the Continental Iron Works on the Greenpoint shore, the USS Monitor was built. The Monitor was a revolutionary ironclad warship, designed by the Swedish-born engineer John Ericsson, with a low, armored hull and a rotating gun turret, something no ship had used in battle before. It was built in about one hundred days and launched on January thirtieth, 1862. On March ninth, 1862, at the Battle of Hampton Roads, in Virginia, the Monitor fought the Confederate ironclad CSS Virginia, formerly the Merrimack, to a standoff. It was the first battle between ironclad warships, and it signaled the end of the age of wooden warships. In McGolrick Park, a few blocks east, look for a monument to the Monitor and its crew.

stops.title: Newtown Creek & the Digester Eggs
stops.text:
End your walk at the Newtown Creek Nature Walk, at the end of Paidge Avenue, on the shore of Newtown Creek, the waterway that separates Brooklyn from Queens.

Look at the giant, shining, egg-shaped structures rising beside the creek. These are the digester eggs of the Newtown Creek Wastewater Treatment Plant, the largest of the city's wastewater treatment plants. There are eight of them, each about one hundred forty feet tall, clad in stainless steel. Inside, bacteria break down sludge from the city's sewage, producing methane gas. The egg shape helps the sludge mix and the process run efficiently. Completed in the 2010s, they've become an unlikely architectural landmark, and they glow blue at night. The plant offers tours a few times a year, including at sunrise or sunset, and the view from the top of the eggs is said to be remarkable.

The Nature Walk was designed by the artist George Trakas, and opened in 2007, as part of the plant's commitment to the community. It's a winding path along the water, with granite steps, plantings, and references to the creek's history. It includes a timeline of the area carved into stone, and features that recall the creek's natural past, before industry transformed it.

Newtown Creek was once a tidal estuary, with marshes and wildlife. The Lenape fished here, and Dutch and English settlers farmed nearby. In the nineteenth century, it became one of the busiest industrial waterways in the country, lined with refineries, chemical plants, fertilizer works, and factories. At one time, the creek carried more cargo than the Mississippi River, by some accounts. It also became one of the most polluted waterways in the nation, absorbing oil, chemicals, and raw sewage.

Today, community groups and the federal government are working on a long, slow cleanup. Kayakers and canoeists now paddle the creek, and scientists monitor its recovery.

It's a fitting place to end a tour of North Brooklyn: a place where industry made fortunes, left scars, and is now being slowly transformed into something new.

overview:
Williamsburg and Greenpoint, along the East River in North Brooklyn, were once among the most intensely industrial places in America. In the second half of the nineteenth century, this waterfront was lined with sugar refineries, oil refineries, breweries, shipyards, ironworks, glass and porcelain factories, and pencil makers. Greenpoint was famous for what were called the five black arts: printing, pottery, gas, glass, and iron, all industries that involved fire and smoke.

Some of the most powerful companies in American history had major operations here. The sugar refinery of the Havemeyer family became the heart of the Sugar Trust, which controlled almost all of the sugar refining in the country. Charles Pratt's Astral Oil Works became part of John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil. Brewers made Williamsburg and neighboring Bushwick one of the beer capitals of America. And in Greenpoint, the shipyards built the USS Monitor, the ironclad warship that changed naval warfare.

Williamsburg was a separate city until 1855, when it merged with Brooklyn. The opening of the Williamsburg Bridge in 1903 brought a flood of new residents from the crowded Lower East Side, especially Jewish families. After World War Two, Hasidic Jews, many of them Holocaust survivors from Hungary and Romania, settled in South Williamsburg, which remains one of the largest Hasidic communities in the world. Puerto Rican and Dominican families settled in the area known as Los Sures, on the South Side. Greenpoint became the heart of the Polish community in New York, often called Little Poland.

As factories closed in the second half of the twentieth century, the waterfront emptied. In the 1990s, artists, musicians, and young people priced out of Manhattan discovered the cheap lofts of Williamsburg, a stop or two from Manhattan on the L train. By the 2000s, Williamsburg had become a global symbol of hipster culture, of indie rock, artisanal food, and fixed-gear bicycles. In 2005, the city rezoned the waterfront, and luxury towers rose where factories had stood. Today, the neighborhood is one of the most expensive in Brooklyn, and the transformation has been a subject of fierce debate.

This tour runs south to north, from the Domino Sugar refinery to Newtown Creek, the border between Brooklyn and Queens.

title: Prospect Park, Park Slope & Gowanus
blurb: Olmsted and Vaux's favorite park, Brooklyn's triumphal arch, the Long Meadow, the Battle of Brooklyn, brownstone Park Slope, and the Gowanus Canal.

stops.title: Grand Army Plaza & the Arch
stops.text:
You're at Grand Army Plaza, the great oval plaza at the northern entrance to Prospect Park, where Flatbush Avenue, Eastern Parkway, and Prospect Park West meet.

Olmsted and Vaux designed this plaza as a grand entrance, a kind of buffer between the city and the park, with an oval shape to direct traffic around it. At its center rises the Soldiers' and Sailors' Memorial Arch, completed in 1892, honoring the Union forces in the Civil War. It was designed by John Duncan, the architect of Grant's Tomb, and modeled on Roman triumphal arches. The sculptures were added later. On top is a dramatic bronze quadriga, a chariot pulled by four horses, with a figure of Columbia, representing the United States, by the sculptor Frederick MacMonnies. On the sides are groups representing the Army and the Navy. Inside the arch, look for bronze reliefs of Abraham Lincoln and Ulysses S. Grant on horseback, by Thomas Eakins and William O'Donovan. The arch is sometimes open for climbing, offering a great view.

North of the arch is the Bailey Fountain, with figures representing Wisdom and Felicity and Neptune with tritons. And on the southwest side of the plaza, there's a bust of President John F. Kennedy, the only official memorial to him in New York City.

On the east side of the plaza, look for the Central Library of the Brooklyn Public Library, completed in 1941. Its striking Art Deco facade is shaped to follow the curve of the plaza, like the spine of an open book. Its entrance is framed by tall bronze screens with gilded figures from American literature, including Moby Dick, Tom Sawyer, Rip Van Winkle, and characters from Edgar Allan Poe. Brooklyn's library system is independent from the New York Public Library, a legacy of Brooklyn's days as a separate city.

On Saturdays, the plaza hosts one of the city's largest greenmarkets.

Eastern Parkway, running east from here, was designed by Olmsted and Vaux as the first parkway in the world, a broad, tree-lined boulevard for carriages, with separate lanes for local traffic and walkways. It was meant to connect Prospect Park with the rest of the city and served as the model for parkways everywhere.

stops.title: The Brooklyn Museum & Botanic Garden
stops.text:
Walk east along Eastern Parkway to the Brooklyn Museum, the grand Beaux-Arts building with a columned portico.

The Brooklyn Museum was designed by McKim, Mead and White, and the first section opened in 1897. It was planned to be the largest art museum in the world, larger even than the Louvre. Brooklyn was then an independent city, and its leaders wanted it to have cultural institutions to rival anything in Manhattan. But in 1898, Brooklyn merged into New York, and the political will and funding for the giant museum faded. Only about one-sixth of the planned building was ever completed. The museum is still one of the largest in the United States.

Look up at the attic of the building, the top of the facade. You'll see a row of statues representing great figures and cultures of the ancient world, created by many sculptors, including Daniel Chester French. Notice that the grand front staircase is missing: it was removed in the 1930s, a decision later regretted. A modern glass entrance pavilion was added in 2004.

Inside, the museum is known for its Egyptian collection, one of the finest in the world, and for its American art, its African art, and its feminist art center, which houses Judy Chicago's famous installation The Dinner Party, a triangular banquet table with place settings for thirty-nine women from history.

Next to the museum is the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, founded in 1910 on the site of a former ash dump. It covers fifty-two acres, with themed gardens, conservatories, and collections. Its Japanese Hill-and-Pond Garden, designed by the Japanese landscape architect Takeo Shiota and completed in 1915, is among the oldest Japanese-inspired gardens in an American public garden. In spring, the garden's cherry trees burst into bloom along the Cherry Esplanade, and the garden holds a festival to celebrate them.

Across the street, the Brooklyn Public Library's Central Library and the museum and garden together form a cultural complex that reflects Brooklyn's ambitions in its days as a great independent city.

stops.title: The Long Meadow
stops.text:
Walk back into Prospect Park through the entrance at Grand Army Plaza, under the Endale Arch, a dark, low stone tunnel. As you walk through it, the park opens up in front of you, and you see the Long Meadow.

This was exactly what Olmsted and Vaux intended. They used the dark, enclosed arch as a kind of threshold, a compression, so that when you emerged, the vast open meadow would feel even more expansive, like stepping from the city into the countryside. It's a classic technique of landscape design, and it's one of the most dramatic moments in any park in the world.

The Long Meadow stretches almost a mile, about ninety acres, making it one of the longest continuous meadows in any urban park in the United States. Olmsted and Vaux shaped it carefully. Notice how its edges curve, and how groups of trees are planted to hide its full length, so you never see the whole thing at once. It invites you to keep walking to see what's around the next bend.

It's the heart of the park: on a sunny weekend, it's filled with picnics, soccer games, dogs, frisbees, and families. Before nine in the morning and after nine at night, dogs are allowed off leash on the meadow, and it becomes one of the best dog parks in the city.

Just like Central Park's Sheep Meadow, the Long Meadow had sheep. A flock grazed here from the park's early years, and in 1934, when Robert Moses removed the sheep from Central Park, he sent that flock here too. Not long afterward, Prospect Park's sheep were retired as well, and the meadow's grass has been mowed by machine ever since.

Look along the western edge of the meadow, near Prospect Park West, for Litchfield Villa, an Italianate mansion completed in 1857, before the park existed. It was built for Edwin Clark Litchfield, a railroad developer and lawyer who owned much of the land that became Park Slope. His property was taken for the park, but the villa survived, and it now houses the offices of the Prospect Park Alliance, the nonprofit that manages the park.

stops.title: The Battle of Brooklyn & Lefferts House
stops.text:
Walk to the east side of the park, near Flatbush Avenue and the zoo, close to the carousel and the Lefferts Historic House.

You're in the area where the Battle of Brooklyn was fought, on August twenty-seventh, 1776. Here's what happened. After the British army landed on Staten Island and then in southern Brooklyn, about twenty thousand British and Hessian troops faced about ten thousand Americans defending Brooklyn. The Americans had built fortifications on Brooklyn Heights, and they posted troops on the Heights of Guan, a forested ridge running across Brooklyn, which today passes through Prospect Park. There were four passes through the ridge. One of them, Flatbush Pass, also called Battle Pass, was right here, along what is now the East Drive near the zoo.

The Americans left the easternmost pass, the Jamaica Pass, almost undefended. The British, guided by local loyalists, marched through it overnight and attacked the Americans from behind. Meanwhile, Hessian troops attacked through the passes here. The Americans were caught between the two forces and routed. Many were killed or captured. The survivors fled west, toward the Gowanus Creek and the fortifications on Brooklyn Heights.

Look for the boulder with a plaque near the zoo, marking the site of Battle Pass, and the Dongan Oak, a giant tree that the Americans felled to block the road.

Nearby, look for the Lefferts Historic House, a Dutch colonial farmhouse with a gambrel roof and a long porch. The Lefferts family were Dutch settlers who farmed in Flatbush for generations. Their original house was burned by the Americans during the battle, to keep it from being used by the British. The family rebuilt it in 1783. In 1918, the house was moved into the park from its original site on Flatbush Avenue. It's now a museum about life on a farm in Brooklyn in the 1820s, including the history of the enslaved people who worked on the Lefferts farm, since slavery was common in Dutch Brooklyn.

Nearby is the Prospect Park Carousel, built in 1912 by the master carver Charles Carmel, with horses, a lion, a giraffe, and a deer.

stops.title: The Boathouse, the Lake & the Ravine
stops.text:
Walk to the Boathouse, the white terracotta building with arched openings on the shore of the Lullwater, a narrow arm of Prospect Lake.

The Boathouse was completed in 1905, designed by the architects Helmle and Huberty in a Beaux-Arts style inspired by the Library of St. Mark's in Venice. It was built to serve boaters on the lake, and it's one of the most photographed spots in the park, reflected in the still water of the Lullwater. In the 1960s, the Parks Department planned to demolish it. A public campaign saved it, and in 1968 it became one of the early buildings designated as a landmark by the city. It's now the Audubon Center, the first urban Audubon center in the country, which offers nature exhibits, programs, and electric boat tours.

The Lullwater flows into Prospect Lake, about sixty acres, Brooklyn's only freshwater lake. In winter in the nineteenth century, the lake was crowded with skaters. Today, people fish, boat, and watch the birds on the lake, including swans, herons, and cormorants.

West of the Boathouse, across a bridge, is the Ravine, the wooded valley at the heart of the park. It's the only forest in Brooklyn, though it's as man-made as the rest of the park. Olmsted and Vaux designed a stream, the Ambergill, which flows through a rocky gorge, with waterfalls and pools, designed to evoke the Adirondack Mountains. When you're in the Ravine, you can't see the city at all, and the sound of water hides the noise. In the 1990s, the Prospect Park Alliance launched a long restoration of the Ravine's woodlands, which had been degraded by erosion and invasive plants.

Look also for the Cleft Ridge Span, a bridge near the lake, built in 1872. It's one of the earliest structures in the United States built of concrete, cast in blocks, with intricate decorative patterns molded into its arch. It was an experiment in a new building material that would later transform architecture.

stops.title: Park Slope Brownstones
stops.text:
Walk west out of the park and into Park Slope, to Seventh Avenue and Sterling Place.

Park Slope rises up the hill from the Gowanus Canal to the edge of Prospect Park, which is why it's called Park Slope. It was developed mostly from the 1870s to the early 1900s, after the park opened, with rows of brownstones and brick houses for the growing middle class. Along Prospect Park West, wealthy families built mansions, and the area became known as Brooklyn's Gold Coast. Walk along the side streets between Seventh and Eighth Avenues, like Carroll Street, Montgomery Place, and Berkeley Place, to see some of the finest rows of nineteenth-century townhouses in America, in Romanesque, Queen Anne, and Renaissance Revival styles. Montgomery Place, a single block, has a remarkable collection of houses designed by the architect C. P. H. Gilbert.

At the corner of Eighth Avenue and Lincoln Place, look for the Montauk Club, a private club housed in a building modeled on the Ca' d'Oro, a Gothic palace on the Grand Canal in Venice, completed in 1891. Look closely at the facade: the friezes depict scenes from the life of the Montaukett, a Native American people of Long Island, after whom the club is named.

This intersection also has a tragic history. On December sixteenth, 1960, two passenger planes collided in the sky over Staten Island. One crashed there; the other, United Airlines Flight 826, crashed here, at Seventh Avenue and Sterling Place. All the people on both planes were killed, along with several people on the ground, including people in a church and in shops. In total, one hundred thirty-four people died. It was, at the time, the deadliest aviation disaster in history. An eleven-year-old boy on the United flight survived the crash, and he was found in a snowbank, but he died the next day. A memorial to the victims is in Green-Wood Cemetery.

A few blocks away, on Union Street, is the Park Slope Food Coop, founded in 1973, one of the oldest and largest member-owned food cooperatives in the country. Members must work a shift every few weeks in exchange for the right to shop there, at prices well below regular grocery stores.

stops.title: The Old Stone House & the Gowanus Canal
stops.text:
End your walk downhill, at J. J. Byrne Park, on Fifth Avenue and Third Street, at the Old Stone House, a small two-story stone farmhouse.

The original house was built in 1699 by a Dutch farmer named Klaes Arents Vechte. On August twenty-seventh, 1776, during the Battle of Brooklyn, this house was at the center of one of the most heroic moments of the Revolution. As the American army fled toward the Gowanus Creek and the safety of Brooklyn Heights, a regiment of about four hundred Maryland soldiers, under Lord Stirling, turned to face the British, who had occupied the house. The Marylanders charged the British again and again, holding them off long enough for most of the American army to escape across the creek. Most of the Maryland soldiers were killed or captured. Watching from a nearby hill, George Washington reportedly exclaimed, Good God, what brave fellows I must this day lose. The soldiers are remembered as the Maryland Four Hundred.

The original house was buried in the 1890s, and the building you see is a reconstruction from the 1930s, using some of the original stones. There's also a twist: in the 1880s, the house served as the clubhouse for the baseball team that later became the Brooklyn Dodgers, which played at a ballpark nearby called Washington Park.

Walk a few blocks west to the Gowanus Canal. In the colonial era, Gowanus Creek was a tidal marsh, famous for its oysters. In the 1860s, it was turned into a canal, to serve the growing industrial waterfront. Factories, coal yards, gas plants, chemical works, tanneries, and cement plants lined its banks. It became one of the most polluted waterways in America, filled with industrial waste and raw sewage. Locals nicknamed it Lavender Lake, for its strange color. In 1911, the city built a flushing tunnel to pump in water from Buttermilk Channel, to flush the canal. It helped, but not enough.

In 2010, the canal was designated a federal Superfund site, and a massive cleanup is underway. In 2021, the city rezoned the neighborhood, allowing thousands of new apartments to be built along the canal. It's a remarkable transformation for a waterway that was once a symbol of industrial filth.

From the battlefield to the factories to the brownstones and the condos, this corner of Brooklyn has seen the whole history of the city.

overview:
If you ask Brooklynites which park is better, Central Park or Prospect Park, many will tell you Prospect Park. And they have a strong ally: Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, who designed both, reportedly considered Prospect Park their finer work.

In the 1860s, the City of Brooklyn was booming, and its leaders wanted a great park to rival Manhattan's new Central Park. The driving force was James S. T. Stranahan, a businessman and civic leader who was also a key promoter of the Brooklyn Bridge. An initial plan for the park would have split it in two with a major road. Vaux, who had been consulted, argued for a different site and a unified design, and in 1865, he and Olmsted were hired. Unlike in Manhattan, they didn't have to work around a reservoir or a rigid rectangle. They had a chance to design a park closer to their ideal: a huge, sweeping meadow, a deep forested ravine, and a large lake, each arranged as a distinct experience, flowing into one another.

The park opened in stages starting in 1867. It covers about five hundred twenty-six acres. Around it, the neighborhoods developed quickly. Park Slope, on the hill to the west, filled with grand mansions along Prospect Park West, and with block after block of brownstones on the side streets. The neighborhood declined in the mid-twentieth century, but in the 1960s and 70s, young families, many of them professionals, discovered its brownstones, bought them cheaply, and restored them. They called themselves brownstoners, and they helped launch the brownstone revival movement that transformed many Brooklyn neighborhoods. Today, Park Slope is one of the most desirable and expensive neighborhoods in New York, famous for its strollers, its food co-op, and its progressive politics.

The land here also holds the story of the largest battle of the American Revolution. On August twenty-seventh, 1776, the Battle of Brooklyn was fought across this terrain, along the ridge that now runs through Prospect Park, and down in the lowlands near the Gowanus Creek. The Americans were routed, and only a heroic rear-guard action and a foggy night escape saved Washington's army.

This walk starts at Grand Army Plaza, explores the park, climbs into Park Slope, and ends at the Old Stone House and the Gowanus Canal.
